en: To Him who, in the act of preservation, abides in the conduct of pure beings; who, in the act of creation, partakes of passion; and [who,] in dissolution...
Salutations to the Existent One, who is beyond the darkness of the world and whose body has cast off the net of duality. ||1||
Relying upon whose grace, the words of even the teachers of the world flow forth with many unfaltering virtues.
May that Sarasvatī herself, whose venerable body is fashioned from the Vedas and Shastras, be the granter of all boons to us. ||2||

Having dispelled the torment of obstacles, may Gaṇeśa—the cloud—though exceedingly white, being entreated by me, cause my seed of purpose to sprout by raining down the showers of his grace, bestowing the desired fruit with unfailing efficacy. ||3||
Though dark-complexioned, he possesses the passion for awakening the lotus of the Vedas;
being peaceful, he brings about the destruction of inner darkness.
Bow down to that Vyāsa, an unprecedented sun in this world, who illuminates even that which is formless by means of thousands of cows (rays).
Having drawn forth [her] from the milk-ocean of the Vedas like Lakṣmī from the sea,
she is the singular embodiment of the source of all worlds, embraced by Him.
I bow to that Śaṅkara, the author of the pure commentary, who bestowed knowledge that grants happiness to all the worlds. ||5||
I bow to that Guru who, through the awakening to the radiant Brahman realized within himself, is one whose experience is non-dual not merely by name but even in actual fact. 6.

I, the ascetic Prakāśātman, having properly attained this knowledge, shall explain the Pañcapādikā according to my learning and according to my ability, out of a desire to dispel it [from others]. (7)
Those who have known all that is to be known do not praise even that which is composed by great men in this world, much less that by one such as I.
Thus, though this expenditure of words is as fruitless as it may seem, I have engaged in it for the sake of purifying my own mind; may the virtuous forgive me. ||8||

For the sake of the unimpeded completion and widespread propagation of the work he intends to begin, as well as for the observance of the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*), he must perform worship and salutation to his chosen deity; furthermore, the meaning of the scripture—the identity characterized by the oneness of the inner self (*pratyagātman*) and Brahman, which is attainable through the discernment of the meanings of the terms *tat* and *tvam*—must be shown in brief in order to state the purport of the entire commentary. Thus, he demonstrates both of these points in brief through both scriptural citation and reasoning: [The text continues with the verse: "Salutations to that Śambhu, who, having assumed the form of a sage, out of compassion for the world, revealed the supreme truth of the Self, which is difficult to perceive, to those whose minds are distracted by various objects. [The commentary then explains: "Salutations" means bowing down with the body, speech, and mind. "To him" refers to the one who is the object of the salutation. "Śambhu" is so called because he is the source of bliss (*śam*). "Who, having assumed the form of a sage" means who, having taken on the appearance of a seer (*ṛṣi*), [revealed it]. "Out of compassion for the world" means out of pity for the universe. "Revealed" means made known. "The supreme truth of the Self" refers to the reality of the inner self. "Difficult to perceive" means hard to understand. "To those whose minds are distracted by various objects" means to those whose intellects are scattered among manifold things. This is the meaning. Now, the purpose of this work is stated: "The purpose of this treatise is the attainment of the knowledge of the unity of the inner self and Brahman, which is the means for the cessation of all suffering. [The commentary then explains: "The purpose" is the goal. "Of this treatise" refers to this very work. "The attainment of the knowledge of the unity of the inner self and Brahman" is the specific purpose. "Which is the means for the cessation of all suffering" indicates the ultimate purpose. "All suffering" includes physical, mental, and divine afflictions. "Cessation" means their destruction. "Means" refers to the instrument. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the connection between the subject matter and the purpose is shown: "The connection between the subject matter and the purpose is that of the means and the end. [The commentary then explains: "The subject matter" is the unity of the inner self and Brahman. "The purpose" is the cessation of all suffering. "Connection" is the relationship. "Of the means and the end" means that the subject matter is the means and the purpose is the end. This is the meaning. Finally, the relationship between the words is shown: "The relationship between the words is that of mutual expectancy. [The commentary then explains: "The words" are those such as "purpose," "subject matter," and "connection. "Mutual expectancy" means that each word depends upon the others to complete its sense. This is the meaning. Thus, having briefly indicated the subject matter, the purpose, and the relationship, he now states the title of the work: "This is the *Vedāntasāra*, composed by Sadānanda. [The commentary then explains: "This" refers to what has been described. "*Vedāntasāra*" means the essence (*sāra*) of the Vedānta (*vedānta*). "Composed by Sadānanda" means written by the author named Sadānanda. This is the meaning. And finally, the benediction is stated: "May the Lord of the Universe, who is the embodiment of the bliss of the Self, grant me peace. [The commentary then explains: "Lord of the Universe" is the Supreme Lord. "Embodiment of the bliss of the Self" means whose nature is the bliss of the inner self. "Grant me peace" means bestow tranquility upon me. This is the meaning. Thus ends the introduction. Now, the meaning of the scripture is being explained in brief, as it is to be attained through the discernment of the meanings of the terms *tat* and *tvam*. To explain the purport of the entire commentary, he shows both [the means and the goal] in brief through scriptural citation and reasoning: [The text continues with the verse: "The Self alone is to be meditated upon; there is nothing else to be known. Having realized the Self, one becomes immortal; there is no other path to liberation. [The commentary then explains: "In this world, the Self alone is to be meditated upon. "Alone" means without a second. "Self" means the inner self. "Is to be meditated upon" means should be contemplated. "There is nothing else to be known" means there is no object of knowledge other than the Self. "Having realized the Self" means having directly perceived the Self. "One becomes immortal" means one attains immortality. "There is no other path to liberation" means there is no way to liberation other than this. This is the meaning. Therefore, the meaning of the scripture is established: the cessation of all suffering is achieved through the knowledge of the unity of the inner self and Brahman, which is the subject matter of this work. This is the conclusion.

"Salutation to Brahman—the witness, whose nature is eternally existent knowledge, immutable, beginningless bliss, and devoid of the web of unreal duality. Thus, the purport of the entire commentary is shown here to be the oneness of Brahman and the Self; for the purport will be demonstrated subsequently by way of detailed analysis.

In this context, devotion directed toward the deity and the guru—augmented by worship, prostration, and so forth—though it fulfills the stated purpose for the speaker, also attains the status of an auxiliary to the knowledge (*vidyā*) for the listeners. Thus, he honors the gurus through the application of speech, mind, and body with such verses as: "Salutation to him whose form is like the sun to the cluster of lotuses that are the heads of the Vedas. He then points out the specific task for which the performance of this auspicious invocation (*maṅgalācaraṇa*) was accomplished, with the words: "by the weight of the stalks beginning with the feet."

Now, an objection is raised: this cannot be considered a *bhāṣya* worthy of being placed on the path of formal commentary, because it lacks the defining characteristics of a *bhāṣya*. For those who know the definition of a *bhāṣya* state: "That wherein the meaning of the *sūtra* is described by means of sentences that follow the style of the *sūtra*, and wherein its own words are also explained—that, the experts say, is a *bhāṣya*. In that regard, regarding the *sūtra* "Then, therefore, the desire to know Brahman," the word "must be done" (*kartavyā*) must be supplied to avoid the charge of mere restatement and to ensure the engagement of persons in the scripture.

In this context, by taking the word *jijñāsā* (desire to know) as indicating the implicit inquiry (*vicāra*), the literal meaning of the aphorism (*sūtra*) becomes: "An inquiry must be undertaken for the sake of the knowledge of Brahman by one who is endowed with the fourfold prerequisites (*sādhana-catuṣṭaya*) and is thus fit for its practice. Consequently, it is established that the knowledge of Brahman is the means to liberation (*mokṣa*) for the qualified seeker; and by virtue of proximity (*sannidhāna*), it follows from both the word and the sense of the scripture that this inquiry concerns the sentences of the Vedānta. Thus, for one endowed with the fourfold prerequisites, [the inquiry is] for the sake of the knowledge of Brahman, which is the means to liberation.

The intended meaning of the aphorism (*sūtra*)—that "the inquiry into the Vedānta texts must be undertaken"—has been understood. In this regard, one might suspect that this *bhāṣya* does not set forth even a portion of the meaning of the aphorism, and therefore is not worthy of being an exposition. Dispelling this suspected defect, [the author] demonstrates that the section of the *bhāṣya* beginning with "Of the objects of the notions of 'you' and 'I'" has as its purpose the demonstration of the subject matter and the purpose, which are implicitly contained within the aphorism: "I am this; this is mine."

The commentary (bhāṣya) ending with the words, "This worldly transaction is innate," concludes with the commentary beginning, "For the abandonment of this cause of evil and for the realization of the knowledge of the oneness of the Self, all the Vedāntas are commenced. This demonstrates that the subject matter and the purpose of the scripture are implicitly indicated by the first aphorism (sūtra).

In this context, the phrase "the commentary ending with 'This worldly transaction is innate'" is connected with the subsequent clause, "it demonstrates the subject matter and the purpose of the scripture."

Now, one might ask: how do these two commentaries alone establish the subject matter and the purpose? We reply: because they present the superimposition (adhyāsa), which is the cause for establishing the subject matter and purpose that serve as the occasion for commencing the treatise; for the statement of a reason indeed proves the very point that has been proposed.

For instance: this treatise ought to be undertaken, because it possesses a probable subject matter and purpose, like the undertaking of agriculture and similar activities; and the treatise possesses a probable subject matter and purpose, because it is the antidote to bondage consisting of ignorance, like the awakening from sleep.

Thus, by pointing out that bondage—which is the opposite of the scripture’s possession of a cause for its commencement, a subject matter, and a purpose—is essentially ignorance (*avidyā*), the two commentaries establish the connection between the subject matter and the purpose. Now, one might object: "The reason—that bondage is characterized by being essentially ignorance—is unproven; how can that which is unproven be used to prove [the thesis]? To this, he says: "[The commentary] concludes with the statement, 'All the Vedāntas are commenced [for this purpose]'."

The meaning is that, by means of the Commentary which establishes the definition, the possibility, the existence, and the means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa) that serve as the grounds for establishing superimposition (adhyāsa)—which itself is the ground for establishing the subject matter and so forth—it establishes its own purpose, namely superimposition, through the definition and other factors, and thereby establishes the subject matter and the purpose. For this very reason, because it establishes the subject matter and so forth both directly and indirectly, the Commentary is taken up in its divided parts, concluding with these [sections].

One might object: "In that case, it should be stated that [the purpose] culminates with the words 'perceptible to the whole world'. True; however, because the commentary on the phrase "of this cause of evil" is intended to demonstrate the connection with the treatise on inquiry (*vicāra-śāstra*) by way of stating the connection with the Vedānta texts—namely, its subject matter (*viṣaya*) and purpose (*prayojana*)—it has been included together with the preceding commentary, on the grounds that they share the commonality of being mediated in the establishment of the subject matter and purpose of the treatise on inquiry.

Now, one might ask: "Even so, why are the subject matter and the purpose presented here, when they are not connected to the aphorisms? To this he says: "The subject matter and the purpose are impliedly indicated by the first aphorism. The word *iti* is used in the sense of a reason (*hetau*). Because they are indicated by implication through the first aphorism, therefore he presents them.

What, then, is the context for this sūtra? It is said: Having studied the Veda-svādhyāya according to the injunction for study which is obligatory (*nitya*), one understands from a superficial examination of the Vedānta passages that [the inquiry is necessary]. This is because the opening statement, "But everything is dear for the sake of the Self," introduces the subject for one who is detached from all else and seeks the Self; and because the concluding statement, "When the Self is known, all this is known," and "This much indeed, my dear, is immortality," establishes that [knowledge of the Self] is the means to immortality.

Having restated the vision of the Self in the words "it is to be seen," the sūtra enjoins that *śravaṇa* (hearing), which is the primary constituent (*aṅgin*), together with *manana* (reflection) and *nididhyāsana* (meditation)—which are its auxiliary constituents (*aṅgas*) that contribute to the result—ends with the injunction "it is to be heard. Furthermore, one investigates: to what extent do the qualifications of the eligible seeker (*adhikārī*) extend; what is this inquiry into the Vedānta texts, and is it already established elsewhere or not; how is the knowledge of the Self the means to liberation; on what authority is that based; and what is the true nature of the Self, and what is its authority?

Perceiving that person to be desirous of knowledge and seeking the human goal, the venerable Bādarāyaṇa composed the aphorism—"Now, therefore, the inquiry into Brahman"—in order to determine, by means of reasoning, the three factors of qualification, subject matter, and fruit required for the injunction that prescribes the investigation of Vedāntic statements for the sake of attaining the knowledge of Brahman, which is the means to liberation, for one who is endowed with the fourfold prerequisites; this is because the uniformity between the Śruti and the Sūtra is understood.

Furthermore, we shall explain later that reflection (*manana*) and meditative contemplation (*nididhyāsana*) are auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) to hearing (*śravaṇa*). Now, an objection may be raised: the injunction "one should hear" (*śrotavya*) cannot enjoin the inquiry into Vedāntic texts for one who possesses the fourfold prerequisites (*sādhana-catuṣṭaya*) for the sake of attaining the knowledge of the Self as Brahman—the means to liberation—because hearing and the other stages have their efficacy toward the comprehension of the object established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*); nor is it possible for them to serve a dual purpose, as is the case with threshing (*avaghāta*) and similar acts.

[Objection: "Like the *apūrva* (unseen potency), which is to be accomplished by two means—perceived and unperceived—here there is an absence of that which is to be accomplished by the unperceived, because the realization of the Self is accomplished solely by perceived means. [Reply: This is not sound, because it will be stated later that the immediate realization of the reality of the Self is to be accomplished by all unseen [potencies], and thus its injunction as serving a dual purpose is established, just like the act of threshing and so forth.

Now, it might be argued that since the Vedāntas would be intent upon injunctions, the nature of Brahman would not be established and other defects would follow; therefore, there is no injunction for hearing [the scriptures] and so forth—this has indeed been shown by the Commentator himself. True, but what was refuted there was an injunction regarding knowledge (*jñāna*), not an injunction regarding hearing and so forth; for in the latter case, the aforementioned defects do not apply.

For how could Brahman be reduced to a subordinate status as the object of the act [of seeing] when the injunction is for "seeing"? However, when the injunction for inquiry is made with the vision of Brahman as its aim, Brahman becomes primary because it serves as a qualification of the vision which is itself the primary fruit; thus, it does not become subordinate. Therefore, when Brahman is presented by the Vedāntas as the primary subject, there is no contradiction whatsoever in the injunction of hearing and so forth for the sake of that vision.

[Objection: But even so, since the opening and the conclusion [of the passage] pertain to the teaching of a single Self, how can the injunctions for hearing and so forth be inferred by means of intermediate sentences? [Reply: We say that this is due to the differentiation of intermediate sentences, just as in the case of the injunction for the connection of sacrifices and other rites with knowledge in the phrase "they desire to know" (*vividiṣanti*); just as in the case of the injunction for holding [the fire] above in the phrase "for it is above the gods"; and just as in the case of the injunction for the collection of observances for one whose clothes are stained.

Alternatively, let the passage beginning with "Therefore, a Brahmin, having become disillusioned with scholarship" (*tasmād brāhmaṇaḥ pāṇḍityaṃ nirvidya*) be the injunction for hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth, because that is its primary purport and because it will be stated by the author of the Sūtras. In any case, there certainly exists an injunction for hearing together with reflection (*manana*) and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*), which serve as its subordinate limbs. Therefore, the Sūtra has been commenced in order to determine the three requirements (*anubandha-traya*) necessitated by that [injunction].

And since the duty of the qualified person—to investigate the Vedāntic texts for the sake of the knowledge of Brahman, which is the means to liberation—has been established by the first Sūtra, and that investigation to be performed will proceed starting from the Sūtra "janmādi" (II.3.1), it must be explained that this Bhāṣya is indeed consistent with the Sūtra, as it describes here the falsity of bondage in order to establish the subject matter and the fruit among the four requirements of an injunction: the qualification, the subject matter, the fruit, and the connection.

Now, one might object: "If the subject matter (*viṣaya*) and the purpose (*prayojana*) are indeed indicated by implication (*arthāt*), then the author of the Commentary (*bhāṣyakāra*) should have demonstrated the operation of the Sūtra with respect to them, and established the subject matter and purpose directly through the process of raising and resolving objections; otherwise, it would follow that neither the author of the Sūtra nor the author of the Commentary intended to address them. To this, he replies: "And this [is shown] more clearly in the Commentary beginning with 'Therefore, Brahman is to be desired to be known' (*tasmād brahma jijñāsitavyam*)."

The phrase "we shall demonstrate what was stated by the author of the Bhāṣya" is to be supplied as an ellipsis. He raises an objection in order to make the very point stated in the first section even clearer by means of an objection and its resolution: "Here he says: 'If this is so... [Objection: But surely, like the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "of this cause of evil," the preceding Bhāṣya also establishes the subject matter and so forth; why then is there an inquiry into that? [Response: He says "no," with the words beginning "I am a human being" regarding the body, senses, and so on.

Since the Sūtra itself has indicated that each preceding item—namely the necessity of inquiry, the subject matter, and the purpose—is to be established by each subsequent one, [the author], intending to state the fixed order of sequence by first establishing the subject matter and the purpose through the proof of superimposition (adhyāsa), says: starting from "It is said" up to the passage preceding "And this he will explain."

Now, one might object: "Since the Sūtra indicates the necessity of inquiry as having the knowledge of Brahman for its purpose, how is it that the cessation of bondage is stated in the Sūtra to be the purpose of both inquiry and knowledge? To this, he replies: "For the knowledge of Brahman, which is indicated by the Sūtra, is the destroyer of the cause of evil. The meaning is that the injunction for inquiry, seeking the purpose of the knowledge to be accomplished through inquiry, establishes liberation as the purpose by way of being a qualification for the qualified seeker.

[Objection: "But surely, misfortune—characterized by falling into hell and so forth—is one thing entirely, while the falsity of the appearance of the body and so forth is what is being proven; thus, how are these two connected? [The author] says "no," for he states: "And misfortune consists in the state of being a subject, primarily characterized by agency and enjoyership. [Objection: "In that case, let it be that the real entity consisting of subjecthood, agency, and enjoyership is what is to be removed by knowledge. [The author] says "no," for he states: "If that were produced by a real entity (*vastukṛta*). For instance, in the case of a variegated whole (*citrāvayavin*):

The cognition of a substance qualified by blue color does not remove its own object, nor that which is inherent in its own object such as taste and so forth, nor a contradictory quality such as yellowness; rather, it is only the non-cognition of its own object that is removed by it. If it is argued that an entity residing in its own substratum is removed by cognition, this is not so, because qualities such as merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) residing in the self are not removed by the cognition of a jar or similar objects. Nor is an entity related to both the substratum and the object removed by cognition.

Because the relationship between the body and the self is not terminated by the knowledge of the self as being merely the body and its objects. Now, it may be argued that the cessation of bondage does not result from knowledge through observed efficacy—by which one could describe it as having ignorance (*avidyā*) as its nature—but rather that it is scripture alone that declares the cessation of bondage through knowledge. To this we reply: surely, for the sake of the logical consistency of what has been heard in scripture, the fact that bondage consists of ignorance must indeed be described.

Just as, in the case of the six sacrifices beginning with the Āgneya, although the status of being the producer of the *apūrva* is heard [in scripture] by virtue of their being the object of the *adhikārāpūrva*, intermediate *antarāpūrvas* produced by the performers of the sacrifices occurring in sequence are postulated for the sake of establishing their capacity to bring about the principal *apūrva* which manifests at a later time; or just as the *apūrva* is postulated for the sake of establishing the very fact that heaven is the means [to the result], so it is here.

[Objection: Is it not the case that in the world there is a rule of pervasion such that momentary actions lack the capacity to produce a fruit that persists over time; and thus, even in the Veda, intermediate *apūrvas* are postulated to establish the *apūrva* of heaven for the sake of the scriptural consistency? [Reply: If so, then here too there must be such a rule of pervasion; to this he says: "Because knowledge is the remover of ignorance alone."

Therefore, since the Sūtra itself functions to establish that bondage consists of ignorance (avidyā), superimposition (adhyāsa) must be described in order to accomplish the purpose of establishing the necessity of investigating the meaning of the Sūtra; this he states with the passage beginning "If that... and ending with "...the utility for establishing the meaning of the Sūtra."

Now, one might ask: why does the author of the commentary (*bhāṣyakāra*), bypassing the primary subject matter to be established by the Sūtra, first explain the secondary meaning (*ārthikārtha*) that is realized later? To this he replies: "It is the introduction (*upodghāta*) to the entire treatise (*tantra*). An *upodghāta* is the explanation of another related matter prior to grasping the subject matter to be established in the mind for its own sake.

The distinction is as follows: first, one makes a formal proposition (*pratijñā*) regarding that which is to be established; subsequently, the description of the reasons for its establishment is the "demonstration" (*pratipādana*). By the term *tantra*, the meaning of the system—namely, the identity of Brahman and the Self—is expressed. Now, one might object: "Granted that superimposition (*adhyāsa*) is the cause for establishing the purpose [of the treatise], how is it the cause for establishing the meaning of the system? Anticipating this doubt, he first states the meaning of the system in order to explain it: "And thus, of this scripture... This connects with what follows: "...the purport (*aidamparya*) has been demonstrated."

He demonstrates that very purport with the words beginning "intent solely on happiness" (*sukhaikatāna*). This is the meaning: that which is the purport of the Vedānta scripture—namely, that the Vedāntas culminate in the non-duality of Brahman and the Self—that has been established by both the Sūtras and the Bhāṣya. Having shown the subject matter of the system (*tantra*), he demonstrates that superimposition (*adhyāsa*) must be described first, because that system depends upon the proof of superimposition, with the words: "And that [is the notion] 'I am the agent, happy, and miserable'."

[Objection: But surely the scripture itself, by casting even that which is considered direct perception (pratyakṣa) into the status of a mere appearance, will establish the identity of Brahman and the Self; what is the use of a separate description of superimposition (adhyāsa)? To this he replies: "First, like sentences such as 'the old cow'... [Objection: If the establishment of the meaning of the scripture is dependent upon superimposition, then that very superimposition ought to have been described explicitly by the author of the Sūtras.

Because that [subject] is primary, otherwise there would be the consequence of a lack of intent regarding it; thus he says there: "And he will state this. One then objects: "In that case, since it is an introductory topic (*upoddhāta*), the sūtra concerning superimposition (*adhyāsa*) should have been composed first. He replies: "Not so, because of the establishment of a specific purpose," for the author of the sūtras has set out in a method of exposition characterized by the formal debate (*vāda-kathā*), which prioritizes the determination of meaning, rather than in an introductory method.

In that case, one might argue that even the author of the Bhāṣya should proceed strictly according to the sequence of the Sūtras and not by transgressing that sequence; to this he replies: "But the author of the Bhāṣya... [He does so] for the sake of easy comprehension—that is, for the purpose of making it an auxiliary to the process of engagement.

One might object: "Even so, this commentary cannot be explained [as such], because there is an absence of an auspicious invocation at the beginning of the treatise; because, being beset by obstacles, there is the possibility of non-comprehension, miscomprehension, or misconception regarding the meaning of the treatise; and because, due to the lack of adherence to the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭa*), it would follow that it was composed by an unreliable author. Thus he raises the objection: "But surely, at the commencement of an undertaking such as the composition of a book..."

[Objection: Is the conduct of the learned regarding spitting and such to be followed by others? [Reply: No; he says, "And the conduct of the learned is our authority. Conduct (*ācāra*) is an action performed as being *dharma* (righteous duty). "Authority" (*pramāṇa*) means it is something that ought to be done. [Objection: Since there is no purpose, what is the use of performing an auspicious rite (*maṅgalācaraṇa*)? [Reply: No; he says, "And the performance of an auspicious rite is well-known. [Objection: But surely there is no obstacle here because the undertaking is small. [Reply: No; he says, "And even in a great [undertaking]."

"Is it not the case that activity for the sake of pacifying obstacles does not arise from mere probability (*sambhāvanā-mātra*), but rather from certainty? To this, he says: 'And it is well-known' (*prasiddhaṃ ca*). "But is worldly renown (*loka-prasiddhi*) not baseless, and thus not a cause for the certainty of obstacles? To this, he says: 'And it is known' (*vijñāyate ca*). He concludes: "So how [is it]? (*tat katham*)?

"Never, in any undertaking, does misfortune befall those in whose hearts dwells the Blessed Lord Hari, the abode of all auspiciousness"—according to this traditional teaching (smṛti), the author has performed an auspicious invocation (maṅgalācaraṇa) characterized by the recollection of the reality of the Supreme Deity, for the sake of maintaining the conduct of the learned (śiṣṭācāra) and for the pacification of obstacles. To this effect he says: "In this regard, it is said. To the question, "What is the authority for that? he replies: "The words 'you' and 'we,' etc. This concludes the commentary (bhāṣya).

The meaning is "the means of valid knowledge" (pramāṇa), or else "the performance of an auspicious invocation" (maṅgalācaraṇa). To the question, "How does this lead to the recollection of a specific deity? he says: "And the meaning of this is as follows. Now, one might object: "In this context, the deity that is the reality of the pure Self is not being recollected; rather, the absence of superimposition (adhyāsābhāva) is being described. True; however, for the sake of that [absence], the Reality itself is also recollected. Thus he says: "That, in some way..."

[Objection: But surely, because it is subordinate to another purpose, the recollection of the deity is not intended [as a primary injunction] and thus cannot produce its effect. [Reply: No, he says—“precisely because it is subordinate to that. Even when the recollection of the deity is for another purpose, it will by its very nature burn away the affliction of obstacles, just as fire, though intended for the sake of smoke, burns grass and the like; this is the intention. He concludes the established point regarding the necessity of providing an explanation: “Therefore. By one who proceeds for another purpose, the two words beginning with “yuṣmad” and “asmad” have been explained by implication.

To explain the latter member [of the compound], he introduces the commentary with the words "of the object and the subject," and so forth. In this regard, contradiction (*virodha*) is of two kinds, and the impossibility of mutual existence (*itaretarabhāvānupapatti*) is likewise of two kinds. How so? One category consists of contradiction as a property of the entities themselves—the incapacity of two things to occupy the same place at the same time—and the resulting absence of the effect characterized by coexistence, which is the impossibility of mutual existence.

The other [type of] contradiction (*virodha*), however, is a property of things (*padārtha-dharma*) consisting in the absence of the capacity for two things to have each other's nature; because the non-occurrence of the effect characterized by mutual identity is caused by that [absence], he asks "What is this contradiction? and so forth, owing to this twofold division. Therein, he refutes the first position with the passage beginning "If, first of all... and ending with "...co-existence has been stated."

In this context, it should be understood that by using the terms "darkness" and "light," the inclusion of shadow and sunlight, as well as cold and heat, is intended; thus, their co-existence even in those cases has been stated. Now, he takes up the second position, beginning with: "It is said that contradiction is characterized by mutual non-identity," and so forth.

Now, some say that darkness (*tamas*) is merely the absence of light, while others say it is merely the absence of the perception of form; how then can this [example] be accepted as an illustration for the seer and the seen, which are both positive entities? It is said in reply: How could darkness—which is perceived as possessing form and is distinguished by specific states such as increase and decrease—fall into either of the two categories of non-existence? For even in a place pervaded by abundant light, one who has closed their eyes perceives the interior of the eyeball.

The perception of darkness is not contradictory, just as one with covered ears perceives internal sounds; and the birth of darkness destroyed by light is established as occurring suddenly from its very primary cause, like the production of a great flash of lightning and so forth.

[Objection: But surely, since it is a rule that a substance possessing color must possess touch, how can darkness—which is devoid of that [touch]—be understood as a substance possessing color? [Response: This is not a fault; for although elsewhere it is a rule that a substance possessing touch possesses color, we nevertheless accept the existence of wind which is devoid of color yet possesses touch. In the same way, by the very rule of its being perceived, it is established that darkness possesses color while being devoid of touch.

Furthermore, smoke, which possesses color, has its tactile quality unperceived elsewhere than in the region where it is seen by the eye; likewise, why should darkness not be devoid of all tactile qualities? For even in a place pervaded by the rays of the sun, the cognition of "darkness" is not observed in the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), the posterior non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), or the mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*) of the lamp's light at the moments of its arising and destruction; thus, darkness is not merely the absence of light. If it were the absence of all light, then it would never cease as long as there was no proximity of all light.

Even for one situated inside a chamber enveloped in dense darkness, because of the perception of the interior darkness along with the perception of forms outside, darkness is not merely the absence of the perception of forms; enough of this excessive elaboration.

One might object: "Surely, the impossibility of the mutual existence of the seer and the seen does not preclude the appearance of their identity, which is the cause of the delusion; for even in the case of mother-of-pearl and silver, which are devoid of identity, a co-location appears as the cause of the delusion—so it may be here as well. To this he replies with the word "How?"—and says: "True;"

There indeed exists in some cases an identity between the substrate consisting of the "this"-portion and the silver being superimposed; and thus, because a superimposition of one portion upon another is observed elsewhere—where a single object possessing both portions is perceived as having a common substratum through the relation of general and particular, or the relation of quality and qualified—so too is it here with respect to the substrate, which is Consciousness (*cit*), and that which is superimposed.

He states that for that which is without self (anātman), "it does not exist," by means of the passage beginning with: "First of all, for the subject, because its sole essence is consciousness, there is no possibility of the 'you' element," and so forth.

This is the intention: [the question] whether the insentient portion of the seer is innate or adventitious. He says it is not innate with the words "by itself" (*svataḥ*). For the object of cognition (*cetya*), being insentient, appears as the objective factor (*karmakāraka*) of consciousness; how then could that which stands in a position opposite to the agent in a single action be the Self? This is the intended meaning. If it is adventitious, it must be either with cause or without cause. If it were without cause, he says in response: "because of the absence of transformation" (*apariṇāmitvāt*).

The intention is that no partless entity has ever been observed to transform by itself into a form possessing parts. He states the reason for this: "because of its stainlessness" (*nirañjanatvāt*). The meaning is that the partless ether (*ākāśa*) has never been seen to transform due to contact with a cause. [Objection: In that case, is it not observed that even a non-self (*anātman*) serves as a substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) consisting of a portion of the self? [Reply: No; he says: "even of the object" (*viṣayasyāpi*).

"Because of equality. This is the meaning: just as one seer is not within the range of perception for another seer, but is only inferable, so too would the object be. Furthermore, there can be no transformation into the form of consciousness (cidākāra) for that which is non-self (anātman), even from something else; for the effect, even if its material cause (upādāna) were inert, would itself be inert. If it is argued that the consciousness of the Self (ātmacaitanya) itself accepts the non-self as its own part, he says in response: "because consciousness does not undergo transference (apratisaṃkrama)."

Therefore, since identity is never observed anywhere, the superimposition of one part upon another by the perception of that other part elsewhere is not tenable; this is the meaning of the passage beginning with "all the more so for its attributes" up until "the non-existence of superimposition alone is logical. The intervening text is clear in its meaning.

[Objection: "But surely, regarding everything from the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) up to the body, the cognition is precisely 'I' (aham), and not 'this' (idam); how then can these be the objects of the notion of 'you' (yuṣmat-pratyaya)? To this he replies: "By virtue of being manifested through its power. The meaning is this: because the ego-sense and so forth are manifested by the power of that consciousness which is the object of the notion of "we" (asmat-pratyaya), even though they lack the status of being the object of "you" in terms of their appearance, they are nonetheless fit to be considered the object of "you" by the defining characteristic of appearing as something immediate (aparokṣatayā).

"Even though they are not separate from consciousness, they appear as if separate"—the meaning is that they appear as if manifold due to the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of the modifications of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇavṛtti).

Even though agency and other attributes in the Self are indeed errors caused by limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), because there is no similarity based on common parts between them, the superimposition (adhyāsa) of the body and so forth is not an error caused by a limiting adjunct; thus, he accepts the possibility of the superimposition of all objects from the ego-sense down to the body upon the Seer, stating: "Even though this is so... and so forth.

He states—by means of the passage beginning with "even so" and ending with "so too is superimposition"—that the very observation of an effect of error that is without limiting adjuncts (nirupādhika) leads one to postulate either another similarity, as in the case of the snake's smell being similar to the scent of the *ketakī* flower despite the absence of common qualities or parts, or another cause, as in the case of the yellowness of a conch shell. He explains the meaning of the word "natural" (*naisargika*) as follows: "inherent in the mere existence of the object itself."

How is it that superimposition (adhyāsa) consists precisely in the conjunction of the defects of agency and enjoyership with respect to the Self? In this regard, the superimposition of enjoyership depends upon the superimposition of agency, because there is no enjoyment for one who is not an agent. Furthermore, agency depends upon the superimposition of the conjunction of passion and hatred, because there is no agency for one devoid of those [defects]. And that conjunction of defects, in turn, depends upon enjoyership.

Because passion and the like do not arise with respect to that which has not been experienced or is of a different nature, superimposition (*adhyāsa*) is innate by virtue of its beginninglessness through a succession of causes, like the seed and the sprout. He shows that the word "worldly usage" (*lokavyavahāra*) denotes superimposition by means of the passage beginning with "The world [thinks] 'I am a man,'" and so forth. "Usage" is fourfold: recognition, naming, grasping, and purposeful action. Therefore, the sense is that the term "usage" is applicable to the cognition and expression "I am a man."

When it is stated that "the appearance of one thing as having the nature of another is ignorance," [the author] accepts his own established doctrine—that ignorance is the appearance of a real entity as being mixed with a false entity—lest there be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that cognitions such as "the cloth is white" would also be ignorance. Having accepted this, he says, "having coupled the real and the unreal," and explains that [statement] with the words beginning, "The Real is consciousness which is not this [object]," and so forth.

[Objection: Surely, because of the employment of the suffix *ktvā*, a difference between actions and a temporal sequence (prior-posterior relation) must be admitted by implication; so how can there be a single meaning for "superimposition" (*adhyāsa*), "pairing" (*mithunīkaraṇa*), and "worldly transaction" (*lokavyavahāra*)? [Reply: No, he says this with the words beginning "having superimposed" (*adhyasya*) and "having paired" (*mithunīkṛtya*). [Objection: Why should it terminate in the mere essential nature [of the object], when the force of the suffix *ktvā* itself should require the admission of a difference between actions? [Reply: No, he says this with the words "And in the conclusion" (*upasaṃhāre ca*).

The intention is this: the sentence-meaning—namely, the object to be qualified (the substantive), which is superimposition (adhyāsa) characterized by the quality of being innate—is not to be split [into separate actions] out of fear that a single word would be rendered meaningless; rather, what is supported by the suffix *ktvā* is a sequence of prior and posterior actions based on conceptual cognition. Thus he says: "Therefore, it is a mere designation, like the statement 'consciousness is the nature of the person'"; the meaning is that it is merely figurative (*upacāra*).

How can a single superimposition (adhyāsa) be distinguished by its specific qualifiers—such as "mutual identity," "the real and the unreal," "I," and "this is mine"—and how can it appear distinct when based on another limiting adjunct (upādhi)? Furthermore, since the cognitions of these qualified objects arise for the speaker in a sequence, the suffix -ktvā is employed by accepting a temporal succession based on cognition and a distinction in the qualified actions due to the difference in qualifiers. In this context, if one were to say simply "ignorance" (ajñāna), it might be understood as "erroneous knowledge" (bhrāntijñāna); therefore, in order to exclude both of those possibilities, he explains the meaning of the terms by defining them with the words "that which is false and that which is ignorance," and so forth.

[Objection: But how can false cognition (*mithyājñāna*) be the material cause (*upādāna*) of superimposition (*adhyāsa*), since we say that superimposition arises when it exists and does not arise when it is absent? [Reply: Is it not the case that true knowledge (*tattvajñāna*) is the obstacle to superimposition, and its absence is ignorance (*ajñāna*); thus, because they relate to the absence of an obstacle, the positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of ignorance with superimposition are established otherwise (*anyathāsiddha*)? This is not sound. For an obstacle is that which opposes the production of an effect even when the complete causal complex (*puṣkalakāraṇa*) is present.

Furthermore, when the full set of causes for superimposition (*adhyāsa*) is present, there can be no arising of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). Therefore, positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) do not have the absence of an obstructing factor as their object. If it is argued that they rather refer to the absence of contact with a contradictory factor, we say no; for an effect first requires its cause, not the absence of contact with a contradictory factor. Consequently, positive and negative concomitance, when supported by reasoning, establish only the production of the cause that is required first.

[Objection: But surely the defect in the object, the sense organ, and so forth, has already been established as the cause. [Reply: True; however, that is merely the instrumental cause (*nimitta*). When there is a requirement for a material cause (*upādāna*), ignorance (*ajñāna*) enters into the picture. Furthermore, every effect must have a material cause because it is a positive entity (*bhāva-kārya*), like a jar and other such things—this follows from inference. Moreover, since even action, quality, and the like arise only by having a substratum, and since the material cause is precisely the substratum of that which is being produced. [Objection: Will not the Self or the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) be the material cause of erroneous cognition? [Reply: No; because the Self is unchanging (*apariṇāmin*).

Furthermore, it is not [the case that the internal organ is the cause], because the internal organ depends on the conjunction with the senses and other factors; moreover, since the object is illusory and exists only as a mental representation, such dependence is impossible, and the positive and negative concomitances of the internal organ are otherwise accounted for by the knowledge of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*). Of the internal organ...

Because it is insentient (*jaḍatva*) and lacks the capacity for cognition (*ajñātṛtva*), and because it would follow that the Self (*ātman*) is subject to error; therefore, superimposition (*adhyāsa*), which consists of false objects and their cognitions and is itself false, requires a material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*). Since it does not reside in the locus [of the Self], while various instrumental causes (*nimitta-kāraṇa*) are being differentiated, ignorance (*ajñāna*)—which conforms to the nature of all effects and is pervasive everywhere—is established as having the Self as its locus. Furthermore, because it is included within the category of the locus of erroneous cognition, false cognition alone is the material cause of superimposition, and not [the Self].

It is well said that the defects consist of the self, the internal organ, the glass, and so forth. It will be stated later that the superimposition based on the self is an error consisting in the association with mother-of-pearl. One raises an objection, claiming that it is contradictory for a single superimposition to be both innate (*naisargika*) and adventitious (*naimittika*), by asking: "But how [is this]?"

In this regard, first of all, in order to demonstrate the lack of contradiction—namely, that there is "naturalness" (*naisargikatvam*) by virtue of being the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*) arising from the stream of superimposition (*adhyāsa*), and "occasionalness" (*naimittikatvam*) by virtue of being the form of individual effects—he establishes the existence of ignorance (*ajñāna*) as a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*) in the Self: "This power of ignorance (*avidyāśakti*) necessarily exists. By the words "necessarily" (*avaśyam*) and "this" (*eṣā*), he indicates that [the proof] possesses two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). First, there is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); for we observe immediate appearances such as "I am ignorant" and "I do not know myself or another."

Is it not the case that this manifestation has the absence of knowledge as its object? No; because it is a direct (aparokṣa) manifestation, like "I am happy," and because absence is the province of the sixth means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). Even for one who maintains that absence is perceived through direct perception, the comprehension of the absence of consciousness in the self is not possible.

In the cognition "I have no knowledge," since knowledge exists in that very locus (*dharmin*), whether it be the self or the object [of negation], once that object is cognized, the cognition of the absence of knowledge is impossible; and even if the locus and so forth are not cognized, the absence [of knowledge] is all the more impossible to cognize. Furthermore, even regarding the absence of knowledge—which is the province of the sixth means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and is inferable from the absence of its effect as a logical mark—the cognition of the absence of knowledge in the self is impossible, regardless of whether the self has been cognized or not.

And in this world, having experienced an ignorance that is turned away from its object—thinking, "I do not know the meaning spoken by you, nor the number, nor the meaning of the scripture"—one engages in hearing it and so forth.

In the theory that ignorance (*ajñāna*) is of a positive nature (*bhāvarūpa*), however, even when the knowledge of its locus (*āśraya*) and its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) exists, it cannot be established that another positive entity is impossible, just as in the case of the absence of knowledge (*jñānābhāva*). Nor does the witnessing consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*), which constitutes the knowledge of the locus and the counter-correlate, remove this other positive entity, namely ignorance; for that [witnessing consciousness] is itself the manifestation of the object of ignorance. Indeed, a thing is not removed by its own cognition.

[Objection: But how can the object that delimits ignorance be manifested by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*), given that the establishment of an object depends upon the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? [Reply: It is said in response: Every object is indeed an object of the witness-consciousness, either as something known or as something unknown. Among these, an object as something known requires the intervention of a means of valid cognition; however, another [object], whether in its general form or its specific form, always shines forth as that which delimits ignorance. Thus, it is established that the perception of ignorance, supported by reasoning, reveals ignorance—which is of a positive nature (*bhāvarūpa*)—as residing in the Self.

Inference also [establishes this]: "The valid cognition under dispute must be preceded by another entity that is distinct from its own prior non-existence, which obscures its object, is removable by it, and resides in its own locus; because it illuminates an unilluminated object, like the light of a lamp first produced in the dark. Consequently, ignorance in the form of a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*), sharing the same locus and object as the cognition, is established.

By the word "power" (*śakti*), he expresses the capacity of the Self to sustain its status as the material cause of all effects by virtue of its dependence upon itself. Its nature is the reality of the Self; the meaning is that it is invariably concomitant with the mere existence of that [Self]. Furthermore, he states that presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is also a means of valid knowledge for the existence of ignorance in the form of a positive entity: "otherwise, the manifestation of false objects would be inexplicable."

In the pure Brahman-self and in the mother-of-pearl, there must be sought some false material cause for the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the ego and silver—which consists of both object and cognition and is itself false. For if it had a real material cause, then because the effect shares the nature of its cause, it would follow that the superimposition itself is real. Furthermore, if that false material cause were itself beginningless, it would lead to the necessity of postulating yet another such material cause. Therefore, it must be conceived as a beginningless false material cause.

And that which is beginningless, inherently false, has a false substrate, and is related to the self—that is ignorance (*ajñāna*). Thus, it has been stated that false superimposition (*mithyādhyāsa*) itself, being otherwise inexplicable without such a cause consisting of the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) of ignorance, leads to the postulation of that [ignorance].

Now, it might be argued that whatever produces an excellence (*atiśaya*) in something is its object (*viṣaya*), and yet no excellence of concealment (*āvaraṇa*) is produced by ignorance (*ajñāna*) regarding the non-self (*anātman*), because there is a lack of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and because the matter is logically untenable. First of all, when the object blue is not known, it is impossible to perceive the function of concealment therein; and when it is not known at all, it is even more so. It might be objected: "Once the object is known, one can understand that it was previously concealed. This is not so; for in the case of an object accessible through a continuous stream of cognitions (*dhārāvāhika-vijñāna*), we observe that what was already known before is known again later.

But does not the very fact of being understood now establish that there was no understanding previously? No; for without knowing the prior non-understanding, the restriction "it is understood only now" would be impossible. Nor does the recognition of identity between earlier and later [moments]—in which non-understanding in the interval is perceived—establish that there was non-understanding in the interval, such that the recognition itself would be untenable.

If it is argued that even though the Self is always cognized as a continuous stream (*dhārāvāhika*), its non-cognition is understood because of the absence of knowledge and memory during the interval, we say no; for even when something is cognized, there is no rule that memory must necessarily follow. If it is further argued that the non-cognition of objects is nevertheless perceived, that is true; however, this appearance arises from the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of ignorance upon the witness-consciousness (*sākṣi-caitanya*) together with the objects. And there can be no concealment (*āvaraṇa*) of that which is superimposed, because—like a double moon—it is not accessible through valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, there is no proof for the existence of concealment regarding the non-Self (*anātman*).

Furthermore, for that which is insentient (*jaḍa*) and devoid of self-luminosity, even the purpose of concealment is not possible. Therefore, due to the absence of any such excellence (*atiśaya*), the non-self (*anātman*) cannot be the object of ignorance (*ajñāna*). To this, he replies: "And that [ignorance] does not obstruct the manifestation of the true nature (*svarūpa*) in insentient objects. The intention is that, rather than that, a different kind of excellence will be produced in the non-self, and it will be stated later that ignorance has that [non-self] as its object. The reason for this is: "precisely because of the deficiency of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-vaikalyāt*)."

Alternatively, one might raise the objection: "Since insentient objects are constantly associated with the light of consciousness as if they were eternal, they would appear eternally; therefore, the function of concealment (āvaraṇa) is indeed possible regarding non-self-objects. Anticipating this, he says: "Precisely due to the deficiency of the means of knowledge" (pramāṇavaikalyāt). The meaning is that because the consciousness which is the means of knowing non-self-objects is deficient—due to concealment alone—the non-apprehension of the object is established; thus, a separate concealment need not be postulated for the object itself. For this reason as well, there is no concealment in the non-self; he states: "Because of the appearance of silver" (rajatapratibhāsāt).

If ignorance were based on the Self and were an obscuration of the non-Self, then, since the manifestation of an object is impossible without the destruction of that obscuration, the ignorance regarding the Self would be removed by the cognition of the object. Therefore, the sense is that because the nature of objects is observed to manifest throughout all three periods of time even while ignorance regarding the Self persists, ignorance is not an obscuration of the non-Self.

Now, it might be argued that the ignorance regarding a mother-of-pearl shell is one thing, which ceases upon the knowledge of it, whereas the ignorance regarding the Self is another, which is observed within the Self; but that is not so. For, apart from an ignorance that has the Self as its locus and object, there is no evidence for the existence of a positive ignorance (bhāvarūpājñāna) directed toward each of the non-Self objects, since the non-apprehension of objects can be accounted for even by a deficiency in the means of valid cognition (pramāṇavaikalya).

Rather, having relied upon a specific excellence (atiśaya) produced by ignorance regarding external and internal objects, the ignorance whose object is the non-self (anātman) has been shown; thus he says: "Therefore, in that case, it is merely the cause for the appearance of another form."

But surely, here too the same logical inconsistency applies: it is your view that the cognition of mother-of-pearl, by subverting the appearance of another form, also subverts the ignorance that is its material cause (*upādāna*). In that case, when superimposition (*adhyāsa*) is being subverted along with its ignorance by the cognition of mother-of-pearl, how is it that ignorance is again observed in the Self? Therefore, one must either accept a distinction between ignorances for each object, or that superimposition does not have ignorance as its material cause, or else that superimposition can be subverted even without the subversion of its material cause.

It is said in reply: in this view, by the cognition of mother-of-pearl and the like, there is merely the dissolution of the superimpositions of silver and so forth into their own cause, just as a jar is dissolved by a blow from a mallet. Alternatively, let it be postulated that the various states (avasthābheda) of the root-ignorance itself serve as the material causes (upādāna) for silver and the like, and these are removed along with the superimposition by the cognitions of mother-of-pearl and the like.

But how can it be maintained that, since in the world one does not perceive that superimposition ceases through the knowledge of reality when it is accompanied by innate ignorance, the cessation of superimposition—accompanied by innate ignorance—through the knowledge of Brahman is postulated by way of an observed precedent? This is not a fault; for we observe that non-apprehension, false knowledge, and the like—which are opposed to the manifestation of reality—cease through the knowledge of reality. Since, in this case as well, positive ignorance and the rest are postulated precisely because they are opposed to the manifestation of reality, their cessation through the knowledge of Brahman is logically established.

Nor does the fault mentioned regarding the side of obscuration (āvaraṇapakṣa) follow here; for an alternative form, distinct from the object, is apprehended by erroneous cognition. Now, if this is so, there can be no function of obscuration caused by ignorance even with respect to the Self. How so? First of all, obscuration is not the destruction of light, because the essential nature (svarūpa) does not perish; nor is it the obstruction of the activity of light that already exists.

Since knowledge, having arisen in the form of the manifestation of its object, lacks both obstruction and expectation regarding its own effect, there can be no ignorance in the form of a positive entity even with respect to the Self, as it would be useless. To this, he replies with the passage beginning with "But in the case of the inner Self, because it is of the nature of consciousness and is self-luminous," and ending with "there is no non-manifestation of that."

The meaning is this: when the full set of causes for such conventional linguistic usages as "it exists" or "it manifests" is present, the convention that takes the reality of the Self as its object—namely, "it does not exist" or "it does not manifest"—is not possible unless there is some form of obscuration (āvaraṇa) of the Self by means of some positive entity.

Since the conventional usage "it shines forth" and so on is observed when the complete causes are present and no obstruction exists—just as in the case of a pot placed nearby—the conventional expression "Brahman does not exist and does not shine forth" implies, by the principle of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) or inference, a positive entity known as ignorance (*ajñāna*), because such usage would otherwise be inexplicable; this is the collective meaning [of the passage].

To establish that [point], he demonstrates its status as the sufficient cause for the conventional usage such as "it shines forth" with respect to the Self, by stating: "because its nature is consciousness. What, then, is the obscuration? To this he replies: "of the non-manifestation of the nature of Brahman. This means: of that fitness to be the objective basis for the conventional usages "it does not exist" or "it does not shine forth," which is itself postulated solely on the basis of observing the effects of such conventions. Furthermore, the effect of error cannot be accounted for there without an obstruction to the manifestation of the underlying substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

The sense is that because the veil is connected with ignorance (*avidyā*), its form being undetermined is also logical. Now, one might object: "In this case too, non-apprehension occurs simply due to a deficiency in the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*. To this he says, "No," for the reason given is "because there is no other cause. Therefore, since there is non-appearance despite the presence of all causal factors, by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), he states what follows: "Its non-appearance is solely due to the obstruction of the power of innate ignorance residing therein. The sense is that no other material substance is possible [to act as the veil].

Therefore, he says: "Hence, that [ignorance] resides in the inward-facing consciousness," meaning that ignorance—which performs the functions of veiling and distortion within the Self—is inferred from the observation of its effects; and because it is impossible otherwise for there to be a cause for both [these effects], it is postulated as being of a positive (bhāvarūpa) nature.

"Is it not the case that we do not perceive any such thing as 'ignorance' (ajñāna) other than non-apprehension, false knowledge, and their latent impressions (saṃskāras), and that these alone obstruct the manifestation of the nature of Brahman—which, though self-luminous—to the individual soul (jīva)? To this he says: 'And in deep sleep, etc. The meaning is that even there, the power of ignorance (avidyā-śakti) remains as a residue of latent impressions; thus, it is not the latent impressions and so forth themselves that constitute ignorance."

How can it be said that, in states such as deep sleep, there is no manifestation of the self-luminous nature of Brahman because the seer is distinct [from it], as is the case with the cognition of another person? This cannot be maintained, because of the scriptural teaching of oneness. Nor can it be due to the obstruction of false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*), for that is absent in that state. Nor can it be due to the obstruction of its latent impression (*saṃskāra*).

This is because the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of error do not act as an obstacle to the manifestation of reality, since we observe the cognition of mother-of-pearl even while the impressions of the delusion of silver persist; nor is it due to an obstruction by non-apprehension (*agrahaṇa*), because the apprehension of its own nature is eternal, and since consciousness is self-luminous, an occasional non-apprehension regarding that object cannot serve as an obstacle; nor do karmic actions possess the power to oppose the manifestation of its own nature.

If it is argued that this would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of consciousness never being manifested even in the slightest degree, and that this objection applies equally to ignorance (*ajñāna*), we say no; for ignorance does not act as an obstruction to the manifestation of the consciousness that has itself as its object. Furthermore, unlike ignorance, actions (*karman*) are not to be manifested by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*) as something eternal, such that the witness-consciousness would have to shine forth unobstructed by virtue of manifesting them. Nor is there any evidence to suggest that actions are contrary to the manifestation of their own substrate.

Furthermore, because actions are *saṃskāras* (latent impressions), like the impressions of error, they possess no obstructive power. Therefore, the conventional usage regarding the non-manifestation of one's true nature during deep sleep and similar states implies that there must be some other obstructing factor—distinct from non-apprehension (*agrahaṇa*), false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*), their impressions, and past actions—which we designate as *ajñāna* (ignorance).

Now, one might object: "Why should another substance be postulated as the obstructor rather than postulating *ajñāna*? This is not so; for it is impossible for the manifestation of its own object to occur without the removal of the obstruction through the knowledge of Brahman, and that which is removable by knowledge is, by definition, *ajñāna*.

In this regard, a certain proponent of universal confusion, who asserts both difference and non-difference and is devoid of the tradition of the profound meaning of the Vedānta, utters these difficult-to-swallow yet charming words: "Indeed, there exists no such thing as 'ignorance' (ajñāna) distinct from non-apprehension (agrahaṇa), false knowledge (mithyājñāna), and their latent impressions (saṃskāra)—an ignorance that serves as the seed of the entire cycle of transmigratory existence, which persists undiminished throughout the three states [of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep], and which stands like a staff until liberation from saṃsāra; rather, ignorance is simply erroneous cognition or non-apprehension."

He should be asked: "What is this delusion? If he says, "It is the notion of a self with regard to that which is not-self, from the ego-sense up to the body," then alas for the forgetfulness of one whose mind is so thoroughly corrupted everywhere!

If you argue that while you establish the cognition of both difference and non-difference—such as "the spotted cow"—as valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), why do you disregard the cognition "I am a human being" as having both difference and non-difference as its object? If you say, "Because of the force of the cognition 'I am not a human being, I am Brahman'," that is not so; for even in the cognition "This is not a spotted cow, but rather a hornless cow," just as there is non-difference of cowness from both the spotted and the hornless [individuals], the validity of the cognition of the non-difference of the individual soul (*jīva*) from both the body and Brahman is likewise established.

If it is argued that this [cognition] is an error, like [the cognition] of silver [in a shell], we say no; for then the same would follow even in the case of "this is a spotted cow," since the usage [of the term "cow"] is not interrupted there. If it is argued that its validity is established by the force of the negative cognition in another individual—such as "this is not a spotted cow, but a hornless one"—where the spottedness is negated within the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of cowness, then that is equally true in the case of "I am a human"; for even in the state of liberation (*mokṣa*), because you [the opponent] are the Self of all, the usage consisting of the conceit (*abhimāna*) regarding all bodies, senses, and so forth, is not interrupted.

If it is argued that where relations such as genus and individual, quality and possessor of quality, cause and effect, qualified and its nature, part and whole, or connection exist, there both difference and non-difference are found—but these do not exist between the body and the self—then why should the relationship between the body and the embodied soul not also be a cause of difference, just like the relationship between quality and possessor of quality and so forth? Otherwise, your long-earned status as a disciple of the Kṣapaṇakas (Jainas), who are proponents of universal confusion (sarvasaṅkara), would be contradicted.
Furthermore, there exists a cause-and-effect relationship between the conscious self and the body, since the conscious aspect of the self is Brahman; therefore, you have no delusion in this matter.

Furthermore, if erroneous cognition (*bhrāntijñāna*) were a transformation of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇapariṇāma*), then ignorance (*avidyā*) would not have the Self as its locus. If it is argued that the transformation of the internal organ itself is superimposed upon the Self, even so, for one who maintains the theory of misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*), there would be no connection between the Self and ignorance, because the relation [between the object and the cognition] would be non-existent. Nor can error be a transformation of the Self, because the Self is unchanging (*apariṇāmin*). Moreover, it is impossible for a substance characterized by the quality of knowledge to undergo further transformation into the form of another quality of knowledge.

Because two qualities of a different intermediate genus cannot co-inhere simultaneously in a single substance—for instance, whiteness does not co-inhere in a cloth at one and the same time—therefore, for one who maintains the doctrine of universal confusion (*sarvasaṅkaravādin*), no such thing as ignorance (*avidyā*) is possible unless they admit the existence of beginningless false cognition. Furthermore, even the connection with beginningless false cognition, being merely conceptual (*kālpinika*) in the self like [the notion of] ignorance itself, does not destroy the immutability (*kūṭasthatā*) of the self, just as the blackness of space does not affect the sky; enough of this digression.

And here, perception, inference, and presumption are presented as the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding ignorance (*ajñāna*) which is beginningless and of the nature of a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*). In this regard, he concludes—stating that "therefore, egoism (*ahaṅkāra*) is also innate"—that its being adventitious (*naimittika*) in its causal form and innate (*naisargika*) in its effect form are not contradictory. The passage beginning with "the attributes of one another" and ending with "shows the nature of superimposition (*adhyāsa*)" is clear in meaning.

Although the superimposition of ignorance and so forth exists as beginninglessly established within that which is a continuous flow of stainless consciousness, whose sole essence is partless bliss, and which is the witness of ignorance and the rest, [the author] speaks by relying on a superimposition that occurs only occasionally: "First of all, 'I' is the primary superimposition. But is this not like [the case of] "this is silver"?

Regarding superimposition (*adhyāsa*), one must also state its "twofold nature" (*dvairūpya*) in the case of the notion "I am. One might object: "Since 'I' appears as a single form, there can be no superimposition"—to this he raises the objection: "But surely 'I' is merely partless consciousness. He then states that the possibility of superimposition exists through its twofold nature: "Just as the inclusion of the other superimposed parts [will be explained]."

Objection: Since the internal organ and the senses are established only as superimpositions—because their existence is not perceived apart from the Self and because scripture does not teach their dissolution by way of their own nature upon the realization of the reality of the Self—they are indeed established as superimposed on the Self both in their own form and in their associated form. However, the body, on the other hand, is not established as a superimposition; for it is grasped by the senses through the notion of "this," it is not perceivable by the pure witness-consciousness alone, it is perceived separately even when the Self has departed, and scripture teaches its dissolution into the elements.

He objects: "But surely this [is so] for the 'I-maker' (ahaṃkartṛ)"—meaning that what is grasped by the notion of "mine" as distinct from the body is all the more non-superimposed. He says: "And [the thought] 'this is mine'"—thereby indicating that it is even more clearly not a superimposition.

Since the nature of entities such as the body is created for the sake of the Self—which is falsely imagined as an agent, enjoyer, knower, and possessed of defects—by way of being an object of action, an object of enjoyment, an object of knowledge, and an object of aversion, its falsity even in its own nature can be inferred by the analogy of a dream; thus he says: "It is said: 'When the ego-maker... and so forth. He shows the application to the case at hand: "'In this way, beginning with the state of being the ego-maker...'"

He states that if the appearance of the object of sight (*dṛśya*) in the seer (*draṣṭṛ*) is due to the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of ignorance (*avidyā*), then the establishment of the subject matter (*viṣaya*) and purpose (*prayojana*) of the scripture will follow as a result: "Therefore, [this is established] up to the experience of the Self as that Brahman" (*atastādṛgbrahmātmānubhavaparyantāt*). The meaning is that such an experience of the Self as Brahman and the cessation of bondage (*bandhanivṛtti*) are both logically possible. To the question, "What follows from the establishment of the subject matter and purpose?", he says: "The undertaking of the inquiry into the Vedānta (*vedāntamīmāṃsā*) which has that as its subject matter is thus justified" (*tadarthaviṣayavedāntamīmāṃsārambhaḥ*). Thus, the necessity of commencing the treatise is established.

The analysis of the compound is as follows: "the cessation of the bondage [consisting] in the experience of the Self as Brahman is the purpose (*artha*)—that is, the motive (*prayojana*) and the subject matter (*viṣaya*)—of this undertaking of Vedānta-mīmāṃsā. He states the purport of the subsequent commentary ending with the words "perceived by all the world" with the words: "He asks: 'Who is this? Now, he explains the intermediate purport by dividing [the text], beginning with: "Even there..."

He introduces the commentary on the subsequent section concerning the possibility of definitions with the words, "If this is so... He asks why the definition and its possibility are not required, and answers that point with the words, "For [a thing] whose form is not ascertained... The meaning is this: it is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) itself that establishes superimposition (*adhyāsa*), which consists in one thing appearing under the nature of another; in doing so, it establishes the object of cognition (*prameya*) as having a possible form within the limiting conditions of its own place and time, and as having a unique form excluded from everything else. Therefore, what is the use of separately propounding the definition and the possibility?

[Objection: Is it not the case that regarding mere objects known through means of valid cognition such as inference, both the possibility of specific characteristics and their distinctness are required? To this, he says: "difficult to establish" (*duḥsampādam*). [He explains] "specifically" (*viśeṣataḥ*) as meaning "by way of being excluded from the uncommon form. In that regard, the proof will be stated merely to the extent that for a seer other than the object, there is an appearance in the form of something else; it does not concern its being ignorance, error, superimposition, or falsity. Therefore, he refutes [the objection] by stating that it is not established by that proof, beginning with: "It is not [superimposed] upon the body, senses, and so forth," etc.

[The opponent] objects: "Surely its falsity is established by the very means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that reveals one thing as having the nature of another, because the object of knowledge (*prameya*) is one and the same. To this he replies with the question: "For what reason? He answers: "Not from experience alone," and explains: "In the world... [The opponent asks: "If there is a means of valid cognition, why is there an absence of experience? He says: "Because of the difference in the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-bheda*). For when there is sublation (*bādha*), that very impossibility of sublation is the proof for falsity.

The sense is that the scriptures are the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the appearance of the non-self within the self, because the practical functioning (*vyavahāra*) of perception and inference would otherwise be untenable. Now, one might object: even here, without a mutual distinction based on sublation, it is impossible to understand that "this is the appearance of one thing as the nature of another"; otherwise, why could it not be the case that a thing appears as its own nature? To this he says: "That [distinction] does not exist here.
