As it is said: "The silver is not real, because it is sublated by a cognition that has as its object the non-existence of that very thing in that very place where it was perceived, just like a dream-object. Also: "The silver is not real, because it is sublated by a cognition that has as its object the non-existence of that very thing in that very place where it was perceived, just like a snake in a rope. Thus, the silver is indeed unreal. And: "The silver is not real, because it is sublated by a cognition that has as its object the non-existence of that very thing in that very place where it was perceived, just like a snake in a rope. Also: "The silver is not real, because it is sublated by a cognition that has as its object the non-existence of that very thing in that very place where it was perceived, just like a snake in a rope. Thus, the silver is indeed unreal. As it is said: "The silver is not real, because it is sublated by a cognition that has as its object the non-existence of that very thing in that very place where it was perceived, just like a dream-object. And: "The silver is not real, because it is sublated by a cognition that has as its object the non-existence of that very thing in that very place where it was perceived, just like a snake in a rope. Therefore, the silver is indeed unreal. As it is said: "The silver is not real, because it is sublated by a cognition that has as its object the non-existence of that very thing in that very place where it was perceived, just like a dream-object. Also: "The silver is not real, because it is sublated by a cognition that has as its object the non-existence of that very thing in that very place where it was perceived, just like a snake in a rope. Thus, the silver is indeed unreal. As it is said: "The silver is not real, because it is sublated by a cognition that has as its object the non-existence of that very thing in that very place where it was perceived, just like a dream-object."

The meaning is that this is not silver, but rather [silver] in another place or at another time, or [merely] in the intellect; for the reason is that such [a qualification] is not apprehended. For a sentence conveys its meaning only to the extent of its expressive capacity; however, since existing in another place is not expressed [by the words], it is not the meaning of the sentence. This is the sense.

If this were so, one might argue that the non-existence of the perceived object here is logically untenable (anupapanna) without its existence elsewhere, and thus the sentence would be understood through presumptive testimony (arthāpatti); to this he says "no"—it is not by arthāpatti. This is because, whether in the theory of misapprehension (anyathākhyāti) or the theory of self-apprehension (ātmakhyāti), we observe the negation of a connection that has been refuted, or of something external, without its existence elsewhere.

Even in the case of the *ākhyātā* sacrifice, when the abandonment of all one's possessions (*sarvasvadāna*) is to be performed due to the interruption of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), that duty is not undertaken there because it is sublated by the cognition of completing the sacrifice without a sacrificial fee (*adakṣiṇa*) caused by a subsequent interruption of the priests; rather, it is understood to exist elsewhere.

If it is argued that "it is simply the activity [of the agent] that ceases in that case," we say no; for it has already been stated that the cessation of activity is not a sublation (*bādha*). Furthermore, in the case of sacrifices and the like, even if activity is obstructed due to the certainty of an impediment such as a king or a thief, there is no established sublation of the cognition of the sacrifice itself. Moreover, as long as the cognition of an uncontradicted duty (*kartavyatā*) exists, the performance of the action will eventually be accomplished at some point or other.

Furthermore, even in the world, when the negation of something occurs only with respect to a specific condition (*upādhi*), one does not assume its existence under another condition belonging to the same class as that negating condition. Thus he says: "as in the case of the absence of a broken jar here. Just as a jar, which has been negated in a perceived location, does not exist in another location, so too, for that which is negated in all conditions—namely, place, time, substance, and everything else—it is not established that it exists in any unperceived condition as its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*). This is the meaning.

"Now, how can there be a realization of the void everywhere? To this he says: "Because that [realization] is established even by that alone. The meaning here is that its cognition is established even by the mere existence of an indefinable, false object.

[Objection: In that case, would there not be a negation based on a difference in time—such as "Previously there was silver, but now there is not"—just as in the case of a jar? [Reply: No, because even throughout the three periods of time, the silver of common worldly experience (*laukikaparamārtha-rajata*) is void here; therefore, a negation without qualifications (*nirupādhika-niṣedha*) is established in relation to it. And by the force of this unqualified negation, the silver perceived as false is subsequently reflected upon after the sublation (*bādha*), as in: "Only false silver appeared."

Otherwise, if there were a difference in time, it would be real silver itself. For a perceptual cognition whose object is mere negation, such as "This is not a snake," does not imply the existence of a snake in another location; how much less so can it be said that a cognition which terminates in the substrate, such as "This is a rope," does not produce a conceptual construction? This is shown by the phrase: "even where [the cognition] is preceded by the sublation of the snake. Thus ends the summary with the words "tadevam" and so forth. The passage beginning with "yadyevam paratra" has a clear meaning.

"Truthful" means "having a clearly manifest object. This is its meaning: regarding the doubt as to whether the word "resembling memory" denotes being produced by a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), or a connection with a prior experience, or a similarity to memory, [the author] stated "it is the manifestation of what was previously seen, not of the seeing itself" in order to clarify that it is indeed being produced by a latent impression. The meaning is "of the same class as what was previously seen," because of the acceptance of indeterminable silver (*anirvacanīya-rajata*). If it were an error, [it would have to be] of a real object.

The reasoning previously stated—that the appearance of a false object as non-distinct [from the substrate] would otherwise lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)—is based on the fact that superimposition (*adhyāsa*) is established by worldly experience. Nevertheless, he says "tathā ca loke anubhavaḥ" and so forth, to show that there is no need for further reasoning.

One might object: "Surely the expression 'a mother-of-pearl shell is like silver' cannot be justified with reference to an error, because [the shell] appears precisely as 'this is silver. Nor can it be justified with reference to sublation, because the word 'like' (vat) is absent there. Thus he raises the objection: "But surely not 'a mother-of-pearl shell'..."

He says: "It is said: 'The apprehension of the mother-of-pearl...'"—this statement demonstrates the connection between the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) and the thing defined (*lakṣya*) by means of this sentence. For, with respect to the subverting cognition (*bādhakajñāna*), the phrase "the mother-of-pearl appears as silver" is the presentation of the definition; or else, by way of being the object of that subverting cognition, or through its power, the falsity of superimposition—which is already established—is denoted by the word "that" (*tat*). Thus, the coherence between the definition and the thing defined is shown therein.

[Objection: "Is it not the case that because of the qualification 'false silver,' one must admit that there is real silver elsewhere? [Reply: No, he says—"falsity also belongs to the silver. The meaning is that the qualification refers to the nature of the object itself, and does not aim at the exclusion of something else. [Objection: "If the silver is false, then since this-ness (idantā) is a property of that silver, its this-ness would also be false; thus, due to the falsity of everything, there would be the undesirable consequence of having no substratum (niradhiṣṭhānatā). [Reply: No, he says—"because of the lack of contact with that [silver]. [Question: "How can that silver, which is not in contact [with the senses], appear as immediate (aparokṣa)? To this he says—"But the appearance as immediate..."

He states the purport of the two examples with the words, "In that regard, by the example of mother-of-pearl," and so forth. "In our own sense" means in the manifestation as "I. He says, "by way of its being the absence of that [objectivity]," meaning that even though there is an absence of the status of being an object of the "you" (the non-self) from the perspective of manifestation, the characteristic of being an object of the "you" still exists in the form of being illumined by consciousness.

Since the aggregate of the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) and so forth is superimposed upon the Seer, whose nature is the light of non-dual consciousness, it must be stated that the Self consists of a triad: the substratum distinct from the object superimposed, the knowledge of the true nature of the substratum—which is the means of valid cognition regarding the reality of the superimposition—and the Seer himself. Consequently, it must be stated that every kind of defect—whether a defect residing in the substratum, a defect in the Seer, or a defect in the instrument of knowledge—all such defects reside in the Self alone.

Because that [triad of causes] is absent—since consciousness (caitanya) is not a produced cognition of an object of superimposition, and because a cognition produced by a triad of causes is impossible in the case of the superimposition of the non-self upon the Self; since the apprehension of a generality whose particulars are unapprehended, which is the cause for being a locus (adhiṣṭhāna), is impossible in the Self; and because the term "in another" (paratra) is inapplicable—the objection is raised that the definition of superimposition, even though stated generally for external objects, does not apply to the Self. This is expressed by the preceding text beginning with "nanu bahirarthe... up to "...ucyate."

[Objection: "But here too, just as in the case of external objects, one might infer that the specific features are ungrasped on the basis of the common property of being an object. [Reply: No, he says—"but here it does not depend on another cause. [Objection: "But even in the manifestation of its own nature, it might be like consciousness, having an ungrasped specific portion. [Reply: No, he says—"of that which is partless. Since the intermediate size has been refuted, the self—whether atomic or infinite—is partless.

[Objection: But surely, like space and other such things, even though it is partless, it does not manifest in its entirety. To this he replies: "Because it is self-luminous" (*svayaṃjyotiṣaḥ*). The meaning is that it manifests as long as it exists. Why? Because of such scriptural passages as, "In this state, this person is self-luminous," and "The Self alone is his light. [Objection: But by the term "light" (*jyotis*), one does not denote a mere quality of illumination;

for that would entail the consequence that the Self is a quality. Therefore, light is a substance possessing the quality of illumination. Thus, since the Self possesses the quality of illumination through the light of produced knowledge (*janyajñāna*) as well, the statement "the Self is light" is not contradictory. [Reply: This is not sound.

Because all entities are associated with other causes and illuminations, the qualification "self-luminous" (*svayaṃjyotiḥ*) is appropriate in order to exclude that same contingency from the Self itself, as indicated by the particle *eva* in the passage, "The Self alone is his light. Now, one might object: why could the qualification "by itself" (*svayam*) not mean that it produces knowledge within its own self independently of any other causal factors? This is not so; for luminosity itself is the subject of the statement, and in that context, the status of being a causal factor does not appear as the primary subject.

Furthermore, since the dependence upon causal factors (*kāraka*) is necessitated by the arising of cognition, in the absence of that [cognition], there is no dependence at all. Now, it may be argued that even birth is necessitated by cognition and not solely by the quality of luminosity (*prakāśaguṇatva*); for, apart from the birth of a substance, the absence of birth within its own substrate is observed in the case of a lamp and similar objects, and here too, from the word "light" (*jyotis*), one ascertains the absence of the birth of the quality of luminosity in the Self. Nor is the transformation into cognition (*jñānapariṇāma*) the emergence of the quality of luminosity even in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

This is because it is accepted that knowledge is a specific modification (*viśeṣapariṇāma*) of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) itself—a substance possessing the quality of luminosity—by its very nature. Furthermore, even knowledge is never observed to have an origin [in the sense of being produced]. If it is argued that it is observed [to originate] in the internal organ, we say no; for knowledge is the manifestation of an object by the knower, and that [manifestation] has the Self as its locus. The designation "knowledge" is applied metaphorically to a modification of the internal organ. Moreover, it is not tenable to claim that "knowledge is a substance whose locus is the Self."

If it is argued that because the Self possesses the quality of luminosity (*prakāśaguṇatva*), its nature as light is not lost, and therefore the quality of inert luminosity is not produced while the quality of conscious luminosity (*citprakāśaguṇa*) is produced—this is not so; for the absence of birth with respect to one's own substance (*svadravyopādhau*) is conditioned by the very fact of being luminous. In the case of mirrors and the like, it is merely the existing luminosity that is made manifest after its concealment has been removed; whereas in the case of lamps and such, the substance itself is born, not the quality of luminosity. Furthermore, from the term "mass of consciousness" (*prajñānaghana*), it is understood that the Self is the light of consciousness (*caitanyajyotis*) and not the light of the inert.

Furthermore, from such scriptural statements as "Consciousness is bliss" (*vijñānamānandam*) and "Brahman is pure knowledge" (*prajñānaṃ brahma*), [it follows that consciousness is the Self]. If it is argued that the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*) denotes the state of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*) and not the abstract quality (*bhāvārtha*), we say no; for this contradicts the well-established usage of the term. Moreover, rather than postulating a new quality of luminosity (*prakāśa*) at every moment, it is better to postulate the persistence of a single quality. And since there is no absence of the quality of luminosity in the Self, there is no evidence for its adventitious nature.

[The opponent] objects: "Is it not the case that the absence of perceived distinctions in the Self is established by experience? [The author] replies: "Indeed, [it is the nature of Brahman]. If that were so, then non-manifestation and error would occur in Brahman itself—as they do with mother-of-pearl—and not in the individual soul (jīva); thus he says: "Not because of its non-manifestation. [The opponent further objects: "Is it not the case that for two substances devoid of the relation of cause and effect, their grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) must reside in a single substance?"

"Just as in the case of [the statement] 'This is Devadatta,' because there is oneness of substance, non-manifestation and error belong only to the movement of the individual soul (jīva)"—thus he objects: "But surely [Brahman] is not other than [the Self]. Then he says, "In that case," meaning that due to the contradiction with the light of knowledge and the absence of a distinction between locus and object, Brahman cannot possess the state of being unknown. To this, he replies: "It is said: it certainly exists. Therein, he first demonstrates the contact of the causal defect of ignorance with the consciousness that is the means of valid cognition within the Self, which is Brahman as the non-dual substratum: "It is said: it certainly exists."

The ignorance already indicated by perception, inference, and postulation is now further demonstrated through scripture (*śruti*) and the postulation based on it (*tadarthāpatti*). Regarding the phrase "Scripture, first of all": since false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*) is absent during deep sleep (*suṣupti*), and since its latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) do not act as an obstacle, and since the occasional absence of apprehension does not inherently oppose the self-evident apprehension [of the Self], it follows that the nature of Brahman should manifest through the very consciousness of one's own essential nature (*svarūpacaitanya*). To show the cause that obstructs this manifestation, [the scripture] points to "unreality" (*anṛta*): "For by unreality... [and so forth].

"They are pushed aside," and "these true desires have untruth as their covering. From this, it is established that there exists an unreal, false entity—an *anṛta*—which is distinct from false knowledge, its latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), non-apprehension, and karma, and which serves as the cause for the failure of manifestation. Furthermore, in the passage, "He grieves while deluded by his lack of lordship" (*anīśayā śocati muhyamānaḥ*), the state of being a non-lord for the Lord who is established by His very nature is nothing other than the non-realization of that state; for the reality [of the Lord] does not perish. Thus, the text shows that delusion (*moha*) is the cause of both the failure to realize the state of the Lord and of grief.

From the word "etcetera," [we understand] the passage: "You do not know him who produced these; another has come between you. Enveloped by mist, prattling and satisfied with food, the reciters of hymns wander. Here, "mist" (nīhāra), "darkness" (tamas), and "ignorance" (ajñāna) are synonymous. By this, it is shown that being enveloped by that very ignorance is the cause for the individual souls' lack of knowledge of Brahman and for their false attribution of prattling and so forth.

Likewise, passages such as, "Remaining in the midst of ignorance, they do not perceive any other excellence," show that ignorance is the cause for both the non-recognition of Brahman—which is the nature of the highest good—and the superimposition of action, its factors, and so forth; and Smṛti texts such as, "Knowledge is veiled by ignorance; by that they are deluded," are also to be understood in this light.

Presumption (*arthāpatti*) also [establishes this]: the scriptural teaching that the cessation of bondage results from the knowledge of Brahman implies that there must exist a cause for the relationship of superimposition (*adhyāsa*), namely the prior lack of realization regarding Brahman; thus, the scriptural mention of the fruit [of liberation] would otherwise be inexplicable. Alternatively, the injunction to "behold" (*draṣṭavyaḥ*) and so forth would be inexplicable without such a prior non-comprehension. Therefore, it has been stated that there exists the defect of ignorance (*ajñāna*), which is the cause of the relationship of superimposition residing in the individual soul (*jīva*) and is the reason for the non-manifestation of the soul's true nature as Brahman.

And here, since the exclusion of non-existence regarding ignorance—which is known by the witness-consciousness—is demonstrated by means of the instruments of knowledge (*pramāṇas*), there is no contingency that it [ignorance] should itself be cognizable by those instruments. To this, an objection is raised: "But surely the individual soul (*jīva*) is not other than Brahman. Here, what is being questioned on account of the identity of the soul and Brahman? Is it the impossibility of a distinction between locus and object due to their identity, or is it the contradiction of consciousness (*cit-svabhāva*) being the locus of ignorance, or the loss of Brahman’s omniscience and other attributes?

Ignorance (*ajñāna*) does not depend on a distinction between its locus (*āśraya*) and its object (*viṣaya*); rather, within a single entity alone, it accomplishes two functions: being the locus and being the veil. This is like the accomplishment of two functions by darkness within the space of a room that is its own locus, because it is non-active in nature and because it is a veil. Indeed, darkness does not appear as depending on two entities. Furthermore, the term "ignorance" is a designation by way of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of knowledge, which necessarily depends on a duality [of subject and object].

It appears as if dependent on a duality. Just as "staying," when expressed by the word "non-going," appears as if dependent on an object—raising the question of whose non-going it is and regarding what object—it is exactly like that. Furthermore, ignorance (*ajñāna*), which veils its own substrate like darkness, is not contradicted by its identity with its substrate. Nor is ignorance contradicted by the illumination of consciousness (*citprakāśa*) residing in its own substrate; for ignorance is not opposed to the illumination of consciousness—the awareness that manifests itself—since the witness-consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*) is precisely what illumines ignorance.
Therefore, there is no contradiction in [ignorance] having consciousness as its substrate.

Furthermore, since it must be admitted by everyone that the self is the locus of ignorance regarding itself and its objects precisely while it is appearing to the produced cognition during the three states, there is no contradiction in its being the locus of ignorance while it is appearing. Nor is mere luminosity opposed to ignorance, because that is absent in the case of one's own cognition. Nor is a contradiction with the association of ignorance ever observed in that which is self-luminous; for such a contradiction is seen only in the case of objects, which are revealed by another.

Since consciousness (*saṃvedana*) is the very nature of the Self (*ātman*), ignorance cannot be admitted as having that as its locus; therefore, it is not an appropriate example [for the relationship between Brahman and ignorance]. Now, if it is argued that ignorance is untenable in the case of identity because it contradicts the omniscience of Brahman, we say no; for it is admitted that the locus of ignorance is the individual soul (*jīva*). But was not their identity already stated? True; yet even though there is identity, just as the darkness and other qualities superimposed upon a reflected self (*pratibimba-ātman*) are not seen in the original object (*bimba*), and the pure whiteness of the original object is seen without contradiction, so too there is no contradiction between omniscience and being the locus of ignorance, even though identity exists.

Therefore, oneness is not contradicted by being the locus of ignorance; rather, it establishes ignorance itself. Thus he says: "Certainly, for this very reason. It is precisely because non-manifestation is observed despite the existence of oneness, self-luminosity, and omniscience that obscuring ignorance is postulated. Otherwise, if there were difference, insentience, and limited knowledge, there would be merely a lack of apprehension; consequently, words such as "darkness," "unreal," "mist," "ignorance," and "obscured"—which denote a positive entity (bhāvarūpa) of ignorance that serves as the cause for the superimposition of non-manifestation—would be sublated.

Now, if there is oneness of substance, what is the basis for the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, by virtue of which the distribution of omniscience and the locus of ignorance are established? One person says the difference arises from delimitation by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); another, from transcendence (*atireka*); and yet another, from the very nature of the relationship between part and whole (*aṃśāṃśibhāva*). He refutes all of these [with the words]: "Therefore, it is delimited by beginningless, established ignorance."

Self-obscuration is simply self-ignorance (*ajñāna*), which is the material cause (*upādāna*) for the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, and so forth; therefore, ignorance is the instrumental cause (*nimitta*) for the delimitation (*avaccheda*) of the soul. This is because that delimitation is itself a phenomenal superimposition whose material cause is that very ignorance. Since it is impossible for that which is truly partless to undergo division, and since the beginningless stream of agency, enjoyership, and association with defects has been shown to exist like a seed and its sprout, ignorance—which is their material cause—is also beginningless. Thus he says: "established as beginningless" (*anādisiddha*).

He states that the beginningless stream of superimposition consisting of the division of the individual soul (jīva) has only beginningless ignorance as its cause, and not the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) and so forth: "delimited by ignorance" (avidyāvacchinna).

Nor can the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) serve as the limiting adjunct (*avacchedaka*); for there is no actual fragmentation [of consciousness] by it, since limitation is merely an illusion (*vibhrama*), and ignorance (*ajñāna*) alone is its material cause (*upādāna*). Furthermore, the internal organ is to be dispelled by perfect knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) because it is a superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of ignorance, and because only that which is itself limited by its own cause can possibly function as a limiting adjunct. Even if it were real, being something with a beginning, it could not be produced by beginningless ignorance; moreover, in states such as deep sleep, the internal organ is absent, which would lead to the undesirable consequence of a lack of limitation [of consciousness].

If it is argued that even then the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) remains as a delimiting adjunct (*avacchedaka*) in a subtle state, what is this "subtlety"? Is it the attainment of partlessness? For if a composite entity were to lose its parts, its very nature would be destroyed. Nor is subtlety merely the reduction of parts, for that would entail the consequence that the persisting whole (*avayavin*) is no longer an effect. If it is argued that it persists in the form of its cause, does this mean that only the cause remains, or that the effect also remains? In the former case, there is an absence of the internal organ; in the latter, there is no distinction from its state of persistence.

Therefore, the attainment of subtlety is simply the persistence of the cause in a state characterized by the potentiality for the impressions of its effects. Consequently, there is no internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) that serves as a limiting adjunct (*avacchedaka*). Thus, since the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman is established through the power of the already postulated *avidyā* alone, there is no room for the postulation of anything additional. If it is argued that the statement "the *avidyā* of the individual soul resides in Brahman" implies that *avidyā* itself presupposes a prior distinction, we say no; for the very notion of "excess" (*atireka*)—as in "the excess of one over another"—is perceived as being preceded by a distinction.

Just as the relationship between a substratum (*dharmin*) and its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), although dependent on difference, is colored by that very difference—as in "the difference of this from that"—so too the relationship between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, although dependent on transcendence (*atireka*), is colored within it as "the transcendence of Brahman from the soul. If this is so, the same applies to ignorance (*avidyā*). Since [Brahman] is partless, difference cannot exist through the relation of part and whole. Therefore, ignorance alone is the cause for the superimposition of difference.

Now, to what does ignorance belong to be the cause of the appearance of difference? Is it not like a substance such as a mirror, which belongs to something else to be the cause of the appearance of difference in a reflected image? If you say it belongs to the face alone, then here too, ignorance—which belongs to the nature of consciousness alone—brings about the distinction in the empirical usage of the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman.

But how is it that ignorance, which is related solely to the essential nature [of Brahman], sets aside the essential nature of Brahman and favors exclusively the differentiation of the individual soul (jīva)? We reply: it is like a mirror or a jar, which, acting as the cause for the division of the space within the face and the space of the sky, sets aside both the original face and the space of the sky despite their connection with them, and instead favors the reflected image and the space within the jar.

Now, what could be the locus of this ignorance? It cannot have as its locus the essential nature qualified by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), because there is no evidence for that. But surely the very manifestation "I am ignorant" is the proof for its having a qualified locus. No; for then it would follow that even the consciousness-light of the experience "I am experiencing" must have a qualified locus. But surely, just as in the case of "the iron burns," where the burning property and the iron appear to be connected to each other due to their common connection with a single fire, [so too here]...

If it is argued that, because experience and the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) are related to a single self, there is such an appearance [of the self as the locus of experience], and not because the internal organ is the locus of experience—then it is equally true that the appearance "I am ignorant" arises from the relation of ignorance and the internal organ to a single self, and not from the internal organ's relation to ignorance. This is so because, when a cognition can be established otherwise, it is improper to postulate a mutual relationship [between the two factors], and because the relation of ignorance to the self is admitted even in deep sleep.

If it is argued that, because it is untenable for [ignorance] to have the mere essential nature (*svarūpa*) as its locus, one must therefore postulate a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*) as its locus—this is not so; for even in the case of a qualified entity, the relation of essential identity (*svarūpa-sambandha*) exists. Furthermore, if an insentient object were the locus of ignorance, it would follow that error and right knowledge would also have that [insentient object] as their locus. [Objection: But is not the untenability equally present in the case of Brahman as the essential nature? [Reply: True; however, rather than postulating two loci that are both untenable, it is better to adopt the locus of the essential nature which is already accepted, since [ignorance] is the locus of a relation only insofar as it pertains to the state of liberation.

In this regard, someone might prattle that ignorance belongs to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) alone. He should be asked: "Is the Self omniscient or partially knowing? If it is partially knowing, then by your own admission you have shown that there is a non-comprehension of objects when the Self does not know something at a certain time.

Now, even if non-apprehension (*agrahaṇa*) and false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*) have the self as their locus, it is claimed that ignorance (*ajñāna*) in its positive form has the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) as its locus. Is this [ignorance] something other than knowledge? If it is, then there is no dispute, for cataracts, jaundice, and the like would also be ignorance. If, on the other hand, it is that which obstructs knowledge, we say no; for we do not observe an opposition between knowledge and ignorance when they reside in different loci, even if they share the same object. If it is argued that ignorance residing in the instrument (the internal organ) is opposed by knowledge residing in the agent (the self), we say no; because there is a lack of evidence for such a claim.

Furthermore, even when another person’s deep sleep is inferred through their internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—which, having dissolved, serves as the instrument for that inference—the cessation of ignorance belonging to that person is not observed. If it is argued that ignorance resides in the instrument because it is a defect causing error, like the presence of a cataract (*kāca*) and so forth, we say no; for this would lead to the same contingency regarding the eyes and other sense organs. If it is argued that since those [senses] have a beginning in time (*sādi*), they cannot be the locus of beginningless ignorance (*anādyajñāna*), then the same applies to the internal organ as well.

If it is argued that the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is not beginningless because one relies on the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*), then the same would apply to the eyes and other sense organs; therefore, the internal organ cannot be the locus of that beginningless ignorance (*ajñāna*). Furthermore, since terms such as "unreal" (*anṛta*) and "mist" (*nīhāra*) denote that the obscuration belongs specifically to conscious beings who have attained knowledge but lack its full apprehension, ignorance does not reside in the internal organ, but rather in consciousness (*caitanya*). Enough of this prolixity. This is what he states: "the infinite individual souls delimited by ignorance."

The reasoning has been demonstrated. As for scripture, the text—"There was another [state] distinct from you; you were enveloped by mist"—shows that ignorance is the intervening factor. And as for the Smṛti: "When the ignorance that produces differentiation has gone to absolute destruction, who will create the unreal distinction between the Self and Brahman? Now, one might object: "But there is no entity other than Brahman that is beginningless. To this he says: "And so the Smṛti [states]. The concluding phrase, "Therefore," is clear in its meaning.

It has been stated that it is logically consistent for self-luminous consciousness to be the locus of ignorance; now, the objection is raised that it is not logically consistent for that which is manifest to be the object of ignorance: "But [is there not] non-contradiction with the means of valid cognition? Indeed, in the experience "I do not know the object you have described," it is precisely that which is appearing which manifests as the differentiator of ignorance. Is it not the case that here the unperceived specific form serves as the differentiator? No; for it is impossible for that which does not appear to manifest as a differentiator.

[Objection: But surely, even for that which does not appear, its status as a differentiator [of other things] is untenable. [Reply: No; because the connection with ignorance has as its very essence mere appearance, and thus its "untenability" is actually an ornament [to our position]. Furthermore, appearance certainly exists. In that case, how could there be an untenability of the perceived being the object of avidyā? Thus he raises the objection: "What is the proof for that? The answer is: "Because it is partless. This means non-difference from consciousness, which is to say, the state of being manifested through immediate intuition.

Furthermore, the distinction from the body is non-different from, or dependent upon, the self-luminous light of the Self’s own manifestation, and is thus indeed immediate (*aparokṣa*); nevertheless, the proponent of the established conclusion (*siddhāntin*) refutes [the objection] by stating, "But [it is not so] for the enjoyer," and so forth. The passage beginning with "But [he is] not the enjoyer" has a clear meaning.

The Mīmāṃsaka, considering himself wise, objects: "But how can there be a cognizer? [His view is that] the knowledge of the categories of objects is itself the knowledge of difference; therefore, the very knowledge of the category of the self as "I" is perception even with respect to difference. He refutes this by stating that superimposition through association is the cause for the non-apprehension of difference, as this is observed everywhere: "I am a human being," and so forth.

Having raised the objection that "even though there is a difference [between the two], the co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) perceived through the direct perception of the objects themselves is merely a figurative appearance (*gauṇāvabhāsa*)," he refutes it with the words beginning, "But is it not figurative? etc. The proponent of the figurative view says: "But if [one were to say] 'I... etc. [Objection: "Surely, setting aside the appearance of direct perception, the distinction [between the self and the body] should be grasped by means of scripture (*āgama*) and inference (*anumāna*) alone. [Reply: He says, "No," with the words, "Even in the case of scripture and inference... etc.

One might object: "Since it is false, the appearance of perception is sublated by those very [means of knowledge], just like the appearance of two moons. To this he replies: "Because of its falsity" (*mithyātvāt tasya*). Let it be so in cases where even a perceptual appearance is immediately sublated and its practical efficacy (*vyavahāra*) cut off by inference and other means, even without prior investigation.

Furthermore, where there is no determination of sublation through the consideration of the relative strength or weakness of two cognitions that have entered the path of critical inquiry, one cannot establish the falsity of perception by means of inference and so forth; having this in mind, he says—from the passage beginning with "How then? up to "it is said"—the meaning of which is clear.

Is the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) said to have as its object a self that is distinct from the meaning-referent (*artha*), or is it so from the perspective of appearance (*pratibhāsa*)? If it is from the perspective of the meaning-referent, he says in response: "Even though [it appears] as distinct from the body and so forth. It is precisely the appearance of distinction that, by being opposed to superimposition (*adhyāsa*), brings about the figurative nature (*gauṇatva*) of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

The intention is that it is not merely the object [that is superimposed]. Now, one might object: since a superimposition of another occurs when there is a perception of a general form but a failure to perceive its specific details, how can there be superimposition in the case of the Self, which is perceived in its specific form? To this he says: "For it is seen... Now, one might suspect that the notion of "I" (ahaṃpratyaya) actually appears as having the distinct Self as its object. He raises this doubt with: "But if, on the contrary, absolutely... He refutes this with: "Therefore, if that [Self] exists..."

When the self is apprehended as distinct through the notion of "I" aided by reasoning-based knowledge (*yoktika-jñāna*), then the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is merely figurative; and since that [notion] is likewise previously figurative, he says—intending this—"Then, after the desire to know (*jijñāsā*)."

Even through inquiry (*vicāra*), the notion of "I" (*ahaṃpratyaya*) has not been shown to have as its object a self distinct [from the body]; rather, the notion of "I" always has only one's own nature as its object, whereas the distinction [of the self from the body] is obtained through rational knowledge (*yauktikajñāna*). Therefore, when that [distinction] is not kept in mind, there is superimposition (*adhyāsa*) just as before; thus he refutes [the objection] with the words, "it is not logical. To this, the objection is raised: "In that case too, there is no superimposition. The rebuttal is: "It would contradict experience."

He raises the objection that superimposition occurs because, even though the letter ‘a’ is absent, the short vowel and so forth are not absent—namely, "But surely, [this is] experience... He replies, "That is not so," meaning that when one of two things is absent, since the two are identical, the distinction between them is established as being mutually absent. The objection beginning with "But this is a great [error]" and its refutation are clear.

Furthermore, is it said that superimposition (*adhyāsa*) is contradicted immediately after discrimination (*viveka*) by the mere notion of "I" (*ahaṃpratyaya*), or rather by rational knowledge (*yauktikajñāna*)? It is not by the mere notion of "I," as he states with the words beginning, "For thus, of the notion of 'I'... Now, one might object: previously, even though the notion of "I" had the Self as its object, it was said to have a distinct [empirical] object due to the proximity of rational knowledge; to this he says, "Therefore, even when the object is discriminated through reasoning..."

The sense is that perceptual knowledge does not become possessed of an object greater than its own [original] object simply because of the presence of another cognition. Since the knowledge produced by inquiry is not followed up (ananusaṃdhāna), and even if it were followed up, it would be mediate (parokṣa), it does not differ from its prior state in being a non-mediately perceived superimposition (aparokṣādhyāsa). He concludes this with the words: "Therefore, according to reason."

Now, it may be asked: "In the case of perception, where there is the superimposition of identity between the subject and the act of milking, what proof has been stated for their distinction that sets aside the cognition of identity? It is replied: it has been stated that distinction is established—just as unity is sublated by the perception of two moons—by means of scriptural testimony supported by reasoning, inference, and the notion of "I. Thus, the passage beginning with "of the self-luminous" (svayaṃjyotiṣaḥ) consists of a restatement of the illustration followed by the statement of the point illustrated; its meaning is clear.

Although the Self is self-luminous, because its specific nature is not grasped by ignorance, the portion of the definition—"the appearance of one thing as another"—is demonstrated by stating that the Self possesses the fitness to be the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*). Within the triad of causes, the valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consisting of the consciousness manifesting the non-dual Self and the causal defect consisting of the ignorance residing therein have been established; now, he establishes the residual impression (*saṃskāra*) with the words: "And because of beginninglessness."

One might object: "Surely, one must speak of a single cognition—having as its objects both the superimposed and the substrate—which is produced by the threefold causal complex; in the absence of such [cognition], there can be no superimposition. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Because there is no separate experience of the fruit regarding the enjoyer and the object. The consciousness of the Self itself appears as the conflation of the Self and the non-Self. Although in its essential nature it is unproduced, it is produced in the form colored by the specific object. And because it is an error, the appearance of the conflation of the object and the subject within a single cognition is possible. Thus, superimposition is established as the cognition appearing as the non-Self in the Self, produced by the threefold causal complex.

He states the purport of the commentary beginning with "How, moreover... as follows: "What is this so-called superimposition?"—this is what is asked by the word *kim* (what). Regarding the words *eva* and *api*: the word *eva* should be understood as applying to both [the question and the objection], while *api* should be understood as applying to the objection alone. The meaning of the objection is this: "In all observed cases, the locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of a superimposition is seen to be an object of the same sensory cognition as that which is being superimposed; since that is absent here, superimposition is impossible. In that regard, for two things to appear as merged within a single cognition, their mere appearance together is required.

Thinking that the qualification "manifestation as an object" is untenable, he offers a rebuttal: "In the first place, this [Self] is not absolutely non-objective. Anticipating the objection that the term "our cognition" (*asmat-pratyaya*) refers to a cognition whose object is the Self, he raises the following challenge: "But [how can there be] a subject... The sense of this is that it is logically impossible for a single entity to occupy, at one and the same time, both the position of the agent in a single act of perception and the opposite position of the objective case (*karman*).

"Let it be, then, that its existence [as a whole] is due to its two parts," he says, "no."—"How so? As for that which belongs to the one. In this regard, just as the light of the sun, which spreads everywhere, has a mirror or similar object as the cause for the manifestation of its specific form in the sky, so too, the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which is a luminous substance superimposed upon the Self, serves as the cause for the manifestation and practical usage of the Self's consciousness through conceptualization (*savikalpaka*). He states: "The *ahaṅkāra* is that which is delimited by the notion of 'I' (*asmat-pratyaya*)."

One might object: "If there is superimposition (adhyāsa), then—as in the case of 'this is silver'—a dual appearance must be stated regarding the 'I'. To this he replies: "That [is] 'this' and 'not-this'. Just as in the expression "the iron burns," there is a dual appearance of both fire and iron characterized by the quality of being a burner, so too there is indeed a dual appearance of the Self and the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) characterized by the quality of being a perceiver in the cognition "I perceive. The point is that the substance itself, such as the Self, when colored by its specific activity, appears as qualified by another entity.

He states that its twofold nature is witnessed by all the world—[namely], as the form which is the object of the love of those in suffering; as the form of the witness to the coming and going [of the body] which has been transformed [into various states]; as the form of consciousness (caitanya) that is woven through the objects of ego-sense and so forth; and as the distinct form [expressed] as "I"—thus he says: "witnessed by all the world."

Now, one might object: "The self is the substratum of the cognition of objects; therefore, how can the *ahaṅkāra* (ego-sense), which appears there as the substratum of the cognition 'I know,' be a part of the 'this' (*idamaṃśa*)? Thus he raises the objection: "What is to be said here? To this, the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntin*) challenges the opponent: "How so? [The opponent replies: "In cases such as 'the iron burns,' even though the iron ball is not the agent, its appearance as being included within the category of the substratum of the act of seeing is possible, just like [the appearance of fire]. Thus the proponent challenges the opponent: "How so?"

Just as fire is seen to be the substratum of the act of burning apart from the iron ball [in which it resides], [the author] establishes through the subsequent text that "I alone am the Self," because the act of cognition is not observed to belong to the Self apart from the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra).

In this regard, the Sāṅkhyas infer an ātman as the prototype, [arguing]: "The manifestation of the reflection of the nature of consciousness (cidākāra) within the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), which is insentient by nature, must be preceded by another such prototype, because it is a reflection, like the reflection of a face. Likewise, the Naiyāyikas and Vaiśeṣikas [infer the ātman]: "Desire and the other qualities are specific qualities (viśeṣaguṇa) belonging exclusively to a substance distinct from the gross elements such as earth, because, while not being perceived in those [elements], they are specific qualities due to being perceivable by a single sense organ."

They infer as follows: since the four elements lack the quality of smell [in certain cases], and since space, time, and the mind are devoid of specific qualities (viśeṣaguṇa), by the method of elimination (pariśeṣa), there must be another substance possessing qualities such as desire, which is the Self (ātman). Likewise, the Sautrāntikas postulate that objects are always to be inferred, arguing that the appearance of the reflection of an object's form within cognitions is preceded by the proximity of a corresponding original (bimba), because it is an appearance of something in what is not that thing, just like the appearance of a face or redness in a mirror or crystal.
To them, he says: "The knower, the known, and the act of knowing are indeed immediate (aparokṣa)."

If the Sāṅkhyas and others consider these inferences to be for the purpose of clarifying the self that is already established by perception, then there is no contradiction whatsoever. However, if they would maintain that the self is eternally inferable, then there is a contradiction with its being known as something directly manifest, like any other object.

Even for the Sautrāntika, if the objects themselves were to appear directly in the inferential cognition of the object, let them appear in the perceptual cognition as well; what fault would there be in that? Thus, because the object itself appears in inferential cognition, the reason [adduced by the opponent] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Furthermore, if even in inferential cognition there were no appearance of the object as a prototype (*bimba*), then since the intended thesis—that [the appearance] is preceded by a prototype—would not manifest, inference itself could not arise. Moreover, inference is contradictory to the appearance of an object that is fit for the conventional usage of being "immediate" (*aparokṣa*).

In this regard, the Vijñānavādins (Proponents of Consciousness-only) say that the immediate manifestation (*aparokṣāvabhāsa*) of an object is caused solely by its non-difference from consciousness; he refutes them [with the statement]: "The object of knowledge (*prameya*) is immediate as an action (*karmatvena*)," because of the experience [expressed as] "I see this. Furthermore, immediacy does not manifest merely from non-difference from consciousness, because even external things such as silver are immediately manifested. If it is argued that even that [silver] is consciousness, we say no; for then there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of there being no sublation (*bādha*) of it, just as there is none for the silver [in a dream]. Therefore, the immediacy of an object consists in its being a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) to consciousness without any intervention.

In this regard, those who follow the Vārttikakāra, the Naiyāyikas, and the Vaiśeṣikas postulate that "the self is directly perceived through a perception produced by the conjunction of the self and the mind. However, the Naiyāyikas and Vaiśeṣikas maintain that the cognition (pramiti) regarding the self is direct only through a subsequent cognition caused by the relation of inherence-in-the-conjoined (saṃyuktasamavāya). The followers of the Vārttikakāra hold that the cognition residing in the object of knowledge (prameya) is direct through a subsequent cognition due to the relation of identity-in-the-conjoined (saṃyuktatādātmya). To them, he says: "But the cognizer and the cognition are indeed exclusively direct."

First of all, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish that another cognition produced by the mind has the self as its object. If it is argued that positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) serve as the proof—since the self is perceived when the mind is present and not perceived when it is absent during deep sleep—we say no; for this is otherwise established by the very experience of objects. Since the self is established just like the object through the mere connection with the experience of the object, it is illogical to postulate another cognition regarding the self and then assume positive and negative concomitance for the mind. Therefore, the self is indeed immediate (*aparokṣa*) even without being an object.

Nor can there be directness (*aparokṣatā*) of an experience within the self or its object by virtue of being an object of another cognition through the relation of inherence in what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*); for since perception depends upon a present object, it would follow that two results [the cognition and the experience] would exist simultaneously. Furthermore, if the experience were manifested through a connection with what is conjoined, it would follow that the dimensions, tastes, and so forth residing therein would also become directly manifest by that very same cognition. Moreover, because no separation between the existence of the experience and its manifestation is observed, it is established that the experience is not accessible to another cognition.

Furthermore, the arising of the experience of an object cannot result from an activity of the self; for, being omnipresent, it lacks motion like an axe or similar tools, and because the fruit of transformation—like a jar or the like—must reside in a single locus of action, if consciousness were to reside in the self, it would follow that the object itself possesses sentience. Nor can the self be sentient merely by virtue of possessing the activity of producing that [consciousness].

Otherwise, it would follow that [the cognition] applies to the mind and so forth as well; and if experience were to have an object and a substrate, there would be no manifestation of the relation in the form "this has been known by me," nor would there be an inference of the act of knowing within oneself, because experience would lack a connection with the self. Therefore, neither of the two possesses immediacy by way of being an object.

[Objection: Surely, it is not logical to postulate that both [the self and cognition] are self-luminous; for if only one of them is self-luminous, then the self alone must be self-luminous. [Reply: No, he says: "Valid cognition is experience. Alternatively, some maintain that the fruit of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) consists of avoidance, acquisition, or indifference; regarding this, he says: "Valid cognition is experience. For it is not logical that avoidance and the others—which are mutually exclusive—should be the fruit of the means of knowledge when there exists experience, which is non-exclusive. This is the meaning.

[Objection: Is it not the case that consciousness itself is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), based on the etymological derivation "that by which something is cognized" (*pramīyate anena*), and that very same consciousness, in its nature as the apprehension of the object, is the fruit of the means of valid cognition? This is the view of the followers of the Sugata (Buddhists). [The author] refutes this with the words: "But the means of valid cognition... "But the means of valid cognition," however, according to the Prābhākaras, is the activity of the cognizer (*pramātṛ-vyāpāra*), which is precisely the contact of the fourfold [factors].

[Objection: But surely the two experiences—the self and the non-self—such as "I know this," are established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as distinct from one another. [The author] says "no" to this: "In that regard, 'I know this'..."

An objection is raised: "Surely, whatever appears does so only as an object of cognition; since this is a rule regarding objects, if the Self also appears, it must appear only as an object and not merely as a substratum. Thus he asks: "Is it not the case that this [consciousness] is not caused by the experience of objects?"

Now, since perceptual knowledge is produced by its object, the object must also be said to possess the status of a causal factor (*kāraka*). In that case, how can there be the connection of two contradictory forms—namely, agency and objecthood—for one and the same thing within a single action? Furthermore, since the agent is subordinate (*guṇabhāva*) and the object is primary (*prādhānya*), does this not entail the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of a single entity possessing two inconsistent natures? To this, he replies: "And in that [object], by way of its substantial form (*dravyarūpatvena*)."

In this regard, he offers a rebuttal—stating that "this is not tenable"—on the grounds that since the universal aspect (sāmānyāṃśa) is common to all selves, it cannot logically constitute the selfhood [of any one], and since the particular aspect (viśeṣāṃśa) is partless, there can be no established distinction between agent and object. Furthermore, he says "because of its unchangeability" (apariṇāmitvāt), because it is impossible for a partless entity to simultaneously undergo transformation into two distinct effects.

Furthermore—does the nature of the subject (grāhaka) also have its establishment as an object, or not? If it does not, there follows the consequence of non-establishment, because one does not admit its self-luminosity (*svayaṃprakāśatva*) or its being the locus of consciousness (*saṃvidāśrayatva*). If its establishment is as an object (*karmatayā*), he says regarding that: "And of the object of knowledge" (*prameyasya ca*). Therefore, since the triad [of knower, known, and knowing] is established by the power of consciousness alone, and since the "I" (*aham*) is established as being partial to the locus of consciousness, the "this-portion" (*idamaṃśa*) is not the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*); thus he concludes: "Therefore, the fruit of the cognition of blue and so forth..."

In order to establish that the ego (ahaṃkāra) is distinct from the Self (ātman), and to prove the self-luminosity of the Self, he presents an alternative: "In this regard, you [must consider] this... The meaning is: "Or even that experience. Therein, the position that the Self is of the nature of consciousness (cit-svabhāva) while experience is an insentient manifestation (jaḍa-prakāśa) is untenable; thus he says: "In that case, not first... [Objection: But surely the fruit of valid cognition (pramāṇa-phala), though itself unmanifest, could illuminate the object like the eye and other senses; why then is there no illumination of the universe? [Reply: No.

Because the eye is an illuminator by generating the manifestation of an object, it is distinct from consciousness (*saṃvit*); however, consciousness itself is self-luminous and does not depend on another light for its manifestation. Therefore, being distinct from the eye and other sense organs, experience (*anubhava*) reveals the object while itself appearing like a lamp. Furthermore, the lamp’s light does not illuminate the object merely by generating the experience of that object—like the eye and other organs—but rather as something entirely separate from that generation.

For instance: the state of being illuminated by light, which is well known as the opposite of darkness, is entirely different from the state of being illuminated by knowledge, which is the opposite of ignorance. The former is produced by light without any mediation, but the eye does not produce both; for it is neither ignorance nor light. Therefore, experience, being independent of any other similar illumination, must itself be manifesting in order to serve as the cause for the conventional usage of "manifestation" regarding its object.

Because it serves, without any mediation, as the cause for the practical usage of "illumination" with respect to its object—just like a lamp or light—it is not the case that the eye is illuminated by another illumination of the same genus, as a jar is illuminated by the light of a lamp; for the eye possesses the quality of illumination intrinsically. If it is argued that the eye produces the illumination of the cognition of its object, even so, the lamp is illuminated only by a cognition of a different genus (vijātīya), and thus has no dependence on light of the same genus.

Therefore, just as a lamp that is obstructed remains unilluminated, if experience itself were unilluminated, it would follow that the entire universe would remain unmanifest, just as the light of a lamp [remains unseen when obstructed].

One might object: "Is it not the case that the consciousness of the subject itself manifests both itself and the object by the power of inert experience? To this he replies: "Not so, for the subject is consciousness. In that regard, if experience were held to be the cause of consciousness being colored by the object—just like the transformation of the intellect (*buddhi*) accepted by our opponents—that would be logical. However, it is untenable that the manifestation of the conscious self should be dependent upon inert experience; thus he says: "Therefore, even though its nature is self-luminous consciousness..."

He refutes [the opponent's view] by stating, "Furthermore, by means of the fruit of the instrument of knowledge," [arguing that] even the act of intending (*cetayatikriyā*)—like the fruit of a prior experience—is an insentient result of experience; for even the conscious [self], being like a lamp, would entail an infinite regress of acts of intending. Regarding the second alternative, he says: "Even in the second hypothesis," [pointing out that] if both were of the nature of consciousness, there would be no mutual dependence for their establishment—as in the case of two separate persons—nor would there be any comprehension of the relationship between consciousness and the self.

An objection is raised: "Surely even the cognition of another person, though it possesses the quality of consciousness (*cidguṇa*), is not self-luminous (*svayaṃprakāśa*) to that other person; likewise, the Self, though possessing the quality of consciousness, does not shine forth by itself. To this, he replies: "The reason for this distinction must be stated. [The opponent might argue: "In that case, even experience (*anubhava*) would not be self-luminous, like the cognition of another person. [The author replies: "If you say 'no' because there is no intervening obstruction (*avyavadhāna*), then that same logic applies to the Self as well"—this is the sense. The phrase "furthermore" (*kiñca*) is for the sake of clarity.

"Let it be, then, that the insentient self is established as the locus of self-luminous experience. To this he says, "Not so—even in the third case. This is the meaning: what is called "cognition" must be either a quality, a substance, or an action. If it were an action, its being luminous and its being a fruit would be untenable. Even if it were a substance, among the possible dimensions—atomic, intermediate, or infinite—if it were atomic in dimension, there would be an appearance of only that much even regarding the object.

It might be so; for a jar in contact with only the light of a firefly does not manifest in its entirety. If [the self] were of great dimension, it would follow that the self, as the substratum of that [light], would also manifest everywhere. If it were of medium dimension, it would possess parts and thus be dependent upon those parts. If it were a quality, then since the self itself would be the quality of illumination, the self would be self-luminous like a lamp. Furthermore, that quality is not produced within the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of its own substratum.

Because it possesses the quality of luminosity, and because it is never absent from the self—just like the luminous quality of the sun and other light sources—it follows that the self alone is self-luminous. This is what he states: "Even for one who does not desire it, the self alone is the light of consciousness."

[Objection: Let it be that the result itself, which has a middling dimension, resides in its own parts, while its dependence on the self is like a jar’s dependence on the ground. [Response: No, he says—because there is no such result existing as something distinct from that. The point is this: based on the experience "I have understood," just as one says "it was illuminated by a lamp," the self alone is the light of consciousness; otherwise, there would be the consequence of it being a mere metaphorical expression, like saying "it was illuminated by wood."

He asks [this] in view of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): "How so? Since consciousness is devoid of the appearance of difference and its establishment depends upon experience, it is not the self (*ātman*) in the same way that objects are; therefore, he states that experience is the one, stable self: "If experience were produced by a means of valid cognition... Furthermore, because of the conceptual complexity (*kalpanā-gaurava*) of postulating distinctions between universals and particulars, he states that the self alone is experience: "...and that which is common to all experiences."

He elaborates upon the very emptiness of the appearance of internal difference with the words: "And there is no experience of blue. Now, having raised the objection that at the time the cognition of blue exists, because the cognition of yellow is absent, the [observed] states of existence and destruction imply a difference between the substrata (*dharmi*), he refutes it with the passage beginning: "But [is it not the case that it is] destroyed or not destroyed? etc. If it is argued: "Since the subsequent cognition has arisen due to the presence of its means of production, and since the coexistence of two cognitions is impossible, the preceding cognition must have been destroyed," [the author replies]: No.

He says, "Because of mutual dependence," namely: "And that [means] in the case of being produced. The intention is that it is a simpler hypothesis to assume that the means of proof is the cause for the coloring by the object of a cognition that is already established, rather than assuming that the means of proof is the cause for the arising of a cognition colored by the object.

The Sugatas (Buddhists) postulate that even though there is an internal difference among cognitions, this difference is not perceived without an external adjunct due to extreme similarity, as in the case of a flame; he refutes them with the words, "by this [argument], 'due to extreme similarity'. Furthermore, if difference were accessible through another cognition, then because of extreme similarity, the delusion of non-difference would arise regarding things that are actually different; however, for that which is self-luminous, difference is non-distinct from the luminosity itself, and thus it is logical that its manifestation consists precisely in being manifest. He states this with the words, "for indeed, of the consciousness-luminosity..."

And the phrase "not as in the case of the individual soul" (na ca yathā jīvasya) has a clear meaning. It was stated that even for a full manifestation, there is an obstruction by ignorance due to its being a single entity; however, here he says—referring to the statement "it has been explained there"—that because the complete cause is unobstructed, there ought to be a manifestation of difference. Now, one might argue that consciousness can be inferred to have its manifestation of difference obstructed by similarity, because it is cognizable by a stable manifesting cognition, like a flame; to this he replies: "For it is not a case of inference from general observation" (na hi sāmānyatodṛṣṭam).

The experience of a single, uniform nature across both the prior and subsequent moments, as well as the necessity for difference to be manifested, constitute the arguments based on experience and reasoning. But how can the self’s consciousness, which is eternal, possess the capacity for the experience of objects? To this, he says: "Therefore, it is of the very nature of consciousness."

One might object: "Even though the self-consciousness (*ātmacaitanya*), which is self-luminous, is the experience of objects, it is precisely by taking that experience of objects as its cause that the self becomes the ego (*ahaṅkāra*) through the reflective awareness 'I am' as the subject. To this he replies: "Certainly, for that very reason. The meaning is that the experience of objects is the cause for the reflective awareness in the form of the subject; otherwise, there would be a manifestation of pure consciousness devoid of the distinction between subject and so forth.

"Not so," he replies by demonstrating the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*): "Because even though the Self (*ātman*) is manifest during deep sleep (*suṣupti*), the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) is not manifest. [The opponent objects: "True, it is so. But surely the manifestation of the nature of the seer (*draṣṭṛ-rūpa*), which consists of the mention of 'I', is caused by the experience of objects; how then could it occur in deep sleep, which is devoid of that? Thus he challenges: "How? [The reply is: The manifestation of objects would indeed be caused by the experience of objects; [but the manifestation of the seer is not].

He offers a rebuttal, stating that because [the object] is insentient (*jaḍatvāt*), the reflective awareness of the conscious self (*cidātmaparāmarśa*) cannot have that as its cause: "And as for the connection with blue in the case of consciousness... Now, one might ask: "In deep sleep (*suṣupta*), since the form of the seer (*draṣṭṛrūpa*) is absent, how can there be that reflective awareness 'I'? He says "No" and replies: "In that case, even if indeed... The point is this: the state of being a seer (*draṣṭṛtva*) consists in having a correlative (*sapratiyogirūpa*); if that were the referent of "I," then the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) would be nothing but the non-self (*anātma*).

[The opponent] objects: "Is it not the case that the nature of the seer (*draṣṭṛ*), which is turned away from all else, is precisely the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*), and that this is experienced in deep sleep?"—this he raises with the words "But surely, 'I'... [The author] refutes this: "No; for you have admitted that the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) is nothing but the Self, devoid of any counter-correlate"—this he states with "This is not sound. [The opponent objects: "Surely the true nature itself must be manifested as 'I' precisely through the experience of objects"; [the author] says "No," with "This is not possible."

Consequently, he states—beginning with "And thus, because of the coloring by objects"—that it would follow, contrary to experience in deep sleep, that the ego (ahaṅkāra), whose nature is characterized by objective coloring and the presence of a counter-correlate, is the Self. The meaning is this: since the Self is the essence of all things, it possesses no exclusion from what is external; rather, the appearance of such exclusion arises solely from the coloring of the "I" (aham). The phrase beginning with "It indeed occurs" has a clear meaning.

The meaning is this: just as on the previous day I existed while conceiving the notion "I am," so too, even though there is an absence of a rule regarding memory for what was thus experienced, there would have to be memory in deep sleep as well, because the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) consists merely of the self that is being remembered. He objects that since the manifestation of the ego-sense and so forth—which is of the nature of eternal consciousness—is indestructible, memory produced by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) resulting from it is untenable; [the objection is stated as] "because there is an absence of latent impressions for that which is indestructible. The rebuttal is: "even that of yesterday... and so forth.

[Objection: But how is there recollection of the ego (ahaṅkāra) in the Siddhānta, given that the witnessing consciousness (sākṣicaitanya) which illumines it is eternal? [Reply: It is said: only the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) as delimited by the mental modification (vṛtti) of "I" attains the status of being an object for consciousness; furthermore, the internal organ as delimited by the recollection produced by the latent impression (saṃskāra) of that modification serves as the delimiting factor for the recollection and the experience—thus, the possibility of recollection is established.

[The opponent objects: "But surely, even for the pleasure experienced during deep sleep (*suṣupti*), there is indeed an experience of 'I' (*ahamanubhava*) in that state, because [the pleasure] inclines toward its own substratum and thus involves the manifestation of 'I'. To this he says: "Surely, there is indeed an experience of 'I' in deep sleep. [The opponent asks: "If pleasure was experienced, then because it is an object (*viṣaya*), the manifestation of 'I' there too must be caused solely by the experience of that object. To this he says: "Not [of anything] other than the Self (*ātman*). The passage beginning with "It is true that it exists" has a clear meaning.

One might object: "How can it be assumed that the reflective awareness of happiness (*sukhāvamarśa*), having abandoned its primary status as having actual happiness as its object, is metaphorically designated as having the absence of opposing suffering as its object? For metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) would apply to verbal cognition; however, the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the reflective awareness of happiness does not admit of metaphorical indication. Thus he objects with the word "how" (*katham*). He answers this by stating, "In a dream, for instance," and so forth, on the grounds that since actual happiness is absent, the absence of suffering—which is the indicated object—is universally accepted.

[Objection: "Surely, by the very force of the subsequent reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), one should postulate that the happiness was indeed primary. [Reply: No; he says this: "If, moreover, the sleeper [says] 'I slept happily'... [The word] "specifically" (*viśeṣataḥ*) means "only as colored by a particular object. He states the indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the fact that the object of the reflective awareness is merely the absence of suffering: "The designation (*vyapadeśa*) also... [Objection: "But there is also an indicative mark for the experience of happiness, such as the clarity of the sense organs and so forth. To that he replies: "As for what [is said] regarding the one who has awakened from sleep... The phrase "that is incorrect" (*tadasat*) is clear in its meaning.

The latter two sections, consisting of the objection and its refutation, are clear in meaning. Therefore, even as the experiencer, no recollection of the "I" is observed during deep sleep. Now, it may be argued that there is no rule that one must necessarily remember what has been experienced; this is true. However, it has already been stated that if the Self were remembered, there would necessarily be a recollection of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) in the form of "I," limited to that extent alone.

[Objection: But surely, even though the absence of suffering exists, it cannot be experienced because of the absence of the recollection of its counter-positive (*pratiyogi*); moreover, the experience of the bliss of one's own nature (*svarūpānanda*) is indeed primary. [Reply: Not so; for that bliss too, being veiled by ignorance, would not be capable of manifesting—this is not the case, since the manifestation of the portion of bliss belonging to the unobscured witness-consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*) is logically possible.

If that is so, why does it not manifest during the waking state? It certainly does manifest as happiness characterized by being the object of supreme love; however, due to being distracted by false cognitions—like the light of a lamp tossed by a violent wind—it does not manifest clearly. In deep sleep, however, because of the absence of that distraction, it is manifested more intensely.

[Objection: Surely there exists for one who has arisen [from sleep] a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the absence of suffering; how can that, being unexperienced due to the absence of knowledge of its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), be reflected upon? [Reply: It is said: it is precisely pleasure that was experienced which, when being recollected by one who has arisen, leads—by means of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*)—to the cognition of the absence of its contradictory, suffering. That is to say: "If pleasure was experienced, then suffering did not exist. Therefore, it is not the absence of suffering that is recollected, but rather it is cognized [through inference]. The same applies to the reflective awareness of the absence of knowledge for one who has arisen.
Ignorance, which is the opposite of knowledge, is established by the very fact that its remembrance—based on having been previously experienced—is otherwise impossible; it is not merely remembered.

[Objection: But how can ignorance, which is experienced even during the waking state, be opposed to knowledge? [Reply: No; for ignorance characterized by a particular state is experienced in deep sleep, and its opposition to the knowledge of jars and other objects is observed even during the waking state at the time of perceiving a cloth. [Objection: Since it is not remembered, the absence of knowledge in deep sleep is merely inferred from that non-remembrance. [Reply: No; for even those cognitions that have passed away exist yet are not remembered.

The absence of an elephant in the morning is also cognized now through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) based on the object that is contrary to the elephant, which is being recollected; it is not established merely from the non-arising of a memory regarding the elephant, because that would be inconclusive (*vyabhicāritva*). Therefore, it should be understood that the absence of knowledge and the absence of suffering are to be known through the impossibility of the experience of specific ignorance and pleasure.

[Objection: But surely, if there is an absence of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) for ignorance, pleasure, experience, and the imperishable witness-consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*), how could one who has awakened have the recollection of these three?
