[Reply: It is said: because the experience of the conceptualization of ignorance, pleasure, and the witness consists in the arising of the reflection of consciousness (*caitanyābhāsa*) which has ignorance as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), and because those reflections of consciousness are distinct due to the different states of ignorance, it is possible that the recollection—born from the impression of their destruction—has the very form of ignorance, pleasure, and witness-consciousness, and is based on the Self as qualified by ignorance, rather than being based on the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

"Since the experience of the bliss of ignorance is possible even in deep sleep in every respect, what has been stated by the author of the commentary is irrelevant"; this is true, but there is no fault, for this was stated relying on the view of another school (paramata), not his own view. He concludes the previously stated self-luminosity and the distinction from the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) with the words: "Thus, this [self] is not [the object] of cognitions such as 'blue'."

This is also for the purpose of indicating the distinction from the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra); since the ego-sense is distinct from the Self, he says—"therefore, for those who know Brahman"—to show that the statement in the Commentary is justified as being rooted in scripture.

And what is that scripture? Having declared the all-pervasiveness of the Brahman called *bhūman* in the passage, "That alone is below, that alone is above," and having stated its all-pervasiveness even in relation to the *ahaṅkāra* (the principle of ego) in the passage, "Now, therefore, the instruction regarding the *ahaṅkāra*," [the text] then speaks of the Self as distinct from the *ahaṅkāra* in the passage, "Now, therefore, the instruction regarding the Self."

[The opponent] points out: "Is it not the case that just as the designation of the identity (*sārvātmya*) between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman is for the purpose of establishing their oneness (*ekatva*), so too might the designation of the ego (*ahaṅkāra*) be for the purpose of establishing its oneness with the Self? No, that is not so—because it is impossible for two things to possess universal identity. In that regard, it is appropriate that the instruction [of identity] between the individual soul and Brahman, which are perceived as distinct, is for the purpose of establishing their oneness; however, since the oneness of the ego with the Self has already been established previously, its separate instruction is understood to be for the purpose of establishing its distinction."

The meaning is that, having taught the nature of the "I" (aham) as the Self in order to establish the perceptibility of Brahman which is otherwise beyond perception, [the text] then teaches the primary nature of the Self by setting aside that [notion of the "I"]. Furthermore, there is the Smṛti text: "The great elements and the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra)."

When it is asked: "In that case, what is the material cause (*upādāna*) of this ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), what is its instrumental cause (*nimitta*), what is its essential nature (*svarūpa*), what is its means of proof (*pramāṇa*), what is its effect (*kārya*), and why does it not appear during deep sleep (*suṣupta*)?"—the following is the response, beginning with "That which is this... and so forth. The phrase "that which is this" and so on is the mention of the material cause. "Ignorance, karma, and prior cognition" means the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of error, action, and previous experience. "Of that" is the indication of the instrumental cause. "The substratum of the two powers of cognition and action" shows its essential nature.

The phrase "agency and enjoyership" is a demonstration of the effects [of ignorance]. The phrase "immutable consciousness" is the presentation of the means of knowledge [for its existence]. The phrase "due to its intermingling with which," etc., states another effect: that it is the cause for the superimposition of all those [attributes] upon the Self. To the question, "Why then would it not exist in deep sleep?", he says: "And that [ignorance] exists in deep sleep. The meaning is that deep sleep is indeed the dissolution of the subtle body, which is the effect of ignorance.

Now, an objection is raised: if the vital breath (*prāṇa*), whose nature is action, exists, how can there be the dissolution of the power of action belonging to the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*)? It is replied: it is not said that the vital breath consists of the ego-sense alone; rather, it is merely stated that the power of action belongs to the ego-sense, which exists as a distinct entity and is the cause of the fivefold functions of the breath. This is because the activity of the vital breath is observed to be dependent upon the mind. Alternatively, one may conceive of the dissolution of the aspect of the power of cognition (*vijñāna-śakti*), while leaving aside the aspect of the power of action characterized by the vital breath; for the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) possesses constituent parts.

Alternatively, by relying on the doctrine of "creation upon perception" (*dṛṣṭisṛṣṭi*), as in the case of dreams and so forth, or with the intention of referring to the perspective of a person in deep sleep, the dissolution of everything therein is shown; for the perception of the vital breath, body, and so forth by another person [waking from sleep] is merely an illusion.

In this regard, the Sāṅkhyas maintain: if it were accepted that the unconscious entity denoted by terms such as *māyā* is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and so forth, then that would be the *pradhāna*—existing independently and not included within the Witness (*sākṣin*) who appears as the "I" (either as His power, His substratum, or His locus)—which undergoes a threefold transformation through the distinctions of qualities (*dharma*), characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and states (*avasthā*). Among these, "transformation of qualities" (*dharmapariṇāma*) refers to its abiding in the form of all effects, beginning with the Great Principle (*mahat*).

Furthermore, the transformation of characteristics (*lakṣaṇapariṇāma*) is the attainment of the forms of past, future, and present characteristics by that very same dharma. For instance: an effect, having attained the future characteristic, abandons that and attains the present characteristic; then, abandoning that, it attains the past characteristic; and again, that very same [dharma] attains the future characteristic once more.

As for the transformation of state (*avasthā-pariṇāma*), it consists in that very [consciousness] assuming states such as being past, more past, most past, future, more future, or most future—namely, the attainment of states such as being new or old. Therefore, there is no need for a conscious entity as the material cause (*upādāna*). To this he says: "And it should not be thought thus. Why? He explains: "Because, in that case, there would be no contact with the 'I-maker' (*ahaṅkṛti*). That in which the act of making "I" (*aham iti kṛtiḥ*) occurs is the witness, the "I-maker."

This is the intended meaning: it has been stated that the appearance of the non-distinction between consciousness and the non-self is neither *akhyāti* (non-apprehension), nor *anyathākhyāti* (misapprehension as something else), nor *ātmakhyāti* (the appearance of the self). Now, if one does not accept *anirvacanīyakhyāti*—characterized by the appearance of the non-distinction between consciousness and false objects manifested through its own ignorance—then there would only be an appearance of consciousness and the non-conscious as absolutely distinct from one another, and never an appearance of their non-distinction.

On this point, the Naiyāyikas maintain: since cognition arises only occasionally even when the self, the sense organs, and their objects are in proximity, one must postulate a "mind" (*manas*) as an instrument that brings about the successive production of mental states such as knowledge, which reside in the self.

In that regard, apart from that [Self], we do not perceive anything called the "internal organ" (antaḥkaraṇa)—which would serve as the substratum for the functions of cognition and action such as knowledge, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort—acting as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) that superimposes non-selfhood upon the Self, just as a mass of iron is to fire, a mirror to a face, or a vessel of water to the moon. If it is argued that this is the "intellect" (*buddhi*), we say no; for the aphorism of Akṣapāda states: "Intellect, apprehension, and knowledge are synonymous."

If it is argued that the intellect knows while the self perceives, we say no; for this would entail a difference in the substrata (dharmin) corresponding to the distinct meanings of the verbal roots [√jñā and √labh]. Therefore, the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) as previously described does not exist; to this, he replies: "And that is a specific modification (pariṇāmaviśeṣa)."

This is the intended meaning: according to the Śruti passage, "By the quality of the intellect and by the quality of the Self, even that which is minute is seen as the size of the tip of an awl," the intellect (buddhi) is understood to be a substance (dravya) because it possesses the quality of transformation (pariṇāma). Likewise: "When the five [sensory] cognitions together with the mind dissolve, and the intellect no longer wavers, there one attains the Supreme Self."

Thus, in the Śruti, intelligence (*buddhi*) is understood to be a substance (*dravya*) by virtue of being the locus of activity (*ceṣṭā*). Likewise, because the Self consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya ātman*) is mentioned separately in the passage, "Consciousness (*vijñāna*) performs the sacrifice," and since "consciousness" and "intelligence" are not different in meaning, intelligence is understood to be a substance by virtue of being the locus of action.

Similarly, from the passages, "By means of consciousness one knows the Ṛgveda" and "For one sees only with the mind (*manas*)," since consciousness and mind fall under the same category of instruments (*karaṇa*) and are identical, and since the mind is heard to possess modifications (*vṛtti*) such as desire and volition, [it follows that it is a substance].

The internal organ (*antahkarana*), which possesses the power of the activity of cognition and is denoted by terms such as *manas* and so forth, is well-established through scriptural authority (*shruti*) and indicative marks (*linga*). Likewise, in such scriptural passages as "By the quality of the intellect and by the quality of the Self," "Becoming one who possesses intelligence, he wanders through this world as a dreamer," and "Consisting of consciousness, consisting of mind," it is understood that [the internal organ] acts as the delimiting factor of the Self and serves as the cause for the attribution of its own qualities and for the Self's movement to and fro.

Likewise, in the Śruti passage, "Upon whose departure shall I depart?", it is understood that even the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which serves as an adjunct (*upādhi*) for the acts of departing and so forth, is a part of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), because two adjuncts cannot coexist simultaneously. Consequently, the internal organ described above is established by both Śruti and indicative marks (*liṅga*). Now, it may be argued that indicative marks found in explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) require logical reasoning (*nyāya*). This is true; however, the very impossibility of movement, limitation, and the like for that which is partless, all-pervading, and unattached—like space (*ākāśa*) when devoid of adjuncts—is itself the required reasoning. Enough of this digression.

[Objection: "Could it not be that the powers of transformation into cognition and action belong to the Self itself? [Reply: No, because transformation is impossible for that which is partless, all-pervading, and unattached; furthermore, since the appearance is otherwise accounted for by its proximity to the transforming internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), [the author] states this with an illustration: "Therefore, it is caused by the coloring of the internal organ. The point is that the redness of the crystal is false, because there is no cause for either the established perception or the existence [of such a quality]. He establishes the absence of both [perception and existence] with the subsequent text.

In this regard, the proponent of the theory of non-apprehension (akhyātivādin) objects: "It is not a false redness residing in the crystal that appears; rather, it is the redness residing in the hibiscus flower itself which, while being perceived, appears as if undifferentiated from the crystal. He raises this objection with the words: "But how [could it appear] in the crystal? To this he replies: "This is not so," beginning with the words: "If [the rays] are reflected by the crystal..."

[Objection: "But surely, due to the power of a defect, there is no apprehension of the configuration because of the absence of contact with the flower. [Reply: He says "no"—"for it does not consist of color alone. The point is that when a quality is perceived through *saṃyuktasamavāya* (inherence in what is conjoined) or *saṃyoga* (conjunction), the substance itself is also conjoined. Otherwise, the proponent of *anyathākhyāti* (the theory of misapprehension) claims that it is color alone which, being reflected, appears as having the nature of a crystal; he refutes this by saying "nor does it belong to its own substratum."

He raises an objection: "In that case, the redness in the region of the crystal is indeed a real substance, either undifferentiated from the crystal itself or perceived as such"—this is expressed in the words, "But surely, as in the case of one who is well-born... Even so, he states that under the theory of *anyathākhyāti* (misapprehension), the relation [between the redness and the crystal] is false, saying: "Nevertheless, it is not red in itself..."

He presents the view of the proponent of non-apprehension (*akhyātivādin*)—namely, that it is the light itself that is red. To this he replies: "In that case, upon the perception of the crystal, there would also be the perception of its color, because of the completeness of the causal factor of inherence-in-the-conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*), or because of an unobstructed conjunction. He says: "In that case, whiteness too [would be perceived]. He raises an objection: "The opposing light has either removed the opposing quality or acted as an obstacle to it. He states the fault in such removal: "In that case, it (the crystal) would be colorless."

The obstruction is the same even for a substance; the meaning is that it is equal due to the presence of a contrary quality by way of its qualities. Anticipating the objection that "even a substance devoid of color might become visible through conjunction with the light of a colored object," he says: "And not from conjunction with a colored object. [Objection: "In that case, since redness has arisen after removing the whiteness, the crystal is visible because it possesses color. To this he says: "Not on account of the light. Having provisionally accepted the existence of light, etc., the rest is clear in meaning.
And then he says that the superimposition of agency and so forth upon the Self is caused by the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) which has been colored [by objects]: "Thus, in this way..."

Now, is it merely that the attributes of the ego (ahaṅkāra) are superimposed upon the Self, or does another false attribute actually arise? If the former, this example would not apply, and there would be the contingency of *anyathākhyāti* (misapprehension). If the latter, there would be the appearance of two agents—a real one and a false one. It is replied: since the ego, together with its own attributes, is superimposed upon the Self and is therefore false, the contingency of *anyathākhyāti* does not arise; for the appearance of a false attribute in one thing due to the proximity of another is precisely what constitutes [the nature of such an illusion].

This is the illustration. Alternatively, even though there are two types of agency, there is no contradiction because the appearance of a distinction between attributes arises from the identity of the two substrates (the self and the ego). Now, one might object: in passages such as "The knot of the heart is rent asunder," the "knot of the heart" is understood to be a cause of misfortune within the Self; how then can it be said to belong to the ego? To this he replies: "Because it consists of both [aspects] merged together. Furthermore, one might argue that the Self would not manifest the ego and its attributes as colored upon itself, because they are equally "colored" [by the Self], just like a crystal and so forth; to this he replies: "Because in that case [the ego] is insentient by nature."

The meaning is that insentience (*jāḍya*) and sentience (*caitanya*) are the causes for non-manifestation and manifestation respectively, not being colored (*uparakta*) or not being colored. Now, one might object: since the sentient [Self] is also devoid of the activity of cognition regarding an object that has colored it, it would be no different from the insentient. To this he says: "But of that which is of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*)," and so on. The point is that the very contact with consciousness without any intervention is the cause of manifestation, not the activity of cognition.

Now, one might object: "If the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) is established as being like the nature of the witness (sākṣin), without the intervention of the activity of cognition (vijñāna-kriyā), how can it possess the character of the 'this-portion' (idamaṃśatā)? To this he says: "By way of its definition" (*tena lakṣaṇataḥ*). This means "by way of the nature of the object" (*arthasvabhāvataḥ*). The meaning is: by its very nature, the state of being the essence of consciousness (*citsvarūpatā*) is the non-"this-portion," while the state of being the object of consciousness (*caitanyakarmatā*) is the "this-portion"; it is not due to the intervention of the activity of cognition. Furthermore, as for how it possesses the "this-portion" from the standpoint of empirical usage (*vyavahāra*), he says: "But from the standpoint of empirical usage" (*vyavahārataḥ punar*).

"Due to the coloring by which" means due to the coloring by that *ahaṅkāra*. "Of that Self" means of that [Self] which has attained the nature of the *ahaṅkāra* (the state of being the *ahaṅkāra*). "By its activity" means by the activity of the *ahaṅkāra*. The sense is that the manifestation as "this" (*idam*) of the body, senses, and objects is established precisely through the mediation of the mental modification (*vṛtti*), whereas their non-manifestation as "this" is established precisely through the absence of such mediation.

[Objection: But surely the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) is separated by ignorance (ajñāna); how then, in the absence of such separation, could there be an absence of the manifestation as "this" (idantā)? To this he says: "Therefore, [it is] 'I'. That is to say, precisely because of the non-manifestation as "this"—meaning, because of the separation consisting of mere ignorance. [Objection: But if it is "you" (yuṣmad-artha) in its actual sense, then the absence of such a manifestation is not logical. To this he says: "And it is observed according to its definition."

[Objection: "But surely, even upon that reflection, the conventional usage of 'made of clay' does not arise; whereas here, upon reflection, the status of being the object denoted by *yuṣmad* (the second person) is conventionally employed. Therefore, this is not a valid example. To this he says: "But those of cultivated intellect... For this very reason, the passage beginning with "having observed most skillfully" is clear in its meaning.

If the superimposition of the non-self upon the self is established by the example of the crystal alone, then there would be no need for the examples of the mirror, water, and so forth, as prescribed in the Vedānta; to this he replies: "As for [the statement], 'moreover, in the case of mirrors, water, etc. Now, since the reflection is perceived as a distinct entity from the original object due to its facing inward and the appearance of difference, how can it be said that "it is that very same thing" without a means of valid knowledge for their identity? He raises this objection: "But how, again, is it that very same thing?"

He offers the rebuttal: "Because of the recognition of the individual," meaning "because of the comprehension of its being a single unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*). Now, one might ask: how can the appearance of difference in direct perception (*abhijñā*) be sublated by recognition (*pratyabhijñā*)? To this he says: "Not if it were a different entity. Now, when there is a doubt as to which of the two appearances—of unity or difference residing in the individual—is sublated by which, he states that the difference of the individual is what is sublated because it lacks any supporting evidence: "Furthermore, [it would follow] from the fact that it is a different entity."

It must be said that the very parts of the mirror have transformed into the form of another individual [the reflection], because otherwise there would be no means for the production of the individual [reflection]; this is the intended meaning. Now, one might object: "This is a counter-seal (pratimudrā) marked by the face, not a transformation (pariṇāma). To this he says "no," for "they possess contradictory dimensions. Let it be then a transformation; to this he says "no," for "if that were so... One might object: "It is indeed always seen. It is not so; for when the mirror is viewed from the side, the previously produced face is not seen.

[Objection: But surely, even when the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) ceases, the effect also ceases; for example, according to the Vaiśeṣikas, when enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) is destroyed, duality (*dvitva*) and so forth are destroyed, and when the conjunction with the hand ceases, the unfolding of the mat ceases. [Reply: No, he says—“Indeed, it is not [destroyed] when coiled up. In all cases, such as molten copper in contact with fire, the destruction of the prior effect occurs precisely through the arising of a contrary effect by means of a complete set of causes (*puṣkalakāraṇa*); and the system of the Vaiśeṣikas is merely a formalism, because that duality and so forth exist simultaneously with the object. This is the sense.

[Objection: But surely the destruction of the previous effect occurs due to the arising of another effect produced by the latent impression (*saṃskāra*), and not from the removal of the instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*). To this, he says: "And thus, as long as... [and so on]. The sense is that if the disappearance of the expansion were due merely to the removal of the instrumental cause, then in the absence of the latent impression, it would contract. If it is argued that here too, the disappearance of the reflection occurs when a contrary effect arises through the force of the latent impression of the previous configuration persisting for a long time, we say: no.

He says, "In this way, for a long time," because it is observed that even when the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of the transformation of the face has persisted for a long duration, the reflection disappears simply upon the removal of the original object (*bimba*). This occurs as soon as the mirror alone has arisen.

[Objection: But surely, even when there is an accumulation of impressions (*saṃskāra*) for the transformation of expansion that has persisted for a long time, just as we observe the cessation of expansion upon the disappearance of the sun's rays, so too the cessation of a reflection that has persisted for a long time should occur upon the disappearance of the original object (*bimba*). [Reply: No; he says: "But as for that of the lotus bud... [Objection: But in that case too, the cause of cessation is simply the removal of the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*), not the bud-state produced by the earthen and other constituent parts. [Reply: To this he says: "Upon its cessation..."

[Objection: "In that case, one should postulate that even in the mirror there is a cause for the transformation into an effect that is the reverse of the face. [Reply: No; he says, "But not in the mirror," because the arising of the surface of the mirror depends upon the work of an artisan—this is the sense. Furthermore, even when the object (the face) is present, one observes that great effort such as heating and cutting is required to make the substance of the mirror assume the form of the face; moreover, [the reflection] is not within the range of touch. And as an additional argument: if there were an intervention by parts [of the face], it would not be visible to the eye either.

In this regard, the formal argument is as follows: there is no other distinct manifestation of the face in a mirror and the like, because it lacks the causes for its production; it is like a horn on the head of a hare.

"In that case, since falsity is established just as it is with silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, there can be no oneness of the face"—this objection is raised, to which [the author] replies here. [The opponent objects: "But surely oneness is understood through recognition. [The author] says "no": "as in the case of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell. The meaning is that even in the case of false silver, recognition is observed, namely: "This is my very own silver. He states the answer: "Not so; for in that case..."

In that case, in the cognition "this is not silver," the very nature of the silver is sublated; however, in the cognition "there is no silver here, but this is that very silver," there is a sublation of the location alone, and thus it is not recognized as being identical with real silver. Therefore, the meaning is that because the recognition of the silver is sublated, the [subsequent] recognition is an error. But here, in the case of "this is not a face," it is not sublated in its essential nature; rather, it is recognized as "there is no face here, but it is indeed my own."

And that [cognition] is not sublated; furthermore, if it were a different individual [face], there would be no sublation such as "there is no face here"—this is the meaning. As for the phrase "but he who," its meaning is clear. Now, an objection: since the parts of one's own face are not visible to the eye, how can there be perceptual recognition? [Reply: Even from the perception of only a few parts, the visibility of the whole (avayavin) is established, just as in common worldly experience.

[The opponent] objects: "The sentence *tat tvam asi* (That thou art) must be intended to sublate the meaning of the term *tvam* (thou), because liberation is impossible without the destruction of the transmigrating self; therefore, this is not a valid example. [The author] refutes this: "Not so," [arguing that] the sentence "That is this Devadatta" is intended to convey identity (*tādātmya*), not the sublation of the other's meaning. Furthermore, the phrase "even scriptural" is clear in its sense. [In the case of the reflection], the sun's being situated in the water is merely utilized as a basis for meditation, but [the sun] does not actually reside in the water.

The proponent of the theory of non-apprehension (akhyātivādin) maintains that what is called a reflection does not appear as something distinct from the original object (bimba) residing within the mirror; rather, it is the original object itself that appears as undifferentiated from the mirror. He restates this view with the words: "But he who thinks... and so forth.

He says that one cannot be considered authoritative if one were to claim: "The face as it is actually perceived—appearing clearly facing west, as if entered into another mirror, as if being observed by another person—does not appear in that way [in the original face]. He states: "Experience itself [refutes such a claim]."

One might object: "Is it not the case that nowhere in the world is a material substance ever seen to exist simultaneously in two places in its entirety? Thus he asks: "But how [can it be] limited? He replies: "We do not [say so]," meaning that a single face, though situated in one place, appears as if divided and situated in different places due to a state of confusion. But what is this entity characterized by division and location in different places within a single thing situated in one place? To this he says: "But the separation... [etc.]
Now, one might ask: "How can even an illusion appear in contradiction with the means of valid cognition? To this, he says: "For [it is not so] in the case of an illusion."

[Objection: But how can the appearance of separation be a manifestation of ignorance (*avidyā*), given that even a tree with its top facing upward is clearly perceived in water as having its top facing downward, and yet there is no ignorance in that case? [Reply: It is said: it has already been stated that ignorance, which consists in the veiling of the object, is not the cause of superimposition (*adhyāsa*). In those cases of error caused by limiting adjuncts (*aupādhika-bhrama*), the adjunct itself is the sufficient cause for the transformation of the Self’s ignorance. Furthermore, it should be understood that in the case of errors involving limiting adjuncts, the knowledge of the true nature of the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) does not oppose the superimposition; rather, this applies only to errors that are without limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhika-bhrama*).

One might object: "If the superimposition of difference, agency, and so forth is an error conditioned by an adjunct (sopādhika-bhrama), then its cessation would not occur through the knowledge of reality, but rather only through the cessation of the adjunct itself. To this, he raises the objection: "But surely, even while the oneness of the image remains unapprehended..."

To avoid the fault already raised, he first dispels another objection: "If the individual soul (*jīva*) is a reflection, it is not capable of comprehending the nature of the original object (*bimba*), because it is a reflection, like the reflection of Devadatta in the pupil of an eye. He refutes this as follows: "Of the non-conscious portion of Devadatta. The point is that the lack of comprehension there is caused by the lack of consciousness, not by the fact of being a reflection; for such is observed in the case of jars and other objects.

Now, the Lokāyata school maintains that the body itself is sentient; to this, he replies: "Of the sentient portion alone. This means [the reflection is not sentient] because it is obstructed by the dullness of the mirror, or by its own inherent dullness. He states another reason for the insentience of Devadatta’s reflection: "And so is the experience. The implication is that if it were ever sentient, it would act independently, even without the movement of the original person.

[Objection: "Is it not observed that Devadatta alone, who is the original object (*bimba*), is the locus of the true knowledge that removes the error? Likewise, because it is the original object (*bimba*), Brahman alone should be the locus of the true knowledge that dispels the error. [Reply: No; he says: "For whose there is delusion... The point is this: being the locus of true knowledge is not caused by being the original object (*bimba*), but rather by being subject to delusion; that, too, is caused by ignorance (*ajñatva*); and that, in turn, has its cause in being a *jīva*.

Now, does Brahman know itself to have the nature of a reflection characterized by the individual soul (jīva), or not? If it does not, its omniscience is lost; if it does know it, then Brahman would perceive saṃsāra within its own self. To this he says "no"—referring to the case of Devadatta who knows [himself].

For Devadatta, although he perceives his own self as possessing qualities such as smallness within the eye-socket, does not grieve because he is obstructed by the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*); likewise, Brahmā also, though seeing transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) in the individual soul (*jīva*) which is his reflection, does not grieve due to his possession of the knowledge of reality. The sense is that the knowledge of reality and transmigratory existence do not remain fixed in one another, just as fairness and darkness do not remain fixed in each other.

[Objection: "But even when unity is understood, the delusion of separation does not cease there. [Reply: True, that is not caused by the state of being a reflection; rather, it is caused by the fact that it cannot be removed by knowledge because its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is not produced by ignorance. Thus he says: "Nor [is it removed] by mere knowledge alone. [Objection: "In that case, since the individual soul (*jīva*) too can be affected by the insentience of its limiting adjunct, it cannot be the locus of either error or right knowledge; and if it were such a locus, it would follow that it is not a reflection. [Reply: No, he says: "The individual soul, however..."

Because the status of the individual soul (*jīva*) as a reflection is demonstrated by Śruti, Smṛti, and Sūtra—such as "He became a counterpart to every form," "He is seen as one and also as many, like the moon in water," and "For this very reason, there is a comparison such as the reflection of the sun and so forth"—and because a reflection of the formless Brahman is possible just as the formless sky, along with its clouds and stars, is reflected in water, since even in water that is only knee-deep, the distant and vast sky is perceived, [there is] the space within the water...

The point is that since it is impossible to say that [the sky] is seen as being joined with reflections such as clouds and so forth, its state of being a reflection and its nature as consciousness—which are established both by scripture and by direct perception—cannot be refuted.

Now, one might object: "Could the individual soul (jīva) not be like the space within a jar, delimited by limiting adjuncts (upādhi)?"—No, it cannot be so. For, since the Brahman residing within the cosmic egg (aṇḍa) would be delimited in its entirety as the individual soul by the limiting adjuncts—both general and particular—it would follow that the undelimited Brahman exists only outside the egg. In that case, Brahman’s omnipresence, its status as the controller of all, and other such attributes would not belong to it; for it is impossible for the undelimited to exist doubly (i.e., both inside and outside) within delimited regions.

If it is argued that all this is said with respect to its own nature (*svarūpa*) and not with respect to Brahman existing externally—no; for in passages such as "He who dwells in consciousness," we hear of Brahman, who is distinct from the individual soul (*jīva*), abiding within a modification by virtue of its proximity to the individual soul.

In the case of the reflection theory (*pratibimbapakṣa*), however, since the space of the reflection is observed precisely where the natural space exists within the water, its occurrence as a doubling in one and the same place is logically established; thus, even for Brahman, its abiding in the delimited states of the individual souls (*jīva*) in the form of a controller and so forth is justified. Therefore, the reflection theory alone is superior. Furthermore, he states that the status of being the locus of the knowledge of the truth of falsity is directly perceived therein: "And that [is] the state of being the agent of the ego" (*sa cāhaṃkartṛtvam*). The meaning is that even the nature of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) appears only through delusion.
Therefore, because the limiting adjuncts cease through the knowledge of reality, their separation and disappearance occur; thus, he says: "Hence, it is logical."

But has it not been stated previously that ignorance (*ajñāna*) is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) for the delimitation of the individual soul (*jīva*); how then can the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) be designated as its limiting adjunct? This is not a fault, because the diversity of empirical usage arises from the degree of diversity in the limiting factors of consciousness. To explain: the pure, non-conceptual consciousness, which is of a single flavor, becomes the basis for slightly conceptual empirical usage due to its connection with ignorance, as occurs in deep sleep (*suṣupti*).

Then, through the delimitation by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) which has that [subtle body] as its material cause, that very same [Self] becomes the substratum for the most gross empirical usage in a dream; furthermore, through the coloring by the gross body conjoined with the internal organ, it becomes even more gross in the waking state. Nor does the difference in limiting adjuncts entail a plurality of individual souls (*jīva*); for it is precisely that which was delimited by each preceding adjunct that is delimited by each subsequent one. Indeed, a plurality of souls would occur only if there were a difference in independent limiting adjuncts.

Now, it might be argued that ignorance (*ajñāna*), colored by the impressions of the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*) together with its subtle form which serves as the material cause of the gross body, cannot delimit the individual soul (*jīva*) during deep sleep; for in that state there is an absence of error, and because the definition of such a division [of consciousness] requires error.

Now, if this distinction is postulated as residing in the object itself, independent of erroneous cognition, then, since that distinction is an effect, it would be absent during deep sleep, dissolution, and so forth; consequently, there would be a confusion of ignorance and the like within Brahman itself. Alternatively, if the distinction were not an effect, its beginninglessness would mean it could not have ignorance as its cause. To this it is replied: in order to avoid the confusion of ignorance and the like within Brahman, it is postulated that the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman exists even during deep sleep and other such states.

[Objection: In that case, the distinction belongs only to the objects and not to the delusion. [Reply: True; however, apart from the distinctions existing in states such as deep sleep, the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman is said to have ignorance (*avidyā*) as its material cause (*upādāna*) because it consists solely of delusion. [Objection: Then the distinction belonging to the objects cannot have ignorance as its material cause, since it is beginningless and is not a delusion. [Reply: True; nevertheless, we maintain that even though it is beginningless, this distinction is dependent upon ignorance. For example, the relation of the Self to ignorance is dependent upon ignorance, yet it does not have ignorance as its material cause.

Since it is impossible for ignorance to exist independently prior to the production of its relation [to the Self], and because the relation between the Self and ignorance is beginningless, ignorance cannot be the material cause [of that relation].

[Objection: But how can the distinction based on the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman be dependent upon ignorance (*avidyā*)? [Reply: It is said: Consciousness (*caitanya*), as qualified by beginningless ignorance, is the locus of the beginningless, conceptual distinction in the form of the beginningless state of being an individual soul, but not in its own nature (*svarūpa*), because that [consciousness] is one. Therefore, the distinction whose locus is the qualified [consciousness], while appearing even in the essential nature, is "qualified" by the ignorance that constitutes its qualification; thus, the distinction is said to be produced by ignorance.

Furthermore, for those things dependent on ignorance (*avidyā*), their indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatva*) and beginninglessness (*anāditva*) are not contradictory, just as is the case with the relationship to ignorance itself. In the world, it is observed that it is only the face and the space as qualified by a mirror or a jar respectively that appear to have a false distinction, and not in their own essential nature (*svarūpa*); thus, the distinction is said to be dependent on limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Therefore, since the individual soul (*jīva*) is merely a division produced by being a reflection in beginningless ignorance, there is no contradiction in all things—such as the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) and so forth—which arise from that [ignorance], being considered limiting adjuncts in relation to the gross reflection, even though they are themselves reflections.

Here, the proponent of universal confusion (*sarvasaṅkaravādī*) prattles on, claiming that because he accepts the unreality of the reflection, the individual soul (*jīva*) cannot be a reflection. To this we reply: in the reflections of both the face and the nature of consciousness (*cit*), unreality is not admitted. Even if one accepts the unreality of distinctions, errors, and so forth, there is no injury whatsoever to the face or to consciousness. Furthermore, we establish the status of the face and consciousness as being the original prototypes (*bimba*) by means of the exclusion of their illusory portions. Bondage and liberation do not belong to the illusory portion, but rather to the essential nature itself.

Even with respect to that which resides in its own essential nature (svarūpa), a distinction of limiting adjuncts (upādhi) has been shown in order to avoid confusion. Therefore, this delusion of the proponent of universal confusion is merely a product of ignorance regarding the opposing school's tenets; for [the opponent] admits that [the distinction] is not a real entity (avastutva).

The distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, as well as the superimposition of the non-Self (*anātma-adhyāsa*), are established by means of two examples based on the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*). When it is asked what purpose the example of the rope-snake (*rajju-sarpa*), prescribed in the Vedānta, serves in that context, he states that its purpose is the removal of another doubt: "But there, for one who is deluded... The meaning is that this is said in order to explain that the superimposition of agency and so forth is conditioned by the ego-sense, which itself is fully produced through the superimposition devoid of limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhika-adhyāsa*).

One might object: "Is it not the case that everywhere superimposition (adhyāsa) is caused by an adjunct (upādhi) distinct from both the substrate (adhiṣṭhāna) and the object being superimposed, and that there is no such thing as superimposition without an adjunct? To this he replies with the words, "Now, even there, if indeed... He answers, "Certainly, here too," meaning that here too there exists at least the adjunct consisting of the mere impressions (saṃskāra) of prior experience; what is being rejected is only an independent adjunct. The underlying point is that there is no fixed rule that the cause of error must be the impressions of a prior experience, rather than the impressions of a prior error.

One might object: "Since superimposition (adhyāsa) with and without adjuncts (upādhi) has already been established by the three examples [of the rope-snake, the shell-silver, and the face-in-the-mirror], there is no further purpose served by the example of the space within a jar (ghaṭākāśa) as prescribed in the Vedānta. Anticipating this, he states—beginning with the words "tatra yadyapy anirvacanīyatayaiva"—that the purpose is to establish the soul's lack of attachment (asaṅgatva) by refuting other objections. [He explains: "In the case of the mingling of a crystal and the like with red color and so forth, through the relation of quality and qualified..."

The logical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: even for that which is fit [to be perceived], because it is inexpressible (*anirvacanīyatayā*), the non-differentiated appearance of redness and so forth is established. But how, one might ask, is the establishment of the Self’s lack of attachment (*asaṅgatva*) achieved through the example of the space within a jar? To this he says: "For in that case... Now, one might object: since the immutability, unity, and lack of attachment of the Self are already established by these very examples, there is no need for scripture (*āgama*). To this he replies: "And all this collection of examples... [is merely illustrative].
The meaning is that since a matter cannot be established by a mere example in the absence of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), there is the possibility of a counter-example.

The commentary (*bhāṣya*) states, "because it is the object of the notion of 'I' (*asmad-pratyaya*)," for the purpose of establishing the possibility of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) upon the Self. Therein, the notion of "I" and the superimposition caused by it have been shown. Now, he explains the meaning of the word "object" (*viṣaya*): "Thus, even though... [and so on]. If the word "object" is used in a figurative sense (*gauṇyā vṛttyā*), what is the common quality (*guṇa-sāmya*) [that justifies it]? To this he says: "And of the object of knowledge (*prameya*)... [Objection: Surely, for a determinate superimposition (*savikalpaka-adhyāsa*), the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) must be described as determinate (*savikalpaka*) itself, because that is how it is observed; it cannot be the indeterminate pure consciousness (*nirvikalpaka-cin-mātra*).

In this regard, one raises the objection: "How can there be a superimposition of the ego (ahaṃkāra) upon the conceptualized [consciousness] through the superimposition of the ego and so forth?"—namely, "But [how can it be] in that which is fit for empirical usage? He replies: "Because it is beginningless. For even in the non-conceptual, a conceptual superimposition is observed; thus, whether by way of the superimposition of ignorance or by way of a prior superimposition of the ego, a subsequent superimposition of the ego is indeed possible within the conceptualized manifestation of consciousness.

Now, it may be objected that for the Self—which is exclusively non-modifying consciousness (*caitanya*), whose nature is stainless bliss (*ānanda*), and which is unattached (*asaṅga*)—the status of being a knower (*pramātṛtva*) is not tenable; for there is an absence of transformation into the activity of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Nor can agency (*kartṛtva*) and enjoyership (*bhoktṛtva*) belong to one devoid of the status of a knower. Thus, since the empirical transaction (*vyavahāra*) characterized by the conjunction of knower, means of knowledge, object of knowledge, agent, action, effect, enjoyer, enjoyment, and the object of enjoyment is impossible in the Self, and because the ego (*ahaṃkāra*) is insentient...

It would follow that this world would fall into a state where all worldly activity is severed, because it would be impossible for [the self] to be their substratum. Alternatively, if it were to illuminate the object solely by means of the light of consciousness established as its own nature, then, due to lack of distinction and because of its omnipresence, it would illuminate everything—thus there would be total lack of order. Therefore, the self must be capable of modification. To this, another says: "This objection cannot possibly apply to those who maintain that the self is omnipresent."

How so? First, if consciousness—or whether it be an action or a quality—arising from the contact of the four factors consisting of the self, the object, the sense organ, and the mind, were to arise as something inhering solely in the self; since it is impossible for that which is partless to have a localized substratum, then, because omnipresence is characterized by conjunction with all corporeal substances simultaneously, consciousness would have to manifest every object whatsoever that is conjoined with its own substratum, the self.

If it is argued that, just as in the case of lamps and the like, the qualities of action and illumination cause an excellence of corresponding illumination in objects conjoined with their own substratum, and thus knowledge is restricted to specific objects by means of the unseen (adṛṣṭa), we say no; for in the case of lamps and such, which illuminate all objects with which they are conjoined, no restriction is observed that transcends the inherent capacity of the object itself. Furthermore, since there is an illumination of all objects—even those like grass that are to be disregarded and do not cause pleasure or pain—the restriction by means of the unseen is untenable.

If it is argued that knowledge illuminates only that which is its cause and not everything, we say no; for this would entail the consequence that the eyes and other sense organs are also illuminators. Furthermore, since the object is being defined [as that which is illuminated], the qualification "that which is the cause as an object" is untenable. Moreover, in the case of lamps and the like, it is observed that the quality of illumination illuminates even objects that are not causes of its own substrate, provided they are in contact with it. This same principle applies even to cognition, which is of the nature of an action; for it is observed that the operations of arrows and the like are causes of excellence (such as reaching a target) whenever there is contact with their own substrate, even if the object is not specifically intended.

If it is argued that because the self is partless, there can be no conjunction with everything, we say: not at all; for nothing would then be manifest. This is because action and quality cannot connect with another thing by overstepping their own substrate, and due to this lack of connection, no excellence (atiśaya) can arise in what is unconnected.

Now, if it is held that cognition inheres only in those parts of the self delimited by the body, and does not inhere in the self as a whole, then the self would possess parts, and there would be no manifestation of objects situated at a distance; for the light residing in the self has no contact with the object, and it has already been stated that action and the like do not transcend their own substratum. Nor can there be manifestation through a connection with a part of the self that is not its substratum; otherwise, everything would be manifested.

[Objection: But surely, just as a malevolent rite (*abhicārakarma*) produces harm in another person who is not conjoined with the region of one's own self that serves as its substrate, so too might it be here. [Reply: This is not sound. For even in the case of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*), based on the capacity of the observed action itself, there is the inference of some other cause—whether it be the divine self conjoined with the regions of both selves, or the Lord (*Īśvara*), or yet another cause. Furthermore, a specific excellence (*atiśaya*) in an object conjoined with a sense organ, which is in turn conjoined with the mind, and which is conjoined with the self, cannot be established through a cognition residing in the person [alone].

Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of the over-extension of the linguistic usage "it manifests" even to other objects that are conjoined with the sense-organ; and because the stream of conjunctions has existed previously, the object does not possess a present stream of conjunctions in the same way that the cognition does. Thus, the same fault applies to the doctrine that the self has the size of an atom or the body. Therefore, for proponents of all these views, the practical operation of means of knowledge and so forth is impossible.

True; however, I shall demonstrate how [this] is possible according to our own position, and thus he says: "In that case, of such an 'I-maker' (ahaṃkartṛ)"—the meaning is "of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), which is the 'this'-portion. By "activity" (vyāpāra), its modification (pariṇāma) is intended. The internal organ, whose nature is luminosity and which possesses parts, being assisted by unseen merit/demerit (adṛṣṭa), the senses, and so forth, undergoes modification in the form of a long beam of light extending from the eyebrows up to the object.

Because light is observed to travel very rapidly over great distances, he states that the connection between the agent and the object occurs through transformation (*pariṇāma*) as a particular state; and that [connection] is produced by the action of reaching (*prāpti*).

It may be that the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) has a connection with objects by way of its own transformation, but how does the Self have the manifestation of specific objects? To this he says: "therefore, it is connected with specific objects. Although consciousness, being veiled everywhere by ignorance, has its nature unmanifested, it is manifested in whatever form the internal organ evolves through its various particular states.

Just as fire, by means of a lump of iron, assumes specific states such as being four-cornered and so forth, the meaning is that consciousness (caitanya), delimited by the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) which is in contact with an object, manifests in the form of that object. Now, one might object: "Let consciousness delimited by the nature of the subject (pramātṛ) appear in that form; how can there be a delimitation of consciousness by an object? To this he says: "Even the objective factor (karmakāraka)," and "engaged in its own operation."

It is said that [the internal organ] has acquired a fitness characterized by the suppression of its own insentience due to its transformation and association [with consciousness]. The meaning is that the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) indeed brings about the fitness for the manifestation of consciousness even within itself, as well as in that which is associated with it.

[Objection: But surely, if there is a difference in the delimiters (*avacchedaka*), then due to the difference in the light of consciousness (*citprakāśa*), how could there be a connection between the experience delimited by the object and the manifestation in the form of the subject? Or, if there is no such connection, how could there be a cognition that manifests the connection between subject and object in the form "this has been understood by me," given the difference in experiences, since it is impossible for two objects to manifest when only one relation is being cognized? To this, he replies: "[The cognition] is of a single nature consisting of immediacy, as delimited by the particular state of the subject produced by the primary action."

The meaning is "one" (ekām). The sense is that because the transformation involves the conjunction of both [the object and the consciousness], there is no interruption of the manifested [consciousness] due to the non-difference of the manifestor. Now, an objection might be raised: "If there is no distinction in the manifestation of consciousness in both cases, would there not be no difference as to whether the cognizer (*pramātā*) is the experience delimited by the jar, or rather that delimited by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)? He says, "No," for: "Therefore, the distinction in the self is produced by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) consisting of the particular state of the internal organ. The word "cognizer" (*pramātā*) is to be supplied to complete the sentence. For the status of being a cognizer belongs to the agent, not to the object.

In this context, since the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is the agent, the meaning is that the knower (*pramātṛ*) is that which is delimited by it. Now, an objection may be raised: "If consciousness is one, it follows that the knower himself is the fruit, which is a contradiction. To this, he says: "The fruit is the non-dual essence of the object's immediacy, designated as the experience of the object. The point is that [consciousness] is the knower when delimited by the internal organ, and it is the fruit when delimited by the object.

[Objection: But surely, since the action and its fruit reside respectively in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and the self (*ātman*), they have different substrates; and since the pot is the object of the internal organ while consciousness is the object of the self, they have different objects. Thus, there is a contradiction with the rule that action and fruit must have the same substrate and the same object. [Reply: No, he says: "Thus, the fruit has the same object as the action. The word "object" (*viṣaya*) is also an elliptical indication of the "substrate" (*āśraya*). Because of the superimposition of identity between the internal organ and the self, they share the same substrate; and because consciousness too is delimited by the pot, it shares the same object.

Now, the Sāṅkhyas maintain that "the person perceives the object situated in the intellect," which contradicts [the view] that "the Self perceives as colored by its own consciousness. To this, he says: "And thus, 'I am the agent' (ahaṃkartā). The meaning is that first the object situated in the intellect, having attained identity with that [intellect], is subsequently perceived. It has already been stated that although the Self is all-pervading, its status as a knower with respect to a specific object depends upon its manifestation through the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the transformations of the limited internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), while its light remains veiled by ignorance (*avidyā*).

Now, what is this manifestation? It is merely the suppression of the veil, not a modification of its own nature. But what is the proof for the aforementioned limiting adjunct (*upādhi*)? It has been stated: "Fear, confidence, and terror—all these are the mind alone. Thus, the mind is consciousness, the intellect (*buddhi*), and that which undergoes transformation as knowledge denoted by the word *dhī*.

Thus, although there is indeed a restriction due to the influence of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), the objection was raised that—because consciousness is not differentiated by all objects—all things would appear simultaneously to it. He refutes this with the words: "And in that case, for the knower who is self-luminous... The point is this: because of the restriction imposed by the limiting adjunct of karma associated with transformation, there is no manifestation of consciousness regarding those things with which it is not associated; therefore, there is no manifestation of all objects to a single knower.

[Objection: "But if consciousness is manifested even in the objective factor (*karmakāraka*), then it should appear to everyone by virtue of being common to all subjects (*pramātṛ*). [Reply: No; he says, "the objective factor also... The consciousness of that object is manifested precisely as non-different from the consciousness of this particular subject, and not as non-different from the consciousness of other subjects; therefore, it is not manifest to everyone—this is the meaning.

Now, it may be objected: since that which is self-luminous, like a lamp, ought to illuminate all things with which it comes into contact, how can a restriction by the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the *ahaṃkāra* be postulated? Nor is it reasonable to say that consciousness, even when colored [by an object], does not manifest objects other than those with which the transformation of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is in contact; for it is precisely the contact with light that is designated as "being manifested."

If it is argued that consciousness is not colored by objects because it is unattached (*asaṅgi*) to other objects, then it follows that it is likewise not colored by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) due to its unattached nature; thus, nothing at all would be manifested even through that limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). It might be replied: "The individual soul (*jīva*), which is a reflection (*pratibimba*) delimited by the internal organ, is limited and can therefore manifest only those objects with which it is in contact. But Brahman, being the original object (*bimba*) and being all-pervading, will illuminate everything."

Furthermore, it is argued that omniscience in Brahman does not follow the individual soul (jīva) as the fairness of the face [does not follow the reflection], nor does the limited knowledge residing in the jīva follow Brahman as the darkness of the face [does not follow the original object]; thus, everything is consistent. This, however, lacks substance. For if that were the case, since consciousness delimited by objects would be the very consciousness of Brahman, there would be no connection with the jīva delimited by the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra); consequently, just like omniscience, the manifestation of objects would also not belong to the jīva.

Now, one might object: "Since there is a mutual connection between the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), which is the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the individual soul (jīva), and the object, the consciousness delimited by both is likewise mutually conjoined; thus, the manifestation of objects by the individual soul is logical. This is not correct; for if that were so, the internal organ would be eternally conjoined with the all-pervading Brahman, and consequently, because the non-difference between the consciousness of the individual soul and Brahman would be manifested within that adjunct, the omniscience of Brahman would manifest to the individual soul as if it were eternal.

Now, it may be thought: although consciousness is all-pervading, because it is veiled by ignorance (*avidyā*), it does not manifest even of its own accord; and since the manifestation of consciousness does not manifest itself, it is incapable of illuminating an object of cognition, unlike a lamp. Just as the sun is obscured even by a finger—though that finger is limited—so too is the all-pervading consciousness concealed by ignorance, however small. In that regard, through the coloring of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), the veil is overcome, and consciousness manifested in that very place illuminates only a certain [object].

That too is not tenable; for it is impossible for the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), being an effect, to suppress its own material cause (*upādāna*), which is ignorance (*ajñāna*). Therefore, the description of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) for limited omniscience is not logical. To this, it is replied: this limiting adjunct is indeed appropriate, because although the individual soul (*jīva*) is all-pervading, it does not come into contact with anything due to its quality of non-attachment (*asaṅgitā*). Furthermore, since light manifests only those objects with which it is in contact, Brahman—being the material cause of everything—manifests the world as non-different from itself, whereas the individual soul does not, because it is not the material cause.
But how can there be a connection with the internal organ for that which is omnipresent—being unobstructed by all things and locations—and yet remains unmixed, being unattached to other objects?

It is said: Just as specific universals such as "cowness" (gotva), though present in the spatial locations of other individuals possessing manes and so forth, and though present in the spatial locations of other individuals such as horses due to their specific nature, are not manifested by those [latter] because of their non-attachment to them, yet are manifested through their connection with a body possessing a dewlap and so forth.

Or, just as the light of a lamp, although it pervades regions such as air, space, taste, and smell, does not illuminate them due to its specific nature, but illuminates only that which is in contact with form (rūpa), so too it is logical that consciousness (caitanya) also conjoins with the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) because of its specific nature, and not elsewhere. And just as grass and the like, though not combustible by fire alone, are burned when mounted upon a mass of iron; so too, objects that are not illuminated by the Self alone are illuminated by the Self when mounted upon the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra). Thus, the description of the ego-sense as a limiting adjunct (upādhi) is justified.

Alternatively—the individual soul (*jīva*), being conditioned by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), is limited and does not illumine everything; for the consciousness delimited by the object is manifested through its contact with the transformation of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which is the cause of the soul's limitation. Thus, its status as the consciousness of the individual soul is not contradicted. Furthermore, because there is no contact with the internal organ transformed into the form of Brahman, it does not follow that Brahman would be eternally manifest. Nor is manifestation admitted to occur merely through contact with the essential nature of the internal organ itself.

Otherwise, it would follow that the attributes (dharma) and so forth residing therein [the Self] would also be perceived. Furthermore, the individual soul (jīva) is manifested by the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) transformed into the ego-function (ahaṃvṛtti) in the form of the living being; otherwise, there would be no such thing as the soul's state of deep sleep (suṣupti). Therefore, because it is limited, it does not illuminate all objects. Alternatively—the soul, veiled by ignorance (ajñāna), not shining by itself, and failing to illuminate various objects, becomes manifested in that very place when the veil is removed through contact with the internal organ; it illuminates the object only through its conjunction with that organ.

And it is observed that the effects of scorpions, trees, and so forth, conceal the nature of their transformations from cow dung, clay, and the like; thus, the established status of the self as a cognizer and so forth is proven.

Since the object is a manifestation (*vivarta*) of consciousness, consciousness—though non-different from it—is said to have the single form of the "I"-manifestation. To this, he raises the objection that it would entail a contradiction with one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*): "But if even the object, such as blue... If every slight similarity were to result in a confusion of tenets, there would be no end to it; however, in this case, there is a great difference between our tenet and that [of the opponent].

The Vijñānavādins maintain that the object is devoid of the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*) and existence (*sattva*) as distinct from momentary consciousness. However, those who perceive reality assert that even though the object is non-different from the non-dual cognition, its capacity for causal efficiency, existence, and permanence remain uncontradicted despite its apparent difference. To show how there is no confusion of tenets in this regard, he demonstrates the unity of cognition, saying: "Not so; because they are mutually excluded," and so forth.

"Let there be oneness due to recognition; yet, difference also appears in the form 'the cognition of a jar' and 'the cognition of a cloth'. To this he replies: "Even when there is an appearance of distinction... The sense is that the recognition of the essential nature [of consciousness] is not sublated by the distinction of external adjuncts (*upādhi*). Now, one might ask: "Even if cognitions are one, why should there not be non-difference of their objects? To this he says: "If it were so... The inference stated is: "The persisting [consciousness] is not non-different from the excluded [objects], because it is persisting, like space or a jar."

Now, he says that even the distinction between the cognition and its object is directly perceived: "Furthermore, even by them... The phrase "cognition whose nature is blue" refers to the blue object itself, because the simultaneous admission of two cognitions—one of the object and one of the subject—is not accepted. "Internal manifestation" means the mere awareness of "I. The meaning is that the distinction exists as a direct perception in the form of agent and object, as in: "I see the blue."

Here the Vijñānavādin objects: "This [distinction] does not apply to both. The meaning is as follows: if blue were other than consciousness (*saṃvid*), it would not appear within that consciousness. If it does appear, why does everything not appear? For there is no specific relation (*viśeṣasaṃbandha*) belonging to the blue. If it is argued that the specific relation is the state of being a generator (*janakatā*) for consciousness, we say no; for this would entail that the sense organ (*indriya*) also becomes an object. Therefore, blue appears in consciousness solely through a natural, unique, and non-differentiated relation (*asādhāraṇābhedasaṃbandha*).

The proponent of the final view (siddhāntin), however, asks: "How can even this appearance of difference, which is directly perceived, be denied by reason? He says: "But how [could one say] 'I know this'? The Vijñānavādin, for his part, replies: "These three do not appear within a single consciousness; rather, these are three distinct consciousnesses occurring in succession. Thus he says: "This is not an appearance of that [single unity]."

If there were sequential occurrence, then at the time of the cognition of one [object], the other would not appear; however, this triad appears directly and simultaneously. Therefore, the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin) states that sequence contradicts direct perception: "But how, then, among those? The Vijñānavādin replies: "It arises from an immediately preceding condition (samanantarapratyaya) accompanied by its latent impressions (vāsanā). Sometimes a cognition arises mounted upon the construction of "I" (ahaṃ-kalpanā); immediately thereafter, a cognition arises conceptualized as an object, such as "this."

These very [factors] are the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) within consciousness. It has been stated that for a cognition of a similar kind, only a preceding cognition of a similar kind is the latent impression, and no other formative force (*saṃskāra*). In this regard, from the conceptual-cognitive state "I know," which is accompanied by these two types of latent impressions, a single three-aspected cognition arises—conceptually constructed as the object, the action, and the "I"—in accordance with its three causes, namely: "I know this. Thus says the proponent of the established conclusion (*siddhāntin*): "But how is it so?"

For indeed, cognitions consisting solely of "I," or "this," or "I know" have never been observed; rather, from the very outset, cognition is observed to consist of the experience of both agent and object in the form "I know this. Therefore, the point is that one must admit an external blue object, distinct from the cognition "I," which possesses causal efficiency exactly as it appears.

We do not say that blue is non-different from consciousness by relying on an empirical experience; rather, we say so because the appearance of blue would otherwise be inexplicable through cognition. For if the cognition and its object were enduring, there could be a unique manifestation of the object due to a specific mutual relationship based on a common causal basis for their activity. However, for a momentary object, in the absence of an adventitious relationship, if even an inherent relationship of non-difference did not exist, then there would be no manifestation at all of that which is unconnected with consciousness.

Therefore, the Vijñānavādin explains that the impossibility of [simultaneous] appearance establishes non-difference—on the grounds that "action is impossible for that which perishes in a moment. In this regard, is the momentariness of cognitions asserted through perception or through inference? Surely, it is through perception; for instance, a cognition appearing as present also makes known its own exclusion from what is not present, just as the cognition of blue makes known blue as excluded from the non-blue.

Therefore, consciousness is perceptible only for a single present moment. To show that there is no manifestation of a distinction between cognitions through perception, he says: "If this were so, [it would apply] to the cognitions of 'I'."

Now, one might object: "Even though difference is manifest, it does not appear clearly due to extreme similarity. To this, he raises the doubt: "Or, because of extreme similarity... What is the intended meaning here? If the intention is that difference is something other than consciousness and is apprehended by another cognition, yet does not appear clearly due to the defect of similarity, then—since the consciousnesses of the locus (*dharmin*) and the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) are not themselves objects of another consciousness—their difference could not be grasped. Or, if they were indeed objects, then the triad consisting of the locus, the counter-correlate, and their difference [would likewise have to be objects].

Regarding whether that [perceived difference] would be imagined as non-different from the cognition, or if it were the very nature of cognition itself—such that difference is nothing but cognition and that knowledge is the cognition—it says in response: "If even of cognition... Furthermore, to postulate similarity when there is an appearance of identity contradicts the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). The error of identity between two distinct things is the basis for postulating similarity; since that [error] is absent, similarity is not established. Thus it says: "Moreover, when its own form appears..."

The proponent of the prima facie view says: "Is it not the case that since the appearance of identity is an illusion, the postulation of similarity is not contrary to valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? Furthermore, the delusion of identity among distinct things is impossible without similarity; thus, the postulation of similarity is based on presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). Therefore, similarity is established. He [the respondent] refutes this, saying: "Not so, because of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*) between the establishment of the delusion of identity and the establishment of similarity. He explains: "Because the cognition of that form [identity] is an illusion. [The opponent objects: "Do not say so; for there would be mutual dependence between the delusion of identity and the proof of similarity. [The respondent replies: "No, because of mutual dependence. (This means: the delusion of identity depends on the proof of similarity, and the proof of similarity depends on the delusion of identity; therefore, neither can be established.)

One might object: "The validity of the appearance of identity is not established intrinsically (*svataḥ*), but rather by depending on the absence of a basis for similarity and its contradiction by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); and since the absence of a basis for similarity and its contradiction by valid cognition belong to the appearance of identity itself, you too face the same fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). To this he replies: "It may be so; even in the case of non-delusion... He refutes this, stating: "This is not intrinsic," meaning that the appearance of identity does not depend on the absence of similarity, but is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by itself.

Anticipating the objection that similarity (*sādṛśya*) is also established by itself, he says: "But the conceptualization of similarity is not [established] by itself. To the question, "From what, then, is the establishment of similarity? he replies: "It is preceded by invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*). The point is that the delusion of identity (*aikyabhrama*) indeed postulates similarity among distinct things.

Now, what is this so-called recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) by the power of which the unity of consciousness is perceived? If it is argued that recognition is a perceptual cognition concerning the relation of a single entity to two points in time, produced by a cause consisting of the present apprehension of an object accompanied by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of a prior experience, then it would not be possible for such recognition to apply to the Self (*ātman*).

How could there be a cause for recognition (pratyabhijñā) in the case of the self, which is of the nature of consciousness? For if the self is permanent—since it is self-luminous and thus not accessible through another cognition, and since there is an absence of any impression (*saṃskāra*) regarding its destruction because its own nature is indestructible—and since there is an absence of impressions for that which is imperishable, and furthermore, since there is no cause for a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) distinct from its present nature for that which is self-luminous, a cause for recognition is not possible in the self. Nor is the knowledge of its own nature itself the recognition.

Because that [consciousness], like the light of a lamp, illuminates the present, it lacks the nature of reflecting upon the past and the future; furthermore, if one accepts the forms of objects in the cognition "I am he," then a distinction between cognitions is established due to the distinction between objects, as indicated by the difference in form between "he" and "I. Therefore, it is established through reasoning that recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) does not apply to the self, and thus its status as a delusion is proven.
To this it is replied: We maintain that recognition pertains to the Self as qualified by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), and not to the mere nature of the stainless Self alone;

for that [Self] which abides in the state of liberation is accessible through scripture alone. This is because, during the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), the nature qualified by the internal organ does not perish, and it is precisely that [qualified Self] which is designated as "enduring" through recognition.

In that regard, since the manifestation of the qualified Self is dependent upon the "I"-notion (*ahaṃpratyaya*) produced by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), it is the internal organ itself—accompanied by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the "I"-modification (*ahaṃvṛtti*) caused by the experience of the Self as qualified by a prior time—that, being the cause for the manifestation of the Self at the present time, produces the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) which has as its object the Self as qualified by both prior and subsequent times.

[Objection: But surely, since the Self is not an object of the two prior cognitions (of recognition), how can it be the object of a single recognition (*pratyabhijñā*)? [Reply: This is not a fault. Just as consciousness, though its nature is self-known, becomes the object of memory produced by its own latent impression (*saṃskāra*) at a later time, so too here, it is not contradictory for that which was not an object of the individual cognitions to be the object of the recognition.

[Objection: But surely, for that which is self-luminous (*svayaṃprakāśa*), the status of being an object (*viṣayatā*) is untenable.
