[Reply: It is not so; for its status as an object is established by way of its being qualified by space, time, and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Just as dharma, though cognizable solely through scripture (*āgama*), is nevertheless cognizable through signs such as the arising of present results—by virtue of its being qualified by attributes such as being on the verge of yielding fruit at this moment—so it is in this case.

But how can there be a simultaneous connection with two contradictory forms—the status of agent and object—within the recognition of a single self? Is it not the case that for all proponents [of the self], the relationship of agent and object is universally accepted as the subject matter of inferences establishing the self as distinct from the body and so forth? That is not so.

In inference and other such cognitions, because the object lacks the status of being a causal factor (*kāraka*) and is an object merely by virtue of its form, the self therein possesses only the status of an agent (*kartṛtā*), not the status of an object (*karmatā*). However, in perception, since the object also functions as a causal factor by way of producing a cognition of itself, the self necessarily incurs the contradiction of assuming two mutually exclusive forms simultaneously within a single action.

It is said: the self’s status as a knower is due to its being qualified by the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), while its status as the object of knowledge is due to its being qualified by prior and posterior time; thus, there is no contradiction because of the difference in limiting adjuncts (upādhi). Furthermore, since the recognition "I am he" is established by one's own experience, some cause for it must be postulated in some way; for, due to the non-contradiction of worldly practice, it cannot be considered an error. Nor is it logical that a difference in cognition arises from a difference in the object merely because of a difference in the form "I am he."

If you argue that consciousness is momentary because there is a difference in objects due to a difference in mental aspects (ākāra), which would otherwise entail the non-existence of the momentariness of consciousness—this is true; if you then claim that the coloring of consciousness by properties such as momentariness is merely a conceptual convention (*vikalpavyavahāramātra*) and does not exist in reality, then there is no distinction [in your position], for conventions such as permanence and so forth are likewise conceptual conventions regarding consciousness, arising from the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of time and other factors.

However, this is the distinction: when time exists, conceptual cognitions such as permanence and so forth—established by experience in the form of "I am that," and so on—are observed to be non-contradictory in worldly practice and capable of causal efficiency; the conventional usages regarding momentariness and the like are not seen to be so.

On this point, the Prābhākaras maintain: "In recognition, this self is not established as the object (*viṣaya*), but rather as the substratum (*āśraya*. This is incorrect; for it is impossible for a self characterized by prior and subsequent times to be the substratum of a recognition that exists for only a single moment, and thus its permanence cannot be established by virtue of being that substratum.

Now, one might argue: "The experience of a previous time, being remembered now, establishes the self as existing at that time which was the locus of that experience; and memory, by having itself as its locus, establishes the self as existing at the present time; thus, there is proof of a self qualified by two points in time. This is not sound.

For memory and prior experience establish the self at their respective times, like the two cognitions of recognition and direct perception; however, it must be explained by what means the connection of a single [self] to two points in time is established—if you say that the pair of cognitions, the prior and the subsequent, establishes it itself, do not say so, because in the case of jars and other objects, recognition is employed as distinct from the two cognitions of recognition [of the object]. Furthermore, the pair of cognitions does not establish itself.

Since each individual cognition lacks a self as its substrate during the two moments [of before and after], nor do the two cognitions—prior and posterior—taken together establish a self possessing them; for they lack a mutual dependence on a single self characterized by the other's cognition. If, however, the two cognitions themselves produce another cognition whose object is the unity of the self as the substrate of the two cognitions—prior and posterior—then it is established that recognition has the self as its object.

Furthermore, because the recollection of a prior consciousness qualified by its substrate—in the form "this was experienced by me"—is established by one's own experience, the existence of the self as previously experienced is now established solely through the fact of being remembered, and not by virtue of being the substrate of that prior consciousness; for that which no longer exists cannot serve as a proof at present. Indeed, it is consciousness itself, while manifesting of its own accord, that establishes the self as its substrate, and not [the self] as something revealed by another through being an object of memory;

otherwise, there would be the absurd consequence that even dharma and so forth, which are established by another, would establish their own substrate, the self. Therefore, it is proven that there is recognition (pratyabhijñāna) regarding the self.

In that case, one might establish momentariness through inference in the case of a jar and so forth, as follows: "Because decay is observed at the end. The existence of a jar characterized by the penultimate moment is called the "end. Its destruction is observed in the moment immediately following its own moment of existence. In this regard, the existences of the jar delimited by each preceding moment prior to the final moment are called the "beginning. These too are pervaded by destruction in the moment following their own moments of existence, because they are existences of the jar.

The inference is: "like the existence of a jar delimited by its final moment. Consequently, since destruction follows immediately after existence, momentariness is established; thus, the unity perceived in momentary things is based on similarity.

In that regard, he states the counter-inference: "Because existence is observed at the beginning. Here, "beginning" refers to the moments delimited by the existence of the jar. "End" [refers to the moments delimited by its destruction].

Thus, the moments intended as the delimiters of destruction are established as follows: it is proven that all final moments are pervaded by the existence of the jar. The counter-inference is: "Because they are times, like a time delimited by existence. One objects that inferring existence at the end contradicts the experience of non-existence—this is raised in the phrase "the experience of decay. In response, he refutes this by stating "here too," meaning that even the inference of decay immediately following the existence of the jar delimited by the moments prior to the final moment would contradict recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).
"The experience of destruction is a direct perception (abhijñā) that sublates inference; recognition is not weaker than inference. To this he says: "No—for it is not the case that both..."

"All entities are momentary because they possess causal efficiency (arthakriyākāritva); that which is non-momentary does not possess causal efficiency, just like a rabbit’s horn. To demonstrate this further inference, he states the impossibility of causal efficiency for a permanent entity, beginning with: "Now, it might be thought: 'That which is considered permanent... and so forth.

The proponent raises an objection: "Is it not the case that only a stable entity, having been modified through conjunction with an instrumental cause (*nimitta*), possesses the capacity to produce an effect preceded by action, whereas a momentary entity does not? The rebuttal begins with "In this way, there is no connection," and so forth. "Successively" (*krameṇa*) means that it would produce multiple effects in continuous succession. He states that [the entity] either produces one or many effects simultaneously and then ceases: "simultaneously" (*yogapadyena*). He refutes the position of succession with the words: "Not at all," and so forth.

If it were capable of performing multiple effects, then—given the presence of its complete causes and because multiple effects are observed from a single [cause]—it would produce them all at once; this is the sense. He refutes the second position with the words: "Nor [can it act] simultaneously. The sense is that existence (*sattva*) is defined by the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*).

Therefore, since there is no further cause for an agent that has already acted once to act again at another time, or else it would not be an agent and thus non-existent, he concludes: "Therefore, precisely because of causal efficiency..."

The proponent of the final view (*siddhāntin*), however, establishes that even for a stable entity (*sthāyin*) that has performed its function once and become silent, there is no attainment of non-existence; this is because existence does not have the characteristic of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*). He explains this with the passage beginning "Now, what is this... and so forth. Regarding that, he says: "The production of a cognition whose object is itself. He refutes this by stating: "In that case, it follows for all [cognitions]," arguing that while such a definition of existence is appropriate for external objects, it cannot be the definition of existence for cognitions, since cognitions do not produce a cognition of themselves as their own object.

[Objection: "But surely, even though cognitions within a single continuum lack the relationship of object and subject toward one another, a cognition belonging to one person can still produce a cognition in another person by way of being its object; thus, cognitions do obtain causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). [Reply: No, he says—“not even in another continuum. The sense is that a cognition belonging to one person is not perceptible to a cognition belonging to another person, but is rather inferable.

If it is argued that, because it is an object of inferential knowledge, the cognition of another mental continuum (*santānāntara*) must be the producer of that [inferential] cognition of another mental continuum, he says "no"—namely, "even in the case of inference. The meaning is that, according to your view, only perception (*pratyakṣa*) is produced by an object, not inference and the like. Now, one might object: "Every collection of cognitions becomes a producer of omniscient knowledge (*sarvajñāna*) by way of being its object, since that [omniscient knowledge] is a direct perception of all objects. To this, he says: "not even in the case of omniscience. [He adds the word] "directly" (*sākṣāt*).

"Along with the disturbances of consciousness" means without interval, by being colored by the knowledge of the Omniscient One; that is to say, through non-difference from it. The reason for this is: "because it would follow that [the Omniscient's knowledge] would have the same nature as the consciousness of transmigratory existence. The sense is that, since one accepts the non-difference between consciousness and its object, the knowledge of the Omniscient One would be defiled by the disturbed cognitions of transmigrating beings. Now, one might object: even if it were colored by all those disturbances, it does not bring about any defect because it is sublated by the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*); however, that very knowledge does not sublate its own disturbance.

Because it is impossible for both apprehension and sublation to occur in a single moment, another cognition cannot have the corruption of a previous cognition as its object, such that there could be a sublation by way of restating it; furthermore, if it were so, there would be no distinction between the corruptions even within the subverting cognition itself. If it is then argued that cognitions are colored [by corruptions] in the omniscient cognition even without those corruptions being present, he says "no"—"if they do not possess that nature. The sense is that since the worldly corruptions do not appear to the Omniscient One, teaching would be impossible.

Now, one might object: "If causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) does not consist in the production of a cognition of its own object, but rather in the production of another moment of the same kind," [the author] raises this with the word "atha" (now). He provides the answer: "It would follow that the final moment possesses the characteristic of non-existence. The meaning is as follows: the cognitions falling within the continuum [of the self], such as "I am," are overwhelmed by defects like passion and so forth, as well as by objects, due to the notions of permanence and continuity; these subsequent [cognitions] arise from the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) characterized by preceding cognitions of objects of the same kind.

In this regard, through the meditation that "all this is momentary," the conceptualization of permanence ceases; through the meditation on specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), the conceptualization of substances, qualities, words, actions, qualifiers, and qualified objects perishes; through the meditation that "this is suffering," the outflows of passion and other defects, as well as the disturbances of pleasure and pain, are exhausted; and through the meditation that "this is empty," the disturbances caused by sense objects vanish.

Then, when the fourfold affliction has been gradually attenuated by the four types of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), a consciousness free from all afflictions arises from the final limit of the excellence of that cultivation acting as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). Since that [final consciousness] is the very end of the continuum of saṃsāra, it would follow that it is non-existent because it lacks any further effect; consequently, it would follow that everything prior to it is likewise non-existent.

[Objection: But surely even the final moment, despite the absence of another cognition within its own continuum, produces the cognition of the Omniscient One by way of being its object? [Reply: No, he says: "And not by the production of the Omniscient One's cognition. The very nature of being a single continuum consists in the causal relationship between two things of identical nature; since the final moment and the Omniscient One's cognition are of identical nature due to their purity, there is an uninterrupted continuum because of their causal relationship—this is the sense. [One might argue: Let there be no interruption of the continuum.

He says "no," because it would follow that liberation is impossible. The point is that liberation is intended to be the cessation of the continuum (*saṃtāna*). Now, if it is argued that liberation is simply the identity of that continuum—since a continuum of an omniscient being produces a similar continuum due to its identical nature—then he replies that there is no production at all by way of being an object: "And consciousness is not the object of consciousness. By the word "object" (*viṣaya*), perceptibility is meant; for the cognition of another person is something to be inferred.

Alternatively, it may be that it is precisely the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) itself that is inferred as being connected to another body; thus, consciousness (*saṃvit*) is not an object of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Or rather, the meaning is this: because there is no difference [between cognitions] insofar as they are of the nature of consciousness—consciousness does not differ from another consciousness by way of the form of consciousness; for if it did, the counter-correlate would result in being non-consciousness, and thus there would be only one single consciousness. Even if there were a difference by way of the form of non-consciousness, consciousness would still be one and the same; therefore, there can be no relationship of object and subject between various instances of consciousness.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "and what [more]": having raised the dilemma as to whether causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is the cause for the existence of a thing or the ground for its cognition, he states the refutation if it were the cause: "of that which is produced by its own causes. The meaning is that the cause is already established prior to the effect. Nor can it be said that even though it is established, it is non-existent prior to the causal efficiency; for that would entail the consequence of it being a non-cause, like the horn of a hare. Regarding the position that it is the ground for cognition, he states the refutation of infinite regress: "in that case, its [cognition] must come from another."

One might object: "Surely, an effect is what is called 'purposeful action' (*arthakriyā*), and cognitions—being subsequent to preceding ones—are themselves self-established; thus, there is no infinite regress of cognition. To this he replies: "But [if it were so], from its own cognitive purposeful action... He then states: "In that case, since cognitions existing as cause and effect are self-established, purposeful action is not the cause for the apprehension of existence": "Then, therefore, not from purposeful action..."

It might be argued that a causal cognition does not depend on a resultant cognition for its manifestation because it is self-luminous; nevertheless, since it manifests by itself and through itself, its own causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) consists in this very self-manifestation. To this he says: "No, for it is not merely its own nature. Therefore, existence is not defined solely by the capacity for causal efficiency; rather, it is inherent. Thus, there is no contradiction in the existence of a persisting entity even when it remains silent after having once performed an effect.

Now, he says that even by performing its effect sequentially, the existence of the entity is not contradicted: "Furthermore, as for [the claim] 'by means of sequence'. He says that even for a potent cause, a sequence of effects is logical in dependence upon a specific sequence in the proximity of auxiliary causes: "Even for that which is stable... He denies the potent cause's dependence on auxiliary causes: "Now, as for the cause... With a hidden intention, he gives the reply: "Not even more so for that which is not a cause."

"In that case, let there be no dependence on auxiliary factors (sahakārin) for either the potent or the impotent [cause]," he says in response: "The entire universe would be without auxiliaries. The sense is that this contradicts the empirical observation that only a potent cause produces an effect by depending on auxiliaries. He raises an objection: "But perhaps only impotent things depend on one another for the production of the causal complex (sāmagrī), so there is no contradiction with experience."

He raises the dilemma as to whether things that are incapable with respect to the effect are nevertheless capable with respect to the causal complex (*sāmagrī*): "Therefore, of that cause... The refutation of both positions is given by: "If [it were] the cause... and so forth. Then, "there is no dependence" explains the meaning already stated.

[Objection: But surely, if there is no mutual dependence between the potent and the non-potent, how can the experience of cooperation be explained? [Reply: Is it not the case that because the effect is equally non-existent [prior to production], why would it not arise from everything? Or, since the cause is devoid of a specific relation [to its effect], why would everything not be a producer? Thus, in the face of such lack of restriction (*avyavasthā*), how do you establish the mere relationship of cause and effect? [Objection: If you say that the restriction of cause and effect is established by the power of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), [we reply: the same applies to the auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*) as well; so he says:

Therefore, [it is] "just as from the cause" and so forth. To the question, "Where then is the utility of the auxiliary (sahakārin)? the author introduces another view and refutes the proponent of the previous position: "But he who thinks [the cause produces an effect] through a particularity (viśeṣa) produced by the auxiliary. One must consider whether that which depends on an auxiliary is capable or incapable of producing a particularity within itself. Regarding its incapacity, he states the refutation: "In the production of a particularity," etc. The meaning is that what is incapable is never seen to accomplish anything, even when a thousand auxiliaries are present.

He states the refutation regarding its being a cause: "Now, as for the cause... In that regard, in order to avoid the fault of infinite regress—which would arise if the first particularity required another particularity—one might argue that some particularity is produced in the cause by the auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*) for the sake of producing the effect; however, in other cases, the effect is produced by the auxiliaries without depending on the production of a particularity in the cause. Thus, he himself demonstrates this lack of fixed rule: "Now, it may be thought that not every effect [requires such a process]."

"It was just that much" means that it was only when there was a specific swelling [of the seed]. He refutes [the opponent's position] by saying, "In that case, even if it does not benefit its own self, the causal factor requires auxiliary causes," thereby showing that your own position has been rejected by you yourself. [The opponent] says, "Even if it does not benefit [it]," to which the proponent of momentariness replies, "It does not benefit [it]. This means that otherwise, everything would result in being an auxiliary cause. To which [auxiliary cause] does it then provide benefit? He says: "But it does not benefit [it] in its own nature."

The meaning is that an effect, while being produced by an auxiliary cause, is indeed assisted [by it]. To this, he offers a rebuttal—showing that there is no contradiction even for an instantaneous effect in terms of receiving assistance: "In that case, even a permanent entity does not admit of any added excellence (*anādheyātiśaya*). He elaborates on this very point: "Just as an instantaneous entity... [and so on]. "[Because it is accomplished by a totality of conditions (*sāmagrī*)" means because it is accomplished by the operations of many causal factors (*kāraka*)."

Furthermore, the connection is as follows: only that which is to be assisted (the effect) depends upon an assistant (the cause), not that which is not to be assisted; [the opponent] raises the objection: "In that case, even if the cause is eternal, it is only the effect that depends upon an assistant, not the cause itself, which is not to be assisted."—Now, [the author says]: "atha" (then).

The view is that even a momentary entity does not depend [on anything]. The connection is as follows: that which comes into being upon the proximity of another depends on it. [Objection: Even in the case of an eternal cause, the effect itself will arise sequentially by depending on auxiliary factors (sahakārin). [Reply: No, he says—“but for an eternal producer”—meaning that because the auxiliaries and the cause are always present, the effect would be produced at all times. [Objection: But surely [the cause] depends on the proximity of the auxiliaries as well. [Reply: No, he says—“what is the reason? [for such dependence].

If the relationship between the cause and its auxiliary conditions is itself the effect, then that [relationship] would also always arise from the cause and its auxiliaries; thus, the meaning is that the production of the effect would occur at all times. Now, one might object: "Why does the effect not always arise even from a momentary cause when it depends upon auxiliary conditions, given that the production of the effect occurs only at the specific moment of existence (sattākṣaṇa), since there is no distinction [in the cause] during the preceding and succeeding moments? To this, he says: "But that which is momentary is the producer."

"This is untenable"—this is the meaning: first of all, it is not possible to understand that the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of fire alone is the cause of the specific characteristic of smoke; for two things that perish in a single moment cannot persist long enough for the pair of cognitions based on positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) to arise. Rather, through positive and negative concomitance between the two continuums (*saṃtāna*) of fire and smoke, it must be established—within the scope of a general category—that the specific characteristics of fire are the causes of the specific characteristics of smoke.

If it is argued that smoke might not arise even from the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of fire residing in glowing embers because of the absence of the specific characteristic of wood, we say no; for that [specific characteristic of fire] also exists within its own continuum (*saṃtāna*). If it is argued that there is a dependence on the conjunction of the specific characteristics of fire and wood, we say no; for if the two continua were eternal, the presence of their cause would also necessarily follow at all times. If it is argued that even in that case there is a dependence on something else, then the same applies here as well.

It is not tenable to claim that, because the presence of auxiliary causes (sahakārin) for an eternal entity occurs only occasionally, there is no risk of its producing effects as if it were non-eternal. Now, one might object: "Even if the emergence of an effect is restricted solely by the presence of auxiliaries, there is still no relationship of 'benefited and benefactor' (upakāryopakāraka) between the series of smoke and the series of fuel. To this he says: "What is improper here? He answers: "Since the restriction exists. The meaning is that even if there is a restriction regarding the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) of the auxiliaries with the effect, the statement that there is no relationship of 'benefited and benefactor' is contradictory.

[Objection: But where has the pervasion of the rule of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka-niyama*) by the relationship between the beneficiary and the benefactor (*upakārya-upakāraka-sambandha*) been observed? [Reply: It has been observed in the case of cause and effect; thus he says: "For instance, whoever... The sense is that in the absence of the relationship between the beneficiary and the benefactor, the rule of positive and negative concomitance would be untenable, as in the case of water and smoke.

Now, it might be argued that the rule of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka-niyama*) applies only to those very specific individualities (*svalakṣaṇa*) of fire and smoke for which a causal relationship has been observed, and not to the continua (*santāna*) of fire and smoke; for if there were no distinction [between the two], then since smoke is seen to exist or not exist depending on the presence or absence of contact with wood in all specific individualities of fire—which are the causes of the specific individuality of smoke—there would have to be a rule of positive and negative concomitance regarding the auxiliary causes, as well as a relationship characterized by mutual assistance (*upakāryopakāraka-sambandha*) based on dependence.

Therefore, the capacity for cause and effect is not attained anywhere other than within the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the cause and effect themselves, but rather within the adjunct of the universal (*sāmānyopādhi*); regarding this, he says: "For in this way the relation of cause and effect is established," and so forth. The intention is that empirical usage is observed to occur within the adjunct of the universal. Let it be granted that there is a rule regarding the capacity for being produced and producing within the adjunct of the universal; what follows from that? To this he says: "In that case, if the cause were not momentary (*kṣaṇika*)," and so on.

He establishes that very point: "For it is because of the connection with a succession of causes. This means that the cause is itself capable [of producing the effect]. Nor does the effect depend upon an auxiliary cause; this means that [the effect] is produced from the cause alone. Now, one might object: "When smoke is produced from the specific particular (svalakṣaṇa) of fire, since contact with wood is also present, that too must be considered an auxiliary cause. To this we say: no.

For even prior [to the production of smoke], since there is an absence of contact with wood—which possesses the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of fire and is capable of generating smoke—there can be no establishment of its status as a cooperative cause (*sahakāritva*) based on mere positive concomitance (*anvaya*) alone, without the observation of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) characterized by its non-causality. Thus he says: "It is called 'accidental' (*kākatālīya*). If it is argued that, in that case, let there be no dependence on a cooperative cause; let there be no cause either, he says: "And thus, the conventional designations of effect and cause [would vanish]."

Therefore, he concludes that because there is no difference in the sequence of the proximity of auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) for both the momentary and the permanent, their causality is likewise undifferentiated: "Therefore, even for the momentary... This is the meaning: just as from a single specific characteristic of fire (*agni-svalakṣaṇa*), due to a difference in auxiliary causes, multiple effects arise from one—namely, fire in the same location, smoke above, ash below, and cognition in a person—so too, from a single cause, through a difference in auxiliary causes at different times, there is a difference in effects.

Therefore, even though there is no difference in the object, the self-consciousness (*ahaṃ-saṃvedana*)—by virtue of its capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-samarthatā*)—exists as something enduring, distinct from the non-dual consciousness (*saṃvedana*) as it appears. Thus, he concludes that there is this great difference from the established doctrine: "In this way, because the agent of the 'I' (*ahaṅkartṛ*) is understood to be always of a single nature."

Because he accepts a confusion of tenets through some degree of similarity [with other schools], because he does not accept the authority of mantras, arthavādas, itihāsas, and purāṇas, because he does not accept deities, heaven, God, or liberation, and because he accepts the existence of only that which is momentary and whose connection with a means of valid cognition is momentary—the Prābhākara is one who has evolved from two parts of the Lokāyata and the Buddhist. Because he accepts both difference and non-difference, and because he does not accept the authority of mantras and so forth, the author of the Vārttika is one who has evolved from two parts of the Lokāyata and the Kṣapaṇaka (Jaina).

But whoever, with the orb of his head bowed at the feet of a Jain mendicant (*kṣapaṇaka*), has the fragments of his discriminative knowledge scattered by the fierce winds of hatred toward the Paramahaṃsas who perceive reality and are devoted to it; whose discernment is rendered distant from the distinction between the merits and defects of his own and others' positions; and who, as if creating a confusion of bondage and liberation through both difference and non-difference, prattles words pleasing to the wicked—claiming that "this Vedānta doctrine is identical to the Vijñānavāda of the Sugata"—he does so because he is devoid of the cultivation gained from hearing the traditional lineage.
One who does not understand the distinction between right and wrong views is not to be censured, but rather to be pitied; therefore, such a person should be disregarded by the wise.

[Objection: Is it not the case that for you, as for [the Vijñānavādin], the imagined nature of the manifold (prapañca) within consciousness is equal? [Response: True; and the fact of appearing within consciousness is also equal for you and him. Thus, why should your own system not be the Vijñānavāda? [Objection: Even though there is an appearance, there exists a distinction between the real and the false. [Response: If this is so, then here too, even though there is falsity, there certainly exists a distinction between the presence and absence of the capacity for causal efficiency (arthakriyāsāmarthya).

If it is argued that this distinction between the real and the false is not established if [the world] is merely imagined (*kalpita*), then even if it is merely an appearance (*pratibhāsya*), the distinction between the real and the false is not established. If it is argued that this distinction is indeed observed, then why should that very observation of the distinction not belong to me as well? If it is argued that the falsity (*mithyātva*) of the pot and so forth is unproven, we say no; for the reality of what appears is likewise unproven. Furthermore, there is the observation of the distinction between the presence and absence of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), and between existence and non-existence, in the case of nacre-silver and a pot respectively.

Moreover, illusion (māyā) is observed to be the cause of affection, hatred, and so forth; and it is heard that in the battles between the gods and asuras, weapons created by illusion serve as the cause of burning, cutting, piercing, and the like. Enough of this excessive elaboration.

One might object: "If the object is also immediate because it manifests consciousness, then the same would apply to inference and so forth; yet this is not observed. Thus he raises the objection: "Now, [it is not so] in the case of inferable objects and the like."

He provides the rebuttal—that there is no immediacy (*aparokṣatā*) with respect to inferential objects and the like—on the grounds that an object becomes a manifestor (*vyañjaka*) of consciousness by attaining a fitness produced through its contact with a transformation of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); since such [contact] is impossible for things that are not present, it is impossible for those two properties [of being a product and being a manifestor] to arise in them simultaneously, and thus they lack immediacy. He states: "There is no immediacy in inferential objects and the like," because "there is no non-exclusion" [of this principle]. The meaning is that the two properties of being a causal factor (*kārakatva*) and being a manifestor (*vyañjakatva*) are incompatible. For redness is certainly not produced in a destroyed jar by contact with fire.

[Objection: But is it not observed that rain and so forth possess presentness by way of their past or future aspects? [Reply: No, because it is impossible for rain to be simultaneously past and present. Furthermore, the present time is not a delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for the property of pastness through its relation as a substrate (*anvayitva*), as it is for a jar or similar object; rather, it is [related] as a counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*). Thus, presentness is not established [for the past].

Furthermore, for that which exists in a past form, there can be no status as the locus of present action or qualities; for we observe that a jar existing in a past form cannot be the locus of the present movement of its red color. Therefore, it is not logical for objects such as those inferred to possess the status of a causal factor (*kāraka*) or to manifest [cognition]. In the case of perception, however, since the contact of the sense organ—which is a quality—cannot function without the operation of the possessor of that quality (the substance), it is logical that the object is included within the causal totality (*sāmagrī*).

How then, in the absence of an operation upon an object, can cognition possess the form of the object in the case of inferable things and the like? To this he says: "Of the mark (liṅga) and so forth themselves. Now, one might argue that just as there is the production of the status of being an object regarding the past, there should likewise be the status of being a causal factor (kārakatva). To this he says "no": "And of the object of knowledge" (prameya). Being an object (viṣayatva) consists in the exclusion of deep sleep with respect to inferable things. And since that [exclusion] is a non-existence (abhāva), it cannot be a property (dharma) of that [object].

Even the fact that consciousness has the form [of an object] is not an operation of the external object, but rather belongs to consciousness itself; thus, there is no causal efficiency (arthakriyākāritva) regarding a past object. Furthermore, the transitivity of the verb "to know" (jānāti) depends upon a result with respect to inferential objects and the like, and not upon an objective factor (karmakāraka); for if it were transitive in that sense, there would also have to be direct perceptibility (aparokṣatā), just as in the case of perception.

Now, in order to explain the meaning, he applies the Bhāṣya passage, "Because it is the object of our cognition," stating: "Thus, the knot of the ego-sense. But surely, the Śruti describes the Self as being conjoined with various limiting adjuncts (upādhi), such as "the embodied one" and "the knower of the field."

In response to the question, "How is it that this designation belongs to the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) alone? he says: "Furthermore, in such a state during waking and dreaming... This refers to the fact that even though the Self has ignorance (*ajñāna*)—colored by the ego-sense and its latent impressions—as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), this designation is caused by various external limiting adjuncts throughout all three states; thus, the phrase "moving back and forth" expresses the coloring by numerous adjuncts.

To one who asserts that superimposition with conceptual content (*savikalpādhyāsa*) occurs only upon a substrate that is itself conceptually determined (*savikalpaka*), the refutation has been stated [by Śaṅkara] as: "Because it is the object of the notion of 'I' (*asmatpratyayaviṣayatvāt*)," etc. Now, he says—starting with "Furthermore, not only..."—that superimposition with conceptual content is possible even upon that which is free from conceptual content (*nirvikalpaka*). [Objection: But how can the Self, which is always inferable (*nityānumeya*), be established as being directly perceived (*aparokṣatayā*)? [Reply: He says "no," stating: "For [superimposition] does not occur when the Self is not well-known. This is because there is no difference between oneself and others regarding the lack of comprehension of the relationship between agent and object in the form "this was known by me."

If it is argued that the distinction between the two [the self and the body] lies in one of them being the substratum of the cognition whose object is experience, we say no; for if there were no experience of the category of the self, it would be impossible to comprehend their relationship. The point is that, since there is no difference regarding the absence of a connection with experience, it is impossible to infer the cognition of one as having the other as its substratum. Let it be, then, that [the self] is established as the substratum of the experience of objects; to this he says: "Nor by means of the cognition of the cognizable."

Now, it might be argued that consciousness establishes its own adjunct (*upādhi*), but not its objective factor (*karmakāraka*). First, the substratum (*āśraya*) cannot be the adjunct, because [consciousness] does not exist in relation to a [separate] object. If it is claimed that the adjunct is both the substratum and the object, one might ask: what is this so-called "objectivity"? If it is defined as "fitness for empirical usage induced by consciousness," then no; for in that case, even the Self (*ātman*) would become an object. If it is defined as "that which, while being distinct from the substratum, differentiates consciousness," then the consequence follows that the eye (*cakṣus*) would also be an adjunct.

Furthermore, an object cannot be that which is fit for the linguistic usage prompted by it while being distinct from its locus; for this would entail the undesirable consequence that even the relation between consciousness and its locus would itself become an object. Nor can you maintain that such a relation does not exist. Therefore, it is only an entity such as the one in contact [with the senses] that is manifested. If it is argued that [the object] may then be known through another cognition whose object is the self, he says "no"—"nor by another cognition."

Whence [is this]? And is that other cognition simultaneous with the experience of the object, or is it at a different time? Regarding its being at a different time, he states the refutation: "If it were at a different time. If it is argued that they are simultaneous, he says in response: "For it is not simultaneous," because [the self] is partless.

The meaning is that two transformations cannot occur simultaneously, whether in the same location or in different locations. It is impossible for a single entity to undergo two simultaneous movements in their entirety, yet transformation is possible; thus he says, "Let it not be so. He further states, "It must not be thus," because even two transformations cannot occur simultaneously in their entirety—since youth and old age reside in the whole body—and because transformation cannot occur by way of parts, given that [the self] is partless.
Therefore, by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), he concludes that [the self] is immediate due to its self-luminosity.

Anticipating the objection that the substrate must be perceptible by the same sense organ as the object being superimposed, and that mere immediacy (*aparokṣatā*) alone is insufficient for this purpose, the author states the purport of the commentary by citing the example of space: "But [it is not so] anywhere... and so forth.

In this regard, since sound is perceptible by a single external sense organ, and because—like odor—it can be perceived as distinct from a substance, it must be classified as a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*). Since it does not coexist with the four qualities beginning with touch, and since space, time, and mind lack specific qualities while being perceptible by external senses, sound is a specific quality belonging only to a substance distinct from the four elements, the self, space, and so forth. The Vaiśeṣikas and others infer that space (*ākāśa*) possesses this quality.

The Buddhists and the Lokāyatas infer that space (*ākāśa*) is merely the absence of corporeal substance, taking non-apprehension as its logical mark (*liṅga*). For the Prābhākaras, however, space certainly exists and has non-apprehension as its mark, because it is merely the absence of corporeal substance, and because absence is itself a distinct kind of entity (*bhāvāntara*). But the followers of the Kṣapaṇaka-Vārtika maintain that space is perceptible by the eye. If that were so, it would also possess tangibility. If you say, "Let it be so," we reply: no.

Because the operation of the eye and other senses is restricted only to substances possessing color and touch, and because the opening of the eyes is established as having another cause (anyathāsiddha) when there is the perception of a mark for inferring space (ākāśa), it is therefore said that "space is indeed imperceptible. Alternatively: the meaning is that it is immediate (aparokṣa) either by being cognizable by the witness-consciousness or by being accessible to the mind alone. "Blue like a sapphire" means it is blue like a sapphire. The passage beginning with "thus it is not contradictory" has a clear meaning.
The meaning is that they consider that object which, when sublated within its perceived substrate, is ignorance, based on the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) of ignorance.

It is not only by virtue of the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with ignorance that [the world] possesses the nature of ignorance because ignorance is its material cause (*upādāna*); rather, it is also because it is the opposite of knowledge (*vidyā*). Thus he says: "by its distinction from that" (*tadvivekena*). Now, one might object: "If the cessation of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) is established by describing ignorance and demonstrating that it is removable by knowledge, what is the purpose of describing superimposition? He raises this objection with: "If this is so, then superimposition... He replies with: "having introduced... (*prakramya*).

He offers a rebuttal, stating "This is not sound," on the grounds that since a person's desire has as its object the cessation of what is harmful (anartha), it must be stated that it is precisely this harmful thing—which is itself ignorance—that is to be removed by knowledge. Since the harmful thing is essentially of the nature of ignorance, there can in reality be no qualities or defects caused by it either in its locus or in its object; thus, through knowledge, the cessation of all harm will result. He states that the subsequent commentary expresses this very point: "In whatever place there is the superimposition of something..."

First, the absence of both defects and virtues resulting from being the object of the superimposition of ignorance (*avidyādhyāsa*) has already been established. Here, the absence of defects and virtues resulting from being the locus (*āśrayatva*) due to the transformation (*pariṇāmitā*) of that superimposition is being explained. How so? Because the beginningless superimposition of ignorance is illumined by eternal consciousness (*nityacaitanya*), there can be no transformation of superimposition within it. Since the occasional transformation of superimposition has ignorance as its material cause (*upādāna*), the status of the Self as the locus [of that transformation] is established through its connection with ignorance. This is the proposition; the author of the Sūtras implies the cessation of bondage through knowledge, which is here stated as the formal enunciation of the Sūtra.

He states the purport of the subsequent commentary (*uttarabhāṣya*) by first reciting its introductory verse: "Thus, [it begins] with the words 'yuṣmadasmad' etc. Here, perception (*pratyakṣa*) is presented as evidence for the fact that the threefold empirical transaction—characterized by the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge; and the agent, the action, and the result; and the enjoyer, the enjoyment, and the object of enjoyment—is preceded by the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of "I" and "mine" upon the body, the senses, and so forth. Now, one might object: it should rather have been stated that "the scriptures are devoted to injunctions and prohibitions," because the entirety of scripture is centered on those two.

Regarding the question, "What is this 'having liberation as the ultimate goal'?", he says there: "And [the phrase] 'having liberation as the ultimate goal'. He shows that the commentary beginning with "But how, again... concerns an inquiry into another means of proof (*pramāṇa*) for the fact that the threefold empirical transaction has superimposition (*adhyāsa*) as its material cause; he does so starting from "Certainly, ignorance is defined as stated above," etc., and he shows the meaning of the objection "But how, again... by saying, "[Ignorance] rests upon the knower (*pramātṛ*)."

He applies the Bhāṣya to this point—that if the means of valid cognition have as their material cause (upādāna) the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) and the self (ātman), which are fully established through the superimposition (adhyāsa) of ignorance (avidyā), then their very validity cannot be established—by asking: "Or rather, how can they have for their object that which possesses ignorance? He explains why there is an impossibility of validity if the material cause possesses ignorance by saying: "If they have for their object that which possesses ignorance. He introduces the introductory summary statement (vastu-saṃgraha-vākya) of the reply, beginning with "It is said: 'The body, the senses, etc.'", stating that it is the detailed exposition (prapañca) of this very point.

The statement that "the triad of empirical transactions has superimposition as its material cause" is intended to demonstrate presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) and negative inference (*vyatirekyanumāna*). He shows the meaning of the commentary on negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*)—namely, "wherever there is an absence of superimposition, as is agreed upon, there an absence of empirical transaction is observed"—with the words: "For [there is no such transaction] with respect to the body, senses, and so forth. He explains the meaning of the terms "body" and so on, and describes the superimposition by distinguishing them, starting with: "Since there is the conceit of 'I' in the body," and so on.

In order to demonstrate another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he restates the perception regarding the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) which is the root of the three types of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*): "For every man [thinks] 'I am [this]'. Herein is the formal argument (*prayoga*): The waking and dreaming states of Devadatta possess the transactions of being a knower (*pramātṛtva*) and so forth, preceded by the superimpositions of "I" and "mine" upon his own body, senses, and other instruments; because they are times other than his state of deep sleep; for whatever time does not possess such transactions is not a time other than his state of deep sleep, just like his state of deep sleep itself.

Alternatively, the threefold empirical transaction is untenable without the superimposition shown as its material cause; for in the state of deep sleep, no such transaction is observed in the absence of superimposition—this is the argument from presumption (arthāpatti).

Now, in worldly transaction, only the relation of agent and instrument is required, not the relation of identity; thus, in order to exclude other possible relations within the two arguments of residual inference (*pariśeṣānumāna*) and presumption (*arthāpatti*), he states that it is not first of all the relation of owner and owned, saying: "not by way of the related term 'ownership'" (*na svatvena saṃbandhinā*). The reason for this is that [the relation of ownership] exists even during deep sleep (*suṣupta*); this is an additional argument. Furthermore, it is precisely the state of being subject to the will [of the agent] that is the cause for worldly transaction.

He raises an objection: "In the absence of that [the relationship], there would be a reversal of worldly activity during deep sleep"—thus another says, "[The relationship is] the state of following the will of the Self. Let it be granted that the relationship between the one who enjoins and the one who is enjoined exists by means of mere will; what follows from that? To this he replies: "From that, of the Self. But what is the proof here that worldly activity is rooted in this relationship? To this he says: "And thus, 'I am rising. [Objection: Even servants and others follow His will; therefore, worldly activity might also occur through His body.

"No," he says, "for that [relationship] does not exist in the case of servants and the like. It is replied: if the relationship were merely the capacity for compliance with one's will, then since that exists even in deep sleep (*suṣupta*), there would have to be worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) even then. If, on the other hand, the relationship were actual compliance through will, then because of its absence in one who is extremely ill, the worldly transaction of being a knower (*pramātṛtva*) and so forth would not occur. Now, if it is argued that this relationship is observed to be the root of worldly transaction, he says "no": "This is not appropriate for one who has great respect for consciousness (*saṃvit*)."

Nor is it figurative, because that would contradict direct experience; thus he says with the words beginning "gauṇī" (figurative). He further states that desire is also rooted in superimposition, saying: "Moreover, even desire is a particular modification. He explains that desire is indeed rooted in the superimposition of the internal organ, saying: "Moreover, even desire is a particular modification. Regarding the point that it is rooted in the superimposition of the internal organ, he cites perception as proof, saying: "And such is the experience. Furthermore, conjunction or inherence between the Self and the non-Self cannot be the cause of worldly transaction, because they exist even during deep sleep.

This is because [the relationship between] the enjoyer and the enjoyed—such as being produced by one's own karma, being governed by one's own senses, and so forth—depends upon the superimposition (adhyāsa) of experience and the like; furthermore, these characteristics exist even in the bodies of servants and others. If it is argued that "being the object of enjoyment without mediation" constitutes the fundamental connection (mūlasambandha), then if this connection is defined as "fitness for enjoyment," it exists even during deep sleep (suṣupti). If, however, the connection is defined as "being currently experienced without mediation," that is not the case; for while the Self is indeed unmediated from all bodies, places, and times, one must still seek the fundamental connection specifically for the occurrence of experience in this particular body.

Therefore, this other type of relation is of no consequence. Consequently, by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*) and through both presumptive reasoning (*arthāpatti*) and inference (*anumāna*), it is established that superimposition (*adhyāsa*) alone is the root of all worldly transaction; thus he concludes: "Therefore, although [the Self] is itself unattached..."

[Objection: Since the proximity of the Self is no different with respect to all bodies, how can there be a restriction of superimposition (adhyāsa) to this body alone? [Reply: Superimposition consisting of ignorance (avidyā) is beginningless. Because it is a transformation (*pariṇāma*) of that [ignorance], or because it is produced by the subtle body (*sūkṣma-śarīra*) which is its effect, or because of its conjunction with it, the restriction of superimposition to the gross body (*sthūla-śarīra*) is not contradictory. [Objection: Is it not the case that the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) alone is the locus of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), and not superimposition? [Reply: No; for the very state of being a cognizer is fully established through superimposition. Thus he says: "Therefore, even though... and so forth.

As for the claim that the invalidity of the means of valid cognition arises because their material cause is the ego-sense—which is fully established through superimposition and conjoined with the self—if by this you mean the loss of that validity which consists in revealing reality (defined as non-sublation by any means of valid cognition within the limits of the perceived substrate), then that is indeed admitted.

Now, if it is argued that when the aspect of ultimate reality (*paramārthasatyatva*) is sublated by scripture (*āgama*), there is a loss of its validity because it ceases to be a factor for things capable of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra-samartha-vastu*), we say no; for there is no such sublation in that case. Thus he says: "In the same way, of those [means of knowledge] which are independent... [and] "...shown by way of affirmation. The meaning is that both are demonstrated: its being a factor for worldly transaction by means of perception (*pratyakṣa*), and its having superimposition (*adhyāsa*) as its root by means of perception, inference (*anumāna*), and presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). Furthermore, this is because it possesses causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-samarthatva*).

Even though words and other means of knowledge are false, their status as causes for purposeful action—characterized by the cessation of ignorance through the perception of sound and so forth, and by the realization of Brahman—is not contradicted.

[Objection: But surely, validity would follow from the correspondence with successful purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). [Reply: No—for the capacity for purposeful action is ascertained precisely from the comprehension of the object, just as the reality of the object is known from cognition itself. Otherwise, even for you, validity would follow merely from the cognition of such reality. [Objection: Since the cognition of Brahman also has superimposition (*adhyāsa*) as its material cause, it too falls into the category of being false. [Reply: If you mean falsity in terms of its own nature (*svarūpa*), that is indeed admitted. But if you mean falsity in terms of its object (*viṣaya*), that does not apply to Brahman, because there is no sublation (*bādhā*) of it.

The world of phenomenal plurality (*prapañca*) is false precisely because it is sublated; it is not so because it is known through a cognition that has superimposition as its material cause. Now, one might object: "Is it not observed that what is produced by a defective cause is also false in respect to its object? To this he says: "But the defect is adventitious. A defect is called a "defect" when it arises subsequently while the causes of valid cognition are already present; such a defect is said to be "adventitious. That which exists as a defect only by virtue of being a cause of valid cognition is not a defect, because it functions as a cause.

However, the superimposition of ignorance (*avidyādhyāsa*) is a defect only with respect to the manifestation of non-duality as consciousness (*caitanya*), not with respect to the manifestation of duality, because that [dual manifestation] is its very cause. Just as a defect of the eye such as a cataract is not a defect when it leads to the inference of the arising of a particular sinful vision, since it serves as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in that regard; such is the meaning. Precisely because it is a defect of consciousness, it manifests an object suitable for empirical transaction (*vyavahāra*) which is the opposite of the Brahman that is to be revealed by that consciousness and is beyond empirical transaction.

And avidyā is a defect because it obstructs the manifestation of consciousness in its true form and is the cause of its appearing otherwise. To the objection—"How can there be the notion of a 'defect' in something adventitious, but not in something innate?"—the author states a mere illustrative example: "And not in that which is common to all. Now, one might argue that the Commentator has stated that even from the perspective of the object, a defect alone is the cause for the falsity of knowledge; to this he replies: "And a defect that is not innate..."

[Objection: "Surely, worldly activity on the part of the non-discriminating will have its root in superimposition (adhyāsa), but that of the discriminating will not. [Reply: No; he says this, stating "and for this reason also, as in the case of animals and so forth. By the example of animals and so forth, he demonstrates that worldly activity has its root in superimposition—namely, "and thus animals and so forth. He states that the worldly activity which serves as the probans (hetu) in the inference of superimposition exists even among the discriminating, as a property of the subject (pakṣadharmatā)—namely, "they share the same acquisition and preservation (yogakṣema)."

In that context, because a cause is observed, one infers the presence of something possessing that cause—namely, "because of observing an effect of a uniform nature. He raises a proof for the existence of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) even in the case of the example of cattle and so forth: "Now, as for cattle and so forth... When two objects are perceived, if their difference is not apprehended through perception, inference, or scripture, superimposition remains as the only possibility; thus he says: "for those of mature intellect. He points out the defect in the view that there is a discernment of difference through natural perception: "It is exactly thus..."

One might object: "Since we observe that even those devoid of investigation through inference and scripture engage in practical activity regarding unseen objects, it follows that discrimination is grasped by perception alone. To this he replies with the objection: "Now, cowherds, women, and so forth... He answers: "Discrimination is not grasped by perception, but rather from the words of a reliable authority," stating: "...it is the practice of those who know it. Furthermore, he says: "And thus, when they are questioned... [implying] that if discrimination were perceptible, they would specifically realize the inner self.

Therefore, he states that the concluding statement is justified: "Hence, what was said is correct. That superimposition (adhyāsa) has as its very time the time of that worldly transaction; and that [superimposition] is common to both animals and those who possess discrimination.

Thus far, the perception and other means of knowledge have been restated as they were previously mentioned. The commentary (*bhāṣya*), which states, "Not by that [self] whose nature is not superimposed," was not explained earlier; it is now explained in this section on the restatement. Here, the following doubt arises: "Granted that superimposition is the cause of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*); nevertheless, like silver and so forth, superimposition is merely the efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*) of the transaction, while the Self alone is the material cause (*upādāna*. To this, he replies: "Not by that [Self] whose nature is not superimposed, because [the Self] is unattached (*asaṅga*)."

The meaning is as follows: since superimpositions such as that of silver are not included within the category of the locus of empirical transaction (*vyavahāra*), and since the empirical transaction of being a knower (*pramātṛtva*) and so forth is observed in the Self even without them, it is logical that they function merely as instrumental causes (*nimittakāraṇa*). In this case, however, because [the superimposition] is included within the very locus of the transaction, and because no empirical transaction is observed in the pure Self during deep sleep, and because the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*) is more fundamental, it is proper to postulate that superimposition—which possesses positive and negative concomitance—is itself the material cause with respect to empirical transaction.

The phrase "the scripture, moreover" expresses a doubt regarding the subsequent commentary. The phrase "of that too" states its intended meaning (*tātparya*). The phrase "in the case of scriptural [activity]," however, permits the cognition of a distinction (*vyatireka-jñāna*) regarding activity for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭārtha*). He challenges this permission with the words: "But surely, [in the case of] the fruit and the obligatory..."

First, regarding the injunction for results (*phalacodanā*): since animals and the like can be obtained in this very life, and since the pleasure produced by them—namely heaven—is not the result of the injunction for animals but is logically the result of the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and other sacrifices, and since unsurpassed bliss is possible in this very life, [the injunction] does not necessitate an *ātman* connected with another body. This is even more so in the case of the injunctions for obligatory (*naiyamika*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites, because they are devoid of results; or, if they were to have results, those could be experienced through the visible [body] alone.

However, since the fruit of expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is the eradication of defects, and since the fruit of those defects can be experienced in this very life, and since another birth is of such a nature [that it would not serve this purpose], and because—in the absence of the appearance of the fruit—it is logical to postulate an obstruction due to a deficiency in its constituent parts (*aṅga*) or an absence of auxiliary conditions, as in the case of the *Kārīrī* sacrifice; and since the enjoyment of heaven and so forth is possible even with this very body through the power of mantras, medicines, and the like, there is no utility in the knowledge of the soul's transcendence of the body.

In this regard, he offers a rebuttal by accepting that the fruit such as heaven—which consists of enjoyments of specific places, times, bodies, and so forth—is established through the authority of the mantras and other sources according to the principle of the section on deities (*devatādhikaraṇa*): "That is true; nevertheless... and so on.

[Objection: "Is it not the case that the distinct Self is sought by the injunctions (*codanā*) themselves, without depending on the authority of the concordance with mantras and so forth? For the author of the Commentary (*bhāṣyakāra*), who was engaged in determining *karma* alone, has already defined the Self. To this, he says: "And thus, [it is] in the operation of the injunctions" (*vidhivṛtte*). The meaning is: if it is indeed required by the injunctions, then it must also be [the subject of] the Sūtra. [Objection: He raises an objection, saying, "For what reason?"—arguing that it is improper for the author of the Commentary to expound something that is neither required nor mentioned in the Sūtra.

He offers a rebuttal by stating that this very Self was indeed indicated indirectly through the authority of the mantras and other sources by means of the portion of the Sūtra: "That is the authority, according to Bādarāyaṇa, because of its independence," following the declaration of the inquiry into Dharma as an investigation into matters of what is to be accomplished.

Thus, having relied upon the authority of the Sūtra’s meaning even regarding a matter of past fact through traditional succession, the Commentator has conducted this inquiry into the Self; how then is it understood that he did not rely solely on the power of Vedic injunction (*codanā*)? To this, he says: "And likewise, for an injunction [can refer] to what is past. If it is then argued that since it depends on injunction, the concordance (*samanvaya*) should also be described right here, he says "no": "And that is the comprehension of its own nature."

[Objection: "But surely, since it is not required even when one is striving for *dharma*, the inquiry into the self (*ātmavicāra*) must indeed be performed. [Reply: No, he says—because of the lack of utility. For *dharma* alone does not require a distinct self; rather, it requires the fruit (*phala*). And Jaimini does not exert effort toward the fruit. [Objection: "If he does require the fruit, then effort toward that is appropriate. [Reply: No; because it is established otherwise, he says: "But the Blessed One, moreover... and so forth.

Now, it might be objected that in that [passage] Brahman alone was investigated, and not the fruit of an injunction; to this he replies: "And in that [case], [the fruit] is to be experienced in another body. And the phrase "all that" has a clear meaning.

[Objection: But surely, since the existence of a self distinct [from the body] is established by the very power of the *samanvaya* (correlative connection), the inquiry into the self is like grinding what has already been ground. [Reply: No, he says—“and its establishment” (*tatsiddhiśca*). [Objection: But since the Word (*śabda*) lacks authority regarding that which is accessible through other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), as well as regarding their absence or contradiction, there is no establishment of the self. To this he replies: “Therefore, he exerted himself for its establishment. This means: by means of an inquiry whose fruit is the removal of contradictions.

He briefly demonstrates the point stated in the passage beginning with "it would be established even without that": "But that exists. This means that there is authoritative validity regarding past objects—that is, regarding [objects such as] heaven and so forth. "Not without that" means not without a distinct self (ātman). Now, one might object: in the *Devatādhikaraṇa*, both the author of the Sūtras and the author of the Bhāṣya have explicitly stated that there is no authoritative validity for mantras and the like regarding deities and such things; how then can they believe that authoritative validity is accepted by the force of a portion of the Sūtra? This is not a fault.

In that regard, [the claim that] the deity possesses a physical form (vigrahavat) is not intended to imply a lack of authority [for the Veda], because it would entail the consequence that the deity is an auxiliary factor acting through direct contact (sannipatyopakāraka), which contradicts the non-perception of such a thing despite its being suitable for perception; furthermore, it was stated with the intention of pointing out a contradiction regarding the ritual action (karman), since even the indicative marks (liṅga) found in explanatory passages (arthavāda) are cited here and there in the *Twelve Chapters* (Mīmāṃsāsūtra) as authoritative means of knowledge.

Nevertheless, the commentary on the passage beginning with "not to be known through the Vedāntas" is clear in its meaning. In that context, by the words "beyond hunger and so forth," the connection with the agent, the connection with the qualified [adhikārin], and the connection with the enjoyer are respectively refuted. Furthermore, the commentary on the passage beginning with "and previously" explains: "from the comprehension of the meaning of the sentence 'That thou art' (tat tvam asi)," and so on.

Furthermore, some maintain that there is no contradiction between the knowledge of distinction (*vyatireka-jñāna*) and the coexistence of superimposition (*adhyāsa*), because they are distinguished as indirect and direct [cognitions], much like the cognition of two moons. Others hold that since the subtle body (*sūkṣma-śarīra*) is an effect of the ignorance of the Self (*ātma-avidyā*), and because cause and effect stand in a relation of both difference and non-difference, superimposition persists even when there is knowledge of distinction, due to the close connection of the gross body with the subtle body—like fire and a mass of iron. The underlying point is that in every case, superimposition does not cease as long as direct realization (*aparokṣa-jñāna*) has not occurred.

"Therefore" concludes the proof for superimposition (*adhyāsa*). Furthermore, the establishment of superimposition is not achieved by perception, inference, and presumption alone; rather, scripture (*āgama*) also demonstrates the appearance of identity between the conscious and the unconscious, by addressing the qualified performer of an injunction through terms such as "Brāhmaṇa" and so forth. He shows this very point with the words "For instance" (*tathā hi*). "One who is suffering from a chronic illness" (*jyogāmayāvī*) means one who is afflicted by a severe disease.

He introduces the definition-commentary (lakṣaṇabhāṣya) beginning with "That which is called superimposition," preceded by a mention of its occurrence, with the words: "Having thus established the existence of superimposition," and so forth. To the question, "Why is there a restatement of the definition already stated here? he replies: "Of what [object] belonging to the category of 'you' (yuṣmad-artha)... He applies the commentary with the words: "In what [object] belonging to the category of 'I' (asmad-artha)... and so forth.

He states that the subsequent commentary is intended to demonstrate, by way of analysis, the superimposition (adhyāsa) already shown through perception in the passage beginning with "placing the mutual superimposition of the self and the non-self before oneself," etc.: "To this he says: 'For example, in the case of one's son, wife, and so forth,' etc. Likewise, the preceding portion of the text up to "the attributes of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa)" has a clear meaning.

In this context, in order to state that the prior superimposition occurs upon that which is already qualified by each subsequent superimposition, he explains the meaning of the word "self" (ātman) by saying, "and the object of the 'I'-notion (asmadartha) is conjoined with the subject of the 'I'-notion (ahampratyayin). Now, one might object: "Is not the body also superimposed? Why then does he say only 'attributes' (dharmāḥ)? To this he replies: "even the substratum (dharmin)"—the word "grasping" (grahaṇa) is to be supplied here. [The opponent asks: "If so, why was the word 'attribute' (dharma) used? To this he replies: "but the word 'attribute'... [and so forth].
And because superimposition upon dharma (dharma-adhyāsa) is primary as it is the root of all scriptural usage, he states that it is grasped primarily: "and caused by that."

[Objection: "But surely desires and the like are attributes of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); since they are understood as being related [to the Self] like a person who is to be punished (*daṇḍya*), they do not deserve to be superimposed [upon the Self]. [Reply: To this he says, "so too the attributes of the internal organ, such as desire and the like. For it is thus: because they exist when the internal organ exists and are absent in deep sleep when it is absent, desires and the like are superimposed as attributes of the internal organ in the sense of a relation [of association], and not in the sense of identity (*tādātmya*). This is the meaning.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the positive and negative concomitances (anvaya-vyatireka) of desire and so forth—which inhere only in the self—and of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) are established as otherwise accounted for (anyathāsiddha) by virtue of their being instruments? [Reply: No; because an effect is necessarily dependent upon its cause, whereas there is no such necessity regarding an instrument; because the postulation of a material cause (upādāna) is more appropriate than the postulation of an instrument; and because of the existence of other instruments such as the eyes.

If it is argued that the self must also be another material cause because of the perceptual cognition "I am desirous" and so forth, we say no; for this is a cognition of a relation, like [the cognition] "one who possesses a staff," whereas if it were a material cause, there would be identity, and the cognition would have to be "I am desire. Therefore, the meaning is that positive and negative concomitance, supported by reasoning, postulates the internal organ alone as the material cause of desire and the rest. The passage beginning with "The internal organ is [the substrate] of the one who has the notion of 'I'" is clear in its meaning.

He explains the two terms “the witness of all its own movements” and “the inner self” with the words beginning with “by the word *sva* [he means] the knot of the ego,” and so forth. He states the meaning of the word “witness” with the words beginning with “by way of non-attachment and changelessness,” and so forth. But how can there be an “inward movement” (*pratyag-añcana*) of the Self, which is within all? He says—in response to this—that it is “with respect to the delusion of entering within the object of mental concentration for one whose consciousness is diffused through the body and other such things,” using the expression “that very [Self] as ‘this’ in the body and so forth.”

[Objection: But surely the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is not known by direct perception (*sākṣivedya*); rather, it is to be inferred from the capacity for the sequential production of cognitions when the self, the sense organs, and the objects are all present together. [Reply: No; because that is established otherwise (*anyathāsiddhatvāt*). The sequential production of cognitions is established otherwise simply by postulating that the self alone possesses the capacity for the sequential generation of cognitions. Furthermore, since it is more parsimonious (*lāghava*) to postulate the capacity for sequence in the well-known self than to postulate the existence of another substance and its capacity for sequence, the latter is a more cumbersome assumption.

[Objection: "Surely I do not postulate the mind through *arthāpatti* (presumption), which would allow for [the argument's] being established otherwise; rather, I do so through inference (*anumāna*). For instance: the production of successive effects by the self, despite its proximity to all objects, depends upon an instrument that acts successively; because the self, though having many objects present, produces effects successively, just as Devadatta, who has many things to be cut down at hand, cuts them successively depending upon an axe. [Reply: This is not sound, regarding the mind.

Because [the reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to the successive operation of contact with each sense-organ when devoid of any other common cause; because it is also inconclusive with respect to the successive contact with space during the falling of a fruit from a tree and with respect to the operation of an axe and so forth; and because it is also inconclusive with respect to the operation of the sense-organs in their contact with their respective objects.

Now, suppose it is thought: "The production of a specific quality (viśeṣaguṇa) depends upon a non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa) characterized by conjunction with another substance within its own substratum, because it is the production of a specific quality in an eternal substance, like the redness produced by heating (pākaja-lauhitya) residing in atoms generated by conjunction with fire"—and that which is this other substance is the mind (manas). This is not so.

Since the conjunction of the body and the sense organs is established, it is impossible to infer a conjunction with another substance [in the case of mental perception]. Furthermore, because the conjunction with the body and other [organs] persists even in cognitions such as dreams and memory, it is illogical to postulate a conjunction with another substance. Therefore, neither inference nor presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) serves as a means of valid cognition for the mind. Moreover, the existence of the mind is already established by scripture (*āgama*), and it is not an object of the senses.
