If the mind were of atomic dimension, it would be incapable [of perceiving objects], like an atom; if it were of infinite dimension, simultaneous conjunctions with all sense organs would lead to the undesirable consequence of the simultaneous arising of cognitions; and if it were of intermediate dimension, since the mind is perceived even during the state of dreaming despite the absence of the sense organs, and because of the experience "my mind has gone elsewhere," the mind is indeed known by the witness-consciousness alone.

Furthermore, it has been shown that there is a superimposition of the inner self (pratyagātman) upon the internal organ and so forth; however, this is incorrect. For if there were a mutual superimposition, both would be the objects superimposed, which would lead to the consequence of both being false. Moreover, if both were the substrata, there would be no distinct manifestation of their specific characteristics. To this, he says: "If [it were] only of the object denoted by 'you' (*yuṣmad-artha*)," etc. The meaning is this: in the case of a superimposition of one upon the other, there would be a manifestation of the generality of one and a manifestation of the particularity of the other alone.

In this context, the manifestation of the distinction between the two in the form of "conscious" and "insentient" leads one to infer their mutual superimposition (*itaretarādhyāsa*), because the manifestation of a distinction is invariably preceded by the state of being superimposed. Nor does this entail the falsity of both; for there is no superimposition of the conscious self’s own nature (*svarūpa*) upon the insentient, since they are superimposed only as being conjoined (*saṃsṛṣṭatayā*). Furthermore, the manifestation of a distinction does not contradict the status of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*); for the distinction is not perceived as a property of the substrate itself, but rather as a property belonging to another substrate.

The text, however, has a clear meaning. Now, one might object: "Superimposition is not possible between two things that appear as both general and particular; if there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), it must be figurative. To this he says, "There is no dispute here. Again, one might object: "It was stated that the appearance of particulars contradicts superimposition. To this he says, "For nothing is impossible in what is actually perceived. He addresses the objection that the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "in the internal organ and so forth" is contradictory by saying, "But surely [superimposition occurs] only in the internal organ upon the inner self (*pratyagātman*)."

"How is it that superimposition occurs only for that which is qualified by the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa)? To this he says: "Precisely for that reason, by its reversal. But [one might ask]: "In that Bhāṣya, how is it stated that superimposition belongs only to the qualified [self]? He replies: "By the force of the mention of attributes (dharma)," namely: "Otherwise, for that which consists of the single essence of pure consciousness alone..."

Although the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) for the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) upon consciousness with respect to an object, nevertheless, it is consciousness itself, as delimited by the object, that constitutes the manifestation; thus, he says, "You have spoken the truth," intending that it was stated [as such] with reference to the appearance of the internal organ. The meaning is that this very object attains the status of being effective toward the Self.

[Objection: But surely, even externally, a connection of the *ahaṅkāra* with consciousness appears in such instances as "I am a human being," and so forth. To this he says: "For this very reason, [it is said] 'in the intellect (*buddhi*) and so on. The meaning is that the delusion of selfhood (*ātmatva-vibhrama*) regarding all objects arises solely from the cognition of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*); otherwise, since the *ahaṅkāra* would be non-different from consciousness, the realization would be that the *ahaṅkāra* itself is the Self.

Now, at the time of the introduction, the portion of the text beginning with "This worldly transaction is innate" and ending before "which impels [one] toward agency and enjoyership" is of clear meaning. Here, all disputants other than the Sāṅkhyas maintain that superimposition (adhyāsa) is the sole cause of activity for that which possesses the powers of agency and enjoyership by its very nature; he refutes them with the words, "therefore, [it is] the agent and the enjoyer. The passage beginning with "perceived by the whole world" is of clear meaning.

He states the purport of the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the words "of this cause of evil" (*asyānarthahetoḥ*), preceded by a reference to what has already occurred: "Thus, first of all, of those two which are [implied] by the sense of the Sūtra..."

[Objection: Should it not rather be said, "for the sake of abandoning what is harmful," and not "for the sake of abandoning the cause"? To this he says: "Because of the abandonment of the cause. He raises an objection against the statement of the purpose: "But surely superimposition, being beginningless, is the cause of what is harmful. [Reply: It might be argued that it should cease through the authority of the scripture; but no, because it contradicts direct perception. Thus he says: "For instance, [the superimposition of] humanity and so forth..."

He resolves [the objection] by stating, "This is not a fault," for neither having a beginning nor being beginningless is the cause of destruction or non-destruction; rather, it is the presence or absence of a contradictory factor. In the world, for instance, even an unoriginated prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) ceases to exist.

The Sugatas maintain that through the excellence of the cultivation of reality (*tattva-paribhāvanā-prakarṣa*), the stream of beginningless latent impressions (*anādi-vāsanā-santāna*) is brought to cessation. The Naiyāyikas and others also hold that the beginningless flow of false knowledge (*mithyājñāna-pravāha*) and the blackness of atoms (*paramāṇu-śyāmatā*) are likewise ceased. The Sāṅkhyas maintain that beginningless non-discrimination (*aviveka*) is ceased by means of discrimination (*viveka*). The Mīmāṃsakas and others hold that the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of the current knowledge of the true nature of Dharma, though beginningless, is ceased. If it is argued that a beginningless entity (*bhāva-rūpa*) does not cease—just like the Self (*ātman*)—we say no; for ignorance (*ajñāna*) is indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*).

The general rule (*sāmānyavyāpti*) is that "what is beginningless does not cease," whereas the specific rule (*viśeṣavyāpti*) is that "ignorance ceases through knowledge"; therefore, the latter alone is more powerful. [Objection: But destruction is the subsequent state occurring within its own material cause (*upādāna*); how then can there be the destruction of that which is beginningless and lacks a material cause? [Reply: No, because it is sufficient that it be the subsequent state occurring within its own substrate (*āśraya*). Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the blackness of atoms and so forth could never cease. [Objection: Because of its difference from non-existence (*abhāva*), ignorance—like the Self (*ātman*)—cannot cease. [Reply: No.

Since it possesses characteristics distinct from existence, why should its cessation not be like that of antecedent non-existence? What, then, is the definitive conclusion? It has been stated that the distinction consists in the concomitance with either knowledge or ignorance.

As for the objection that superimposition does not cease even when there is knowledge of difference, he replies: "From such sentences as 'That thou art' (*tattvamasi*). Now, one might ask: what is the distinction between the knowledge of difference and the knowledge of Brahman as the Self regarding the cessation of superimposition? To this he says: "For that [knowledge] cuts off [the Self] from Brahman. Furthermore, it has been shown through scripture and the presumption of its meaning (*arthāpatti*) that transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) is not caused by a lack of understanding of difference, but rather by a lack of understanding of Brahman. Therefore, the sense is that it ceases upon the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).

[Objection: Surely knowledge is the remover of ignorance alone; how then can there be the removal of superimposition? To this he says: "Therefore, upon the removal of the cause... [Objection: But even the notion of "I" (ahaṃpratyaya) has, in its actual object, Brahman as its true nature; why then does it not remove ignorance? He says: "But the notion of 'I'... because it does not manifest the identity of Brahman and the Self. [Objection: Surely another cognition arising from inquiry and discrimination would remove it; no, he says: "Nor another cognition... because it is a cognition lacking valid authority (apramāṇa).

Now, one might object that the purpose of the scripture is not merely the cessation of what is undesirable (*anartha*), but rather the attainment of unsurpassed Brahman-bliss; thus, he again challenges the statement regarding the purpose: "But is it not heard that Brahman is unsurpassed bliss? [The author replies: Just as the attainment of bliss is the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman produced by the scripture, so too is the cessation of what is undesirable heard in the scriptures; how then can there be a challenge to the purpose? To this he says: "But surely, of the undesirable as well..."

[Objection: "In that case, the entire fruit must be proclaimed, not merely a portion of the fruit. [Reply: He raises this objection with the words, "Then both... [The author replies: No; the attainment of bliss (ānandāvāpti) need not be stated as the purpose (prayojana), because the status of being a purpose is established by the very fact of its being indicated as the object (viṣaya), since a person's desire is fulfilled by that alone. Thus, the completeness of the purpose is established through both scripture and meaning, and the indication of the object is obtained; therefore, this designation is appropriate. This he says with the words beginning, "It need not be stated," and so forth.

[Objection: "Let it be that the identity of Brahman and the Self (*brahmātmatā*) alone is the subject matter (*viṣaya*), while the attainment of bliss (*ānandāvāpti*) should be specified separately as the purpose (*prayojana*). [Reply: No, he says—"And that [attainment] is not external to the subject matter. The meaning is that the very identity of Brahman and the Self is the attainment of bliss. [Objection: "Since the cessation of evil (*anarthanivṛtti*) is also included within the scope of the statement regarding the fruit, that too must be the subject matter of the scripture. [Reply: No, he says—"The destruction of evil along with its root. The point is that the identity of Brahman and the Self alone is the subject matter of the scripture, whereas the fruit is established by implication.

In that case, he says—"Then the cessation of evil is indeed the subject matter of the scripture concerning the identity of Brahman and the Self, not the subject matter of the statement regarding the fruit"—meaning that even the grasping of the cause of evil [is included]. Now, one might object: "But even in sentences such as 'That thou art,' the cessation of evil is not understood as a subject matter. To this he replies: "Because in all the Vedāntas... The meaning is that although the meaning of the sentence is positive in nature, since the referent of the word "Brahman" is presented precisely as being characterized by the absence of evil, that too is a subject matter.

One might object: "Is there not no sentence that establishes the meaning of individual words, but rather only one that establishes identity? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "For example, 'Being alone, my dear, this was in the beginning,' and so forth; [this] constitutes a single sentence by way of presenting [the identity]. The meaning is this: because the referent of the word *brahman* is not an object of worldly experience, having established that referent, the sentence consisting of the statement of identity forms a single syntactical unit. One might further object: "If Brahman is devoid of phenomenal expansion (*niṣprapañca*) and is the subject matter of the scripture, how can the cessation of the miseries residing in the individual soul (*jīva*) be the subject matter of the scripture? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "That being so, by means of such a referent of the word *tat* (That)."

Even so, he offers this rebuttal: "If that is the case, [then] the inherent absence of conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañcatā*) is the subject matter of the scripture, whereas the removal of ignorance and its effects is obtained through the power of realizing the identity of Brahman as the self devoid of conceptual proliferation; it is not itself the subject matter of the scripture, because the non-appearance of ignorance and its effects—which is the very opposite of their appearance—cannot be established by the scripture. Thus he says: "If that is so, [the removal of ignorance] is inseparable from the realization of Brahman as the self."

Now, it might be argued: "Just as the meaning of the sentence cannot be realized as qualified by the absence of that [illusory object] because of its contradiction with the illusory ignorance and its effects, so too, because of the contradiction with the appearance of the world in Brahman, Brahman devoid of the world cannot be made known as the Self through such scriptural passages as 'not gross' (asthūla) and so forth. To this it is replied: First of all, the world is not established in Brahman by means of perception and other such pramāṇas, since Brahman is not the object of those [means of knowledge]; nor is the connection of Brahman with the world understood merely by the establishment of the world itself.

Because that [scripture] merely imagines the cause [of the world]. Now, one might object: "In passages such as 'All this is what this Self is,' the world-appearance (prapañca) manifests within Brahman. True; however, since those passages—by restating the universal identity of Brahman established through the capacity of Brahman as the material cause of all—serve to provide the objects to be negated, they are syntactically connected with the prohibitive sentences as a single coherent whole, and thus they do not contradict the state of being devoid of the world-appearance.

Furthermore, even if it were established that [Brahman] is the self of all by virtue of being the material cause of everything, its state of being the self of all could not be demonstrated through sentences containing manifold conceptual elaborations (prapañca). Nor, when it is possible for negative sentences to form a single syntactical unit with others by supplying the objects to be negated, [can they be taken otherwise].

By making a division of the sentence, it is possible to cognize independently that which possesses manifoldness (saprapañca) as being purposeful, while that which is devoid of manifoldness (niṣprapañca) is contrary to human purpose and devoid of purpose. Furthermore, the state of the conscious self being free from manifoldness during deep sleep is observed to be a human goal. It is also heard in scripture: "Having realized that which is soundless, touchless, formless, and imperishable, one is released from the jaws of death. Moreover, the state of the conscious self possessing manifoldness is observed to be productive of evil, and no fruit [resulting from it] is heard of in scripture.

Therefore, the syntactic unity with the prohibitions is abandoned. Nor does the appearance of the restatement of the phenomenal world (prapañca)—which is the object of prohibition—sublate the cognition of the non-phenomenal (niṣprapañca), because that restatement exists for the sake of that [prohibition].

Now, an objection is raised: having first established the non-existent phenomenal world (*prapañca*) in Brahman by means of sentences describing it as possessing such a world, its subsequent negation would indeed be useless, according to the maxim: "It is better to avoid touching mud from afar than to wash it off. To this it is replied: For the sake of realizing the non-dual Brahman, the phenomenal world—which is already implied in Brahman by the very power of the teaching that He is the material cause of the entire universe—is restated and then negated; this negation is appropriate for the sake of accomplishing the supreme human goal of non-duality.

[Objection: But then, by the very power of being the material cause of all, the cognition of the world as having manifoldness (*saprapañcatā*) would necessarily follow. [Reply: No; for when there is a contradiction with a direct scriptural negation of that manifoldness which was established by the power of scripture, the former is weaker. [Objection: In that case, the attainment of manifoldness through its being the material cause of all does not occur. [Reply: No; for as long as it is not sublated, the appearance of manifoldness occurs precisely by the power of its being the material cause as taught in scripture, just like the appearance of silver in mother-of-pearl and similar cases.

Only that which has already been established is sublated by a stronger means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), not that which is unestablished, nor that which has already been cognized. Furthermore, Brahman is not cognized in such a way (as having manifoldness) by the sentences containing elaboration (*saprapañca*) read within the context of meditative worship (*upāsanā*); for those [sentences] have other purposes and are contradicted by sentences whose sole purpose is [the realization of Brahman]; because meditation is possible even through a superimposed form; and because the sentences concerning creation, being intended to provide the objects to be negated for the realization of non-dual Brahman, merely serve to establish what is already [provisionally] established. Therefore, neither verbal nor worldly cognition is obstructed in the case of the cognition of Brahman as the Self devoid of elaboration (*niṣprapañca*).

[Objection: But surely the individual soul (*jīva*) is also the object of the comprehension of the meaning of the [great] sentence; since that world of manifestation (*prapañca*) is known through perception, how can there be comprehension of the meaning of a sentence whose content is the absence of manifestation? [Reply: It is said in response: First of all, the world of manifestation consisting of agency and so forth is not cognizable through inference and the like, because it is immediately present (*aparokṣatvāt*). Nor is it cognizable by the eyes and other external senses, because the inner self (*pratyagātman*) is not an object of the external organs. If it is argued that it is cognizable through mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*), what is the proof for that? If it is argued that positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*) are the proof—namely, that bondage is perceived in the self while the mind exists, and is not perceived when the mind is absent in deep sleep—that is not correct.

Because it is otherwise established (*anyathāsiddhatva*); for even as the cause of the existence of the manifold of agency and so forth within the Self, positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) are possible. Furthermore, regarding the non-appearance of agency and so forth during deep sleep, there is doubt as to whether it is due to the absence of the mind or due to its own [the Self's] own absence, since the negative concomitance is thus doubtful. If it is argued that cognition also requires an instrument, we say no; for manifestation is possible through the very consciousness of the Self itself, without any intervention.

Now, it may be argued that the Buddhists and the Prābhākaras postulate that even agency, enjoyership, attachment, aversion, pleasure, pain, and so forth, are self-luminous within the Self; however, this is not tenable. If these [qualities] were substances, it would be more parsimonious (laghīyaḥ) to postulate a single quality of luminosity for the Self itself and then derive the luminosity of the others through their inherence in that [Self], rather than postulating multiple qualities of luminosity for those [others] and thereby postulating the luminosity of the Self as qualified by them. Furthermore, if they are qualities, they cannot be self-luminous because a quality cannot possess another quality.

If it is argued that these [states] themselves possess the quality of luminosity (*prakāśaguṇa*), we say no; for the quality of luminosity does not arise within its own substrate, as is the case with the sun and other such objects. Furthermore, the fact that bondage is never perceived apart from its own existence does not imply that it is self-luminous (*svayaṃprakāśamāna*); for this is possible even through its connection with the eternal luminosity of the Self (*ātman*). Nor is it reasonable to postulate another causal instrument of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the direct perception of bondage when the established causes are absent.

Because it would contradict the scriptures which teach the absence of phenomenal proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), and because it would necessitate the postulation of another false cause—as in the statement, "Indra by means of his magical powers" (*indro māyābhiḥ*)—the cognition of the non-proliferated Brahman-self as reality does not sublate the cognition of the world as having phenomenal proliferation. This is because the world is known solely through the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*), which is common to both real and unreal entities such as ignorance (*ajñāna*). Therefore, since the absence of the appearance of the world consisting of ignorance and its effects cannot itself be cognized as a qualification of the Brahman-self due to its very opposition to that [world], it is well said that the cessation of illusory bondage occurs as an inseparable consequence of the realization of the Brahman-self.

Now, if the cessation of what is undesirable (*anartha*) is not the subject matter of the treatise, how can it be obtained through the power of understanding the subject matter? In this regard, is the cessation of the undesirable itself being questioned, or the appearance of its cessation? If it is the cessation [itself], he says: "And this is logical. The sense is that [the undesirable] is opposed to the manifestation of reality (*tattva*) and is the effect of ignorance (*avidyā*).

One might object: "In a case where there is the cognition 'this is not silver,' it subverts the error 'this is silver'; however, here the cognition 'I am Brahman' is grounded in the true nature of reality and does not have the negation of the phenomenal world as its object. Therefore, how can there be the removal of error in that case? To this he replies: "But [error] is removed by means of the negative particle and so forth. In that regard, there are two types of knowledge that oppose error: the knowledge of another entity, such as mother-of-pearl, which is the opposite of the error, and the knowledge of the non-existence of the reality of the superimposed object.

In that regard, he provides the following rebuttal: "In the case where [one says] 'this is not silver,' there is no dependence on a negative particle (*nañ*) for the removal of the superimposition through the knowledge of the absence of the reality superimposed, because it is the knowledge of another entity that is its opposite. However, he states that in the case of Brahman, the cessation of superimposition occurs through the knowledge of another entity that is its opposite: "But here, on the other hand, such knowledge itself [is what effects it]. Now, an objection is raised: "Indeed, every operation accomplishes only its own object, not some other unintended thing."

Therefore, it must be stated that the operation of knowledge has as its object the removal of error, not the existence of some other entity; thus he provides an example: "like the operation of the rising of a scale. He establishes that the necessary concomitance of one object with another is proven through an operation directed toward a different object: "For instance, the operation of rising..."

[Objection: But surely, since the activity itself has both as its object, both are established by way of being objects, and neither one is merely incidental; [Response: No, he says—"And not for that which causes the upward movement."

"Let it be granted that through the knowledge of the mother-of-pearl and Brahman as the Self, there is the necessary concomitant (nāntarīyaka) removal of silver and bondage; but how is there the cognition of that removal? To this he says: "That too is necessarily concomitant"—namely, "Thus, when the object is grasped erroneously. The word "thus" means that just as there is the removal, so too is there the cognition of it. He demonstrates this by means of a gesture: "I am not the agent; I am Brahman. The connection [of the words] follows the reverse order.

In the comprehension of the meaning of the sentence "I am Brahman," the realization that "if I am indeed Brahman, then I am not the agent" follows as a necessary consequence (*nāntarīyaka*). This same logic applies to the statement "this is not silver. Now, one might ask: why should the sentence itself not be the [direct] meaning? He says "no"—for the cognition "this is mother-of-pearl" is itself complete and free from further expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣa*). The term "restatement" (*anuvāda*) means a restatement of that which is established as a necessary consequence of the knowledge of the sentence-meaning.

He provides an example for the manifestation of the inseparable connection (*nāntarīyaka*) of the cognition of one object through the cognition of another object, stating: "Therefore, of the verb... Since the verb expresses the action that constitutes the sentence-meaning, it possesses the status of a sentence (*vākyatva*). By the very power of the cognition of the action, when there is the comprehension of the connection of all means (*sādhana*) with the action through alternation (*vikalpa*), the other words serve to restrict [the means] to one or another; however, when the connection is comprehended as constant (*nityavat*), they serve to exclude others by way of restatement (*anuvāda*). This is the meaning.

And the cognition of a constant concomitance is possible, since it is logical for a single [action] to have multiple means of accomplishment. Thus they say: "In the injunction 'he sacrifices' (yajati-codanā)," and so forth; this is another example where the understanding of a different meaning arises through *śrutārthāpatti* (presumption based on what is heard). Anticipating the objection—"How can substance and deity be understood as the meaning of the root *yaji* (to sacrifice), given that they are only known through the necessity of otherwise explaining the scriptural mention of 'sacrifice'?"—the author says: "How [can they be the meaning] of that which denotes action alone?"

Now, it might be argued that where a statement concerning the nature of another entity, which is the opposite of an object grasped through error, removes that error, there—since the statement lacks the capacity to establish the removal of the error itself—the cognition of the removal must be considered an invariable concomitant (*nāntarīyaka*). However, where perception is the sublater, there the sublater is precisely the cognition of another entity qualified by the removal of the error; in that case, the cognition of the removal of the error is not an invariable concomitant.

Anticipating the objection that even here, since bondage ceases through immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*), the cognition must have both as its objects, and that one is not necessarily dependent upon the other, he says: "Even of the sublation by perception" (*pratyakṣabādhasyāpi*). First of all, the absence of silver is not cognizable through non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), because [silver] is being seen in the location before one. If it is argued that [the sublation] is produced by sense-contact (*saṃprayoga*), he says "no," because "its object is not in contact" (*asaṃprayuktaviṣayatvāt*). The meaning is that neither the silver nor its absence is fit for sense-contact. The conclusion, "that very [sublation] is verbal" (*tadeva śābdam*), is clear in its purpose.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) is the removal of the cause of misfortune, and not the fruit of the commencement of the Vedāntas? In that case, how can it be said that "the Vedāntas are for the sake of abandonment"? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The use of the dative case as well... The term "upādāna" (taking up) means the commencement of the Vedāntas. [Reply: If so, since the scripture has the knowledge of Brahman as its fruit, the removal of misfortune cannot be its purpose. [Response: No; for it is established that even through a traditional sequence (*paramparayā*), it serves as a purpose desired by the person. Thus he says: "And [its] being the purpose..."

Regarding the phrase "for the attainment of knowledge" (*vidyā-pratipattaye*), he introduces the word *pratipatti* (attainment) because knowledge is not like a cow or similar objects. For knowledge, both in reality and from the perspective of its appearance, is indeed attained by the knower simply through its arising; this is the meaning. In that regard, among other forms of perception, knowledge consists in the immediate manifestation (*aparokṣāvabhāsa*) together with its own object, and by the word "attainment," the intended meaning is the certain conviction of immediacy regarding the object. He says, "This is not possible here," and explains: "True, it is so in other cases."

Here, by the word "knowledge" (*vidyā*), that valid cognition which arises from the word—assisted by an investigation into its power and intended meaning—is designated. Its "establishment" (*pratiṣṭhā*) is the direct perception (*aparokṣya*) of it together with its own object. In this context, "impossibility" (*asambhāvanā*) refers to the mind's unfitness for one-pointed mental modification (*ekāgra-vṛtti*) caused by the lack of accumulated contemplation upon Brahman as the Self. "Contrary conception" (*viparīta-bhāvanā*) refers to the accumulation of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) resulting from the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the body and so forth [upon the Self].

Now, it might be argued that there is no observed case where, regarding an object grasped by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that produces immediate manifestation, there is a lack of immediate certainty due to both types of mental defects; to this he says: "And so, in this world, in this place and time... Just as in the case of a moist *marīca* fruit situated at a great distance, because one lacks the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) from seeing such an object and possesses contrary latent impressions, one does not reach certainty even though the object is seen through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

The meaning is that a direct certainty regarding a specific aspect that was previously unestablished does not arise. [An objection: "But how can something not ascertained by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) be ascertained by a conceptual cognition (*tarka-pratyaya*)? To this he says: "Therefore, of the means of valid cognition... The meaning is that when the collection of auxiliary factors (*sahakāri-sampatti*) is well-known, the accomplishment of the result follows. [Another objection: "If *tarka* were also a means of valid cognition, how could the ascertainment of an object arise from two means of valid cognition? And if it is not a means of valid cognition, then all the more so [it cannot]. Thinking thus, he asks: "Now, what is this [tarka]?"

He states that even though inference (*tarka*) is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is indeed an auxiliary factor because it is a specific kind of cognition: "The object of the power of the means of valid cognition... The term "that" (*tat*) refers to the reality (*tattva*) of those [means of cognition]. The meaning is that inference is the cognition of possibility and impossibility regarding the reality of the means of cognition and so forth; it does not have the nature of a definitive certainty (*niścaya*).

In this regard, the following has been determined in the First Tantra: Some maintain that for cognitions, both validity (*prāmāṇya*) and invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) are intrinsic (*svataḥ*). Others hold that both are extrinsic (*parataḥ*). Still others claim that validity is extrinsic while invalidity is intrinsic. The proponents of the Veda (*vedavādinaḥ*) assert that invalidity is extrinsic while validity is intrinsic. Among these, it is first of all not tenable to say that for cognitions both validity and invalidity are intrinsic, because of their mutual contradiction. Now, one might object: "The distinction is established by the difference between individual instances. True, in fact it is exactly so.

From the perspective of common experience (*pratīti*), however, because there is no distinction between the appearances of valid and invalid cognition, it is impossible to determine what belongs to whom; this would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the absence of all worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*). Furthermore, the distinction between valid and invalid cognition does not manifest through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) in the same way that the distinction between the corporeal and the incorporeal does. Nor is it established by the object (*artha*) alone when there is a difference in individual instances. Nor is both [validity and invalidity] extrinsic (*parataḥ*); for a cognition devoid of the distinction between validity and invalidity has no cognizable nature of its own.

Nor is validity—the capacity to determine an object—comprehended extrinsically through the cognition of the excellence of its causes, for that would lead to an infinite regress. Nor is validity produced by a cause distinct from the cause of the cognition itself.

Because that [reliance on external causes] is impossible in the case of a cognition that perishes in a mere moment; because, since there is no distinction between erroneous and correct cognitions from the perspective of their appearance, there would be the undesirable consequence of the absence of practical activity prior to the ascertainment of validity, as such validity has not yet been apprehended; and because even the cognition of the excellence of the eyes and other sense organs—which is the cause of validity—cannot serve as the basis for the ascertainment of validity without first being apprehended as being produced by further excellences, since, like error, it is indistinguishable from the perspective of its appearance and thus its production by excellences cannot be self-evident.

Because the presence of qualities in knowledge and their positive and negative concomitance are otherwise accounted for by having as their object the absence of defects that obstruct validity; and because no qualities are observed in the sense organs and so forth apart from the removal of defects, there is likewise no simultaneous production of validity with the cognition from any other source. Even if validity were determined through a cognition that accords with purposeful action (*arthakriyā-saṃvāda*), the same fault of infinite regress and so forth would apply.

If it is argued that validity belongs only to instrumental cognitions (*sādhana-jñāna*) because they accord with purposeful action (*arthakriyā-saṃvāda*), but not to resultant cognitions (*phala-jñāna*) because there is no further purposeful action [to verify them], and therefore there is no infinite regress—then, for that very same reason, validity for instrumental cognitions would also have to be intrinsic (*svataḥ*). Otherwise, one who has acted would determine validity from the resulting purposeful action, and from that validity there would be the initial activity; thus, there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*). Furthermore, activity does not occur for the sake of determining validity, because cognitions are by nature free from doubt regarding their objects.

If it is argued that in the examination of form and so forth, the determination of an object is seen to arise from the four conditions (*pratyaya*), we say no; for it is the first cognition alone that dispels obstacles such as doubt, whereas subsequent cognitions do not. Therefore, since the practical engagement with an object is observed to be occasioned merely by the arising of a cognition, validity (*prāmāṇya*)—the determination of an object—is both through perception and in reality *svataḥ* (intrinsic). As for invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*), its production arises from causes accompanied by defects, and its perception arises from sublation (*bādhaka*); thus, it is logical that invalidity is *parataḥ* (extrinsic).

If it is argued that the production of invalidity from another source is not possible because it is preceded by the non-existence of validity (*prāmāṇya-prāgabhāva*), we say no; for non-validity—consisting of ignorance, doubt, and false knowledge—is of a positive nature (*bhāva-rūpa*). If it is asked, "How can there be extrinsic invalidity for that which is intrinsically valid? This would contradict its very nature," we reply: through the force of defects and obstructions, it is not contradictory, just as the sensation of coldness does not contradict fire. Furthermore, precisely because of intrinsic validity, practical activity (*vyavahāra*) is observed based on the cognition itself until the presence of a defect is apprehended.

Therefore, it has been established that validity and the cognition thereof depend neither on excellences (*guṇa*) nor on another cognition; rather, knowledge by its very existence is the cause for ascertainment and linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*). An objection is raised against this: "If knowledge determines its own object by depending upon rational inquiry (*tarka*), then this contradicts [the principle] stated. He answers: "It would not [be so] by its own power alone," and so forth.

It has been stated that since the determination of an object's direct manifestation arises from the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) itself, and since reasoning (*tarka*) is employed only for the removal of obstacles to that [cognition], reasoning is not the cause of the ascertainment of the object.

[Objection: "Surely, since it is possible for there to be an obstruction to valid cognition regarding external objects, let there be the assistance of reasoning (*tarka*) to remove that [obstruction]; but it is not so with respect to the Self, because, being self-luminous, there is no such obstruction. To this, he says: "And thus, in the sentence *tat tvam asi*, the referent of the term *tvam*... By the word "not conceiving," the absence of immediacy (*aparokṣya*) is expressed, and by "contrarily," mediacy (*pārokṣya*) is expressed.

The intention here is as follows: in the world, the immediacy (*aparokṣatā*) of an object arises either from its non-difference from consciousness, or from the object’s production of its own consciousness without mediation, or from its connection with the sense organ which is the cause of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); for it is observed that objects such as those inferred, which lack these three aforementioned causes, possess mediacy (*parokṣatā*).

In that regard, since Brahman alone is the material cause (upādāna) of all cognition, even in the consciousness produced by verbal testimony (*śabda-pramāṇa*) which has the form of Brahman, Brahman also appears immediately as something directly perceived (*aparokṣa*), either because it is non-different from that [consciousness] or because it is its generator. However, that [direct perception] is obstructed by the mind’s extreme subtlety, by the defect of lack of one-pointedness (*anekāgratā*), and by the defect of the latent impressions of error (*viparyaya-saṃskāra*); consequently, due to delusion, it appears as if it were indirect (*parokṣa*).

In this regard, by the force of the injunctions for sacrifices and the like, as well as for practices such as *nididhyāsana* (meditative contemplation), directed toward immediate (*aparokṣa*) knowledge, the sense organ—having its obstructions of impurity removed by sacrifices and the like, having the defects of contrary activity restrained by tranquility (*śama*) and other means, being illuminated by the lamp of the excellence of conviction regarding the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) and so forth as revealed through reflection (*manana*), and possessing the quality of one-pointedness produced by the accumulation of *nididhyāsana* focused on the extremely subtle reality of the Brahman-Self—[functions] by removing the obstruction caused by the delusion of mediacy (*pārokṣya*).

It is understood that from the word alone there arises the cause for immediate certainty; for in the world, it is observed that in determining an extremely subtle object, one depends upon a particular state of one-pointedness of mind. And by the word "reasoning" (*tarka*) here, such a mirror of the mind that dispels all obstacles is meant; because reasonings that dispel logical impossibilities, doubts, and contrary impressions are included within the initial knowledge.

And thus, the fact that the word [the Upanishads] is shown to be the cause of the realization of Brahman by means of the secondary derivative suffix (taddhita-pratyaya) in the phrase "that which is known through the Upanishads" becomes logical; for it is only immediate realization that constitutes perfect knowledge.

Another opinion holds: it is not the very first verbal cognition that becomes a direct manifestation (*aparokṣāvabhāsa*) depending on the removal of obstacles; rather, the word itself, having first produced a mediate cognition (*parokṣajñāna*) regarding Brahman, subsequently produces a second, direct cognition by depending on the aforementioned auxiliary cause, the mirror of the mind.

Because words and the like have the capacity for application toward immediate knowledge through the use of secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) and so forth—just as sensory contact, having produced direct cognition (*abhijñā*), subsequently produces recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) by depending on the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of prior experience—so it is here. Furthermore, with respect to Brahman, which is self-luminous, indirect knowledge is not an error; for even in the case of what is self-luminous, such as the consciousness of another person, [indirect knowledge occurs].

"Because we observe inference regarding things beyond the senses. Since immediate realization (*aparokṣya*) must be obtained through a further effort regardless of the means, he states that it is appropriate to mention the word "realization" (*pratipatti*) separately: "Therefore, even though knowledge has previously arisen... By what auxiliaries, then, is immediate realization obtained from the authority of the Word? To this he says: "And the manner of attainment is pointed out in the Vedāntas alone."

Now, an objection may be raised: how is it understood that reflection (*manana*) and meditative cultivation (*nididhyāsana*) are auxiliaries to hearing (*śravaṇa*), given that reflection—which consists of the repeated mental conviction regarding Brahman produced through the investigation of the possibility and logical consistency of the meaning—arises only after the Self has been understood from hearing, which is defined as the ascertainment of the words of the Vedānta endowed with both literal power (*śakti*) and intended purport (*tātparya*)?

Furthermore, even when the object has been ascertained through both valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and reasoning (*yukti*), there arises *nididhyāsana*, which is the one-pointed concentration of the mind upon that very object. Thus, since hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*) are understood to be subsidiary (*aṅga*) to it by virtue of assisting in the nature of *nididhyāsana*, it is not logical for reflection and meditative absorption to be subsidiaries of hearing.

To this it is replied: In that view where the ascertainment of the word qualified by its power and purport first produces a mediate knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*) regarding Brahman, and subsequently—depending upon the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) refined by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of reflection (*manana*) and meditative concentration (*nididhyāsana*)—produces immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*), there, although the mediate knowledge of Brahman is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to meditative concentration because it assists it, reflection and meditative concentration [are auxiliaries] to hearing (*śravaṇa*) in the production of immediate knowledge from the ascertainment of the word qualified by its purport.

[The two] attain the status of being auxiliaries that assist toward the fruit. Now, one might object: "Even when the fruit arises through direct perception (*aparokṣa*), why could *śravaṇa* and *manana* not be auxiliaries to *nididhyāsana*, since all three are equally immediate auxiliaries? Or rather, why could they not be of equal primary importance, like the *darśa* and *pūrṇamāsa* sacrifices? It is replied: The ascertainment of the specific word becomes the cause for the comprehension of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) without any mediation; for a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) reaches the comprehension of its object without mediation.

Reflection (*manana*) and meditative contemplation (*nididhyāsana*), however, serve as causes for the experience of Brahman by means of their effect: the one-pointed mental modification (*ekāgra-vṛtti*) perfected through the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the mind’s inclination toward the inner self (*pratyagātman*). Thus, since they are remote from the result, reflection and meditative contemplation are accepted as its auxiliary members (*aṅga*) with respect to the specific determination of the word (*viśiṣṭa-śabdāvadhāraṇa*), which is the immediate instrument (*karaṇa*) regarding that result.

However, when first a cognition resulting in immediate experience arises from the word alone, yet—due to defects in the internal organ such as the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of error and distraction—it persists with respect to the object as if it were a result of mediate experience through delusion; at that time, reflection (*manana*) and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*) serve as auxiliaries that assist the fruit of the means of knowledge, by removing obstacles such as the defects of mental distraction, and thus acting as causes for the establishment of the result of immediacy. This is not contradictory.

Furthermore, it is not possible for the fruit of immediate experience (*aparokṣānubhava*) to arise from meditative contemplation (*nididhyāsana*) alone without the instrument of verbal testimony (*śabda*); for the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of that [contemplation] is not established. If it is argued that because the immediate experience has as its object the Brahman-Self as understood through words, its validity is determined by means of those words—this is not so; for it is better to assume that the cognition already arisen is produced by a well-known means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), rather than assuming its validity depends on the determination of the existence of its object through another means of valid knowledge.

Otherwise, [validity] would depend on something else (*parataḥprāmāṇya*) in one case and be intrinsic (*svataḥprāmāṇya*) in the other. Therefore, it is logical that reflection (*manana*) and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*) are auxiliary factors (*aṅga*) that contribute to the fruit of hearing (*śravaṇa*).

[The opponent] objects: "Surely even the direct realization (*aparokṣajñāna*) of Brahman is not the cause for the cessation of suffering, because we observe that saṃsāra continues even when that realization exists; otherwise, the body would fall away immediately. Thus he challenges [the view]: "Now, as for the attainment of the knowledge of the oneness of the Self... [The author replies: "But surely the distinction between the knowledge of difference (*vyatirekajñāna*) and the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) has been shown. True; however, there is no distinction in terms of the result. Thus he says: "For instance, in the case of the individual soul (*jīva*). This is not correct.

He says, "Let it be that there [is the cessation of ignorance]," because the cessation of superimposition (adhyāsa) along with its root occurs through the direct realization of reality (tattva-aparokṣa), as established by both positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) and the scriptures. [Objection: But surely, just like the cognition of the negative concomitance (vyatireka-avagama) which opposes superimposition, let it be inferred that the knowledge of reality (tattva-avabodha), though opposed to superimposition, does not remove it. [Reply: No; he says, "For not [of the individual soul] (jīvasya). The meaning is that the knowledge of reality, which is opposed to non-knowledge (anavabodha), is not the same as the cognition of negative concomitance.

He raises an objection: "In that case, because direct realization occurs only for one who still possesses a body and sense organs, the body would fall away immediately"—this is expressed by the words, "Now, from the knowledge of Brahman... He states that even when ignorance is ceased through the knowledge of reality, a recurrence [of worldly existence] is possible: "Not so, due to residual impressions (saṃskāra)... He elaborates on this very point with the words, "For instance..."

[Objection: Is it not the case that a residual impression (*saṃskāra*) can only arise from action (*kriyā*) and knowledge (*jñāna*), and not from ignorance (*ajñāna*) and its effects? [Reply: No, because we observe residual impressions of odor and the like, and because it is admitted that all effects leave residual impressions during the state of cosmic dissolution (*pralaya*). Furthermore, in all cases, one can infer the production of a residual impression based solely on the fact of destruction; and since ignorance and its effects consist of erroneous cognition (*bhrāntijñāna*), a residual impression is established through the admission of a semblance of cognition (*jñānābhāsa*) which serves as the delimiting adjunct (*avacchedaka*) for the witness-consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*) even in the case of ignorance and so forth.

[Objection: But how can there be an immediate manifestation of duality from a mental impression (*saṃskāra*), which is merely a cause for memory? [Reply: We say that it is because the mental impression, like ignorance (*avidyā*), is a defect of consciousness. For it is established that a defect residing in the cause of an immediate manifestation is the cause of an immediate error; furthermore, since ignorance has the Self alone as its locus, it is logical that the mental impression also has that same locus. Moreover, only effects distinct from ignorance and its impressions have ignorance as their material cause (*upādāna*).

Even though the self does not possess the status of being the material cause (*upādāna*) of false mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), there is no contradiction in its being their locus-condition (*āśrayopādhi*), just as it is the locus-condition for ignorance (*avidyā*). Furthermore, since the cessation of impressions occurs gradually through the continuous pursuit of the knowledge of reality, liberation while in the body (*videhamukti*) is not contradicted by the fact that one remains for some time; or rather, it is faultless to say that a "residue of ignorance" (*avidyāleśa*), like a residue of darkness (*tamoleśa*), is designated by the term "impression."

[Objection: Is it not the case that "not all Vedāntas" has a clear meaning? In that regard, he shows that within those Vedāntas intended for the realization of the attributeless Brahman (*nirviśeṣa-brahman*), meditations on the qualified Brahman (*saguṇa-brahman*) are merely incidental—thus [he says]: "It is true, but the act of meditation... [Objection: If the attributeless Brahman is what is to be realized, how can the Brahman with its manifold world (*saprapañca*), which serves as the support for the meditation on the qualified Brahman, be a subordinate element (*aṅga*) such that an injunction is stated by depending upon it?

Intending to refer to the principle of superimposition and negation (*adhyāropāpavādanyāya*), he says: "And that [Brahman] is one from which the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*) has been removed. To the objection—"If the phenomenal world is being negated, how can there be an injunction for meditation (*upāsanā*), given the contradiction with the cognition of negation?"—he replies in that regard: "And in this state... Now, an objection is raised: "If [meditation] is enjoined by depending [on Brahman], then, like the *godohana* vessel, it would result in an eligibility restricted to those already qualified [for liberation]; thus, only one who seeks liberation (*mumukṣu*) would have the eligibility even for meditations. To this it is said:

Since the carrying forward of water (praṇayana) is the subject at hand, it cannot be established as something to be performed by means of the injunction regarding the *godohana* vessel; therefore, because the carrying forward is already established as the subject, and because the desire for cattle is not established for one who is independent [of that context], it is shown that only one qualified for the New and Full Moon sacrifices who desires cattle has the qualification for the *godohana* as well, based on the carrying forward that is already established.

Furthermore, since the practice of Brahman with its manifold elaborations (*saprapañca*) is obtained from the scripture without distinction for both those seeking liberation and those not seeking it, an injunction based upon that is possible even for those not seeking liberation; thus, there is no need to postulate a qualification of the seeker of liberation, but rather it is merely an injunction based [on that common ground], which is faultless. Therefore, he concludes that the commencement of the primary purport is directed toward Brahman: "Therefore, because it depends on that as its object."

Now, the meaning of the passage beginning with "Surely there are also meditations on what is not Brahman" is as follows: all Vedāntas are intent upon the realization of the identity of Brahman and the Self, whether directly or indirectly, by means of the purification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). To state that the subject matter and purpose of the science of inquiry (*vicāra-śāstra*) are precisely those of the Vedāntas, he says: "And how this meaning [is established]. He states the purport of the Commentary (*bhāṣya*) with the words: "Regarding the matter already proposed. The passage beginning with "The body alone... has a clear meaning.

Even though the Vedāntas have the Śārīraka (the Self) as their ultimate purport, he explains how the inquiry itself has that same purport with the words: "In this context, of the Vedāntas... Now, one might object: "The meaning of the Sūtra is merely the necessity of the inquiry; therefore, the mention of the subject matter (*viṣaya*) and the purpose (*prayojana*), which are not explicitly stated in the Sūtra, is inappropriate because they are related only to the Vedāntas and their inquiry. To dispel this doubt, he states the intent of the subsequent commentary by first mentioning what has preceded: "When there is the desire for liberation, immediately thereafter," and so forth.

How is it that liberation is the purpose established by the meaning of the knowledge of Brahman? To this he says: "The desire for the object that is the human goal. By "activity" (pravṛtti) is meant the state of being a means to a desired end within the scope of activity; for we shall explain that this alone is the injunction (vidhi). That verbal root-meaning in which the status of being a means to a beneficial end is taught by words such as the optative suffix (liṅgādi), that verbal root-meaning, being generally a means to a beneficial end, is connected—by implication—with a specific result through the qualification of the qualified person (adhikāriviśeṣaṇa).

Because a general understanding is untenable without its resolution into a specific instance; therefore, the meaning is that inquiry, being understood in a general sense as a means to the beneficial, culminates in the specific fruit of liberation for the qualified seeker by way of the knowledge established through its own inherent capacity.

Now, an objection may be raised: "Where an injunction (*niyoga*) is taught for one who desires a human goal (*puruṣārtha*), that injunction implies that the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is a means to that human goal. Therefore, let it be assumed—by the power of the injunction itself—that the inquiry being enjoined is a means to liberation; why then resort to the assumption of the power of an injunction to enjoin [an act] as a means to a desired end? This is not sound, because there is no logical inconsistency [in our position]. To explain: first of all, the very nature of an injunction is not logically untenable without a connection between the fruit and the meaning of the verbal root.

If it is argued that [the Veda] cannot be the instigator [of action] because it is not observed to function as such in the case of an unauthoritative injunction (*anāpta-niyoga*) or a mandatory injunction (*naiyamika*), then if even the desire for a result (*phala-kāmanā*) must be required by the injunction for activity to occur, then that desire alone is the cause of activity, not the injunction; for in the case of perception and other means of knowledge, it is seen that they operate independently [of a desire for a result]. Alternatively, if the desire is not required, then when a person is impelled by an injunction regardless of a desire for a result—like one being driven by a powerful current of wind and water—there would be no occasion to postulate a connection with a result, as this would lead to the absurd consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the same would apply even to being driven by water and so forth.

Is it not the case that an injunction (*niyoga*) being cognized as pertaining to one who desires a fruit is untenable without a connection to that fruit? Otherwise, there would be no injunction for one desiring a fruit. What is the intended meaning here? If you mean that desire for a fruit cannot be a qualification of the person entitled to the injunction (*adhikārin*) without a connection between the fruit and the meaning of the verbal root, that is not so; for we observe that even such things as "living" (*jīvana*), which are not themselves to be accomplished, serve as qualifications of the person entitled to the injunction.

If it is argued that it is untenable for the object to be a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), we say no; for by this [qualification], its status as the "thing-to-be-accomplished" (*sādhya*) cannot be established as an already existing fact. If it is argued that its status as the thing-to-be-accomplished exists by its very nature (*svarūpeṇa*), we say no—because it is not intended to be so expressed. To explain: since the word is intended merely as a qualifier for the purpose of excluding other specific types of qualified persons (*adhikāriviśeṣa*), the status of being the thing-to-be-accomplished is not what is intended to be expressed. Nor is there an intention to express its status as the thing-to-be-accomplished even by implication (*arthāt*), because no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has yet been seen for that. Furthermore, desire itself, having an already established nature, is the qualifier of the qualified person, since heaven serves to distinguish that [desire].

Furthermore, even that which is to be accomplished by another is seen to function as a qualification of the person entitled (adhikāriviśeṣaṇa) in other contexts—such as in "one desiring to study should beg alms," "one desiring another's wife should perform penance," and "one desiring a village, eat. Nor is it possible for the desire for heaven to be a qualification of the person entitled, because neither the exclusion of non-connection (ayogavyavaccheda) nor the exclusion of connection with others (anyayogavyavaccheda) is possible here. To explain: the term "one desiring heaven" [does not exclude] the non-connection of the person with the injunction (niyoga) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices.

It does not exclude [others], because the connection of the person with the rite is already established by the obligatory injunction (*nityavidhi*) itself. Nor is the qualification intended to exclude the connection of the injunction with one who does not desire heaven, for even in this case, there would be a contradiction with the connection to the obligatory *darśapūrṇamāsa* injunction. Furthermore, there is no difference between the obligatory and optional injunctions, since the injunction regarding the *darśapūrṇamāsa* along with its subsidiaries remains identical; the only difference lies in the qualified performer (*adhikārin*).

Therefore, just as in the case of the statement "the bearer of the staff recites the directions," this injunction is intended to refer to heaven as a qualifier and not to a person qualified by it; thus, the word *svargakāma* (desirous of heaven) is a statement of the result (*phala*). By implication, one who desires heaven becomes the qualified agent (*adhikārī*). Furthermore, since a statement of the result must be expressed as connected with a statement of the means (*sādhana*), there is no room for the expression of a mandatory injunction (*niyoga*). Consequently, the meaning of words such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is simply that which is the means to a desired end; this is the injunction (*vidhi*).

Others think as follows: when the mandate (niyoga) is being denoted as distinct from both the object and the person to be enjoined, the connection between the object and the person to be enjoined is understood through implication (*sāmarthyāt*). Otherwise, since the agent would not be connected with the object—due to the lack of connection between the agent and the action—the mandate could not be fulfilled if the object were not performed. Consequently, the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), being connected with the qualified person (*adhikārī*), is also connected with heaven, which is its qualification; for that which is connected with a qualified entity is necessarily connected with its qualification as well.

In this regard, since a logical connection (anvaya) is not possible without a relationship of primary and subordinate status, it follows that heaven is the primary element and the ritual action is subordinate; thus, the relationship between the goal to be accomplished and the means of accomplishment is established.

This is not sound: for even with the qualification of "burning of the house while living" (*jīvanagṛhadāha*), there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the sacrifice being construed as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to that [act]. If it is asked, "What is the fault?", [the answer is: if life and so forth were construed as subordinate to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), then an extended application (*atideśa*) would apply to the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*). In that case, one would have to say, "As long as one lives, one should offer the *saurya* oblation. If, on the other hand, [life] were construed as the primary element, then life itself would become something to be accomplished by the ritual action.

Therefore, the term *svargakāma* (one who desires heaven) performs an *anvitābhidhāna* (denotation of what is already syntactically connected) with the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and other such words, which generally express an injunction for a means to the good (*śreyaḥ-sādhana*) by way of referring to a specific result. Now, an objection may be raised: "If the connection with a specific result occurs through verbal cognition itself, then it is improper to say that the connection with the specific [result] arises from the capacity of the general [injunction] to culminate in being a means to the good. This is not a fault; for, by the force of the injunction regarding the general means to the good—which stands in need of a specific [result]—the term *svargakāma* is inferred to refer to that specific result.

This is because the intention (*tātparya*) of another word is based upon the requirement for a prescription (*vidhy-ākāṅkṣā*). Consequently, it has been stated that the connection with the fruit [of the action] arises through the power of the injunction (*vidhi-sāmarthya*). Now, an objection might be raised: since there is the qualification "not already expressed by a finite verb (*tiṅ*), a primary derivative (*kṛt*), a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), or a compound (*samāsa*)," if the instrumentality (*karaṇatā*) of the sacrifice were expressed by the optative suffix (*liṅ*), then the instrumental case ending in "by means of the *Jyotiṣṭoma*" (*jyotiṣṭomena*) would be untenable. This is not so; there is no fault here because of the distinction between the instrumentality colored by the difference between the meanings of the bases—the general term "sacrifice" (*yāga*) and the specific term "*Jyotiṣṭoma*" (*jyotiṣṭoma*). Enough of this digression.

"How is the subject matter established? To this he says: "That being so, from where [is it known]? This is a restatement of what was already said in the passage beginning with "Thus, in this way. The statement "First of all" is an explanation of the intent (*tātparya*) of the *Bhāṣya*. Now, an objection may be raised: "The subject matter is understood precisely by the definition of Concordance (*samanvaya-lakṣaṇa*), and the purpose (*prayojana*) is determined by the fourth chapter alone; why then are the subject matter and the purpose indicated by the first aphorism (*sūtra*}? To this he replies: "This is the beginning of the scripture."

Now, one might object that it is improper for a single sūtra sentence to have multiple meanings; to this, he says: "And this sūtra... Therein, he states the purport of the commentary—which explains the words beginning with "atha"—by first mentioning what has preceded: "Thus, by virtue of being the beginning of the sūtra..."

Thus ends the first section, titled the "Commentary on Superimposition" (*adhyāsabhāṣya*), in the *Pañcapādikā-vivaraṇa*, composed by the venerable Svaprakāśānubhava Bhagavat, the disciple of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ananyānubhava Pūjyapāda.

In this regard, the connection of the injunction for inquiry with its result, as well as its connection with the object of inquiry—namely, the nature of Brahman which is not immediately present—has already been stated. Now, in order to demonstrate that the connection with the object of inquiry which is not immediately present requires an undertaking not otherwise established, [the author] first raises an objection: "But surely the desire to know Brahman is already established. The meaning is that the collection of logical principles required for the determination of the meaning of the Vedāntas has already been set forth in aphorisms such as "Then, therefore, the desire to know Dharma" (Jaimini Sūtra 1.1.1).

Anticipating the objection that "the determination of the meaning of injunctive sentences is what is undertaken there," he says: "because the meaning of the entire Veda has already been investigated. This means that the Veda is concerned solely with what is to be done (kārya). Now, one might object: "Brahman is understood from the purport of the Vedāntas, not something to be done; and that which is not understood cannot be the object of a sentence's cognition. To this, he says: "And of the knowledge of Brahman..."

[Objection: "But has not the entire collection of injunctions regarding action (*kriyā*) already been described? This [work] is now begun for the purpose of describing the injunctions regarding knowledge (*jñāna*). [Reply: No, he says: "Therefore, it is already established. The meaning is that since the forms required by injunction—namely, origin (*utpatti*), application (*viniyoga*), performance (*prayoga*), and qualification (*adhikāra*)—have been described without distinction for both action and realization (*pratipatti*).

Now, an objection is raised: just as the authority of the Veda was established in the first chapter; the distinctions among the originative injunctions of ritual acts in the second; the relationship between primary and auxiliary elements among those enjoined in the third; the extent of what is to be performed, prompted by either the sacrifice or the human agent, in the fourth; the sequence of performance in the fifth; and in the sixth...

The determination of qualification is required by the injunction; thus, with the first six chapters, the investigation required by the injunction regarding the archetype (*prakṛti*) has been completed. An injunction joined with all its constituent parts is called an archetype, while one joined with deficient parts is called a modification (*vikṛti*). Among these, in the seventh chapter, the extension (*atideśa*) of the constituent parts taught in the archetype to the modification was determined.

In the eighth [book], however, the specific extended application (*viśeṣātideśa*) of the auxiliary elements taught in the archetype—such as "a cake on eight potsherds for Agni"—to the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), such as "one should offer a pap for Sūrya," by way of commonality regarding substance, deity, and so forth, was determined. In the ninth [book], however, *ūha* (adaptation) is demonstrated: when there is a difference between the substance and deity of the archetype and the modified sacrifice regarding the mantras, *sāmans*, and purificatory acts extended from the archetype to the modified sacrifice, one must set aside the words concerning the substance and so forth belonging to the archetype and substitute words concerning the substance and so forth belonging to the modified sacrifice.

For example: in the modification (*vikṛti*) of the mantra "pleasing to Agni" (*agnaye juṣṭam*), there is the substitution of the word "pleasing to Sūrya" (*sūryāya juṣṭam*). However, in the tenth [book], it is shown that the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) extended by analogy (*atideśa*) to a modification—which have their place in the archetype (*prakṛti*)—are sublated by the instruction of specific subsidiaries belonging to that modification, just as the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) obtained for the modification through extension from the archetype is sublated by the specific instruction in the modification: "the sacrificial grass consists of *śara* grass."

In the eleventh [book], however, that which is called *tantra*—the equal benefit to all the principal rites (*śeṣin*) resulting from the single performance of a subsidiary (*śeṣa*) enjoined by multiple principals—is explained. For example, as in the case of the three rites of the full-moon sacrifice: "The cake on eight potsherds for Agni," "He performs the *upāṃśuyāja* in between," and "The cake on eleven potsherds for Agni-Soma"; through the single performance of the *prayāja* and other subsidiaries enjoined by these three rites, there is benefit to all three principals.

In the twelfth [book], however, *prasaṅga*—namely, the assistance rendered by the performance of subsidiaries enjoined for one [principal] to another principal that lacks the capacity to independently motivate that performance—is demonstrated; as, for example, the assistance rendered by the subsidiaries enjoined for the animal sacrifice (*paśu*) to the animal-cake offering (*paśupuroḍāśa*).

Thus, by refuting various objections chapter by chapter, the different components of the injunction have been examined. Likewise, since Brahman—the object to be realized—is not established through perception and other means of knowledge, there arises the doubt that an injunction for realization is impossible; it is with the intent of refuting this doubt that the [next] section begins. Regarding this, he says: "Because there is no further objection. The meaning is that Brahman is established just like the sacrificial post (yūpa) or the Āhavanīya fire; or, even if it were unestablished, the meditation would be accomplished by means of a superimposed form.

In this context, the proponent (pūrvavādī), in order to refute certain partial adherents of the Siddhānta who accept that the Vedāntas are centered on injunctions, demonstrates the manner in which those [Vedāntas] are commenced specifically to dispel the further doubt they have raised—introducing them with the words, "In this regard, some... (atra kecit).

One might object: "Even when an injunction (*vidhi*) is heard in only some instances, the collection of Vedānta passages—though separated by distance—is connected as a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) by providing the required auxiliary elements (*anubandha*); so what need is there for an injunction to be heard everywhere? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Even where an injunction is heard... The sense is that even there, the injunction is untenable.

[Objection: But surely, even though the *kṛtya* suffixes are prescribed for the sense of the action (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*), since they are remembered in the rule "And the *kṛtyas*" (*Pāṇini 3.3.163*) as being prescriptive, knowledge is enjoined by the suffix *-tavya*. To this, he says: "In that case, although [the suffix] is called a *kṛtya*... The meaning is that nevertheless, an injunction is not possible here. [Objection: Let knowledge be enjoined just as "one must go" (*gantavyam*) is an injunction to go. [Reply: True; it is appropriate that there is an injunction when the suffix *-tavya* refers to the action (*bhāva*). Thus he says: "That which denotes the action (*bhāva*)."

The term *bhāva* refers merely to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). The sense is that this [meaning of the root] can be enjoined primarily for the sake of an independent result. Now, one might object: even from an optative suffix (*vyapratyaya*) denoting an object (*karman*), an injunction regarding the meaning of the root is understood—as in "One's own Veda is to be studied" (*svādhyāyo 'dhyetavyaḥ*). To this he replies: "But where the object is expressed as primary... [and so forth].

In that regard, is the action enjoined for the sake of an independent result, or for the sake of a result residing in the object (the *karmakāraka*)? Regarding this, he first states that it is not for the sake of an independent result: "In that [case], [the action] is subordinate to the substance. Then, if it were an injunction for the sake of a result inherent in the object as the locus of the action, he says: "If the substance were the primary [aim]. Now, one might argue that through the power of the action enjoined with respect to the Self, there would be a purification (*saṃskāra*) consisting in the removal of impurities such as ignorance and demerit; to this he replies, "No," saying: "And of that which is purified."
In that regard, because of the scriptural statement "he offers groats" within the context of a sacrifice, it is understood that the offering of groats is an auxiliary part of the sacrifice.

In this context, the auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) are of two kinds: *arthakarma* (primary acts) and *saṃskārakarma* (purificatory acts). Those prescribed independently, without depending on the assistance of a sacrifice, such as the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, are *arthakarma*. Those which serve as subordinate qualities (*guṇa*) to the instrumental factors (*kāraka*) such as rice-grains (*vrīhi*) are *saṃskārakarma*. Among these, the *saktu-homa* (the offering of groats) is certainly not an *arthakarma*, because the substance of groats (*saktu-dravya*) is subordinate, just like the act of sprinkling water (*prokṣaṇa*).

And the action of consecration (*saṃskārakarma*) is of two kinds: consecration of that which has already been employed (*viniyuktasaṃskāra*), such as the consecration by sprinkling and so forth directed toward rice-grains already employed in the injunction "one should sacrifice with rice-grains"; and consecration of that which is about to be employed (*viniyokṣyamāṇasaṃskāra*), such as the consecration by means of the fire-laying (*ādhāna*) of the *āhavanīya* fire which is about to be employed in the injunction "one offers oblations in the *āhavanīya*"; the meaning is that there is an employment of what has been consecrated.

In that case, just as it was determined that the flour (*saktu*)—which has been reduced to ashes by the oblation—is neither employed in the sacrifice in either way (as a means nor as an end), and since its uselessness would otherwise follow—it must abandon its status as a preparatory act (*saṃskārakarma*). Thus, setting aside the primacy of the flour itself as expressed by the word "flour," and adopting the primacy of the action by treating the flour as a subordinate factor (*guṇabhāva*), it is established as a fruitful act (*arthakarma*); likewise, one might object: "Let us set aside the primacy of the self as the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*) expressed by 'the self,' and instead, by accepting the self as a subordinate factor in the phrase 'one should meditate by means of the self,' let meditation be enjoined as the primary act for the sake of an independent fruit. This is the doubt raised in the words: "But then, on the contrary..."

In this regard, just as even though the oblation (*homa*) is primary, because the verbal root is transitive, the groats themselves are reduced to ashes as the object (*karman*) of the action, so too, since comprehension (*avagama*) is also transitive, there is no injunction [of it] in the absence of an object in reality; thus he provides the rebuttal: "Even there, it is not known. Although it is the instrument (*karaṇa*) in terms of the word, in terms of its actual meaning...

He raises the objection that the status of being an object belongs to the self alone—namely, "Now, it is known. In that case, since there is the factor of being an object (*karmakāraka*), some excellence (*atiśaya*) must be stated regarding the self; for in its absence, knowledge cannot be enjoined as something devoid of an object. Thus he says: "In that case, that very [objection] has arrived. Now, one might argue that attainment through the state of being manifested is the fruit of the enjoined action upon the self; to this he says, "No," because "that would be a useless repetition of what is already accomplished" (*tac ca kṛtakaraṇamanarthakam*).
The meaning is that because it is attained through the manifestation of eternal consciousness, it does not possess the status of being an object of knowledge.

Furthermore, the preceding section [of the text] has a clear meaning.
