According to those who maintain that it is a separate beginning, the cessation of ignorance, dharmas, and so forth is "formative force" (*saṃskāra*); yet, there is no requirement for that which is formed to be employed elsewhere, because it is itself a human goal. Since a formative force that is itself a human goal requires employment [for something else], this [section] is begun for that purpose. This is the view of those who argue for a separate beginning.

The meaning of the passage beginning with "Others, however, undertake [the inquiry] in this way" is as follows: although the fourfold method required for the injunction of practice was already established in the *Prathama-tantra*, the scripture must nevertheless be commenced in order to define Brahman, which is its subject matter; yet that commencement is not possible, because there is an absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding Brahman.

To this it is replied: the preceding portion of the text is clear in meaning. Regarding the phrase "by way of being the object of the injunction for the qualified person" (adhikāriniyogaviṣayatayā), the sense is as follows: the connection of knowledge with its fruit is understood; that [knowledge] is to be performed by one who desires that fruit; and since performance proceeds from an injunction, the point is that it is understood as the object of an injunction for one who desires the fruit.

To this, [the author] replies with the words "atrocyate" (here it is said), etc., whereby the proponent refutes the two previous arguments. If one objects that in common worldly usage the *kṛtya* suffix does not convey an injunction (*niyoga*), he says "that is not so"—namely, "tat svayam eva" (that [suffix] itself). Then, regarding the Veda, he says "and this is well-known. Therefore, the meaning is that for those who accept the injunction to study (*adhyayanavidhi*) by means of the first sūtra, this inquiry is already settled. As for the passage beginning with "nanu caturvidhasya," the meaning has already been stated.

Furthermore, even if the self were the instrument (*karaṇa*), since it is the very agent of the action (*karman*) and is eternally established as being intrinsically immediate (*aparokṣa*), it cannot be the object of a manifestation produced by an enjoined action; thus, because it is not an object (*akarma*), it has been stated that knowledge devoid of an object (*niṣkarmaka*) cannot be enjoined. To this he says: "That also is not so."

Since there is no fourfold fruit in the Self, even though it is not an object of action (*akarma*), there might be a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) regarding the stream of knowledge that manifests it, for the sake of the fruit of liberation which inheres in the agent; just as the injunction "one should wear gold" is a restrictive rule for the attainment of prosperity (*abhyudaya*) regarding something not otherwise established, so too is this case—thus he says: "of that which is already established. Now, one might object: since the stream of knowledge is uninterrupted even during the three states [of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep], there can be no restrictive injunction. To this he replies: "Indeed, not even by way of an injunction..."

"In that case, for the sake of removing the appearance of a non-self, the restrictive injunction (*parisaṅkhyā-vidhi*) would have an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). To this he says: "In that case, then... The sense is that since the matter has already been established, there is no further doubt to be raised. He says, "Furthermore, from the knowledge of the Self... and so forth, meaning that even if an injunction to know were made, the treatise would not be commenced because there would be no purpose. Nor does the stream of cognition—which, though not itself a cause for the cessation of what is harmful—remove that harm simply by virtue of being enjoined; the meaning is that there is no distinction [between such an enjoined stream and one not enjoined].

One might then object: "In that case, let the knowledge of the transcendental reality of the Self, which has the cessation of defects such as ignorance as its fruit, be enjoined. To this he replies: "But [if it is argued] 'from that which is determined by the notion of "I"... No; because an injunction is untenable with respect to something that is absolutely unestablished. Thus he says: "That is incorrect; for an injunction..."

The meaning is this: just as, with reference to a sacrifice that is generally well-known, another individual instance similar to previously experienced instances of sacrifice—which exists only as a mental construct—is enjoined; so too, with reference to the knowledge of the transcendent Self which is generally well-known, another instance similar to previously experienced instances of knowledge is apprehended in the intellect, and it is that which is to be enjoined as something to be performed.

[Objection: Since knowledge in general (*jñānasāmānya*) is established in the world, if it were enjoined with reference to that [general category], then that specific instance (*tadvyaktitvena*), namely the knowledge of the extraordinary Self (*alaukikātmajñāna*), would be understood as something to be performed. [Reply: No, he says: "If indeed that is knowledge... The meaning is that because such knowledge of the Self is not established as a specific instance of the general category of knowledge, it is impossible to place such knowledge upon the intellect as something to be performed.

Now, if such self-knowledge were already established, would it be in one's own self or in another person? If it were in another person, since that other qualified person does not perceive it for themselves, it is impossible to conceive of such another individual as something to be accomplished. If, on the other hand, it is in one's own self, he says in response: "What is the use of an injunction? The meaning of the passage beginning with "As for the view of other schools" and so forth has already been explained. The phrase "for the investigation of that" means for the investigation of Brahman; thus, the meaning is that the scripture is commenced for the purpose of investigating Brahman.

"Another opinion," he says. That very proponent of the injunction for realization (pratipatti-vidhi) establishes his own position: "True; since Brahman is also understood from the Veda even though it is directed toward a task (kārya), an injunction for realization is appropriate. He states this with the words, "But surely, merely that much... [Objection: "Is this not contradictory—that the understanding of one thing arises from a word whose primary purport is another thing? To this, he replies: "When that exists... (tasmin sati).

The meaning is that, by virtue of the authority of the injunction (*vidhi*), other entities associated with that injunction are also established as being required by it. He provides an illustration for this, stating: "Just as for the eye whose object is color, everything in contact with it is its object"—that is, "just as when there is color... [and so forth]. Now, one might object: "In passages such as 'He is to be seen' (*draṣṭavyaḥ*), non-perceptual knowledge is not what is enjoined; for, being a direct experience of bliss, it is a human goal (*puruṣārtha*) like heaven and such, and thus cannot be an object of an injunction. Nor is verbal knowledge [what is enjoined]; [the text continues].

In this regard, he raises an objection: "Because no injunction (*vidhi*) is heard there"—asking, "How so? He replies: "An injunction exists in verbal cognition"—saying, "It is said. Now, one might object: "This sentence is intended to enjoin the non-self-nature of the Self; therefore, because it does not serve a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*), it cannot be enjoined. To this he says, "No—it is not 'the state of being all forms'": the meaning is that, having taken as the objective something already understood, it is precisely the unapprehended self-nature that is enjoined.

He states another objection: "If the Self possesses all forms... [The opponent asks: "What, then, is being enjoined? To this he replies: "Therefore, of everything... By reflecting on such statements as "not this, not this," he says that it is the Self alone that is to be enjoined through the sublation of the non-Self: "...by means of the dissolution of the nature of the non-Self. [The opponent objects: "But surely this statement is intended to establish the non-duality of the Self; no injunction is perceived therein, whether with respect to knowledge or the object. To this he replies: "But surely no injunction is heard here..."

He says, "Let it be postulated," as in the case of [the mantra] "Pūṣan has the portion of ground flour" (*pūṣā prapiṣṭabhāgaḥ*) and so forth. The meaning of the passage beginning with "When the meaning of the injunction is already perceived" is as follows: When a ritual action—unspecified by the three times and fit for performance—is understood through the power of the word, and when the *niyoga* (the mandate) in the form of "that which must be done" is cognized because that [understanding] would otherwise be inexplicable, is the injunctive word (the prescriptive term) then postulated as the meaning of the injunction? Or rather, is it postulated when such an object is not yet perceived, being merely a thing unfit for performance?

If it is argued that "the injunctive word is postulated once [the object] is understood," we reply: Is the word postulated for the sake of valid cognition (*pramiti*) or for the sake of restatement (*anuvāda*)? It serves no purpose as a restatement. If it is for the sake of valid cognition, he says regarding that: "When [the object] is already understood, the postulation [of the word] is useless. This means that the postulation of words such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*) would be useless because they function as conveyors [of what is already known]. Since there is no cause for postulating an injunction when there is a comprehension of an object that is not to be performed, he states: "But if it is not understood" (*athāpratīte*). This means that through the word, there is no comprehension of something to be performed in that case.
The sense is that there would be the undesirable consequence of having to postulate [an injunction] even in cases of mere explanatory passages (*arthavāda*).

Anticipating the objection—thinking that because the defects of the two alternatives (*vikalpa*) apply everywhere, no injunction can be postulated anywhere—the opponent raises the following: "But [in the case of] what is not heard... In that regard, the relationship between the substance and the deity, being cognized as untouched by the three times (past, present, and future), leads to the inference of the sacrifice (*yāga*) which is inseparably connected with it; and the sacrifice, in turn, leads to the mandate (*niyoga*) which is inseparably connected with it. Thus, the meaning of the injunction is understood from the very power of what is heard in the text. In that context, for the sake of mere worldly practice, the abandonment of the flour-substance with Pūṣan as the intended deity must be performed.

Thus it is concluded: the meaning is that here [in this case], the sense of the injunction (*niyoga*) is not understood by the force of what is heard [in the text] as it was there. He says: "True, that is appropriate there. But one might object: "In this case too, the injunction is understood by the force of the Self (*ātman*) which is heard [in the text]. To this he says: "But here too there is the word 'Self' (*ātmapada*). No; for while the sacrifice and the injunction are untenable without someone who understands the injunction, there is no such untenability regarding the understanding person [the Self] without the injunction. He says: "This is not sound; for the injunction..."

[Objection: Is it not the case that whatever connection is apprehended in the Veda is necessarily connected with an injunction, either directly or indirectly? For even in passages such as "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest," an indirect connection with an injunction is admitted; and since there, the essential nature of everything is invariably concomitant [with action], it brings the injunction to mind. To this, he replies: "Even so, let it be granted. The intention is that because an injunction has the meaning of a verbal root (bhāvārtha) as its object, it does not have the connection with an existing entity (bhūta) as its object.

If that is the case, then the meaning of the verbal root (bhāvārtha) is also an object of the injunction, being invariably concomitant with it through mere association; thus, he says: "It is postulated together with the verbal root itself."

He asks "What is this? with the intention of expressing the defects inherent in all possible meanings of verbal roots (*dhātu*). First, he introduces the root *kṛ* (to act), because there is no reason to bypass the general meaning of all roots at the outset, by saying: "If, first of all, it is 'that which is to be done' (*kartavyam*). He states the refutation of that position: "In that case, it would lack the nature of the Self (*anātmasvabhāvatā*). The sense is that the vision of the Self occurs precisely through the dissolution of phenomenal expansion (*prapañca*). He states another refutation: "And if [it were defined] by its manner of performance (*itikartavyatayā*)."

The meaning is that tranquility (*śama*) and so forth constitute the procedural requirements (*itikartavyatā*) for knowledge, not the procedural requirements for the dissolution of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*). He states another verbal root with the word "now" (*atha*). He refutes [this] with "even so" (*evamapi*). For when women and the like are perceived as fire and so forth, their status as women and the like does not cease; the point is that the cognition of what is to be enjoined (*vidheya-buddhi*) lacks authoritative validity (*aprāmāṇika*). He states another objection against enjoining the meaning of the verbal root in either case: "and it would be an instruction on an impossible object" (*aśakyārthopadeśaśca*).

[Objection: "But in the case of [meditations on] women, fire, and so forth, there is a mental act (*mānasī kriyā*); however, knowledge (*jñāna*) when enjoined brings about the cessation of the non-self (*anātman*). To this he says: "For one thing does not become the essence of another thing. [Reply: "In that case, by means of the dissolution of the person's own nature—just as the valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consisting in the ascertainment of a post [dispels the error of a man]—the valid cognitive knowledge that ascertains the Self through the dissolution of the non-Self is merely restated (*anūdya*), and a mere injunction (*vidhi*) is supplied from elsewhere. To this he says: "In that case, 'it is to be known' (*jñātavyaḥ*), etc."

In that case, one must state that the cognition of Brahman—which is already established from another source—is a restatement (anuvāda) distinct from the meaning of an injunctive sentence; yet, there is no other means of valid knowledge [for its establishment]. To this he says: "From what [source] is its attainment? [The opponent objects: "But surely [its attainment comes] from the designations in the Vedāntas, which are distinct from injunctive words. To this he replies: "From designation" (abhidhānataḥ).

"In that case, since the realization of Brahman is established through the authority of the designation itself, without depending on the performance of the causal factor of an injunction, there is no need for an injunction. To this he says: "In that case, the injunction is purposeless. "But surely, even when realization has been accomplished, another such manifestation is enjoined? To this he says: "As something to be performed again. "But what is to be done with that, since the purpose is already fulfilled by the former one? To this he says: "Just as in the case of mantras."

The meaning is this: mantras, having been acquired solely by the rule of private recitation (*svādhyāya-vidhi*), and having established themselves by producing a cognition of their own meaning for one who has grasped the relationship between words and word-meanings, remain devoid of the purpose of engagement or avoidance, because their own meaning is not something to be performed and is already known through the sentences of the *Brāhmaṇas*.

In this regard—mantras such as "With the Aindrī [verse] [one approaches] the Gārhapatya fire," "I cut the barhis grass, the seat of the gods," and "They took up this rein of the Rta" [the horse's halter], and so forth, are said to be purposeful because they are enjoined as auxiliary parts of the ritual action (*karmāṅga*) by means of scripture (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), syntactical connection (*vākya*), and so on, just like rice and other materials; they serve a purpose by way of accomplishing the primary transcendental result (*apūrva*). Among these, by what... [are the mantras [distinguished]?]

When it is observed that they assist because the accomplishment of the *apūrva* (the transcendental result) is not possible otherwise through mere assistance, since the injunction for study has the purpose of knowing the meaning, and because it is improper to postulate an unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) benefit when a seen (*dṛṣṭa*) benefit exists, it is inferred that at the time of performance, the mantras—having produced the "disposal" (*pratipatti*) of the substances, deities, and so forth which require such disposal—assist the *apūrva* by means of that disposal. Consequently, it is understood that the accomplishment of the *apūrva* occurs through the performance of recollection by means of the mantras alone, and not by means of the sentences of the Brāhmaṇas.

In this regard, the rule for performance (*prayogavidhi*) causes the production of an unprecedented benefit (*apūrvopakāra*) through the constituent parts (*aṅga*), and causes the knowledge of the meaning through the mantras. Just as the injunction of performance, by means of the mantras, enforces a further cognition that produces an unprecedented benefit—distinct from the cognition first produced—so too, another realization of Brahman (*brahmasaṃvedana*) is performed for the sake of the fruit of liberation.

[The opponent objects: "But surely, in that case, it is logical that for mantras which have ceased [their function] after producing a cognition of their own meaning, there is a further necessity for the performance of that cognition by means of the *prayogavacana* (injunction of performance), due to the power of the application (*viniyoga*) established by direct statement (*śruti*) and so forth; however, there is no such *prayogavacana* regarding the knowledge of the Self. To this he replies: "In that case, the *prayogavacana* is the enjoiner. [The proponent asks: "In that case, is it not also brought about here? The proponent replies: "In this case as well, the *prayogavacana* is the enjoiner."

First, an originative injunction (utpatti-vidhi) characterized by the verbal expression "one should produce knowledge of the Self through the Vedānta texts"—similar to the injunction "one should sacrifice with Soma"—is supplied. Then, that injunction, observing the various requirements of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) as to how that knowledge is to be produced, becomes an application injunction (*viniyoga-vidhi*), applying the injunctions for tranquility (*śama*) and so forth—which are read within the same context and situated near the fruitful injunction for the knowledge of the Self—as the constituent parts of the procedure.

Furthermore, seeking an eligible agent who understands "this is my duty" regarding the ritual action along with its auxiliary parts, [the injunction] subsumes liberation mentioned in the explanatory passages (arthavāda) according to the principle of the *Rātrisatra* sacrifice, and thus becomes an injunction of application (*viniyoga-vidhi*) and an injunction of qualification (*adhikāra-vidhi*), stating: "One desiring liberation should produce self-knowledge by means of the Vedāntic statements, which are assisted by the procedure consisting of tranquility and so forth. Again, that same [injunction], impelling the qualified agent to perform that knowledge of reality along with its auxiliaries, becomes an injunction of performance (*prayoga-vidhi*).

Furthermore, the proponent of the final view (siddhāntin) states the distinction between mantras and Vedāntas: "Now, regarding the mantras... [he says]. "Being intent upon the cognition" means that the purport of mantras lies solely in the cognition that assists toward the unseen potency (apūrva), and not in the actual state of the object; whereas in that regard, the Vedāntas have their own meaning as their injunction because they bring about the understanding of an unknown object that serves a purpose.

In this regard, he says—"even though [the word] is introduced for another purpose"—to show that there is no contradiction between its being intent upon an injunction (*vidhi*) and its being intent upon an unknown object (*ajñātārtha*), by way of conveying the cognition of what is to be accomplished (*vidheya*). Now, one might object: while permanent entities may have multiple effects either sequentially or simultaneously, how can a word—having a single cause of action due to its intended meaning (*tātparya*)—be intent upon both? To this, he replies: "or just as in the case of word-meanings."

The proponent of the final view (siddhāntin), in order to demonstrate that the human goal is accomplished simply by accepting the primary denotative cognition regarding Brahman—and thus that there is no need to postulate the injunctions of origin, application, qualification, and performance for a secondary cognition as is required for mantras as subordinate elements of an injunction—states their distinction from mantras: "This [Brahman] is, as it were, not yet defined."

The remainder of the sentence is as follows: because it is not observed that a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*)—such as the passage concerning women, fire, and so forth—which has its remainder established by an injunction through the surrender of its subject matter to that injunction, or the knowledge produced thereby, is intended to have [only] the object of cognition (*prameya*) as its primary purport. Now, one might object: since an object of cognition is accessible through ordinary means of valid knowledge (*laukikapramāṇa*), it lacks such primary purport; however, in this case, because both the injunction and Brahman are *alaukika* (transcendental), there would be a dual purport. To this he says: "Nor can both be [the primary purport] simultaneously."

With respect to knowledge (*jñāna*), Brahman possesses primacy as the object of cognition (*prameya*); it possesses the status of a subordinate element (*guṇabhāva*) as a qualifier of the enjoined knowledge; it possesses the status of being something to be accepted (*upādeyatā*) because it is an object of cognition; it possesses the status of being the objective referent (*uddeśyatā*) with respect to the injunction; it possesses the status of being enjoined (*vidheyatā*) because it is an object of cognition; and it possesses the status of being restated (*anuvādyatā*) for the sake of the injunction. Thus, if Brahman’s own knowledge were the object of an injunction and were subordinate to the resulting comprehension of it, then primacy, the status of being accepted, and the status of being an object of cognition would coexist in that single verbal cognition alongside their opposites—the status of being subordinate, the status of being the objective referent, and the status of being restated. This results in a logical contradiction within a single cognition produced by words.

This is a contradiction. [Objection: Is it not the case that there is no contradiction because the first cognition is directed toward the object, while the second cognition, by virtue of having an injunction as its object, is directed toward that [injunction]? [Response: No; for if the word does not have both as its purport, it is impossible for the cognition produced by it—even if generated repeatedly—to have both as its purport.

One might object: "Surely the consequence of heterogeneity does not constitute a fault, for otherwise the injunction of subordinate actions (*guṇakarma*) would be untenable. To this he replies: "But if this were so, [regarding] subordinate actions... Subordinate actions are those rites intended for the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the factors of action (*kāraka*) that serve as auxiliaries to the sacrifice. In that context, heterogeneity is asserted by accepting the position that the factor of action (*karmakāraka*)—as qualified by a specific excellence (*atiśaya*) produced by the action—is precisely what is denoted by the case-ending expressing the factor of action.

In the case of rice (*vrīhi*), since its existence is established by other means of knowledge and it functions as a causal factor (*kāraka*), its status as a subject of restatement (*anuvādya*), its subordinate nature (*guṇatva*), and its status as the object of reference (*uddeśyatva*) are established. Furthermore, because it possesses an excellence (*atiśaya*) produced by the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) which is to be enjoined, its status as something to be taken up (*upādeyatva*), its primacy (*prādhānya*), and its status as the object of injunction (*vidheyatva*) are understood through the power of the case-ending (*vibhakti*). Thus, there is a discrepancy regarding the various forms of subordinate actions (*guṇakarma*) within a single cognition. In that regard, the excellence produced by the action is not denoted by the case-ending itself; rather, it is understood through the necessity of enjoining the purposeful action for that [excellence].

Therefore, in verbal cognition (*śābdajñāna*), only the qualities of being a subordinate factor (*guṇatva*), being the object of a prescription (*uddeśyatva*), and being the subject of a restatement (*anuvādyatva*) are perceived; whereas predominance (*prādhānya*), being the object of knowledge (*prameyatva*), and being the object of a prescription (*upādeyatva*) appear in another means of valid cognition, namely inferential realization (*arthāpatti*). Thus, because there is a difference between the cognitions, he resolves [the objection] by stating that "there would be no fault of inconsistency" (*na nirākṛtaṃ syāt*). [Objection: In this case as well, since there is a difference between the knowledge of Brahman and the enjoined knowledge, the three contradictory triads would appear in a state of fixed distinction. [Reply: He says "no," with the words "But where, however, from another means of valid cognition... (*yatra punaḥ pramāṇāntarāt*).

[Objection: "In this case as well, let it be accepted that there are indeed two cognitions. What, then, is the difference in their causal complexes (*sāmagrī*)? For even a thousand cognitions produced by a single causal complex cannot possibly have different objects of knowledge (*prameya*). [Reply: Let it be then that the collection of words other than the injunctive word first establishes the nature of Brahman as a distinct entity, and then, having generated a subsequent cognition that restates it, it assigns that [nature] as the object of the injunction; thus, through the injunctive word, there is syntactic unity (*padaikavākyatā*)."

He says "no"—"and that very [text] is not the *samanvaya* (harmonious connection). Now, one might object: "In that case, those words which form a single syntactical unit with an injunctive word (*vidhipada*) would have a separate connection, and thus the attainment of Brahman would be subordinate to them. Anticipating this, he asks: "Then what about the words of the *arthavāda*? One might further object: "Even here, because they refer to an existing fact (*bhūtārtha*), they must be subordinate to an injunction, just like the knowledge produced by an *arthavāda*. He says "no": "But here, however, it is not touched upon [by an injunction]. The sense is that subordination to an injunction exists for the sake of reaching a purpose (*prayojana*), not on account of the fact that something is an existing reality.

Although the failure to grasp [the truth] is removed by verbal knowledge (*śābdajñāna*), nevertheless, the cessation of ignorance—consisting of false knowledge and its latent impressions—occurs through immediate experience (*aparokṣānubhava*). And since that [immediate experience], which does not arise from verbal knowledge as its result, must be established, [the opponent] raises the objection that knowledge is enjoined [as a means to it]: "But then, from verbal knowledge... [In response, the author says: "If that is so, then one must state the instrumental factor (*karaṇakāraka*) for the knowledge being enjoined, just as in the case of rice and the like; but that is not possible," and thus he asks: "What is that knowledge?"

[Objection: But is it not well known that perception and the other means of knowledge are instruments for producing immediate (aparokṣa) cognition? [Reply: No; because it would follow that they have the same result as previous cognitions. Thus he says: "And verbal [cognition]... and so forth.

Now, it may be argued that verbal knowledge is what is being enjoined. Is that knowledge, by virtue of being enjoined, something whose fruit is indirect—the initial cognition or its continuous stream? It is not the initial one; thus he says: "That is incorrect, as for that which... This is because, as has been shown, there would be a lack of uniformity if the sentence were intended to convey both [the cognition and its result]; this is the remainder of the sentence.

One might object: "Once Brahman has been understood through the first cognition, let a continuous stream of cognitions (pratyaya-santāna) be enjoined with that as its object; from the accumulation of their latent impressions (saṃskāra), direct perception (aparokṣa) will be established. To this he raises the following doubt: "Now, is it that very same cognition [which is enjoined]? Is this understood through the force of an injunction for meditation (upāsanā-vidhi), or rather through the force of the injunction for seeing (darśana-vidhi) in the passage, "One should see the Self in the Self alone"? In the first place, no injunction for meditation is heard [in the relevant texts].

This is because passages such as "One should meditate [on him] as the Self," "One should meditate on the Self alone as the world," and "The wise man, having known Him alone," are intent upon establishing the subject of the extraordinary Self by employing a cognition that is established by its own nature; furthermore, because of the hearing of the restrictive particle *eva*, the sentence is intent upon the qualification, and since there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) if both were being established simultaneously; and because in the passage "He is to be meditated upon" (*nididhyāsitavyaḥ*), the statement is intended as a praise so as not to cause a syntactical split within the sentence devoted to establishing the Self.

Now, as for the argument that [the injunction of meditation follows] from the force of the injunction for seeing (*darśana*), he says "no"—for how could that be obtained through the two terms "worship" (*upāsti*) and "meditation" (*dhyāyati*)? If it is argued that because knowledge is everywhere inseparably connected with its continuous flow, the injunction of knowledge implies an injunction for that continuity, he says "no"—it is not by means of knowledge alone. Nevertheless, perhaps the injunction for worship might somehow be inferred from the injunction for profound meditation (*nididhyāsana*).

Nevertheless, since meditation is not a cause for direct perception—which is the fruit—he says: "Nor from practice. Because practice is not a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and because the object is not in contact [with the senses], there is no direct perception of the reality through practice; rather, the meaning is that it is merely a false directness.

Is it not the case that meditation is heard of as having direct perception as its fruit in the passage, "But then, meditating, he beholds Him who is partless"? True; in one instance, the concentration of the mind serves as the cause for one-pointedness, and by means of that one-pointed mind acting as a cooperative factor, the word itself—by the force of the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) in the term "aupaniṣadam" [that which is known through the Upaniṣads]—produces direct knowledge.

Because of the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) of the statement, "Meditating, he sees by means of the clarity of knowledge" (*dhyāyamāno jñānaprasādena paśyati*); because one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgrya*) is the cause for perceiving subtle objects; because when the benefit is accomplished through what is perceived, it is improper to postulate something unperceived (*adṛṣṭa*); because one who desires direct perception engages spontaneously in meditation (*upāsanā*); and because the injunction for profound reflection (*nididhyāsana*) has a perceptible purpose—it has been stated that there is no injunction here. This is what [the author] expresses: "Nor is it heard. The meaning is that since the sentence is a restatement of a perceptible capacity, no injunction is heard therein.

One might object: "Since it serves as a cause for direct realization through the door of one-pointedness, let it proceed even by way of a visible result. Thus he raises the objection: "But what is the need for hearing (śravaṇa) in this matter? The passage containing the reply is clear in its meaning. Therefore, the sense is that because there are not two distinct cognitions, and because it is impossible for a single cognition to serve both purposes, the knowledge of Brahman cannot be something enjoined.

The phrase "yat punar" (as for what was further said) has a clear meaning. He states that the determination of the function of a word—which depends upon the intended purport (*tātparya*)—is not achieved through the illustration of a stable entity (*sthāyivastu*), saying: "That is appropriate there. Now, one might object: the five sentences—"He sacrifices the *samidhs*," "He sacrifices *tanūnapāt*," "He sacrifices the *iḍās*," "He sacrifices the *barhis*," and "He sacrifices with the *svāhā*-utterance"—enjoin five ritual items and also enjoin their sequence. Therefore, he reiterates the point that the word itself would be rendered redundant, saying: "As for this which was said..."

He offers a rebuttal—that only the word-meanings (padārthas) are accessible through verbal testimony, whereas sequence is accessible through presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) and not through verbal testimony—by the words "yattāvat pratyekam" ("as for that which [is said] regarding each"). This means "those [meanings] indeed. The ellipsis to be supplied is: "there is no injunction of their sequence."

Is it said that sentences convey a sequence that is a distinct entity from the word-meanings, or is it the conveyance of a sequence consisting merely of the word-meanings themselves? It is not the latter alternative, as he says: "Nor are those [word-meanings] denotable by the word 'sequence'. But surely a subsidiary (aṅga) is enjoined, and the injunction of performance (prayogavidhi) employs that which is a subsidiary.

Therefore, since sequence is also to be enjoined because it is employed by the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*), one must accept that even though sequence is not the meaning of a word, its injunction is to be derived from the sentences themselves. To this he says: "Even the injunction of performance [does not enjoin it]. The meaning is: because only what has been enjoined is to be employed, and it is only the ritual items (*padārtha*) that have been enjoined. Otherwise, there would be a circular dependency: the injunction of performance would apply to what is enjoined, and the injunction of performance would require the assumption of an injunction [for the sequence]. Now, one might argue: "The sequence is nothing other than the ritual items themselves; therefore, while employing the ritual items, one also employs the sequence. To this he says: "It has already been stated that those [items] are not the sequence."

Another says: "There is no such thing as 'succession' (krama), because it is not observed in any single object; for if it were based on multiple objects, succession would be impossible due to the simultaneity of those objects, and if there were no simultaneity, it would be impossible for a property to reside in both. To this he replies: "And there is no such thing as succession... [The opponent objects: "But surely, like conjunction (saṃyoga), if it resides in both, there must be simultaneity of the objects," as was stated. To this he replies: "In that case, succession is a real entity (vastubhūta). The sense is that precisely because it is succession, there is no requirement for simultaneity.

[Objection: But surely, no sequence is perceived without the apprehension of limiting conditions (*upādhi*) such as place, time, and substance. To this he says: "Those very [things]... [Objection: But surely, because the objects to be performed (*anuṣṭheya-padārtha*) have not yet attained their own nature, there can be no sequence of place, time, or substance. To this he says: "It is merely the cognition of memory... The meaning is that the sequence of the text itself, when being remembered, becomes superimposed upon the objects to be performed. "In every way" is the conclusion.

Now, one might object: "A prescriptive injunction for the sequence must be stated. We reply: No; because sequence is not something that can be enjoined. Rather, sequence is established as a qualification of what is to be performed (*anuṣṭheya*), but it is not itself enjoined, since it is not something to be performed. By what, then, is it established? It is established by the impossibility of a single agent performing multiple ritual items [simultaneously], as he says: "And that [sequence] is due to the oneness of the agent," and "and due to proximity. This means that in the absence of a sequence based on purpose (*arthakrama*), there is a sequence based on textual order (*pāṭhakrama*).
Therefore, the meaning of this section is that in all cases, the two types of objects to be known are established by these two means of knowledge alone.

The passage beginning with "In this case, there is not a duality of cognitions" and ending with "the Veda makes [it] understood" has a clear meaning. He states that while the eye is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) independently for each object with which it comes into contact, the word is not a means of valid cognition for every individual thing; rather, it is a means of valid cognition only by coming together [with other words] where there is an intended meaning (*tātparya*). Thus he says: "In that case, it is logical that it makes known whatever it [intends to] convey."

One might object: "Surely the knowledge of the reality of the Self derived from verbal testimony should not be solely concerned with an object of cognition (*prameya*); rather, by being the object of an injunction and thus being the object of the injunctive cognition produced by an injunctive word, it must be subordinate to that injunction. To this he says: "Let it not be so" (*mā bhūt*). "How then is the realization of Brahman as the Self established? To this he says: "When that [injunction] has been enjoined, [it follows] by implication" (*tasmin vihite 'rthāt*). "But by what inconsistency is the establishment of that reality [brought about]? To this he says: "Because it possesses an object" (*saviṣayatvāt*). The meaning is: precisely because the attainment of comprehension would otherwise be impossible.

He refutes this, saying: "Even so, the meaning is not intended. The sense is that it is contradictory to claim that regarding a single object, the first apprehension is invalid while the second cognition of that very same object is valid; likewise, it is contradictory to say that the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) is not a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), yet the presumptive testimony based on that revelation (*śrutyarthāpatti*) is a means of valid knowledge, and so forth. Furthermore, he states that the impossibility of enjoining a cognition does not imply that the object of cognition is a real entity: "Nor is it by necessity," etc. [Objection: Since cognition is intrinsically valid (*svataḥprāmāṇya*), it is logical that its object must be exactly as it is.

"Otherwise, there would be no purpose for a positive injunction regarding superimposed knowledge"; to this he replies: "For they have imagined objects. The sense is: why should the verbal cognition not possess intrinsic validity even prior to its connection with a positive injunction? Now, it might be argued that even for the cognition of what is to be enjoined, the observed result is simply the correct apprehension of its own object; therefore, setting that aside, to claim it has a superimposed object would involve the postulation of something unobserved. To this he replies: "This very point is the reason here."

The meaning is that, since it contradicts all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is more logical to postulate the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) than to postulate what is already observed (*dṛṣṭa*). With the words, "Therefore, since the Veda culminates in action," the proponent of non-commencement (*anārambhavādī*) concludes his refutation of the partial Siddhāntin.

[Objection: "But if the Vedāntas lack the status of having dharma and Brahman as their subject matter, would they not become useless, since they are included [in the curriculum] by the injunction for Vedic study? [Reply: No; he says so with the words, "And this being the case, 'this Self is Brahman,' etc."

In this regard, the Vedāntas culminate in the injunction for the origination of meditation upon the Self as qualified by all the attributes proclaimed in the Vedāntas; in the injunction of application (*viniyoga-vidhi*), they culminate through the inclusion of tranquility (*śama*) and other requisites as the procedure (*itikartavyatā*); in the injunction of qualification (*adhikāra-vidhi*), they culminate by relating the person desiring liberation as the one to be enjoined; and in the injunction of performance (*prayoga-vidhi*), they culminate by impelling the qualified person to perform the rite along with its constituent parts. All of this has already been established.

In this regard, is it being said that the entire Veda is determined to be intent upon action (kārya) because words possess the capacity to convey their own meanings as connected with action, or is it due to the authority of the statements of the Sūtra-author and other experts? It cannot be the first alternative, because that will be refuted in the *Samanvaya* Sūtra. As for the claim that it is due to the authority of the statements of experts, he says in response: "This would be so if [it were true] that the entire meaning of the Veda [is such]."

[Objection: Even though *dharma* alone was the subject introduced at the outset, this *brahman* has been defined as a secondary topic (*prāsaṅgika*). [Reply: No; he says "and it has been investigated" (*vicāritaśca*). How is it understood that the inquiry proceeded under the heading of the meaning of the Veda? He says: "Insofar as it is concerned solely with the goal to be accomplished" (*kāryaniṣṭha eva*), based on the force of the statements of the authors of the Sūtra, the Bhāṣya, and the Vārttika.

The intention here is as follows: "Now, therefore, the inquiry into Dharma. This is the subject matter of the Mīmāṃsā-śāstra on Dharma. The deliberation is whether it should be commenced or not. The prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that it should not be commenced, because perception and other means of knowledge are not instruments for determining the meaning under investigation, and because the Veda is employed for the sake of transcendental merit (*adṛṣṭa*) due to the injunction to study it. For that purpose, it is deliberated whether the injunction to study has a transcendental purpose or a perceptible purpose.

Since an injunction is inappropriate when the means [of knowledge] is already perceived, and since an injunction implies a restriction regarding what is not yet perceived, it follows that the injunction has an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). [Objection: But surely the Veda (*svādhyāya*), being understood as the object of the act of study, must be either something to be refined (*saṃskārya*) or something to be attained (*āpya*); since a visible result is possible, how can it have an unseen purpose? [Reply: No; for there is no authority (*pramāṇa*) for the application of the refined text to another ritual, and that which is already attained would be fruitless.

[Objection: But surely, since the comprehension of the meaningful content—which has a visible fruit—is obtained from the sacred tradition (āmnāya), one cannot postulate an unseen fruit (adṛṣṭa). [Reply: No; for if activity toward the means of a visible fruit were to proceed from something else, it would result in the redundancy of the injunction (vidhi). [Objection: But how can study, whose primary factor is the object of action (karmakāraka), be postulated as having an independent unseen fruit? [Reply: No; because the object of action is itself fruitless, one must postulate the opposite—that the fruit belongs to the act—according to the principle of the *saktu* (barley-meal) injunction: "one studies by means of the Veda" (*svādhyāyenādhīyīta*). [Objection: But no fruit of study is heard even in an explanatory passage (arthavāda). [Reply: That is not so.

By means of the commonality of being "study," the fruits of recitation and study—such as streams of clarified butter and so forth—are extended even to the initial study; thus, according to the logic of the *Rātrisatra*, there is a modification of the fruit in the injunction: "One desiring streams of clarified butter and so forth should study with the *svādhyāya*. Furthermore, because it is not a mere purificatory act (*saṃskārakarma*), the mention of the fruit is not a mere explanatory praise (*arthavāda*).

[Objection: "But even if the purpose is unseen (adṛṣṭārtha), what loss is there to the inherent capacity for understanding the meaning? [Reply: No; for we observe that in the case of mantras employed for other purposes such as the removal of poison, there is a suppression of the intention to convey the meaning. Therefore, since the Veda lacks the intention to convey meaning, since it is not an object of perception and the like, and since inquiry serves only to assist other means of valid cognition, it follows that an inquiry into Dharma, being without a basis, should not be commenced. [Conclusion: This inquiry must indeed be commenced;
this is the established position (siddhānta), because its duty to be performed is established by the injunction for the study of one's own Vedic portion (svādhyāyādhyayana-vidhi).

[Objection: But has it not been stated that [the Veda] is without a basis? [Reply: No, because the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) is its basis. [Objection: But was it not shown that its purpose is unperceived (*adṛṣṭa*)? [Reply: No, because study has the object of action (*karmakāraka*) as its primary element, and thus it is impossible for it to have an independent unperceived purpose. [Objection: But was it not said that there is no purpose whatsoever in the object of action? [Reply: No, because both are possible: the *svādhyāya* (one’s own Vedic text) is acquired through study by way of a perceived means, and it is also refined by the force of the injunction to study the text along with its auxiliary limbs (*aṅga*).

But has it not been stated that there is no application (*viniyoga*) for the refined [text]? No; for its application is established precisely through the authority of its being adopted by the injunctions of the ritual (*kratu-vidhi*). Indeed, the injunction of the ritual, desiring the comprehension of its own subject matter, adopts the Veda as a refined text because it serves as the generator of that comprehension. But is it not the case that the authority of adoption adopts merely the Veda as the generator of knowledge, and not the refinement? True; yet—

By the very force of the injunction for study (*adhyayanavidhi*), it is postulated that only a sacrifice performed by one who possesses the specific knowledge produced by the refined *svādhyāya* generates the *apūrva*. Therefore, observing the force of the injunction, the injunction of the ritual (*kratuvidhi*) takes up the *svādhyāya* as something refined, insofar as it produces knowledge of its own subject matter. Now, it was argued that an independent unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) should be postulated; but this is not so.

Since the attainment of an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*)—which is the inherent cause (*samavāyin*) for the apprehension of the meaning and syllables of the text and the knowledge produced thereby—is established, it is illogical to postulate an independent *adṛṣṭa* by assuming a reversal of causal factors that would contradict the Vedic revelation (*śruti*). Just as in the case of the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*), there is no contradiction in study being beneficial to the ritual (*kratu-upakāritva*), even though it is not a direct subsidiary (*anaṅga*) of the ritual itself. Now, one might argue that the suffix *-tavya* denotes an independent *apūrva* colored by the meaning of the verbal root; but that is not so.

Even if the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) were denoted [by the verbal suffix], it would be better to denote the *apūrva* residing in the object-kāraka (*karman*) denoted by a single word, rather than denoting an *apūrva* colored by the meaning of the stem (*prakṛti*) conveyed by separate words. This is merely because the *apūrva* is produced by the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*) and not by substances (*dravya*) and so forth; however, as for its inherence (*samavāya*), that is possible wherever it may be. Furthermore, if the Veda (*svādhyāya*) lacked the intention to convey meaning because it served only an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatā*), then the injunction to study (*adhyayanavidhi*) would also lack the intention to convey meaning, and consequently, the very injunction to study for the sake of an unseen purpose would not exist.

Therefore, since the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from the injunction to study the Veda along with its auxiliary limbs depends—by virtue of being inherent in the agent itself—upon visible results such as the grasping of syllables, the comprehension of meaning, and engagement in sacrifices, there is no inherent obstacle to the comprehension of meaning caused by the nature of the *svādhyāya* (one's own recitation). Consequently, one should undertake the inquiry into Dharma (*dharmavicāra*) by relying upon the sacred tradition whose meaning is intended to be expressed.

Thus, since the commencement of the treatise is intent upon demonstrating the occasion for investigating the nature of *dharma*—and not for establishing an investigation into the meaning of the entire Veda—it is established that the investigation about to begin has *dharma* as its object, and not merely the meaning of the Veda as a whole. He demonstrates this with the words: "For thus, at the commencement of the treatise... Now, one might object: based on the indicative mark (*liṅga*) found in the commentary, such as "one should investigate the Vedic sentences," it is understood that the commencement of the investigation concerns the meaning of the Veda as a whole. To this he asks: "How so?"

Since the author of the Bhāṣya has demonstrated both the general consensus and the specific disagreement regarding *dharma*, he states that it is precisely this which is to be investigated: "What is called *dharma* is something to be accomplished... Having thus shown the disagreements concerning the subject matter, he says—starting with "In this regard, [it is] characterized by the Agnihotra and so forth"—that the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) arises specifically regarding the subject of *dharma*. The particle *na* (not), however, is to be connected with both the preceding and the following words. The portion of the text prior to "When this has been suspected" is of clear meaning.

When the commencement of the treatise has been thus questioned, he introduces the aphorism of the established conclusion by stating its subject matter: "The Vedic sentences are for the sake of dharma. Since an inquiry is only appropriate for that sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) whose meaning is intended to be expressed, there is an inquiry into its intended meaning. He demonstrates the meaning of the aphorism—the inquiry into dharma, which is the occasion for the inquiry into the intended meaning—by means of the application of the aphorism: "Having studied the Veda, immediately thereafter... To the question, "What follows from this?", he says: "This being the case..."

To the question, "What is intended there that is understood? he says: "But [it is] beyond dharma. The meaning is this: when it should have been stated that "an inquiry into the meaning of the Veda must be undertaken by demonstrating the intention regarding the meaning of the Veda," the author of the Sūtras, by employing the term "dharma," intends to convey that let there be no promise to investigate the entire meaning of the Veda; rather, this is an investigation of only one part. This is how it is understood.

An objection is raised: "Is it not the case that the words 'atha' (then) and 'ataḥ' (therefore) state that the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*), having already been accomplished, is the cause for inquiry? For the study of one's own Veda is indeed a cause for inquiry into its own meaning, but not a cause for inquiry into Dharma; therefore, because of the contradiction with the words 'atha' and 'ataḥ', an inquiry into Dharma cannot be proposed. To this, he replies: "How so? As for that which was said... [and so on].

Because of the capacity of the word *dharma*—which denotes the primary subject under investigation—to imply both the general and the particular; because it is that [dharma] alone which is desired to be known due to the existence of conflicting views regarding it and its being the means for achieving the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*); and because prior to the demonstration of its authority, there is no comprehension of the general understanding, the specific conflicting views, or its status as a means to human goals regarding the meaning of the Veda, and thus such inquiry would be impossible—it is *dharma* alone that is investigated.

Thus he says: "It is said: 'That which is called dharma... and so forth. In that context, by demonstrating that dharma is fit for inquiry, he intends to show its absence in the case of the Vedic text (*vedārtha*) through the phrase "from worldly report" (*lokapravādāt*). Now, it was argued that in the inquiry into dharma, since the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*) has already been accomplished, its status as a cause is established, and thus the demonstration of the intention regarding the meaning (*arthavivakṣā*) is useless. This is true;

Since even the *agnihotra* and other such rites constitute branches of dharma (*dharmaskandha*), and since they are dharma by virtue of leading to the state of the gods (*devagati*), they are useful; thus he says: "The *agnihotra* and so forth are also the meaning of the Veda. The phrase "because" means "because they constitute a branch of conflicting views" (*vipratipattiskandhatvāt*). Therefore, the intended sense is that this [Veda] must be shown to be the object of one's own study (*svādhyāya*). Now, if the inquiry into dharma is for the sake of human ends (*puruṣārtha*), then since that is accomplished through mere study (*adhyayana*) alone, what is the use of an inquiry into dharma? To this he says: "And not from study alone."

Therefore, he says that there is no contradiction with the words "atha ataḥ": "immediately after the study [of the Veda]. Furthermore, because the word *dharma* is the primary subject, even if there were a contradiction with the words "atha ataḥ," an inquiry into *dharma* alone would be appropriate; thus he says that the inclusion of the term *dharma* is justified in order to express this. For people desire to know *dharma* itself, not the meaning of the Veda; for even that [meaning] is included because it is prompted by its being *dharma*. Thus he says: "not the meaning of the Veda."

It has been stated that the first sūtra is devoted to the inquiry into dharma by means of the apprehension of generality, the contradiction regarding particulars, the purpose of human endeavor, and the apprehension of the word "dharma. He says that the second sūtra is likewise: "That which again [is the cause] of dharma... The Prābhākaras maintain that this sūtra is primarily concerned with the definition of dharma, while the apprehension of its means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) follows by implication. The followers of the Vārtika maintain that the apprehension of the means of valid cognition is explicit, while the definition of dharma follows by implication. In any case, both are intended to be expressed.

In this context, since the mention of "Veda" might lead one to think that the entire Veda is the subject matter of Dharma, he says—"That, indeed..."—to make it understood that only the *codanā* (injunction) is intended.

One might object: "The mention of *codanā* (Vedic injunction) is not intended to exclude all the Vedas from being authoritative regarding *dharma*; rather, it has some other purpose. To this, he says: "Now, as for the mention of *codanā*... [and so forth].

The meaning is as follows: the operation of words such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*) has for its object the *bhāvanā* characterized by human activity, which culminates in that which is to be brought about (*bhāvya*). It has the cognition of the word itself as its instrument (*karaṇa*) and the cognition of explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) containing praise or censure as its procedure (*itikartavyatā*). Although it is expressed by the specific optative suffix—despite the general verbal nature (*ākhyātatva*) shared with other verbal endings which denote the *bhāvanā* of the action—it is called the "verbal *bhāvanā*" (*śabdabhāvanā*). Alternatively, the word itself, as qualified by the three aforementioned factors, is the verbal *bhāvanā*; or else, it is a quality of the word.

For in all cases, an instrument (*karaṇa*) becomes an instrument with respect to the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) only by way of accomplishing that which is to be brought about (*bhāvya*), being assisted by the procedure (*itikartavyatā*). In this context, the knowledge whose object is the verbal efficient force (*śabdabhāvanā*)—which is produced by words such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and is assisted by knowledge of praise and so forth—is the cause of a person’s engagement or withdrawal because it is a motivating knowledge; thus, by way of accomplishing that which is to be brought about, it is called the instrument with respect to the verbal efficient force.

And that verbal productive energy (śabdabhāvanā), in producing a person's inclination toward action, is unable to do so without the object of that action being a human goal (puruṣārtha); for a person does not engage in what is not a human goal.

Consequently, because the activity of a person is impelled by an injunction (*codanā*), the verbal root-meaning—which is not a human goal and is expressed by the same word—is set aside as the objective (*bhāvya*). Instead, even though it is a qualification of the person, heaven (*svarga*) and the like are adopted as the objective. Thus, the activity of the person—having the verbal root-meaning as its instrument (*karaṇa*), the *prayāja* offerings and so forth as its procedure (*itikartavyatā*), and being directed toward heaven and the like as its objective—becomes the "objective-efficient-force" (*arthabhāvanā*). Therefore, the term "injunction" (*codanā*) is employed to indicate that the "verbal-efficient-force" (*śabdabhāvanā*) is the prompter for the accomplishment of such an objective-efficient-force.

This is not the essence; rather, the rebuttal begins with "the injunction for study," and so forth. Its meaning is as follows: in the statement "one's own Veda is to be studied," the operation of the suffix *tavya* is the verbal productive energy (*śabdabhāvanā*). This has as its goal the objective productive energy (*arthabhāvanā*) characterized by the person's engagement in study; it has as its instrument the knowledge that impels one toward its own object; and it has as its procedure the cognition of the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) and other elements that constitute the fruit of study.

And that [verbal productive energy] brings about the objective productive energy—characterized by the person's engagement, having study as its instrument, culminating in the Veda as its goal, and having facing east and so forth as its procedure.

And that [study], being incapable of producing the mental realization (*arthabhāvanā*) without being the cause for generating a fruitful cognition of the subject matter to be cultivated (*bhāvya*), implies—through the power of the injunctive suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth contained within the Veda—that the ritual realizations (*kratubhāvanā*) denoted by those words have heaven and the like as their objects, albeit indirectly. Thus, by the very force of the injunction to study, it is established that the Veda conveys mental realizations whose objects are specific fruits.

Therefore, by the mere mention of the Veda, it is established that these mental realizations, setting aside the primary meaning of the verbal roots, have heaven and the like as their objective supports.

Moreover, if "injunction" (*codanā*) were used, there might be a suspicion that the Vedāntas have a different purpose; to dispel that, it is more appropriate to use the term "Veda. Thus he says: "Furthermore, [he uses] the mention of the Veda itself. He states another doubt: "For if 'injunction' were mentioned... [The objection: "But having promised an inquiry into Dharma immediately after the study of the Veda, by saying 'characterized by injunction' (*codanā-lakṣaṇa*), he speaks only of Vedic injunctions. [Reply: No, because there is no distinction [between them] in that context.

And by this sūtra, why should there not be, even in that case, the universal application of *codanā* (injunction)? He states the restriction of Vedic injunctions in another way: "Now, in the section concerning the Vedas (*vedādhikaraṇa*). He offers a rebuttal, saying, "This is a common proverb," implying that one who sets aside the mention of "Veda" obtained in the definition-sūtra (*lakṣaṇasūtra*) and applies it elsewhere would not be acting with deliberate intent. Therefore, he says, "Hence, from the mention of *codanā*," meaning that the term *codanā* is used for the purpose of excluding the possibility that the Upanishads (*vedānta*) have *dharma* as their primary subject matter.

Therefore, according to the intention of the authors of the Sūtra, Bhāṣya, and Vārtika, [the work] has Brahman alone as its subject matter, not Dharma; thus he says: "In this way, the author of the Sūtras... and so forth.

[Objection: Is it not the case that there exists a statement enjoining precisely those [Vedic texts] as pertaining to *dharma*? To this he says: "But surely its purpose is seen. True; however, by the force of the introductory context of the aphorism on the injunction of *dharma*, the subsequent general statement is restricted to the specific subject at hand. Thus he says: "True; by the power of that introductory context. Having stated the rebuttal in general terms, he states it for each [case] individually: "Moreover, its purpose is seen."

One might object: "Is it not the case that by the word *āmnāya* (the Veda), the application of the entire Veda to the comprehension of *dharma* is clearly established? He answers this with the question, "How so? He refutes this by stating, "After the study of the Veda," and so forth: the commentary (*bhāṣya*) does not intend to convey the totality of the application (*viniyoga*), but rather intends to establish the existence of the meaning of the *āmnāya*. Just as when it is said, "Form is perceptible," this does not mean that every instance of perception is applied to form, but rather merely states the connection of form with perception—so it is here. Thus he responds.

"Exclusion of non-connection" (*ayogavyavaccheda*) means that, having refuted the Vedas' lack of connection with the comprehension of ritual action (*karman*), their connection is established. It does not mean "exclusion of connection with something else" (*anyayogavyavaccheda*); the meaning is that it is not being asserted that the Vedas have no connection with other objects. Now, one might ask: since the word *karman* refers to the object of knowledge in general, would it not apply equally to both Dharma and Brahman? To this he says: "And by the word 'karman'... [etc.].

"How can a word that is well-known in the sense of an action or a mere object have the action as its primary meaning? To this he replies, "Because of the context," stating: "Since it leads to the understanding of that [Brahman]. "Therefore" is the conclusion.

The phrase "what more" (*yat punaḥ*) is a restatement of what has already been said. By the word "uselessness" (*ānarthakya*), either the absence of a denotable meaning or the absence of a purpose is intended. He first states that it is not the absence of a denotable meaning with the words: "In that case, if 'uselessness' means the absence of a meaning," and so forth. Then, having restated the lack of purpose with the word "now" (*atha*), he states the refutation: "Let it be [the case of] 'He wept' (*so'rodīt*). [Objection: But surely a purpose can be postulated for those [sentences] as well, just as in the case of syntactic connections such as "Pūṣan has the ground flour as his portion" (*pūṣā prapiṣṭabhāgaḥ*). [Reply: No, he says: "Because they form a single sentence" (*ekavākyatvāt*).

[Objection: "But surely, just as the injunction 'carrying the fuel below, one should run after [the fire], for [it is] above for the gods' establishes the carrying above as part of a single syntactical unit with the preceding [text], let a purposeful injunction be postulated here as well. [Reply: No, he says—because it is impossible to postulate [such]. [Objection: In that case, the Vedānta passages too must have action as their purpose because they lack a [distinct] purpose. [Reply: No, he says—those, however, which have discarded all that is inauspicious...

Therefore, he states that the Sūtra refers to sentences read within the context of ritual action (kriyāprakaraṇa): "Because it is not itself a human goal" (*ataḥ svayamapuruṣārthatvāt*). He provides the evidence for the point that it is only those [sentences] read in the context of ritual action that are shown to be connected with action as commendatory statements (*stāvaka*) when they lack a purpose of their own, and not the Vedāntas: "And likewise, only those of that kind" (*tathā ca tadvidhānyeva*). The meaning is that no Vedānta sentence whatsoever has been cited in the section on Arthavāda (*arthavādādhikaraṇa*) as being subordinate to ritual action.

The phrase "even some" indicates the manner in which the Prābhākaras commence their treatise. This is the underlying intention: the injunction for Vedic study (*adhyayana-vidhi*) indeed enjoins inquiry (*vicāra*). And that [injunction], desiring that the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*) culminate in its fruit, would enjoin inquiry into the meaning of the Veda as a whole, not specifically inquiry into *dharma*. Now, it may be objected: an object of inquiry deserves investigation when there is a general consensus regarding it and a specific disagreement; such is not the case with the meaning of the Veda. To this he replies: "Rather, [it is for] one who has studied the Veda... and so forth.

In the statement, "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the *udbhid* [sacrifice]," there arises a doubt regarding the mode of expression (*vacanavyakti*): is the sacrifice enjoined with reference to one who desires cattle, or is the qualification of being one who desires cattle enjoined with reference to the injunction of the sacrifice, or is it both? Similarly, in the case of the *sattra*, where the sacrificers themselves are the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), is the status of being an officiating priest enjoined with reference to the sacrificers, or is the status of being a sacrificer enjoined with reference to the officiating priests? It is because of such doubts concerning the mode of expression that this inquiry is undertaken. "Now, therefore, the inquiry into Dharma. The subject matter (*viṣaya*) is the investigation into the meaning of the Veda.

The inquiry is whether that [Veda] should be studied or not. For now, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it should not, because there is no means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for its objective basis (*ālambana*). [Objection: But surely the inquiry would have the Vedic revelation (*āmnāya*) as its objective basis. [Reply: No; because the revelation, being a subordinate element (*śeṣa*) to the injunction for teaching (*adhyāpana-vidhi*), lacks the intention to convey its own meaning. How so? First of all, the act of study (*adhyayana*) attains the status of being subordinate to that [injunction] because its performance is prompted by the injunction for teaching.

Furthermore, the "Veda as one's own recitation" (*svādhyāya*)—by way of accomplishing the act of study—is also intent upon accomplishing the act of teaching, like sentences concerning the removal of poison and so forth; thus, according to some, it does not deserve to convey its own meaning.

Others, however, maintain that because the suffix -tavya in the injunctive sentence regarding the private recitation (*svādhyāya-vidhi*) establishes an *apūrva* (transcendental result), the status of the Veda as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of that *apūrva* is first understood. Since the injunction for teaching (*adhyāpana-vidhi*) necessitates the performance of the enjoined study, the act of teaching is accomplished through study without setting aside the previously understood status of the Veda as a subordinate element of the *apūrva*. Consequently, since it is a subordinate element of the *apūrva*, its literal meaning is not intended to be expressed; thus, the conclusion follows that no inquiry into the meaning should be commenced.

In this regard, an inquiry must be undertaken, because the Vedic study (*svādhyāya*) has a meaning intended to be expressed. Now, it was argued that Vedic study is a subsidiary part of the injunction for teaching; but this is not so, because being a subsidiary cannot be established by mere motivation. For the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*) does not become a subsidiary to subsequent sacrifices merely through the motivation of those sacrifices. [Objection: But gender, number, the fore-sacrifices (*prayāja*), and so forth, achieve the status of subsidiaries because their performance is motivated by the injunctions for the sacrifices; [Response: No.

The status of being an auxiliary (*aṅga*) arises from the force of the means of proof for application (*viniyoga*), such as context (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth; and because it is an auxiliary, its performance is prompted by that [primary act]. However, no such means of proof for application exists here [in the case of the Veda]. Nor does the status of being an auxiliary follow merely from being prompted; this is the distinction. Therefore, because of its independence, the Veda has the intended meaning as its purpose.

As for the claim that it is a subordinate factor (*aṅga*) of the *apūrva* of study, even there, since the *apūrva* requires a purpose and because it is improper to postulate an unseen result when a seen one is available, a purposeful cognition produced by the capacity of the *svādhyāya* (the Vedic text) is postulated as the fruit. [Objection: But that is not something arising from a ritual injunction (*naiyogika*); rather, it is a fruitful cognition produced by a seen capacity. [Reply: True; it is precisely a fruit that does not arise from an injunction.

An unseen potency (*apūrva*) is postulated as the benefit [accruing] to the cognition by virtue of its being an auxiliary to the performance [of the rite]; or else, it is postulated that the intentionality (*tātparya*) of the cognition is dependent upon its having a result produced by a mandate (*naiyogika*). This is because the causes for worldly intentionality, such as the desire to speak (*vivakṣā*), are absent. Thus, since its meaning is intended [to be conveyed], the scripture (*śāstra*) ought to be commenced.

In that regard, he offers a rebuttal—stating "even there, not the entire meaning of the Veda"—to show that even at the commencement of the inquiry into the meaning of the Veda, the Vedāntas are not redundant (gatārtha). The sense is this: although the inquiry is conducted under the condition of being the "meaning of the Veda," by the force of the inclusion of *dharma*, it is understood that only one part of it has been investigated. One might object: "How can an inquiry impelled by the injunction to study the whole [Veda] have as its object only a single part? To this he replies with the objection: "How so? He then provides the answer: "If that were the case, then [the sūtra would begin with] 'Now, therefore... (*tathā sati athātaḥ*). This implies that if the inquiry were restricted to a single part, the introductory words of the *Brahma-sūtra* would be inappropriate.

The meaning is as follows: because of the difference in the operation of injunctions (*vidhi*) and the difference in their respective purposes, there is no contradiction in the fact that even when investigating only a single portion [of the Veda], it is impelled by an injunction; just as the injunction "one should see form with the eye" remains operative even when one sees only a blue color—a mere part of form—so it is here. Otherwise, if one intended to investigate the entire meaning of the Veda in accordance with the injunction, the mention of *dharma* alone would not have been made; thus he says: "since [the inquiry concerns] dharma."

He raises an objection: "The purpose of including the word 'dharma' is indeed the exclusion of the investigation into only a portion of the Veda's meaning; however, the true purpose is the establishment that the meaning of the Veda serves the goals of human life (puruṣārtha). He replies: "True; nevertheless, [this refers] to the authors of the treatises. He refutes this further: "In that case, then... For one must state the basis for using the word *dharma* to denote the meaning of the Veda. It cannot be based on conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), because there is disagreement regarding its application even to such things as the worship of *caityas*.

Now, if the word *dharma* denotes that which is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) as a means to the highest good (*śreyas*), and since the subject matter of the Veda is of such a nature, the word *dharma* applies there as well—then, in that case, since Brahman, though being cognized from the mere recitation of one's own Vedic study (*svādhyāya*), lacks the status of being denoted by the word *dharma*, and because its nature is the highest good, it is excluded by implication; therefore, it is appropriate to conduct an inquiry [into Brahman] under the heading "Dharma."

Otherwise, the intention is that one should have stated "the desire to know the meaning of the Veda" (*vedārthajijñāsā*) in order to indicate the inclusion of both Dharma and Brahman as they appear at first glance. For it cannot be said that the nature of Brahman as something to be attained (*anuṣṭheya-śreyorūpa*) is not understood prior to inquiry merely from the connection with the word *brahman*.

He states that the *Lakṣaṇasūtra* also has *dharma* as its subject matter, not the meaning of the Vedas—thus he says, "and likewise the subsequent [sūtra] as well. For a definition (*lakṣaṇa*) is intended to remove confusion regarding the application of other [definitions] to the thing to be defined (*lakṣya*). And in this case, it is precisely *dharma*—such as the worship of shrines (*caityavandana*) and so forth—that is the object of dispute due to its being erroneously applied, not the meaning of the Vedas. Therefore, he says that *dharma* alone is defined so that the definition may fulfill its purpose: "it is intended to remove disputes concerning the true nature of *dharma*."

[Objection: "But are there not also disagreements regarding the meaning of the Veda—namely, whether the meaning of the Veda is characterized by *arthavāda* (explanatory passages) or characterized by *codanā* (injunctions)? Therefore, the definition [of the Veda] is stated in order to refute that. To this, he replies: "Otherwise, in the case of disagreement regarding the meaning of the Veda... The sense is that since no action (*kārya*) is perceived in the mantras and so forth, and according to the rule that "that which is perceived by something is the meaning of that," there can be no such disagreement.

[Objection: "But even when *dharma* is mentioned, why is it not established that the meaning of the Veda is characterized by *codanā* (injunction), after having set aside the characterization as being merely explanatory (*arthavāda*)? To this he says: "Because, when *dharma* is mentioned... The meaning is that since there is no appearance of refuting contradictions regarding the meaning of the Veda in general, but rather an appearance of refuting contradictions regarding *dharma* specifically, it is impossible to grasp the refutation of contradictions concerning the meaning of the Veda which has not [yet] been understood.

Now, one might object: "Since the word *dharma* is used in the sense of the Veda's meaning (*vedārtha*), let it be intended that the very refutation of misconceptions regarding that [meaning] is what is desired. To this he asks: "How so? In that regard, it has already been stated that the word *dharma* is not used in the sense of the Veda's meaning by relying on conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), nor is it used through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*); for if something other than the primary denotation were the indicated meaning, it would follow that the Veda's meaning would be non-dharma (*adharma*).

Now, it remains to be considered whether activity toward that [Veda] occurs by adding its own specific meaning, or whether the word alone is employed as being intent upon the relationship between the name and the named. Regarding this, he first states that it is not by adding its own specific meaning: "As for the claim that 'the object characterized by the injunction (codanā) is [Dharma]'... If [Dharma] were merely characterized by the injunction, it would not be determined that "the meaning of the Veda is only this much," because the words *codanā* and *dharma* do not denote the same thing.
