The sense is as follows: just as when it is said that "whatever is visual is color," it does not follow that color is the object of every instance of perception, so it is here. With the words "But if, on the other hand... and so forth, he refutes the view that the Sūtra is intended to define *dharma* by means of injunction (*codanā*). He states the refutation while conceding [the opponent's point] with the words "But somehow... The underlying intention is this: if that which is characterized by injunction were the meaning of the Veda, then the word "object" (*artha*) would be redundant.

Since the Śyena sacrifice and others are characterized by Vedic injunction (*codanālakṣaṇa*) and constitute the subject matter of the Veda (*vedārtha*), it is impossible to exclude them [from the definition]. If they were not characterized by injunction and were not the subject matter of the Veda, then the exclusion of the Śyena and other such acts would follow from those two criteria alone, rendering the word "artha" (purposeful/wholesome) redundant; furthermore, its mention as a mere restatement (*anuvāda*) in the defining statement would be untenable. Moreover, the word "artha" would also be redundant in the formal proposition regarding the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇapratijñā*). In the context of the inquiry into Dharma (*dharmavicāra*), the purpose is to establish that the Śyena and similar acts—which are objects of prohibitive injunctions—are non-Dharma (*adharma*) precisely because they are harmful (*anartha*).

Likewise, the word "codanā" must also be understood as referring by implication to the entire Veda. How so? Is there a portion of the Veda distinct from "codanā," or is there not? If there were none, then the definition "an object characterized by codanā" would result in the identity of the definiendum and the definition, as it would simply mean "the meaning of codanā."

If it exists, that portion of the Veda must either be meaningful or meaningless. If it is meaningful, how could the meaning of a non-injunctive (non-*codanā*) portion be cognizable through an injunction? If, on the other hand, the portion of the Veda distinct from the injunction were devoid of meaning, then how could the meaning of the injunction constitute the meaning of the Veda as a whole—a collection consisting of both the meaningful and meaningless portions? Therefore, the word "injunction" (*codanā*) is intended as a metaphorical designation for the entire Veda.

With the intention of refuting two words in the sentence "the meaning of the Veda is characterized by injunction" (*codanā-lakṣaṇa*), he says: "even so, somehow. This being the case, since the determination of the meaningfulness of the Veda through its authority would have already occurred prior to the inquiry, then regarding the doubt as to whether the meaning of the Veda is characterized by injunction or characterized by explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) and the like, the Sūtra would have to be intended to provide the conclusion that "the meaning of the Veda is not characterized by explanatory passages and the like, but rather is characterized by injunction. And that is untenable, because the meaningfulness [of the Veda] has already been ascertained; thus he says: "this being so, 'characterized by injunction'..."

[Objection: But surely, since the intention to convey meaning (*arthavivakṣā*) has been demonstrated in the first sūtra, and since the meaningfulness [of the Veda] is thereby ascertained, it is appropriate to formulate the definition with reference to that [meaningful Veda]. [Reply: No; for as long as its validity (*prāmāṇya*) is not ascertained, the intention to convey meaning is impossible. In that context, the intention to convey meaning was shown merely by refuting the invalidity resulting from the injunction to study (*adhyayanavidhi*); however, validity was not established there by refuting invalidity based on causes such as being of human origin (*pauruṣeyatva*) or having a subject matter accessible through other means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntarayogyaviṣayatva*).

Therefore, because its meaningfulness is not yet ascertained, it is impossible to restrict the definition of the Vedic meaning as being "characterized by injunction" (*codanā-lakṣaṇa*). Now, if it is argued that the definition is formulated precisely by accepting its meaningfulness on the strength of the first sūtra itself, to that he replies: "In that case, the subsequent demonstration of its validity would be inappropriate. [Objection: But surely it is demonstrated again for the sake of strengthening that very point. [Response: No; for if its meaningfulness were already certain, there would be no purpose in strengthening it, and if it were uncertain, the application of the definition would not even occur.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the demonstration of the Veda’s authority is also for the sake of [establishing] the Veda’s purpose, and not for the sake of ascertaining the Veda’s meaningfulness? [Reply: No; for if the Veda’s authority were also a subject matter of the Veda, it would follow that the Veda has authority regarding an already established entity (*siddha-vastu*). Furthermore, when the author of the *Bhāṣya* begins the second chapter, he shows by saying "the definition of authority has been completed" that the authority of the Veda itself was established by the first chapter; this is appropriate only if the inquiry is preceded by the ascertainment of the Veda’s meaningfulness.

Therefore, he says that by the second sūtra, either the definition or the very status of the Dharma as a source of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is established: "And [the phrase] 'the definition of the means of valid knowledge has been stated'. Furthermore, since the authority of Mantras and Arthavādas regarding the Dharma is refuted in this very sūtra, the section on Arthavādas (*arthavādādhikaraṇa*) would become unnecessary; thus he says: "And [if one objects] regarding the Mantras and Arthavādas... If it is argued that the section exists for the purpose of demonstrating the manner of their application as commendatory statements (*stāvaka*), we say no; because their authority regarding the Dharma is refuted right here, there is no possibility of a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) arising there [in the Arthavāda section] based on them being the expounders of the Dharma.

He concludes: "Therefore, by the reasoning previously stated, it has been established that only those portions of the Veda which have the *kārya* (the task to be accomplished) as their purport were undertaken for investigation and have been investigated, but not those portions whose purport is the *vastu* (the existing reality). Hence, this [work] is commenced in order to investigate that portion of the Veda whose purport is the true nature of reality (*vastutattva*). Thus ends the second section (*varṇaka*) in the *Pañcapādikā-vivaraṇa*, the work of the venerable Svaprakāśānubhava Bhagavat, disciple of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ananyānubhava.
Now begins the third section: "Then, therefore, [there should be] the desire to know Brahman."

In this world, four meanings of the word *atha* are well-established through its usage in the linguistic conventions of the elders: immediate succession (*ānantarya*), introduction of a topic (*adhikāra*), auspicious invocation (*maṅgalācaraṇa*), and the state of being a different matter from the subject at hand (*prakṛtādarthādarthāntaratva*). Among these, since the word *atha* is employed here to denote immediate succession by way of excluding the others, he states the purport of the preceding portion of the commentary—extending up to the words "and when it has the sense of immediate succession"—with the passage beginning: "In that case, the word *atha* [signifies] the sense of immediate succession," and so forth.

How so? Since the word *jijñāsā* possesses meaning through its etymological components (*avayavārtha*), it is illogical for the desire [itself] to be that which is to be undertaken; furthermore, because it cannot be the subject matter explained in every section (*adhikaraṇa*), the word *atha* does not signify "commencement" (*adhikāra*). Moreover, since the purpose of the desire for knowledge of Brahman as an auspicious invocation (*maṅgalācaraṇa*) is already well-known, and even if it were not well-known, it would result in the word being a mere explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) intended for glorification, the Sūtra does not have the purpose of serving as an auspicious invocation.

Furthermore, since the fact that desire arises from some previously mentioned object is more well-known than its arising from anything else, there is no need for it to be explicitly stated; thus, the word *atha* does not have that [desire] as its meaning. Now, one might object: "Is it not also well-known that desire follows immediately after something? True; however, because the immediate succession is intended here in the sense of a causal relationship (*hetu-phala-bhāva*), the word *atha* illuminates the sufficient cause previously mentioned by means of expressing that immediate succession.

[Objection: Is it not true that, by the very power of the arising of a desire culminating in activity toward the knowledge of Brahman, the complete cause is inferred; what then is the purpose of the word *atha*? [Reply: There is no fault, because the word *atha* aims at conveying the specific qualification of the qualified person (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*) which has previously occurred and serves as the complete cause for the entire effect—beginning from the arising of the desire up to the arising of the desired knowledge.

And that comprehension, by way of generating a desire that culminates in activity toward the knowledge sought, becomes an auxiliary factor for such activity; thus, it is well said that the word "atha" (then/thereupon) signifies "immediacy" (*ānantarya*) in order to indicate the four previously established means (*sādhana-catuṣṭaya*), as it serves as the complete cause for the entire process beginning from the arising of a desire characterized by the motive for activity up until the arising of the knowledge itself, by means of denoting this immediacy.

One might object: "How can the word *jijñāsā*, which is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in the sense of 'investigation' (*vicāra*), be accepted as having its meaning through its etymological components (*avayavārtha*), according to the maxim that 'convention overrides etymology'? He raises this objection with the words beginning from "But this word *jijñāsā* is a term for investigation" up until the point where the text says "the passage [thereafter] has a clear meaning. The response begins with "It is said: this is not the word *jijñāsā*," and so forth. The underlying intention is as follows: there are four modes of the application of words.

In this context, *rūḍhi* (conventional usage) is as follows: in the linguistic practice of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*), there is an indivisible relationship of denotation that arises solely from the capacity of usage, without depending on anything other than the denoter and the denoted. *Yoga* (etymological derivation) is the denotation of a specific meaning by a word—which has attained the status of a single compound through *samāsa* and so forth—by means of the multiple denotative powers residing in its own constituent parts. Both of these are called the primary function (*mukhyā vṛttiḥ*). *Gauṇa* (secondary/metaphorical usage) is the function [of a word] toward another object, distinct from its own denoted object, by way of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) due to the connection with a quality (*guṇa*).

In that regard, when it is possible for a single word, which is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in one sense, to have a derivative application (*yoga-vṛtti*) in another sense, the conventional meaning is adopted by setting aside the derivative meaning, according to the maxim: "Conventional usage overrides derivative etymology. Furthermore, when both conventional and primary derivative applications are possible, the secondary (*gauṇa*) meaning is discarded; for in a case where a word already possesses an established capacity for a certain meaning through its derivative application, there is no reason to postulate an additional power for that same word in that very context, as there would be no other effect to account for.

[Objection: But surely, in the case of words such as *paṅkaja* ("mud-born"), another mode of operation (*vṛtti*) called "etymological-conventional" (*yogarūḍhi*) must be postulated. [Reply: No; because even there, the meaning is understood through the etymological mode of operation alone. [Objection: But since we observe that, setting aside other objects such as blue lotuses (*utpala*), the word *paṅkaja* immediately brings about the cognition of the red lotus (*tāmara*), two distinct powers (*śakti*) must be postulated. [Reply: No; for even when the capacity is no different, the first cognition is observed due to the frequency of usage.

Just as, although there is no difference in the capacity [of the word] with respect to nine different meanings, the first comprehension from the word "cow" (go) occurs only regarding the form possessing a dewlap and so forth, due solely to the frequency of its usage; therefore, since the occurrence of usage and comprehension is possible through the already established capacity alone, there is no need to postulate another capacity—thus he says: "This is not the word *jijñāsā*. The preceding passage, up to the question "How?", is of clear meaning.

But surely, even by means of etymological derivation (yogavṛtti), it is only the connection between the meanings of the word's components that is conveyed by the word; however, "inquiry" (vicāra) is not the meaning of the components of the word "desire to know" (jijñāsā). How then can the understanding of that [inquiry] be established as otherwise accomplished through a capacity already [established]? Thus he raises the objection: "How is there establishment otherwise? (kathamanyathāsiddhatvam).

He provides the rebuttal: "Because it has the sense of inquiry (vicāra) implicitly included within it. [The opponent objects: "But how can mere cognition, which is what is intended, be invariably concomitant with inquiry? To this he says: "In this way, [there is] the usage and the cognition. [This means that] even though the word itself lacks the meaning of its constituent parts (avayava-artha), since the usage and the resulting cognition are established through indication (lakṣaṇā) based on the invariable concomitance (avinābhāva) between the word and the connection of the meanings of its parts, there is no need to postulate a further power (śakti). This is because there is no effect that cannot be otherwise accounted for (ananyathāsiddha). Thus he concludes: "Because it has the sense of inquiry implicitly included within it. Now, one might ask: "How is mere cognition invariably concomitant with inquiry? To this he says: "In this way, [there is] the usage and the cognition."

Indeed, knowledge that is desired is intended to be understood together with its object, because there can be no desire for knowledge whose object is not understood. Consequently, when an entity has already been apprehended, the knowledge desired regarding it is expected to have the result of certainty in the case of what is doubtful, or the result of direct perception in the case of what is remote.

Since both of these are to be accomplished through the effort of investigating the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth, the specific knowledge desired regarding an apprehended entity leads to the investigation of the *pramāṇas* by way of invariable concomitance; this is the meaning of the application of the two cognitions (*prayoga-pratyaya*) toward the knowledge to be accomplished by investigation.

[The opponent] objects: "Is it not the case that the Sūtra does not intend to establish mere desire, since there would be no purpose [in doing so]? Rather, by way of demonstrating the knowledge sought after, it indicates the inquiry (*vicāra*) as its underlying means; thus, that [inquiry] alone is what is intended to be established by the overall purport (*tātparya*). Therefore, the word *atha* serves to introduce one of these three—the inquiry, the knowledge, or Brahman—as the subject of the purport. To this he replies: "Even so, how is this known? He elaborates on that very point: "by relying on the inquiry that is implied within [the Sūtra]."

The connection is that [the inquiry] is based on an investigation which is implicitly included by virtue of the primary meaning of the term *artha*. Therefore, the construction is: "having accepted that one of the three [meanings] is being undertaken.

In this context, he offers a rebuttal—stating "it is said: because it would follow that the scripture is not to be commenced"—by showing that if the word *atha* does not, through its expression of immediate succession (*ānantarya*), logically present a specific qualified candidate endowed with the fourfold means prescribed by the scriptures, then the inquiry, being enjoined as something to be performed for the sake of commencing the investigation, would be without a qualified subject and thus unpracticable.

[Objection: But surely the injunction for inquiry itself, by the logic of the *Viśvajit* sacrifice, will imply a specific qualified person (*adhikārin*) and culminate in activity; what then is the purpose of the word *atha*? [Reply: But surely the inquiry, once understood as something to be performed, also implies its commencement as a matter of course; so what is the use of the word *atha* for the purpose of commencing the inquiry? [Objection: But when both [commencement and qualification] are obtained through the force of the injunction, what is the determination there? [Reply: Since it serves as a necessary adjunct (*upādhi*) required by the injunction, it is more appropriate to provide the qualified person precisely by way of expressing immediate succession (*ānantarya*); thus he says: [The author] states: "Since it serves as a necessary adjunct (*upādhi*) required by the injunction, it is more appropriate to provide the qualified person precisely by way of expressing immediate succession (*ānantarya*)."

The meaning is that if [the word "should" (*kartavya*)] were intended merely to indicate eligibility (*adhikāra*), it would be purposeless—that is, it would lack a culminating purpose reached through the gateway of activity. Now, one might object: "A person desiring liberation (*mokṣakāma*) can be postulated [as the eligible person]. No; for this would entail the fallacy of a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*). To explain: when it is said "it should be done," since no specific qualification is mentioned, all persons would be understood as eligible. However, because such universal eligibility is untenable, one would have to postulate a specific eligibility [by implication]. Therefore, the sense is that it is better for the scripture itself to provide the specific eligible person directly by means of the word.

One might object: "Surely, following the principle of the *rātrisatra* sacrifice, one should take either liberation or the knowledge of Brahman—though mentioned only in an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*)—and transform it into a goal to be accomplished; thus, one who desires liberation or desires the knowledge of Brahman should investigate [the scriptures]. Consequently, at the time of understanding the injunction, there would be an injunction characterized by a specific qualified agent. To this, he raises the objection: "But [if you say] the knowledge of Brahman is the purpose..."

In this regard, the following must be stated: Is this scripture said to have universal eligibility (*sarvādhikāra*) because everyone desires its fruit, or does it have restricted eligibility (*viśiṣṭādhikāra*)? If there is restricted eligibility, then since eligibility depends upon the comprehension of the injunction (*vidhi*), the assumption of an eligibility obtained through incapacity would result in the same persistence of the cumbersome operation of both positive and negative prohibitions.

Therefore, since the injunction for inquiry is understood as being preceded by the comprehension of the qualified seeker—one who possesses the fourfold means (sādhanacatuṣṭaya) and is mentioned in the context of the injunctions to "hear" and so forth—this fault does not arise; thus, it is appropriate that the word *atha* itself provides the specific scriptural qualification of the seeker.

Now, regarding the claim that the scripture has universal authority (*sarvādhikāra*), it is not a case of absolute negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), nor does it require dependence on words to confer authority upon specific [persons]. To this, it must be said: Is the scripture of universal authority by way of its result (*phalataḥ*) or by way of its injunction (*vidhitaḥ*)? It cannot be by way of its result, because not all people possess a desire for that result; thus he says: "Because the purposefulness of the knowledge of Brahman is not established [for all]. The preceding passage, ending with the words "let there be no purposefulness for the knowledge of Brahman," is clear in meaning.

One might object: "Since the injunction for Vedic study (*adhyayana-vidhi*) has the three higher castes as its qualified agents (*adhikāra*), and since the inquiry (*vicāra*) is prompted by that injunction, the scripture possesses universal qualification (*sarvādhikāra*) precisely because of the injunction. [The author replies: "Let it not be for the sake of the knowledge of Brahman. [The opponent asks: "But surely an injunction (*vidhi*) is the cause for the performance of its own subject matter or of what is auxiliary to it; and inquiry is not the result of the act of understanding the meaning of the subject matter enjoined by the injunction for study. Therefore, does the injunction for study not also impel one to perform the inquiry for the sake of accomplishing that result?"

If it is asked: "Is it not observed anywhere that an operation (*vyāpāra*), distinct from both the object and its auxiliary, is to be performed as impelled by an injunction (*vidhi*) with a view toward the production of a result—as in the case of threshing (*avaghāta*) and the like?"—the answer is no. This is because it is precisely the threshing, which is itself the enjoined act (*vidheya*), that is repeated until the result is reached. However, one must explain how deliberation (*vicāra*), being a distinct and independent verbal action (*bhāvārtha*), can be enjoined. This is not a fault;

for just as the status of being enjoined is postulated for repetition—which is itself not enjoined and does not assist the enjoined act—because otherwise the injunction would fail to culminate in a result, so too is such a status established for deliberation.

In this regard, is the result of study—the knowledge accomplished through inquiry which has the determination of meaning as its fruit—a visible result established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*); or is it a scriptural result, being a qualification of the eligible person (*adhikārin*) due to the injunction being made with that [determination] as its aim; or is it a result obtained by the force of the injunction’s capacity to extend to its purpose? It is certainly not a visible result, because the determination of meaning does not arise from mere study, even when that study is characterized by repetition, and because superficial perception (*āpātadarśana*) does not depend upon inquiry.

Therefore, the act of study would not have the determination of meaning as its observed result. Now, it may be argued that by means of the suffix *tavya*, the verbal efficient force (*śabdabhāvanā*)—which is the agent’s own operation—is denoted in the form of an injunction; and this verbal efficient force, while bringing about the objective efficient force (*arthabhāvanā*) which has study as its instrument, postulates the comprehension of a meaningful purpose as the human goal to be accomplished by that objective efficient force.

Since human effort cannot be directed toward that which does not serve a human purpose (*puruṣārtha*), and since no other thing to be accomplished (*bhāvya*) is obtained [from the text itself], the study—due to its status as a subordinate element (*guṇa*)—attains the state of being the instrument (*karaṇa*) of the productive activity (*bhāvanā*). It becomes the instrument by way of accomplishing the comprehension of meaning, which is the thing to be accomplished. This is because even tools such as axes are seen to be instruments for the productive activity of cutting only by way of accomplishing the splitting of wood, which is the object to be produced by the action. Therefore, it is established that the comprehension of meaning is the fruit of study, precisely because the injunction to study could not otherwise function as an impeller (*pravartaka*).

Otherwise, since the study itself—being expressed by the same word—would be the objective (bhāvya), it would follow that even the acquisition of the Veda (*svādhyāyāvāpti*) could not be the fruit of the injunction. Therefore, he says: "For that [acquisition] ends with the grasping of the syllables, because its fruit is the acquisition of what is being studied. This is the intended meaning: when the object of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) is denoted by the suffix *-tavya*, and the Veda is both that object and the fruit of its own acquisition, no further objective need be postulated; for that would contradict the word which denotes the object of the productive operation.

Now, it might be objected that human activity is not produced by an injunction merely through the fact of something being an object to be brought about (*bhāvya*), but rather only in expectation of a human goal as the object to be brought about; therefore, even if there is a contradiction with the literal words, since the understanding of the meaning is the object to be brought about for the sake of accomplishing the productive operation (*bhāvanā*), one might suspect that this is what is intended. To this he replies: "Then let the course of the barley meal be [the object]. He refutes this: "Let it be so, then, that the barley meal is the destination."

The intention is as follows: since the determination of meaning does not result from mere recitation, and since the Veda being heard would otherwise be fruitless, and since mere recitation cannot serve as the objective to be realized (*bhāvya*) due to its lack of purpose, it is inferred that one should realize heaven through the study of one's own Vedic text (*svādhyāya*).

[The opponent] objects: "Since grammar is also an auxiliary limb (*aṅga*), the determination of meaning arises as a visible result from the study of the Veda together with its limbs, as prescribed by injunction; and for the sake of resolving contradictions therein, inquiry is employed. Therefore, when a visible result exists, it is not logical to postulate an invisible one. [The author] replies: "That too is not so; [the Vedas] are purposeful because of their syllables. He refutes [the objection]: "In that case, they are not purposeless."

The meaning is as follows: since the comprehension of the meaningful purpose is established through the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of study directed toward the very action characterized by the audible *svādhyāya*, and because even things like cattle or food—which are themselves means toward a further goal—are seen to function as the objects to be cultivated (*bhāvya*), the operation of the injunction extends only as far as the attainment of the audible *svādhyāya*. Now, one might object: "If the operation of the injunction extends only as far as the grasping of the syllables, then the comprehension of the meaningful purpose would be without a cause. To this, he replies: "The comprehension of the purpose is indeed prompted by the fruit [of the injunction]."

This is the intended meaning: since it is observed that the words of trustworthy worldly authorities convey their meaningful content even without an injunction, and because there is a connection [between study and result], and because—unlike in the case of threshing and other such acts enjoined by injunctions—there is no rule regarding the production of an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), the comprehension of meaning is not the fruit of the injunction; rather, the fruit is that which arises from the mere recitation of one's own accepted Vedic study.

Since the result of an injunction is indeed some unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) effect that coexists with the seen (*dṛṣṭa*), when the unseen is established without contradicting the seen result, it is not proper to postulate an independent unseen effect that contradicts it. Furthermore, since the injunction to study has as its result the comprehension of the meaning of what is fruitful, for whichever person has the qualification for a particular rite, there would be study only of the sentence pertaining to that rite, and not the study of other sentences.

In that case, because there would be an absence of results such as engagement [in ritual action], the mastery of the entire Veda would not be established; thus he says: "Furthermore, the injunction ends with the grasping of the syllables. Now, one might object: even if the study of the entire *svādhyāya* is enjoined as an obligatory duty (*nitya*), how can the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) inherent in the acquisition of the whole *svādhyāya*—which resides in the passages concerning rites for which one lacks qualification—be a cause for the establishment of the *apūrva*, given that it does not lead to the comprehension of meaning or the performance of rituals? This is not a fault; for it is possible for it to assist in the production of the *apūrva* through means such as expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*) and recitation (*japa*).

[Objection: But surely [the result] is the acquisition of the syllables from study. [Reply: But surely, what is the distinction [between the two]? There is indeed a distinction here: "acquisition" (*avāpti*) is the property of the syllables consisting in their being capable of being uttered independently, whereas "study" (*adhyayana*) is the activity of speech and mind directed toward that [acquisition].

One might object: "Surely, study must be enjoined with the aim of understanding the meaning, for an injunction cannot be formulated without a specific qualification (*adhikāra*). Moreover, when the utterance of words is enjoined specifically for the purpose of understanding the meaning, the intended purport (*tātparya*) of the sentence is established; for in common worldly usage, we observe that the purport of a word-utterance directed toward understanding the meaning is prompted by natural inclination (*rāga*). To this, he raises the objection: "But surely, the injunction for study has no explicitly heard qualification (*aśrūyamāṇādhikāra*)."

*Adhikāra* (qualification) is that by which one is authorized for this action; it refers to the cause for the relationship between the injunction and the person, such as the desire for livelihood and so forth. Now, one might object: "Let the qualified person be inferred according to the *Viśvajit* principle," or alternatively, "Since initiation (*upanayana*) is the subject under discussion—as seen in the Vājasaneyins' text beginning with 'He comes for studentship'—let it be inferred by the authority of the context (*prakaraṇa*) that the initiated person is the qualified one. To this he says "No," adding: "And the comprehension of meaning is observed to follow from the grasping of the syllables; this, by obstructing the assumption of a [separate] qualification... and so forth.

Granted that there may be an injunction stating, "One desiring comprehension of the meaning should cultivate it through study," even so, the engagement in inquiry is not enjoined by the injunction for study in the form, "One should cultivate comprehension of the meaning through inquiry. To this, he replies: "In cases where there is a visible purpose, [the engagement occurs] directly."

In this regard, is it said that the comprehension of meaning is the fruit of study—either directly or indirectly—by the very force of its purpose (*arthasāmarthya*), or rather because it is enjoined with reference to one who desires such comprehension? With this intention, he says: "To this, it is replied. Accepting the first alternative, he says: "It would follow from the injunction for study. He states that the second position is untenable: "It cannot be the cause of qualification (*adhikāra*)."

The meaning is that since the comprehension of the meaning (*arthāvabodha*) has not yet been apprehended prior to the study, a desire for it is impossible; therefore, the injunction is not intended for one who desires the comprehension of the meaning. Now, one might ask: how can there be a non-apprehension of the comprehension of the meaning? Because prior to the study, the meaning of the Veda is not apprehended, and as long as the qualifier is not known, the comprehension qualified by it cannot be understood. One might further argue: "Since the Veda is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), its meaning exists just like the words of a trustworthy person (*āpta*); thus, the mere existence of the meaning is apprehended through inference. To this we say: no.

Since the mere knowledge that [the Veda] possesses meaning is established through inference, there can be no desire for that knowledge. Furthermore, since specific sentence-meanings such as the *agnihotra* have not yet been apprehended, there can be no desire for knowledge qualified by them. If it is argued that the specific meanings of sentences like the *agnihotra* are indeed apprehended through instruction (*upadeśa*), then, because those specific cognitions of sentence-meanings would already be established, no desire for them could possibly arise.

If it is argued that determinate knowledge (*niścaya-jñāna*) is desired because the knowledge derived from instruction (*aupadeśika-jñāna*) is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*), [we reply]: when its invalidity is certain, there can be no desire for determinate knowledge regarding it, since the object of the instructional knowledge is merely an illusion; when it is doubtful, the occasion for inquiry is into its validity itself, not into the study [of the scripture].

Furthermore: because it is impossible to designate all cognitions of sentence-meanings simultaneously by means of a single cognition; because if one were to utter a word while designating [meanings] in a general sense, it would follow that the word’s purport (tātparya) extends to the mere cognition of the object; because there would be no purport regarding specific cognitions such as the *agnihotra* sacrifice; and because, by postulating a purport toward a qualified meaning in accordance with the power of the sentence, it would follow that the injunction to study (*adhyayana-vidhi*) does not have the cognition of the meaning as its motive.

Therefore, since specific cognitions are not established prior [to the study], there can be no injunction directed toward them; thus he says: "And prior to that, there is a need for the knowledge of qualification. Furthermore, even if there were an injunction directed toward [a result], comprehension of meaning would not be established merely from the act of recitation as a visible fruit, because it is not observed; thus he says: "Therefore, it is not from the injunction. Now, in common worldly usage, one observes an intention (*tātparya*) in the utterance of words directed toward the comprehension of meaning; however, the utterance by the listener is certainly not the cause of that intention.

Because that [intention] does not exist in the world, there is no utterance by a speaker; for if the Veda were not of human origin, it would follow that it lacks intentionality (*tātparya*). Therefore, since a word is inherently capable of conveying meaning, one requires the utterance of a word directed toward the cognition of meaning in order to eliminate defects caused by connection with a person. Furthermore, it will be explained that intentionality is a property of the word itself, to be understood through the sixfold indicators (*liṅga*), and is not a property of a person.

Now, in order to establish that the injunction for study possesses a permanent entitlement (*nityādhikāra*), [the opponent] challenges the engagement in study by asserting that it cannot occur due to the absence of a specific qualification for the entitlement: "If this is so, because no such entitlement is heard."

In that regard, an injunction (vidhi), being understood as that which impels toward its own object, implies—since it could not otherwise be accounted for—that there exists an eligible person capable of acting who understands, "This is my mandate. However, when the performance of the object of the injunction is accomplished through some other cause, then the injunctive power of the injunction is obstructed.

Furthermore, an injunction (*vidhi*) that functions as an impeller through a state of being intrinsically connected does not impel by first postulating an owner who is the qualified agent (*adhikārin*) for the sake of accomplishing the activity. In this regard, the Prābhākaras object, saying: "Even the injunction for study (*adhyayanavidhi*), because its own subject matter consists of an execution prompted by the injunction for teaching (*adhyāpanavidhi*), does not itself function as an impeller through a state of being intrinsically connected by postulating a qualification. To this he says: "In this matter, some say..."

Now, an objection: in the Vedic injunction, "One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa at eight years of age" and "One should teach him," the injunction for teaching has no explicitly stated qualification (*adhikāra*). How, then, can it impel the act of studying? If it is argued that a qualification must be inferred here [for the teacher], we reply: no; rather than inferring a qualification for the teacher, let the study itself be understood as being prompted by its own injunction, for which a qualification can likewise be inferred.

[Objection: Because of proximity (*sannidhāna*), [the answer is: surely, since study is an act performed for the sake of the injunction to teach within the context of a postulated qualification (*kalpitādhikāra*), no qualification for that [study] is postulated there. [Reply: Why should it not be the reverse? Since teaching is an act performed for the sake of study within the context of a postulated qualification, no qualification for that [teaching] is postulated there.

Now, it might be argued that since the injunction for study is fulfilled by the recitation from a written text, the injunction for study prompts the act of teaching; if that were so, then since the injunction for teaching would be fulfilled even by an unenjoined study, the injunction for teaching would not prompt the enjoined study. Alternatively, it might be argued that because of the similarity in the auxiliary requirements (*aṅga*)—such as the pupil facing east and holding the sacred grass-bundle (*pavitra*) in his hand—for both study and teaching, the injunction for teaching prompts only the enjoined study. This [objection] applies equally to the case of teaching being prompted by the injunction for study.

Furthermore, because of the restrictive injunction, "Be dependent on your teacher; study the Veda," reading from a written text is not appropriate. If it is argued that [the injunction] is prompted by the rule for becoming a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇavidhi*)—since it occurs subsequent to teaching and the meaning of the sentence "Study" implies this—[we reply: no, because one hears of the status of being a teacher (*ācāryatva*) from the mere act of initiation (*upanayana*), as in the statement, "That is his second birth; he is a teacher because of that. Since the status of being a teacher is already established through the etymology "one who causes [others] to grasp right conduct" (*ācārān grāhayati*), the word [in the injunction] must be supplied with the ellipsis "prompted by the rule for becoming a teacher."

Because resorting to a future state [of the agent] is indeed more parsimonious. Therefore, since the assumption of a governing rule (*adhikāra*) is equal and the mutual requirement (*itaretaraprayukti*) is also equal, and since the application of its own injunction (*svavidhiprayukti*) is possible, how can it be that study is prompted by the injunction for teaching? To this he says: "The performance [of study] is prompted by the injunction for the production of the status of a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇavidhi*)."

The intention is as follows: according to the rule "the root *nī* takes the ātmanepada when [used in the sense of] honoring, lifting up, acting as a teacher, knowing, wages, counting, and expenditure," the ātmanepada is prescribed for the root *nī* when honoring and the other aforementioned actions are to be accomplished.

In this context, from the understanding that "he should initiate him (*upanayīta*) and he should teach him (*tam adhyāpayīta*)" constitutes a single syntactical unit (*ekaprayogatā*), it is seen that because the boy (*māṇavaka*) is a subordinate factor (*guṇabhūta*) with respect to the act of teaching—as being the object (*karmakāraka*) of the teaching—he must, in response to the inquiry of how he might fulfill the injunction for teaching, be understood to assist the injunction for teaching by performing his own study through the act of approaching [the teacher].

In that context, regarding the interpretation of the phrase "having initiated [the pupil], he should teach," if one assumes a single unified action, it follows that the very act of becoming an *ācārya* (teacher), which is accomplished by the act of leading [the pupil] (*nayan*), is understood as the fruit of the teaching (*adhyāpana*) as well. Consequently, because one merely assumes a connection with desire (*kāma*) for the status of being an *ācārya*—which is the very fruit mentioned in the scripture as "having initiated, he should teach, desiring the state of being an *ācārya*"—the injunction for teaching becomes one that possesses a qualified agent (*sādhikāra*). Alternatively, [one may consider the verse]: "But that twice-born man who, having initiated a pupil, should teach him the Veda..."

"One who possesses the ritual procedure (kalpa) along with the secret doctrines (rahasya) is declared to be an Ācārya. Because the performance of the initiation (upanayana) and the teaching (adhyāpana) are one and the same, because an injunction is heard regarding teaching, and because the fruit of being an Ācārya is heard, the injunction "one who desires the status of an Ācārya should initiate the boy and teach him" is established. However, the distinction is that in the case of the student's own study (adhyayana), no specific cause for entitlement (adhikāra-nimitta) is heard in the scripture.

[Objection: But if study is not a subsidiary part (*aṅga*) of the injunction for teaching, then how can that study—which is enjoined by an independent injunction—be performed as prompted by another independent injunction? To this, he says: "Just like the laying of the fires (*ādhāna*), which is prompted by texts [stating] specific desires (*kāmaśruti*). This is the intention: it is heard in scripture, "A Brāhmaṇa should lay the fires. In that context, the laying of the fires is not enjoined independently and eternally with reference to a person; rather, it is enjoined as a means to an end. Thus, although the laying of the fires is itself enjoined by an independent injunction, its performance is prompted by another independent injunction, namely the texts stating specific desires such as, "One who desires heaven should lay the fires. Similarly, although study is enjoined by an independent injunction, its performance is prompted by another independent injunction, namely the injunction for teaching. Therefore, there is no fault. Furthermore, the laying of the fires is indeed enjoined independently by the text, "A Brāhmaṇa should lay the fires," yet its performance is prompted by the texts stating specific desires. Likewise, although study is enjoined by an independent injunction, its performance is prompted by the injunction for teaching. Consequently, there is no contradiction. Similarly, although study

Because it is understood as a *saṃskārakarma* (a preparatory rite) acting upon the instrumental factor (*kāraka*), like the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) of grains due to its being directed toward a substance (*dravyaparatayā*), and because no fruit is heard [in the text], it cannot have the status of an independent optional (*kāmya*) entitlement (*adhikāra*). Nor can it have the status of both a compulsory (*nitya*) and optional entitlement through a reversal of the subordinate and principal roles according to the logic of the *saktu* [grain-powder] injunction; for the fires consecrated by such rites are employed in other sacrifices, as seen in the rule, "One offers in the Āhavanīya fire. Therefore, an injunction for the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) that lacks both types of entitlement is not capable of inducing one to perform the establishment.

In that case, the performance of the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*) would be prompted by the injunctions for subsequent sacrifices. To this it is replied: the fire-consecration is not a performance prompted by the injunctions for the obligatory *darśapūrṇamāsa* and other such rites. This is because the *āhavanīya* fire, being the objective (the goal), is not something to be brought about as an action; therefore, it cannot be something to be performed as prompted by the injunctions for sacrifices. Indeed, an injunction impels the performance of only that which is "to be brought about" (*upādeya*); otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that even those such as "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) would have to be performed. Therefore, the performance of the fire-consecration is prompted solely by the injunctions for subsequent optional rites.

For desire, unlike an injunction (*vidhi*), does not compel one to perform only that which is to be adopted (*upādeya*); rather, whatever object—whether it be an end or a means—is indispensable for the fulfillment of what is desired, all of that the injunction compels as a necessary auxiliary. This is because we observe a distinction between injunction and desire. For example, regarding the injunction, "One should sit upon a golden seat," if such a seat is unavailable, the injunction does not compel its performance; however, desire, even by producing such a seat, causes one to sit upon it.

Thus, the very desire to become an *ācārya* brings about the act of study for the student by means of the teacher's instigation, for the sake of accomplishing the teaching. In this context, in order to demonstrate that it is the injunction of study itself—which possesses a mandate through its obligatory character (*nityādhikāra*)—that impels one toward study, [the author] refutes the application of the injunction of teaching, stating: "That is incorrect, says another. The intention is as follows: first of all, it is not logical that the status of being an *ācārya* should itself be the thing enjoined.

Since the injunction has as its object the essential meaning of the acts of initiation (*upanayana*) and teaching (*adhyāpana*), teacherhood (*ācāryatva*) does not possess the nature of an injunction by virtue of being denoted by the injunctive word itself, because it is denoted solely by the middle-voice (*ātmanepada*) suffix. Nor is teacherhood the fruit resulting from the injunction (*naiyogika-phala*), because teacherhood—being based on the status of the instigating agent (*prayojaka-kartṛtva*) in the sense "he causes [the pupil] to grasp the rules of conduct" (*ācārān grāhayati*)—is worldly (*laukika*). If it is argued that teacherhood is non-worldly (*alaukika*) because it is produced by the act of leading (*nayati*) with the student as its object, that is not so.

Because the Smṛti states, "since he is the teacher," it is understood that the worldly status of being a cause with respect to the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the student (*māṇavaka*) alone is the basis for the application of the word "teacher" (*ācārya*); furthermore, since the acts of honoring (*saṃmānana*) and so forth mentioned alongside it lack a non-worldly character, even if the status of being a teacher were non-worldly, it will still be the fruit of the injunction (*niyoga*) of the initiation (*upanayana*).

Therefore, how could there be a qualification for the injunction of teaching? If it is argued that because the single performance [of the act] is understood from the statement "one should teach him," the injunction transforms into "having initiated [the pupil], one should teach him," even so, the fruit of the subsidiary (aṅga), which is an explanatory passage (arthavāda), should not be imagined as the cause for the qualification of the primary injunction, namely: "one who desires to become a teacher should initiate and teach the boy."

Thus, since the injunction for study also belongs to the context (*prakaraṇa*) of initiation (*upanayana*) for the Vājasaneyins, and because its status as having a qualified agent is established through the authority of the context in all Smṛtis—namely, "one who has been initiated should study"—it is logical that study is prompted solely by its own injunction. As for the statement from Manu that was cited, it does not enjoin anything for one desiring to become a teacher, either on its own or by inferring a source-Vedic text; rather, due to the connection with the word *yat*, it merely provides the designation "teacher" (*ācārya*) for the agent, while restating the acts of initiation and teaching.

[The text] ordains [this], because of the statement, "They call him the Ācārya," and because the designation [of 'Ācārya'] is a constituent part of the injunctions for salutation, worship, and so forth, which will be described later. Therefore, the application of the injunction for the office of an Ācārya is incorrect—[one might object]. But even so, it is not proper to assume a qualification (adhikāra) in both cases.

Since the application of one is established by means of the other alone, when the question arises as to which of the two is to be postulated, [the opponent] objects: "How so?"—observing that because the boy (*māṇavaka*) is unawakened, he is incapable of undertaking his own obligation and performing the practice; therefore, the injunction for teaching (*adhyāpana-vidhi*), being itself possessed of an obligation, impels the study (*adhyayana*). To this, he gives the reply: "One should initiate a Brahmin who is eight years old. This means that this is the mandate for the teacher, i.e., the mandate for one who desires to become a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇa*).

This is the intended meaning: the injunction for becoming a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇavidhi*) does not impel one toward study that has not been enjoined; for those who are ineligible for study, there can be no engagement with it as a subordinate element of the teacher's qualification due to its lack of purpose for them. If, on the other hand, it impels one toward study that is indeed enjoined, then it must be asked: does the injunction require both an eligible person (*adhikārin*) and a subject matter (*viṣaya*) as conditions for determining its own nature, or not? It requires the subject matter as a condition for its own nature, but not the eligible person.

If it is argued that the student is the qualified person because he is the one who initiates [the action] and serves as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), then, since the specific student for whom this injunction is intended would remain unknown, anyone at all might teach it. To address this, he says: "The boy is not enjoined. Alternatively, if the injunction requires a qualified person solely by virtue of his own essential nature (*svarūpa-upādhi*), then it is established that the injunction to study possesses a qualified subject. In that case, through the context (*prakaraṇa*), the initiated boy becomes the qualified person.

Furthermore, if the injunction for study possesses an objective (sādhikāra), its status as an instigator (prayojayitṛtva) is also established. If it is argued that when performance by another is possible, even an injunction with an objective does not act as an instigator, to that he replies: "And for one who is not enjoined, there is the study of one's own Veda" (svādhyāyādhyayana). The term "not enjoined" (aniyuktasya) means one who has not been set in motion by the very injunction pertaining to his own objective. Now, it might be argued that even if one person does not engage in it, another will, and thus the teaching of the Veda is established in the form of a continuous stream (srotorūpeṇa); but this is not so.

Because the act of initiating (upanetṛtva) is also a constituent part of that [teaching]; one should initiate him by oneself and teach him, not one who has been initiated by another. Otherwise, due to the deficiency of a constituent part, the qualification would not be fulfilled, and the fruit of the status of a teacher (ācāryatva) would not be attained. If it is argued that one might therefore initiate and teach others as well, that is not so; for all boys do not engage in an activity that serves no purpose, and thus teaching would not be accomplished.

Now, one might object: how can a child comprehend his own duty? [We reply: There is no contradiction, for just as there is a comprehension of the duty to perform the *saṃdhyopāsana*, the fetching of fuel, and so forth, there is likewise a comprehension of the duty to study through the power of instruction. Furthermore, he says—"Moreover, the injunction regarding the appointment of a teacher"—because if the obligatory study were performed by means of a non-obligatory injunction, then upon the cessation of that [non-obligatory] injunction, it would be impossible to accomplish the obligatory study.

This is the intended meaning: that which is desired by the teacher is not itself a human goal (*puruṣārtha*); for, ultimately, the human goal consists only in the attainment of happiness and the cessation of suffering. In this regard, when there is an expectancy for a purpose for either the status of being a teacher or merely the act of teaching, since it is improper to postulate an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) when a seen result (*dṛṣṭa*) exists, [teaching] serves as a means for acquiring wealth, as stated: "Of these six occupations, three are the livelihoods: officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and the acceptance of gifts from the pure."

Because of this traditional authority (*smaraṇa*), and because the giving of a teacher’s fee (*gurudakṣiṇā*) and so forth is prescribed as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the boy’s study, the injunction for teaching—which enforces the performance of the primary act (*aṅgin*) of study—does not enforce the performance of the auxiliaries such as the fee and service; rather, the acquisition of wealth itself is the purpose. Since it possesses a purpose in that way, it is optional (*kāmya*), and thus its status as something to be performed as a constant obligation (*nitya*) is not established. [Objection: "In that case, approaching the teacher (*upagamana*) and studying would be non-obligatory. [Reply: No, he says—"But the sacramental rite (*saṃskāra*) called initiation (*upanayana*) is obligatory."

But is it not the case that a fault is also heard of when a penance (*prāyaścitta*) is not performed—namely, "When a long time has passed, one deserves a double vow"? In that regard, how can the compulsory nature (*nityatā*) of initiation (*upanayana*) be established on the basis of hearing of a transgression? It is replied: the double vow is not prescribed for the sake of removing a fault caused by the non-performance of a penance; rather, it is said that for a fault already existing which must be removed by a penance, its removal depends upon a double vow only when a long time has elapsed.

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of an infinite regress regarding expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*). Now, one might object: "Even if the sacrament of initiation (*upanayana*) is mandatory, how is the necessity of Vedic study established? To this he says: "And the sacrament... Because it is prescribed as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) with respect to its primary element (*aṅgin*), the necessity of the subordinate element—being conditioned by its primary—implies the necessity of the study itself, which is its own condition. But one might further object: "Since the study is taught independently (without being introduced as a subordinate part), how can it be a subordinate element of initiation? Moreover, the injunction for the sacrament of initiation alone cannot, on the grounds of logical inconsistency, imply the study as its principal purpose (*śeṣin*)."

In the absence of a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) based on specific connections such as direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), the connection with a particular study is not established; just as the injunction "gold is to be worn," although it appears from the literal sense to be for the purpose of purifying gold, does not attain the status of being an auxiliary to any [particular] sacrifice—because there is no evidence of a specific connection via *śruti* and so forth, because if it were connected to sacrifices by virtue of the capacity of the substance gold to be purified, it would follow that it applies to all sacrifices, and because it is impossible for a single purification to be beneficial to all sacrifices—it does not become an auxiliary to anything else.

Having abandoned the status of being a preparatory rite (*saṃskārakarma*), an independent injunction (*vidhi*) that has prosperity as its fruit is accepted; likewise, the initiation rite (*upanayanavidhi*)—lacking the authority of direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) and other means of proof, and failing to become a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to another because it would otherwise entail a connection with a sacrifice due to the capacity of the boy to be consecrated—should, having abandoned the status of a preparatory rite, be independent and have prosperity as its fruit. For every injunction regarding the nature of an action, by its very inherent power, generally establishes the relationship between the principal and the subordinate.

Since it is only when assisted by direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) and other means that [the injunction] can establish a specific relationship, the status of initiation (*upanayana*) as a purificatory rite (*saṃskārakarma*) is not established. |||

To this it is replied: The injunction for Vedic study itself, by virtue of its independence from such means of knowledge as direct audition (*śruti*) and so forth, accepts approaching a teacher as its own subsidiary through the authority established in the fourth book [of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtras]; for, since prohibitions against reading from written texts and the like are in force due to the formulation of restrictive injunctions such as "Study the Veda remaining under the authority of a teacher," the student's accomplishment of study would be impossible without approaching a teacher.

[Objection: Surely, approaching the teacher (*ācāryopagamana*) may be taken up as a visible requirement through the force of the injunction for study (*adhyayanavidhi*); but how can the invisible refinement (*saṃskāra*) of initiation (*upanayana*) be taken up as a subsidiary (*aṅga*)? [Reply: It is said: the very injunction for approaching the teacher, when assisted by a manifold collection of procedural details (*itikartavyatā*), produces an invisible refinement. And that injunction, seeking its purpose as impelled by another injunction, finds it possible to assist the injunction for study through the visible act of approaching the teacher, and thus does not postulate an invisible result.

Because it is illogical to postulate an unseen result when a seen one exists; that is to say, since a superior seen result is possible, it is illogical to postulate an independent unseen result. Thus, when the teacher’s attendance is undertaken by the force of the injunction for study, the connection of the purification produced by the injunction for initiation—which rests upon that attendance—with the injunction for study is established through that very means by the force of the injunction for initiation itself. Therefore, it is established that initiation is an auxiliary to study, due to the force of the undertaking of both injunctions.

Now, once it is established that initiation (*upanayana*) is a purificatory rite (*saṃskārakarma*), there arises in the injunction for the purificatory rite a requirement for its purpose; consequently, by means of the visible channel of approaching the teacher—which is itself implied by the injunction for Vedic study—the injunction for initiation, through its own inherent capacity, cognizes its status as a subsidiary (*aṅga*) to Vedic study.

As for the claim that there is no evidence for the *upanayana* being a purificatory rite (*saṃskārakarma*), it is replied as follows: Since the relationship of principal and subordinate between the *upanayana* and the study of the Veda (*adhyayana*) is established by the very force of their mutual mention, when the doubt arises as to whether the *upanayana* is a subordinate element as a purificatory rite—like the sprinkling of water (*prokṣaṇa*) and so forth—or rather a subordinate element that assists toward the fruit of the study—like the *prayāja* offerings and so forth—it is accepted as a subordinate element by way of being a purificatory rite.

Because it benefits the essential nature of the principal act (*aṅgin*) by being a directly contributing subsidiary (*sannipatyāṅga*), and because there is an absence of those subsidiaries that benefit through the result (*phalopakāryaṅga*) due to their remoteness; and since it is logical to prefer proximity over remoteness, it is established—by the force of the inclusion of both types of injunctions—that initiation (*upanayana*) is a subsidiary that benefits the essential nature of study (*adhyayana*) by way of purifying the student (*māṇavaka*).

Furthermore, since the modification of the sentence—"An eight-year-old Brāhmaṇa should approach [the teacher]"—into "He should study" will be stated later, it is the very hearing of the word *saḥ* (he) that, referring to the boy consecrated by the initiation (*upanayana*), enjoins him to the study of the Veda (*svādhyāya*). Thus, the injunction for initiation, being supported by this direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), establishes its own status as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the study. It is not correct to say that the rite of consecration is not referred to by the word *saḥ*, but rather that only the boy is referred to.

Because the formative element (*saṃskāra*) is immediately present as the subject matter, because it has been shown that initiation (*upanayana*) and Vedic study (*adhyayana*) stand in a state of mutual expectancy, and because the revealed scripture (*śruti*) provides what is so expected; furthermore, even though the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) lacks a case ending, it conveys the relationship by virtue of expressing its meaning as connected [to other factors]. Therefore, it is only the injunction (*vidhi*), supported by the revealed scripture, that authoritatively establishes the relationship between the subordinate and the principal (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*).

Furthermore, since among the Vājasaneyins and in the Śrutis inferred from all the Smṛtis, the injunction for study is prescribed with reference to the initiation (*upanayana*), the injunction for initiation—being supported by the context of fruitful study—establishes its own status as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to study. Therefore, it is correct to say: "And the sacrament (*saṃskāra*) is for the purpose of the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*). [Objection: Even if it were optional (*kāmya*), the injunction for becoming a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇa-vidhi*) would still be obligatory (*nitya*), because its fruit is something eternally desired.

And then, he raises the objection that there is no contradiction regarding the conjunction of the eternal and the non-eternal, starting with: "But how [is it] by means of the office of a teacher? etc. He refutes this by accepting that the fruit is eternally desired: "This would indeed be its eternity by virtue of the fruit, but not from the word. [The opponent objects: "Whether it is to be performed through the force of the fruit or through the force of the word, if it is an eternal duty, what is lost by the distinction of the means of knowledge? To this he replies: "Nevertheless, because the fruit is eternally desired..."

The meaning is that it is based on the actual capacity of the thing to produce a result. Now, one might object: "In some cases of teaching, the understanding of its being a duty is dependent on the desire for a specific result as a means; in other cases, however, the desire for the result in teaching is dependent on the verbal understanding of its being a duty. What, then, follows from this regarding the understanding of teaching as a mandatory duty? To this, he says: "For when there is a verbal understanding of its being a mandatory duty... There is indeed a distinction here. How so? For the injunction to teach...

One who has understood [the duty] from the word as being permanent (nitya) is prompted to act by generating a desire for performance at all times toward everyone, within the specific scope of his own qualification; this is because there is no restriction upon the understanding of a mandatory obligation (*kartavyatā*) that is grounded in valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*) regarding its own scope. However, if the comprehension of the obligation were dependent on one's personal desire, then due to the very restriction of that desire, the comprehension of the obligation would likewise be restricted, and thus teaching would not be established as a permanent duty.

[Objection: But surely even a desire dependent on a scripturally established obligatory duty (nitya-kartavyatā) may, in certain places, times, or regarding certain objects, be obstructed by the lack of capacity in the agent and so forth, due to considerations of propriety (aucitya); how then can there be a performance as if it were obligatory through a constant desire dependent on that obligatory duty? To this he replies: "Even when [the conditions of] propriety and so forth are absent. The meaning is that, according to the authority of the means of knowledge, the injunction for teaching is indeed eternal; out of fear of sin and the like, it compels the qualified person to perform it through the medium of desire and so forth, to the extent that it is possible.

The word "tena" (by that) has a clear meaning. Now, one might object: "Just as the necessity [of performing a rite] is established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), why could the necessity of its performance not also arise from [the teacher's] will? To this he says "no": "But when the understanding of the duty to act arises by force of the result," where the ellipsis to be supplied is "that [duty] would be non-eternal. Now, one might argue: "Since the goal is eternally desired, the desire which is the cause for the understanding of the duty to act must also be eternal. To this he says: "Even though... Even if the goal to be attained is eternal, because there is a variety of means, the duty to teach is also non-eternal; this is the meaning. Now...

[Objection: For someone who is incapable of any other means, since that [initiation] is the sole means, it must be performed as an obligatory duty (*nitya*). To this, he replies: "Even though it is the sole means... Therefore, there is a contradiction regarding the conjunction of the obligatory and the non-obligatory (*nityānitya-saṃyoga-virodha*). Now, one might object: even if initiation and instruction are not obligatory in themselves, because they are subordinate to the injunction for procreating a son—which is obligatory—there is no contradiction regarding the conjunction of the obligatory and the non-obligatory. Thus he raises the objection: "But surely, for the father, there is the injunction for procreating a son..."

In this context, the purpose of the injunction for procreating a son is to bring about the satisfaction of the ancestors who have departed to the other world by means of performing the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* and other rites in this world. And such performance is not possible apart from the initiation (*upanayana*), Vedic study, and the knowledge of the meaning [of the scriptures]. Therefore, the sentence "Therefore, [one should instruct] the son" prescribes instruction as a subordinate element (*śeṣa*) to that [injunction], which is required for the fulfillment of the fruit of the obligatory injunction for procreating a son.

Consequently, by the force of the injunction for the perpetual procreation of sons, the necessity (nityatva) of the injunctions for initiation (*upanayana*) and so forth is established. Furthermore, since the instruction (*anuśāsana*) culminates in the knowledge of the meaning, study (*adhyayana*) also has the knowledge of the meaning as its fruit; thus he asks: "Or how [is it] of study? He answers: "By this, the instruction of the son is not being enjoined."

Now, therefore, follows the rite of entrustment (*sampatti*): when one intends to depart [from this world], he says to his son, "You are the Veda, you are the sacrifice, you are the world. This refers to the entrusting to the son of the Vedas, their meanings, and their fruits—all of which were previously to be performed by himself. The son replies, "I am the Veda, I am the sacrifice, I am the world"; this acceptance by the son as something to be performed by him is the rite of entrustment.

The point is this: since it is impossible to encompass all duties all at once without prior instruction, this sentence merely restates as an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) the instruction that was already established previously and was implied by the injunction for producing a son, which culminates in the attainment of its fruit. Let it be granted, then, that this sentence does not enjoin the instruction itself.

Nevertheless, by the very force of the injunction for the constant procreation of a son, the injunction for the father’s instruction—beginning with the initiation (*upanayana*) and so forth—is established as being constant; to this he replies with the words "at the eighth year from conception," etc. The meaning is this: since there is no fixed rule regarding the lifespan of a father who is entitled to the injunction for the constant procreation of a son, it is impossible for him to remain until the completion of the instruction; therefore, "instruction" (*anuśāsana*) consists merely in the imparting of the things to be done, not in the actual enforcement of their performance.

Therefore, even because it is implied by the injunction for the production of a son—which is itself obligatory—the injunction for initiation (*upanayana*) and so forth is not necessarily permanent. Now, one might ask: "How is it understood that the instruction regarding what must be done by the father consists merely in the teaching [of the son], and not in the actual performance of the initiation and other rites? To this he says: "And likewise there is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the case of Śvetaketu. Consequently, the contradiction between the permanent and the non-permanent remains just as it was; thus he says: "That very same [injunction] by means of the permanent..."

[Objection: "But surely the student himself, once his duties toward one teacher have ceased due to that teacher's death or other causes, will summon another teacher and thereby accomplish the lifelong study. [Reply: No, as the author says: "Furthermore, when the teacher has passed away... It is not the case that the student, impelled by his own obligation, procures another teacher in order to fulfill his own duty, because he does not accept such a mandate; nor is it by the teacher's mandate.

Because in the absence of an eligible person (adhikārī), there is no comprehension of the duty to perform the ritual injunction (niyoga); and because it is impossible to accomplish the means [of the rite] by performing what is not one's duty. Now, an objection might be raised: "Just as one may take a substitute for other required materials, one might likewise take a substitute for the eligible person so that the boy (māṇavaka) could accomplish the duty. To this he says: "No, the eligible person is not substituted. For a substitute is taken when the primary person is absent, in order to perform that which must necessarily be done, since there would be sin (pratyavāya) from the non-performance of such a mandatory act.

In the absence of an eligible person (*adhikārī*), there can be no comprehension of the relationship expressed as "this is mine," and thus no injunction (*niyoga*) that must be performed. For whose sake, then, would a substitute (*pratinidhi*) be taken for the mandatory performance? It cannot be for the deceased, because the cause for his connection with the injunction has ceased and he no longer possesses any duty to perform. Nor can it be for the substitute himself, because the duty belongs to the teacher (*ācārya*), and the status of being a substitute occurs only after the teacher’s duty has been fulfilled. Therefore, there is no connection between an eligible person and a substitute.

In that case, there would be no occasion for the doctrine of a substitute in every instance; thus he says: "The qualified person [acts] for the sake of accomplishing his own qualification. Now, one might object: when the teacher has died, some other teacher will take charge of the student to fulfill his own duty; what need is there for the student's act of choosing another teacher? This is not so, because there is no second initiation (*punarupanayana*). Since the status of being an initiator (*upanetṛtva*) is already established, he does not take on another student, nor would he teach one who is uninitiated, because the constituent factor (*aṅga*) [of initiation] has already been completed.

If it is argued that "gathering" (saṃgraha) means for the purpose of increasing one's livelihood, we say no; for it would follow that a poor young student could not be accepted, and there would be no reason for a teacher to travel to another village to provide instruction for young students living in nearby villages. Indeed, in those [nearby] places, neither instructors nor those learned in the Vedas (śrotriya) are seen.

And thus, for the sake of accomplishing the initiation (*upanayana*) and other rites of the student (*māṇavaka*), it is heard in scripture that he goes to the teacher himself: "Satyakāma Jābāla, indeed, will dwell as a religious student under your lordship; I shall approach your lordship," and so forth. He concludes: "Thus, this [position] is full of many faults."

[Objection: "But if [the acts of] approaching [the teacher] and studying are prompted by their own injunctions, then since the initiation (*upanayana*) and teaching (*adhyāpana*) are established as being prompted by those [acts], the injunction for them [the teacher's acts] would be purposeless. [Response: This is not an injunction regarding the operations of the prompter (*prayojaka*), but rather an injunction regarding the operations of the agent (*kartṛ*)—namely, approaching and studying. Thus he says: "Therefore, the mandate (*niyoga*) belongs to the boy alone."

One might object: "Since the injunctive word expresses a meaning already associated with the sense of the causative suffix (*ṇic*), the connection of the injunction with the agent's activity contradicts the authority of the sentence. Thus he asks: "How can there be a relation between the quality and the agent's activity?"

Is it said that there is a contradiction with logic (*nyāya*) or a contradiction with scripture (*śabda*)? It is not a contradiction with scripture, because [such a usage] is seen elsewhere; thus he says: "Just as by this [rite] for one desiring a village. Nor is there a contradiction with logic; because, by restating the village, there is the injunction of what was previously unestablished; thus he says: "for one desiring a village."

[This is explained] by the passage beginning with "the sacrifice is enjoined. Now, an objection is raised: "In the case of teaching and sacrificing, since two distinct operations—one of the agent and one of the instigator—are understood, it is reasonable that one is enjoined while the other is restated as a reference. But in the case of initiation (*upanayana*), since the meaning of the verbal root is the operation of the instigator, how can the operation of the agent, which is not explicitly expressed, be enjoined? He raises this objection with the words "It is reasonable in the case of 'he should cause to sacrifice,'" and so forth. Now, an objection might be raised: "Let there be no injunction of the boy's operation regarding initiation; however, there will be one regarding study (*adhyayana*). That is not so.

He states that it is because of the similarity of the sentences: "Thus, because it is impelled by the injunction for the office of a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇavidhi*). In that context, although the root *nī* (to lead) denotes the activity of the prompter (*prayojaka*), the activity of the boy (*māṇavaka*)—though not explicitly denoted—is nevertheless understood; therefore, it is that very [activity of the boy] which is taken up by the root through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and enjoined, and not the activity of the prompter, because the latter is already established [by other means]. He resolves this with the words: "It is said: this [activity] belongs to the boy alone."

One might object: "How is the activity of the boy understood as something implied, or how is the activity of the instigator a mere restatement of what is already established? Thus he raises the objection: "How, first of all... To establish that the activity of the boy is implied, he first establishes that the activity of the teacher is not something to be enjoined, stating: "Both from the explicit statement of 'he should initiate' and from logical reasoning."

When it is said, "He initiates the boy," the boy's movement toward one's own self is understood from the direct expression, not one's own movement toward the boy; otherwise, the statement would have been, "He should go toward the boy. This is also understood through reasoning: just as an ordinary man teaching letters to children does not become subordinate to the children, but rather brings the children themselves under his own authority.

But even so, the activity of the teacher would not be a restatement of what is already established; for, once the student's study—accompanied by the ancillaries such as service—is enjoined, and once that study is prompted by its own injunction, the teacher’s activity would follow as a means of livelihood (*vṛtti*).
