And when that activity for the sake of livelihood has already been established, one could then enjoin the student's activity, such as study, by way of restating it. Thus, there arises the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).

Now, one might object: "In the case of the injunction 'one should cause him who desires a village to sacrifice,' this same fault applies; for there too, having referred to the instigating activity (prayojakavyāpāra) which is generally obtained as being for the sake of livelihood in other sacrifices prompted by their own respective injunctions, a specific sacrifice is enjoined for one desiring a village. If that is so, then here too, let the student's activities—such as approaching the teacher and studying—be enjoined by way of referring to the instigating activity generally obtained in other acts of study.

Alternatively—the activity of the instigator (prayojaka) will be obtained through the very force of the injunction regarding the activity of the boy (māṇavaka); it is not that the activity of the boy, which was never previously established, is enjoined by first restating a future attainment based solely on the injunction of the instigator's activity. Thus he says: "And all this [activity] of the Brāhmaṇa is obtained from another source precisely because it serves as the means for the performance (vṛtti)."

[Objection: But surely, having merely restated the activity of the prompter (prayojaka) as already established, why could the sentence not be intended as a specific injunction regarding qualities, eligibility, and so forth? [Response: First of all, the sentence is not intended as an injunction of eligibility, because the eligibility for the obligatory and optional rites such as living (jīvana) and so on has already been heard. Therefore, he says—referring to the phrase "there, one should teach someone"—that only an injunction of a quality (guṇavidhi) remains, just like "one should offer with curd" (dadhnā juhoti). [Objection: Let it then be an injunction of a quality. [Response: No, he says—referring to the phrase "the activity being already established there"—that this is not so.

The intention is as follows: when the qualified object (*viśeṣya*) itself is being cognized, then that single qualified object is cognized as characterized by various attributes; thus, there would be no split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*). However, when the attributes are cognized after restating the qualified object, then—since the attributes do not attain unity through mutual qualification and are instead cognized individually without mutual dependence—the sentence is split due to the plurality of objects of cognition (*prameya-bheda*).

"Is it not the case that everywhere the qualificand (viśeṣya) is merely restated by way of its universal aspect? True; the qualifiers (viśeṣaṇa) are likewise so, yet things are cognized as objects through their specific forms and as being mutually qualified. Therefore, he concludes—'Thus, for the Teacher [Śabara]...']—that injunctions regarding origin (utpatti), entitlement (adhikāra), and quality (guṇa) are not possible with respect to the activity of the instigator (prayojaka)."

In this context, he raises an objection in order to show that the activity of the boy (*māṇavaka*), though being understood [only] through implication (*lakṣaṇā*) by the verbal root (*dhātu*), is indeed what is to be enjoined: "But surely, [the activity] of the boy also... He provides the reply with the words beginning, "We say that it exists," and so forth. He raises another objection: "Surely, in actions such as going, the activity is seen to belong only to the agent (*kartṛ*), and not to the object (*karmakāraka*) such as the village; and since the boy is the object of the action denoted by 'leads' (*nayati*), how can he possess an implied activity? To this, he asks: "How [is that so]?"

He refutes [this objection] with the words: "at the very moment he initiates [the student]" (*yadaivopanayīta*). The phrase "even the one to be refined by the initiation rite" (*upanayana-saṃskārya*) means "even the one who goes toward [the teacher]" (*upagantṛ*). The point is that the act of going on the part of the one being led—the object of the verb "to lead" (*nī*)—is well known. [Objection: In that case, the boy's going is accomplished solely through the activity of the instigator (*prayojaka*); why then is it enjoined? [Reply: No; because it would not be established without an injunction. Thus he says: "and for him, being a discerning person" (*prekṣāvataḥ*).

[Objection: "But even if it is an injunction, it might be an optional injunction (*kāmyavidhi*). [Reply: No; he says, "even though it already exists. If so, how then is it an injunction? He says, by way of elimination, that it is a mandatory injunction (*nityavidhi*), stating: "by virtue of the injunction, there is a necessity to perform it. If so, how is the sentence to be interpreted? He says: "Therefore, [the text] 'an eight-year-old Brahmin... etc.

[The opponent] objects: "But even if [the act] is enjoined as something eternal (*nitya*), the relationship between the injunction and the person, or the activity caused by that relationship between the injunction and the person—which constitutes the meaning of the term 'qualification' (*adhikāra*)—is not obtained. He raises this objection with the words: "But even for these [eternal acts], qualification is not obtained. The intention is this: [one might argue that] for a person who is understood in a general sense [to be the agent], there is no specific qualification such as "an eight-year-old Brahmin..."

[Objection: "By hearing these qualifiers, this very [combination] will constitute the ground for eligibility (*adhikāra-nimitta*). [Reply: It is not so; because it is untenable for each qualifier individually to be the ground for eligibility, and because there is no mutual qualification between the two qualifiers. If it is argued that—even though each qualifier is connected to the action in its denotative sense—there is nevertheless a ground for eligibility through their mutual qualification by virtue of the contextual implication (*artha*), as in the case of "a one-year-old reddish-brown cow" (*aruṇayā ekahāyanyā*) and so on; [we reply: No, because this would entail that the ground for the person's connection to the injunction would not be expressed by the words (*aśābdatva*).

He refutes [the objection] by stating: "There is here a cause for entitlement (*adhikāra-hetu*), namely, a constant occasion (*nitya-nimitta*). The meaning is that it is not the cause for the commencement of the relationship between the injunction and the person. Regarding the word "constant" (*nityam*): it means that it necessarily occurs for a specific person as long as he lives. Furthermore, the occasion for entitlement is not exclusively verbal (*śābda*) in all cases; for even the capacity to perform the ritual action along with its subsidiaries—which is non-verbal—is an occasion for entitlement, since only one who is capable possesses the entitlement.

Alternatively—since the two words intend to convey a qualified entity by means of expressing the connection with the action, the verbal nature of the qualification for eligibility (*adhikāra-nimitta*) is not destroyed. Even so, one raises the objection that the qualified entity itself cannot be the qualification for eligibility: "But surely, the genus (*jāti*) and age (*vayas*) are qualifiers of that which is to be enjoined (*upādeya*)."

This is the intended meaning: that which is to be accepted (*upādeya*)—whether directly or indirectly—is that which is to be performed as the object of an injunction (*vidhi*), and its qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) consist of the collection of actions, factors of action (*kāraka*), and their qualities. Among these, the qualifiers of the thing to be accepted are the qualifiers of the agent, such as in "the staff-bearer recites the *praiṣa* formulas" and "the priests wearing red turbans proceed with the ritual"; the qualifiers of the instrument (*karaṇa*), such as the plurality [of grains] in "one should sacrifice with rice-grains" (*vrīhibhir yajeta*); and the qualifiers of the recipient (*saṃpradāna*), such as in "to Indra, the self-sovereign" (*indrāya svārājñe*).

Furthermore, the qualification of the object to be enjoined (*upādeya*) is not the cause for the connection with the entitlement (*adhikāra*); for, as a qualification of the causal factor (*kāraka*) to be performed, it is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*) with respect to the injunction, whereas the entitled person (*adhikārin*) is connected to the injunction primarily as its master (*svāmin*). How, then, is the status of the boy (*māṇavaka*) as the object to be enjoined understood here? It is said: the accusative case-ending, which expresses the boy’s status as the object (*karman*) with respect to the activity of the instigator (*prayojaka*), implies his status as the agent (*kartṛ*) with respect to his own activity.

Because the activity of the instigator (prayojaka) has the agent as its object, in this case, while restating the activity of the instigator already established, there is merely a transformation [of the injunction] to connect it with the activity of the agent; the agency of the boy (*māṇavaka*), which is already established by the words of the text, is not set aside. Thus, age characterized by caste—which is a qualification of the boy who is to be enjoined (*upādeya*)—is not the cause for entitlement (*adhikāra*). But what, then, is the cause for entitlement? To this he says: "A non-enjoined qualification (*anupādeya-viśeṣaṇa*) is the cause of entitlement."

That which is connected to an injunction (*vidhi*) is non-subordinate (*anupādeya*), provided it is distinct from that which is to be performed as enjoined by the injunction and its specific qualifications; for example, "one who lives," "one whose house is burning," or "one who desires heaven. To avoid the charge of contradicting his own established tenets, he accepts the position of the mandatory injunction (*niyoga*): "True; this is indeed the settled rule."

The meaning is as follows: where an injunction (*niyoga*) is presented as the sentence-meaning by means of a word such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*), there, because the connections with other word-meanings are caused by the requirement of that injunction which constitutes the sentence-meaning, and because the injunction itself requires the qualification (*adhikārin*) and the object (*viṣaya*) as its own formal conditions—expressed as "whose [injunction]? and "with respect to what?"—the person desiring heaven (*svargakāma*) is connected as the qualified agent through the requirement of the injunction: "This injunction is mine. Being connected as an owner is what is meant by being the "person to be enjoined" (*niyojya*), that is, being the qualified agent (*adhikārin*).

In this regard, first one understands, "This is my mandate (*niyoga*)," and through the realization that the mandate is something to be accomplished, one subsequently relates to the meaning of the verbal root as the agent for the sake of performance. For the mandate, being understood as that which is to be achieved, is logically untenable without the connection of an agent to the meaning of the verbal root—which is capable of effecting the fulfillment of the mandate—on the part of the primary correlate, the qualified person (*adhikārin*), who has realized, "This is my mandate. Thus, the Prābhākaras maintain that the connection with the agent is preceded by the connection with the qualification.

In that regard, let it be granted that a qualification of the non-adopted (anupādeya) may be the cause of entitlement; however, in the doctrine of *bhāvanā*, even a qualification of the adopted (*upādeya*) is a cause of entitlement. Thus he says: "But the experts in logic maintain that entitlement belongs to the agent."

This is the intended meaning: when the activity of a person (*puruṣapravṛtti*) or the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) is presented as the sentence-meaning by means of suffixes such as the optative (*liṅ*), then—since a relation is necessitated by the requirement of a principal element, and since an action, by virtue of its own nature, requires an agent, an instrument, and an object, and since the human goal and the meaning of the verbal root are respectively connected as the end to be achieved (*bhāvya*) and its means (*tatkaraṇa*)—it follows by process of elimination that those such as "one who desires heaven" are connected as the agent (*kartṛ*).

Consequently, since those [words] such as "desiring heaven" (*svargakāma*) are connected—by way of being qualifiers of the agent—for the purpose of restricting that [agent], through their connection with living (*jīvana*) and the burning of the house (*gṛhadāha*), it follows by elimination that they establish a connection as the agent. Because the fruit belongs to the agent alone, one subsequently experiences the connection of entitlement (*adhikāra*), characterized by ownership of the ritual act, in the form: "This ritual act, which is the means to the fruit, is mine. For the very fact of being the enjoyer of the fruit of the ritual act constitutes the connection of ownership (*svāmyanvaya*) with respect to that act.

Consequently, since the qualifiers of the agent themselves establish the connection of ownership toward the ritual act by virtue of that very agent being the enjoyer of the fruit, the status of the agent constitutes the basis for entitlement (*adhikāra*). Thus, the sense is that even by adopting the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) as the meaning of the sentence, the entitlement of the student (*māṇavaka*) is established. Alternatively, just as in the *Rājasūya* sacrifice, the quality of being a king (*rājatva*), which is a qualifier of the agent, becomes a qualifier of the entitled person because it cannot be accomplished by any other entitled person acting as the agent; so too should it be here.

[Objection: Surely this solution is not tenable; for the means to the highest good (*śreyaḥ-sādhana*) is denoted as the sentence-meaning by the cognitions of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, and that [means] first requires connection with a qualified person (*adhikārin*). How so? For the highest good indeed requires an enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*); therefore, its means also becomes connected to an enjoyer.

Furthermore, because we observe an expectation regarding the connection with an owner—such as, "Whose is this means to excellence? This is my means for achieving what I desire"—just as one asks, "Whose is this injunction? and [answers], "It is mine," so too, *bhāvanā* (the efficient force), being understood as an action that has an agent as its substratum, requires such an agent. Now, it may be argued that an injunction (*vidhi*) is simply a means to excellence that is fit for performance; [and] a means to what is desired by the agent...

Since it is accepted that [the word "vidhi"] denotes an injunction (*vidhi*), and since an action (*kṛti*) requires an agent (*kartṛ*), then—given that the mandate (*niyoga*) is also understood as something to be accomplished—it would follow that the connection with an agent caused by that action must occur [for the mandate as well]. Now, one might object: "The action is denoted by the word only as subordinate to the mandate; and the syntactic connection of word-meanings does not occur through the requirement of what is subordinate, but rather through the requirement of the principal. Therefore, due to the requirement of the principal mandate, the connection with the qualified person (*adhikārin*) occurs first. To this we reply: this is exactly the same in the case of a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhana*) as well.

Because the action (*kṛti*) is denoted as a subordinate element (*upasarjana*). Now, an objection might be raised: since even the "good" (*śreyas*) is subordinate, how could the connection with the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*), which is obtained through the force of that [good], belong to the means (*sādhana*)? This is not a fault; for the "good" is a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) to the very nature of being a means, and because that [good] is invariably connected with the enjoyer, it is established that the means—which is common to both the agent (*kartṛ*) and the enjoyer—is necessarily connected with the enjoyer in accordance with its own adjunct, the "good."

Therefore, [the agent] first requires the connection with the qualification—namely, "this is the means for accomplishing my desired end"—by means of the injunction, which constitutes the sentence-meaning as the means to the highest good (*śreyas*). Subsequently, by the very power of the injunction, that same [agent] attains the connection with the action (the verbal root-meaning), which is the locus of being the means for accomplishing the desired end.

He says that even so, there is no contradiction in this case: "Furthermore, here the boy (*māṇavaka*) is not enjoined as qualified by [his] caste or age. When the injunction—characterized by being the means for attaining what is generally desired—is conveyed by the word regarding the boy’s activities such as initiation (*upanayana*) and study, then, since that general [injunction] requires a specific excellence of welfare (*śreyaḥ*), one postulates a specific excellence of welfare residing in the boy, namely the initiatory rite (*saṃskāra*) which is a means to human goals through a causal chain; and thus, the injunction characterized by being the means to that [specific welfare] [applies].

The injunction (*vidhi*) is established as pertaining to the activity of the boy (*māṇavaka*); consequently, by virtue of being the enjoyer of the fruit of the sacramental rite (*saṃskāra*), the boy relates to the injunction as its owner (*svāmin*). In that context, the qualification of "being a Brāhmaṇa" and so forth serves to restrict that ownership; subsequently, it restricts the agent's connection to the boy’s activity regarding the object of the means for what is desired. This is the meaning of the text.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the connection with the status of agent (*kartṛtva*)—as being the object of the instigator’s activity—is understood from the sentence? [Response: True; however, because of the force of its connection with the injunction (*vidhi*), one understands the connection with the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*), and thus the restriction to the connection with the agent is postulated.

[Objection: But even so, it is not established that study has an [independent] entitlement (*adhikāra*). To this, he says: "Thus, because initiation (*upanayana*) is for the purpose of study... And it is well-known in all the *Smṛti* scriptures that initiation is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to study. Furthermore, for the Vājasaneyins, study is enjoined with reference to initiation. And the capacity of these two injunctions is demonstrated by the means of proof known as "appropriation" (*upādāna*).

Here too, in the phrase "he should teach him," the word "him" (tam) refers back to the initiated student; and since the subsidiary (the teaching) and the principal (the learning) share a single qualification, it follows that "the initiated Brāhmaṇa should study. Since there is no rule that the time which serves as the occasion for the qualification for the subsidiary must necessarily apply everywhere to the principal, age is not the occasion for the qualification for study. Now, one might object: "Could it be that the injunction for study, by virtue of its obligatory qualification, has the comprehension of meaning as its goal? To this he says: "And merely by the grasping of syllables... and so forth.

If it is argued: "Since the injunction for obligatory study is fulfilled by studying just once, how is repetition (āvṛtti) obtained? Or, in the view that the fruit is the comprehension of meaning, how is it obtained, given that it is impossible for the result to terminate [with the first instance]?"—this objection applies equally here as well, because the attainment of the syllables is the fruit. If it is argued: "The fruit of the injunction is indeed the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa)," this is equally true in the case of the comprehension of meaning.

Now, it might be argued: "The observed result inherent in [the study of] the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) is the comprehension of meaning; and since that depends upon the acquisition of the syllables and their investigation, repetition is established for that purpose"—but this is not so. Since the comprehension of meaning is seen even from the human-authored sentences of other Vedic branches (*śākhāntara*) when they have been repeatedly studied, it is not logical to require repetition for that purpose. Furthermore, repetition is postulated for the acquisition of the syllables by virtue of the injunction for recitation and private study (*japa-svādhyāya-vidhi*), and not by virtue of the capacity for comprehending meaning.

Alternatively, the word *adhyayana* (study) primarily denotes the entire operation extending up to the acquisition of what is being studied; however, in cases such as a single recitation, it is used in a secondary sense (*gauṇa*). Thus, the necessity for repetition (*āvṛtti*) is established. Now, one might object: "By stating that the Veda itself, independent of anything else, is the cause for inquiry, the author of the Commentary (*Bhāṣyakāra*) has merely stated that the injunction to study (*adhyayanavidhi*) is the cause for inquiry. To this he replies: "But surely, in this way, one becomes a student of the Veda... [and so on].

True; he provides the rebuttal that the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*) is the cause for inquiry by way of presenting the subsequent injunctions that motivate inquiry, and not by way of being something enjoined by the injunction for formal study—stating "True, it is exactly so," and so forth. Now, one might ask: how can a subsequent injunction, which is only superficially understood from the study of one's own Veda and remains uncertain, impel one toward inquiry? To this he says: "For one who has studied the Veda [realizes] that these [rites] must necessarily be performed."

Since those who have entered upon the initial [stages] require knowledge of the determination of what is to be performed regarding the daily obligatory rites (*nityavidhi*), the inquiry (*vicāra*) is necessitated for the sake of that determination. Furthermore, even the inquiry into the texts concerning optional rites (*kāmyavākya*) is prompted by the desire for the results, just as the rite of establishing the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) is. Now, one might object: "It would be better to assume that the inquiry is prompted by the injunction for Vedic study (*adhyayanavidhi*), rather than assuming multiple promptings from various injunctions"; but this is not so.

Since it has been stated that the injunction for study lacks a purpose because reflection—which is distinct from both the object to be accomplished and its auxiliaries—is not required, and since it has also been stated that there is no injunction for reflection even on the basis of a result—just as the repetition of threshing is not prompted by a separate result—reflection cannot be prompted by that [injunction]. However, because reflection serves as an auxiliary to what is enjoined by subsequent injunctions, its being prompted by them is possible. Furthermore, a difference in injunctions is not contradicted by the fact that there is a difference in the resulting determinative knowledge for each individual sentence.

Otherwise, even the performance of sacrifices and other rites would be prompted by the injunction for study, because the fruit of the injunction for study extends as far as the attainment of heaven and so forth. Now, it might be argued that study itself must be prompted by subsequent injunctions, since without study, the investigation, determination, and performance [of rituals] cannot be accomplished. To this, he says: "Therefore, because there is no understanding prior to study."

The meaning is that prior to the study [of the Vedas], because the subsequent injunctions have not been understood, they cannot be the motivators for the study. Furthermore, the injunction for study—like the injunction for the twilight worship (*sandhyopāsana*) and others—impels one toward action when heard from fathers and others; however, it has already been stated that it is impossible to hear all the subsequent injunctions before the study [of the Vedas]. One might then argue: "Let it be that the inquiry into Brahman is also motivated solely by the subsequent obligatory injunctions (*nityavidhi*) to which the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*) are entitled. To this he says: "Not so, as regards the knowledge of Brahman."

Nor does the injunction regarding the eternal *agnihotra* and other rites investigate Brahman for the sake of establishing the distinction between *dharma* and Brahman; for, by mere superficial observation, it has as its object distinct, empirical entities. The phrase "Therefore" (*tasmāt*) concludes the intermediate section (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*), while "Thus, in this manner" (*tadevam*) concludes the main section (*mahāprakaraṇa*).

Now, one might object: "The syllable *oṃ* and the word *atha*—these two emerged from the mouth of Brahmā after piercing the throat; therefore, both are auspicious. Since the word *atha* thus possesses an auspicious meaning, and since at the commencement of a treatise an auspicious rite (*maṅgalācaraṇa*) must be performed to preserve the tradition of the learned and to pacify obstacles, it follows that the word *atha* has that purpose. To this he says: "Even of auspiciousness... [and so on].

First of all, auspiciousness does not connect with the inquiry into Brahman within the meaning of the sentence through the relation of agent, instrument, or object, because there is no evidence for it being any one of these [three] factors (kārakas), and because other kārakas are already present. Nor is there a connection by way of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), such that "the inquiry into Brahman is auspicious"; for that would result in its being a mere explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*) intended for praise. Now, if it is argued that the performance of an auspicious rite must indeed be undertaken, he replies: "because it is useful merely for the sake of the sacred revelation (*śruti*)."

One might object: "Is it not the case that the word *atha* is also employed with the intention of expressing a different topic from the one under discussion? For example, when one topic has been stated and another is intended, one says, 'Now you think thus' (*athaivaṃ manyase*); therefore, the word *atha* has that [new topic] as its meaning. Thus he raises the objection: "Is it not [the case] from the matter being introduced? (*nanu prakriyamāṇāt*) and so forth.

He offers a rebuttal, stating that "it is not distinct from immediate succession," on the grounds that when immediate succession is expressed by way of the relation between cause and effect, the fact that it is a different matter from the subject at hand is established by implication, and thus need not be stated separately. He raises an objection: "How so?"—that is, why is it not understood that the very fact of being a different matter implies immediate succession?

In this regard, is it a specific entity that, having occurred previously, is invariably established as the cause by being illuminated? Or is it that any entity whatsoever, having occurred previously, is required? Regarding this, the first alternative is not tenable; for without the expression of immediate succession (*ānantarya*), the restriction of a specific preceding entity as the cause cannot be established. Thus he says: "Thus, that which is about to be produced [requires] what has invariably occurred previously. Now, as for the second alternative, he says: "Otherwise, in whatever [entity]..."

[Objection: But even in the case of immediate succession (*ānantarya*), a preceding factor is not understood as being the cause. [Reply: True; however, the immediate succession of the effect from the complete cause (*puṣkalakāraṇa*) is indeed primary, because it is uninterrupted and because it is non-deviant (*avyabhicāra*). On the other hand, the immediate succession between a non-cause and its effect sometimes deviates and sometimes is interrupted; thus, it would be merely secondary (*gauṇa*).

Therefore, when the preceding event—the abundant cause—is illuminated by the mention of primary immediate succession (*ānantarya*), the state of being a different matter (*arthāntarabhāva*) is also included therein; however, when a different matter is mentioned, primary immediate succession is not included. He concludes: "Hence, the causal matter must be expected. He introduces the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the stated point with the words: "He says this. Now, if the result is indeed perceived, what is the use of understanding the abundant cause? It is not necessary.

He states—“And since, when [the word *atha*] has the sense of immediate succession (*ānantarya*), [it is so]”—because the desire reaching as far as the fruit, being a qualification of the qualified person (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*), depends upon an understanding [of what precedes] for the commencement of inquiry and so forth. Now, having raised the objection that the prerequisite (*pūrvavṛtta*) is already well-known from the inquiry into Dharma (*dharmajijñāsā*), he says: “But the immediate succession to the study of one’s own Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayana*) is common [to both]. He explains the meaning of the Commentary with the words beginning “without which, as a rule,” etc. He states another interpretation: “Or else,” meaning that [the inquiry into Brahman] is not the complete cause [for the knowledge of Dharma].

An objection is raised: "But surely, since the study of the *svādhyāya* is enjoined by the single injunction for study (*adhyayana-vidhi*), it must have a single purpose, namely liberation (*mokṣa*). Even if the inquiry into the meaning of the entire Veda is not prompted by the injunction for study, because the inquiries into Dharma and Brahman share a single fruit through their relationship as mutual helper and helped, it is said that the inquiry into Brahman—the thing to be helped—occurs immediately after the comprehension of Dharma—the helper. Thus he objects: "But here, the sequence following the comprehension of ritual action (*karman*) is a specific distinction."

He demonstrates the relationship of mutual assistance between the investigation of *dharma* and the investigation of *brahman*, stating: "And so it has been described in another commentary. *Adhikāra* means activity (*pravṛtti*). *Saṃskāra* means the fruit (*phala*). The meaning is: by way of a succession of activities and a succession of fruits. Alternatively, "purification" (*saṃskāra*) refers to the purification of the person (*puruṣa*) through ritual acts (*karma*). And "from the word" (*śabdataḥ*) is stated there as the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). "Immediately after having understood" means immediately after the understanding of *dharma*.

Regarding this point, he cites another agreement with the author of the Śāstra, beginning with the words: "It has also been described by others in their own commentaries," and so forth. He states that the relationship of mutual assistance between the inquiry into Dharma and the inquiry into Brahman does not necessarily depend on the fact that they share a single result: "No; for even prior to the inquiry into Dharma, there is one who has studied the Vedānta. He explains this Bhāṣya with the passage beginning: "Even though the study of the Vedānta... and so forth.

One might object: "In the inquiry into Dharma (*dharmajijñāsā*), since one has already mastered the authority of the Veda, the meanings of words and sentences, and the logic required for them, it is possible to investigate Brahman [at that very stage]. To this he replies with the question, "How so? In order to show that [the inquiry into Dharma] provides no assistance, he analyzes the inquiry into Dharma, stating: "In that regard, first, three things have occurred in the inquiry into Dharma. He asks, "What are they? and answers with the passage beginning, "The twelve-lakṣaṇa [work]," and so forth. Therein, in order to demonstrate that even the logic (*nyāya*) provides no assistance, he discusses the logic as well.

He analyzes this with the words: "In that regard, that which [is stated] in the first sūtra," and so forth. It is true that the logic required for the injunction to study—namely, that its fruit culminates in the comprehension of the visible meaning—is indicated by the word *atha*; and the entire logic required for the authority of the Veda is indeed indicated by the first pāda. As for the question "Why is there a dependence on the first pāda?", this was stated while provisionally accepting that point, and thus there is no contradiction.

[Objection: "But since the means of knowledge such as direct scriptural statement (śruti) and indicative mark (liṅga) are required here as well, the other system [of Mīmāṃsā] must also be presupposed as having preceded this. [Reply: No, he says—"but as for the other," etc. For the system required for the operations of originative injunction (utpatti-vidhi), applicatory injunction (viniyoga-vidhi), injunctive injunction (prayoga-vidhi), and injunction of qualification (adhikāra-vidhi) was propounded there [in the Pūrva-mīmāṃsā]. And that [system] is not useful for the presentation of an already existing entity (vastu) which is not something to be performed (ananuṣṭheya).

The sense is this: even when the purpose to be accomplished (*kārya*) is the same, a distinction in reasoning (*nyāya-bheda*) is required due to the difference in the intermediate subjects of knowledge (*avāntara-prameya*) in each chapter; how much more so, then, must it be said regarding the difference in subjects of knowledge consisting of entities that are not themselves effects? Furthermore, the *Śruti* and other means of knowledge are employed exactly as they are well-known in the world. An objection is raised: "But surely Brahman has also been determined there [in the ritual sections] as being subordinate to the ritual act (*kārya-śeṣatayā*). He says "No," because [Brahman there] was not one whose "all [impurities] were entirely dispelled" (*nirasta-aśeṣa*). Another objection is raised: "Even though it was not formally proposed (*apratijñātasya*), the reasoning required for it was shown by way of another purpose. He says "No," because "there was no exposition of that" (*na tat-pratipādana*).

[Objection: But surely the principle required by the injunction is also to be relied upon through the combination of qualities (*guṇopasaṃhāra*). To this he replies: "That which, moreover, is established by the first mantra... [Objection: But even knowledge associated with qualities (*saguṇavidyā*) is indeed knowledge itself. To this he replies: "And in that case, it is a mental action (*mānasī kriyā*). The phrase "Thus, in this way" is the conclusion.

It might be argued that the meaning of the word *atha* (then) is not immediate succession to the desire to know Dharma (*dharma-jijñāsā*), but rather immediate succession to the inquiry into the authority of the Veda; to this he says, "no," in the words: "As for the further point that the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*) is useful for the comprehension of its meaning. The sense is that merely by knowing "the Vedas are authoritative," no one would engage in the inquiry into Brahman, which involves manifold effort. Then, could the knowledge of the determination of Dharma be the cause for the qualification (*adhikāra*) to inquire into Brahman? To this he says, "no," in the words: "As for the further point... [and so on].

It must be stated whether the determination of Dharma (dharmanirṇaya), when being utilized, is useful for engaging in the inquiry into Brahman (brahmavicāra) or useful for the determination of Brahman itself. First, he states that it is not the former alternative: "For knowledge whose object is something else [is not useful here]. Nor is it the second, as he says: "That too does not exist here. The sense is that since Brahman can be inferred even through the phenomenal world (prapañca) by means of the relationship between cause and effect, the determination of Dharma is not required.

He says that, by process of elimination, the utility of ritual actions remains; thus, "therefore, the utility of ritual actions is what remains. However, the sense is that even this is not possible under certain views. Regarding that, he states, "What is this succession of qualifications? meaning that neither a succession of qualifications nor an assistance toward the knowledge of Brahman is possible.

[Objection: Is this not a tradition of practice? For instance, beginning with the *saṃdhyopāsana* (twilight worship), by abandoning each preceding lesser rite and adopting each succeeding greater rite, one eventually reaches a state of unsurpassed action after a thousand years; then, by way of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), one enters into the knowledge of Brahman. [Reply: No, he says: "Just as for one desiring to ascend a palace," and so forth. This is because there is no authoritative evidence (*prāmāṇa*) for either the abandonment of the previous rite upon the adoption of the subsequent rite, or for the entry into the knowledge of Brahman by way of elimination.

In that case, one might object: "If the fruit of all actions is attained through a succession [of stages], then since there is no desire for those [lower fruits], one whose desires have ceased would enter into that [highest state] out of a desire for supreme bliss. To this he says: "Now, with a mind afflicted by desire" (*atha kāmopahatamanāḥ*). He elaborates on that very point: "And thus, [starting from] the status of a sovereign of the whole earth (*sārvabhauma*), etc. This means: by a succession of qualifications—that is, by a succession of fruits. He refutes this: "In that case, it must be stated that [the sequence] follows immediately after the performance of ritual action" (*karmānuṣṭhānānantaryaṃ tarhi vaktavyam iti*).

The meaning is that since the inquiry into Brahman occurs immediately after the attainment of the fruits of performing ritual actions (*karmānuṣṭhāna*), the scripture would not have humans as its qualified practitioners. Furthermore, ritual actions do not assist the knowledge of Brahman by means of dissolving desires; rather, [the author] says: "Or how could the fulfillment of desires be the cause for the cessation of desires? The portion preceding the word "satyam" (it is true) is clear in meaning.

He says that because the enjoyments of Hiraṇyagarbha and others perish moment by moment, the desire for a future accumulation of enjoyments arises; therefore, there is no entry into the knowledge of Brahman through the dissolution of desires. [The opponent replies: "True, this is logical, provided that the enjoyment is that of Hiraṇyagarbha. [The author asks: "Then from what source does the dissolution of desires occur for all people? To this he says: "Therefore, because of the perception of defects such as decay in sense objects. He concludes with the words: "Therefore, in all cases..."

Furthermore, is the cessation of desire upon the attainment of all objects stated through the authority of scripture (*āgama*), or through the power of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)? It is not the first; thus he says: "And there is no such scripture. He then raises the objection that it must be through the power of *anvaya-vyatireka*: "But surely, upon the attainment of desires... The refuting passage, however, is clear in its meaning. The third section [of the work] holds that all Vedic words, taken together, aim at the cognition of the dissolution of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) such as the identity of the body and the self;
and that [position] is rejected precisely because it contradicts direct experience (*pratīti*).

[The opponent] objects: "In that case, since actions being performed serve as purifications of the person (*puruṣasaṃskāra*), they are effects of the knowledge of Brahman; therefore, the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*) should follow the performance of dharma. [The author replies: "Let it be then, by way of purification. [The opponent objects again: "But how can these rituals—which, according to the text 'All these become possessors of meritorious worlds,' are means for achieving independent human goals—be considered subordinate acts (*guṇakarma*) serving as purifications like the act of sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), on the strength of Smṛti? [The author replies: No, because that would contradict Śruti.

Now, an objection: purification (*saṃskāra*) consists either in the imparting of a quality or the removal of impurity. In this regard, the removal of impurity as a purification of the self is established by such texts as, "By dharma one casts off evil," and "Yogis perform action, having abandoned attachment, for the sake of self-purification. Alternatively, the imparting of a new quality to the self is understood through the fact that the injunction would otherwise be inexplicable. Therefore, its status as a purificatory rite (*saṃskārakarma*) is indeed known from scripture, as evidenced by the scriptural statement: "By this, this limb of mine is purified."

Nor is it the case that the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) for obligatory rites (*nityakarman*) is prescribed as a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the substances that are auxiliary to a sacrifice (*kratvaṅga*), such that there would be a contradiction with their own independent results; rather, like the injunction for the acquisition of wealth, it is merely a source of assistance (*upakāramātra*). This is true; however, since the result of prosperity (*abhyudaya*)—characterized by the destruction of sin and the production of a new unseen potency (*apūrva*)—is understood from scripture, it is impossible to determine that these rites are subordinate to the knowledge of Brahman, even on the strength of Smṛti. To this, it is replied:

If the means of knowledge—such as hearing, reflection, meditation, and practice—are accomplished for the self that has been refined by the performance of obligatory and occasional rites, then those purificatory rites, through a specific auxiliary factor, bring about the realization of the Self; however, when there is an absence of such auxiliary causes, they result in the fruit of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*). Since this systematic arrangement is thus established, there is no mutual contradiction between the Śruti and the Smṛti.

Now, an objection is raised: from the statement, "He for whom these forty-eight purificatory rites (saṃskāras) exist," followed by, "he goes to union with Brahman (sāyujya) and to the same world as Brahman (sālokya)," the attainment of Hiraṇyagarbha is understood as the fruit of the ritual acts of purification, because of the indicative mark (liṅga) of *sālokya*; it is not the attainment of the Supreme Brahman, by which—through the power of auxiliary factors and by way of purifying the person—the rituals would have liberation as their fruit. To this, it is replied:

First of all, the word *saṃskāra* (purification) indicates that actions are subsidiary to a substance which serves as the means for an independent result, just like the purification of curd or rice. Since all actions are connected here as purifications, it is inferred—by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*) and presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*)—that they have liberation as their fruit by being subsidiary to the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), because two fruits are mentioned: "union with Brahman" (*sāyujya*) and "residing in the same world as Brahman" (*sālokya*).

For thus the Blessed One said: "A man, devoted to his own particular duty, attains perfection"; and having further stated, "Learn from Me how he, having attained perfection, reaches Brahman," He continued: "Endowed with a purified intellect, having restrained the self with fortitude, constantly intent on the yoga of meditation, and firmly established in dispassion."

By stating, "Then, having known Me in truth, he enters into Me immediately thereafter," [the Lord] shows that for one who has been purified by obligatory rites (*nityakarman*), whose internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is denoted by the term "perfection" (*saṃsiddhi*), and who possesses the necessary auxiliary factors such as the yoga of meditation (*dhyānayoga*), liberation occurs through the arising of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). Furthermore, by the words "in their respective duties," the obligatory rites are meant; and by the word "perfection" (*saṃsiddhi*), the purification of the self and the attainment of fitness for the knowledge of Brahman are expressed.

This is because the supreme perfection will be described later, and because it has been stated: "Yogis perform action, having abandoned attachment, for the purification of the self. Likewise: "By the great sacrifices and by [other] sacrifices, this body is made fit for Brahman"; "Knowledge arises in men from the destruction of sinful karma"; and "When the impurity has been cooked away by actions, then knowledge proceeds."

Therefore, by the force of the term "saṃskāra" (refinement) and from other scriptural authorities, the obligatory rites (*nityakarman*)—by means of purifying the person through the removal of impurities and the instilling of qualities—bring about fitness for the knowledge of the Self; thus, by generating the knowledge of reality, they are combined with [liberating] knowledge for the sake of liberation. This is just as the preparatory rites (*saṃskārakarman*), such as the sprinkling of rice grains (*vrīhiprokṣaṇa*), are combined with [the fruit of] heaven by being causes for the production of the essential form of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*).

[Objection: But surely, because they share a single agent [with the primary rite], the obligatory rites (nityakarman) must be subsidiary actions (guṇakarman), just like the act of sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) and so forth. [Reply: No; for the knowledge of Brahman is not something to be enjoined (avidheya), and the Self, as that which is being refined, cannot be a subsidiary to an action that is to be enjoined. [Objection: In that case, it is not a purificatory action (saṃskārakarman); for such a status is well-known in the case of purificatory acts directed toward substances that are themselves enjoined as parts of a rite. [Reply: No; for it is well known that there is a purificatory act involving curd (dadhi) as a part of eating, even though eating itself is not enjoined.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the obligatory rites (*nityakarman*), which are enjoined as instruments (*karaṇa*) in the instruction of a [specific] injunction, would—contrary to their status as instruments—become subsidiary procedures (*itikartavyatā*) for the knowledge of the Self, just like the preparation of curd and other materials? [Response: This is not a fault; for we observe that the *Sautrāmaṇī* and the *Bṛhaspatisava*—though enjoined elsewhere as independent instruments by separate injunctions in such texts as "Having piled the fire-altar (*agni*), one should sacrifice with the Sautrāmaṇī" and "Having sacrificed with the Vājapeya, one should sacrifice with the Bṛhaspatisava"—function as subsidiary procedures (*itikartavyatā*) for the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*) and the Vājapeya, respectively.

If it is argued that, due to the distinction between the means (*karaṇa*), the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), the injunction (*vidhi*), and the authoritative testimony (*pramāṇa*), it is appropriate for the Sautrāmaṇī and similar rites to possess a dual nature, we reply: True; however, provided there is no contradiction in meaning, let this dual nature—consisting of being both a means and a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*), and thus being both a subsidiary to an independent fruit and a procedure toward the knowledge of the Self (*ātmajñāna*)—be postulated here as well. This is on account of the force of the obligatory injunction (*nityavidhi*) and the force of the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) inferred from the Smṛti concerning purificatory rites. Moreover, it is not merely a procedure because it is simply a purificatory rite of materials intended for another purpose.

If it is argued that [the injunctions regarding ritual action] are not auxiliary to knowledge because they are not seen in the context of the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration)—since that rite has the consecrated fire as its objective—[we reply: here too there is no contradiction, because the means to knowledge are prescribed with reference to one who has been purified, whose internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is cleansed, who is dispassionate, and who desires to know (*vividiṣu*). Perceiving through direct experience that purity and the inward-turning of the mind are the fruits of ritual action, and inferring that such results were produced by actions performed in previous births, he will proceed to engage in the internal means of knowledge.

Therefore, just as the acquisition of materials prescribed by other independent injunctions serves as a subsidiary (śeṣatva) to both the sacrifice and its enjoyment due to the difference in the attainment of auxiliary causes, so too it is not contradictory that obligatory rites (nityakarman) serve as subsidiaries to both the knowledge of the Self and worldly prosperity (abhyudaya) through the difference in their auxiliary causes. Furthermore, whoever is a proponent of the doctrine of residual impressions (saṃskāra) who—having distanced himself from the subtle meaning of the Vedānta—denigrates the Vedānta and asserts that obligatory rites do not have the purpose of producing residual impressions, should be disregarded because he lacks knowledge of the distinction between the various meanings of the scriptures.

Alternatively, he states—by means of the passage beginning with "by sacrifice, by charity," and so on—that all ritual actions, though enjoined by originative injunctions (*utpatti-vidhi*), shall become subject to another injunction of qualification (*adhikārāntara-vidhi*) such as "one desiring the experience of Brahman should perform sacrifices and the like," due to a difference in connection (*saṃyoga-bheda*), just as there are other injunctions of qualification for those desiring livelihood and so forth.

How, then, is the direct experience (*aparokṣānubhava*) of the reality of the Self understood to be something to be accomplished through meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), like heaven and other such goals? Because it is a human goal (*puruṣārtha*). For when verbal knowledge has already arisen, there can be no desire for it; and when it has not yet arisen, there can likewise be no desire for it because its object is not yet known. Therefore, it is logical that one desires a direct knowledge of what has been understood through words. And it has been shown previously that this [direct knowledge] is to be accomplished by means of another effort. In that regard:

Since sacrifices and the like are understood—by virtue of being subordinate to desire and by virtue of being presented as the instruments (*karaṇa*) of the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) denoted by the verb—to be connected only with that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), it is understood that sacrifices and the like are the means for the realization of Brahman. Consequently, the injunction takes the form: "One who desires the experience of the Self should perform sacrifices and the like. Nor is there a connection [of the sacrifice] with mere desire, because that [desire] is understood not to be something that can be accomplished. Nor is there a contradiction with the present tense in the word "desire to know" (*vividiṣanti*), since the injunctive *leṭ* suffix is accepted, thereby revealing the injunction itself.

Nor is there any contradiction with the obligatory (*nitya*) and optional (*kāmya*) modifications [of the Agnihotra], because it is understood that a single ritual action can be connected to multiple injunctions regarding its performance. [Objection: But surely, just as in the case of the *Kuṇḍapāyinām Ayana* sacrifice—where the statement "They offer the Agnihotra for a month" establishes a distinct ritual because of its difference in context (*prakaraṇāntara*) from the well-known Agnihotra—it cannot be assumed here that the well-known Agnihotra and other rites are to be employed, since the sentence concerning the desire for knowledge (*vividiṣā-vākya*) likewise constitutes a different context.

Therefore, it is not correct to say that other distinct rites alone are enjoined here along with their originative injunctions (*utpatti*) and qualification injunctions (*adhikāra*); for in the *Kuṇḍapāyināmayana*, the word "Agnihotra" is a non-worldly designation (*alaukika-abhidhāna*). Because it is dependent on the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), it denotes the meaning expressed by that suffix; thus, it is impossible for it to independently refer back to the Agnihotra enjoined in another location. Furthermore, the verb *juhoti*, which expresses a general action, cannot abandon the distinct rite defined by the factors (*kāraka*) situated in its own proximity.

It was stated that because it is impossible for [the word] to refer back to the Agnihotra which is separated [by other passages], another ritual action alone, qualified by the attribute of "monthly" (māsa), is enjoined; however, in this case, since the words "study," "sacrifice," "giving," "austerity," and "fasting" denote worldly activities and thus possess independence, it is logical that they refer back to the study and other acts enjoined in other locations, and that those very same actions are enjoined through a difference in connection (saṃyoga-bheda).

[Objection: Even so, since the knowledge of Brahman is produced by a causal complex consisting of perceptible means of knowledge (*dṛṣṭapramāṇasāmagrī*), it does not depend on the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*); for when the causes of knowledge are present, there is no absence of the arising of knowledge due to the absence of sacrifices and the like. [Reply: This is not so. Since the establishment of perceptible causes is included within the means of knowledge of positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*), dependence on those [perceptible causes] is appropriate; however, in this case, even though the perceptible causes for the face [in a mirror] are complete and there is an absence of mere negative concomitance (*kevalavyatireka*), there is nevertheless dependence on the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) because of the injunction—so it is also with regard to perfect knowledge (*samyagjñāna*).

The dependence on the unseen (adṛṣṭa) follows precisely from the injunction itself. Now, it may be argued: "Since there is no means for the application of ritual acts (*karman*) toward knowledge (*vijñāna*), their application must be postulated toward liberation (*mokṣa*), which is the fruit of knowledge. To this we reply: Just as intermediate *apūrva*s are postulated by the force of the injunction itself to account for sacrifices and other rites prescribed with heaven and so forth as their goal, so too here, let a door such as the purification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgrya*) be postulated.

Furthermore—since it is impossible for that which is directly heard [in scripture] to be a means to knowledge, it is better to assume that it is a means to that [knowledge] even through a mediated succession (*paramparā*), rather than assuming it is a means to its result [liberation]. This is because the instrumental case-ending (*karaṇavibhakti*) is seen even when there is a mediated means, as in the expression "he cooks with wood" (*kāṣṭhaiḥ pacati*); whereas it would be inconsistent [to use the instrumental] even if [the wood] were a direct means to the result. Moreover, in this sentence, liberation is not heard as being accomplished by sacrifice and the like; rather, the Self is understood as the object of knowledge and thus as being accomplished by that [knowledge], not as being accomplished by sacrifice and the like.

Furthermore—only after avoiding contradiction with other means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is it proper to abandon what is explicitly stated in scripture and assume what is not; and there exists a prohibition against actions being a means to liberation in such passages as, "There is no other path," and "Neither by action nor by progeny. Moreover, he states that the assumption of actions being a means [to liberation] even through a traditional succession (*paramparā*) is contradicted by another means of valid knowledge: "One should sacrifice with whatever [is available]," and so forth. This is intended as an illustration of the collection of scriptural statements whose ultimate purpose is the purification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

Now, one might ask: if both [the paths of] *saṃskāra* and *vividiṣā* result in the state of being a knower (*jñānitva*) through the door of purification, what is the distinction between them? It is said in reply: *Saṃskāra* accomplishes perfect knowledge (*vijñāna*) only when there is the attainment of auxiliary causes such as hearing, reflection, meditation, and practice; in their absence, it results only in worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*). In the case of *vividiṣā*, however, since knowledge is the fruit of action, the means produce knowledge only upon reaching that fruit—this is the distinction.

In this regard, a certain person—a proponent of universal confusion even within Vedānta, whose speech regarding difference and non-difference is as senseless as the blustering of a fool—imagines that ritual actions are a means to liberation based solely on the *vividiṣā* injunctions. Such a person is to be disregarded due to his lack of expertise in both logic and scripture. Furthermore, although in the expression "one desires to go by horse" the horse is sometimes seen to persist until the completion of the return journey, this is not a valid illustration for the claim that ritual actions are a means to liberation.

However, it has been stated that through both reason and scripture, knowledge alone is the means for achieving the goal; for in the case of rituals whose fruits are remote, there is no attainment of performance until the fruit is reached, since cessation is established only after one understands that the fruit consists in the mind’s inward orientation. When the opponent has thus argued, the proponent establishes his own position: "True, this is so; provided that [knowledge] was indeed practiced in the same birth."

The intention is as follows: this word *atha* is intended to set forth the specific qualification of the eligible person (*adhikārin*)—which must be understood in the preceding moment—as a condition for the authority to engage in action, starting from the arising of the desire that culminates in activity and extending to the object of experience. In that regard, since actions whose fruits are separated by many births do not require comprehension at the very time of engaging in the fruit, the word *atha* is not used there for the purpose of such comprehension.

[Objection: But surely, even the knowledge of the duties performed in a previous birth becomes a cause for the qualification to inquire into Brahman; for the connection with the debts is contingent upon this present birth, and only one who has discharged the three debts possesses the qualification for liberation. To this, he says: "By this [it is shown] that even by way of the discharge of debts... [Objection: But it is recorded in Smṛti: "Having discharged the three debts, one should fix the mind on liberation; but he who pursues liberation without having discharged them goes downwards. [Reply: True.

He states that it is a *apasmṛti* (erroneous tradition) because it contradicts the *śruti*: "And thus there are the *śruti* and *smṛti*: 'Or otherwise, [one may attain liberation] from the state of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) itself. Now, an objection is raised: "There is indeed a *śruti* which says, 'A Brāhmaṇa, being born, is born with three debts'. True; however, an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is set aside when it contradicts an injunctive *śruti*. Furthermore, do the words "debts" refer to the son, sacrifice, and celibacy themselves, or rather to the injunctions for them? In the first case, a connection with a son and so forth is not possible for one who is being born, because this would contradict the non-perception of what is capable of existing. Nor...

There is a connection with that injunction (*vidhi*); for one who lacks the capacity to comprehend an injunction has no entitlement (*adhikāra*), and capacity is a qualification of the entitled person. If it is argued that "a householder, being born, is born burdened with three debts," we say no; because such an assumption would contradict the injunction, "one should go forth from the household. Furthermore, in that case as well, there is an equal contradiction with non-perception of the fit (*yogyānupalabdhi*) regarding the birth of a householder as being connected to the birth of sons and so forth.

Furthermore, it is not logical to connect the injunction regarding sons and so forth with the time of one's birth as a householder, because at that time there is an absence of the capacity to perform the injunctions concerning sons and the like. If it is argued that this statement is intended to prevent the connection with other conflicting injunctions prior to the attainment of the qualification for sons and so forth starting from birth, we say no; for such an interpretation would contradict another injunction regarding renunciation (saṃnyāsa). Therefore, this is merely an explanatory passage (arthavāda).

[Objection: But surely, since there is a contradiction with the injunction, "Having completed the stage of studentship (brahmacarya), one should become a householder," how can renunciation (saṃnyāsa) be enjoined immediately after studentship? [Reply: No; for renunciation has as its subject those who are detached and seek liberation, and thus there is no contradiction with the general injunction. [Objection: Why could renunciation not have as its subject those who are ineligible for ritual action, such as the blind and the lame? [Reply: No.

Because of the scriptural statement without qualification, "One may renounce from the stage of studentship, from the householder's life, or from the forest-dweller's life"; because those who are ineligible—such as those described as "whether he be one who has not taken vows or one who has taken vows, whether he be one who has not performed the ceremonial bath or one who has performed it, or one whose sacred fires have been extinguished"—are mentioned separately from the [standard] stages of life (āśramas) precisely as being eligible for renunciation; and because even the blind and others are not established as ineligible since they possess eligibility for rites such as the five great sacrifices (pañcamahāyajña) through their sons; and because even the blind and others who lack dispassion (vairāgya) are ineligible for renunciation—it follows that dispassion alone is the cause for renunciation.

"May my body be observant; may my tongue be most sweet; may I hear much with my two ears. Since, through such passages as "Food, breath, sight, hearing, mind, and speech," proficiency of the body, senses, and so forth is prayed for the sake of self-knowledge (*ātmajñāna*), and since renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is a subordinate element of self-knowledge, as well as from Smṛti texts such as "One should place one's feet on ground purified by sight," it follows that only one whose senses are exceptionally sharp is qualified for renunciation.

Since renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is enjoined in every context concerning the knowledge of the Self (*ātmajñāna*), it is established that renunciation has the knowledge of the Self as its fruit by virtue of being an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to hearing [the scriptures] and so forth. But how can it be determined that both actions and their abandonment have the knowledge of the Self as their fruit? We reply: they are like the two options regarding the taking of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup, which are auxiliaries to the sacrifice. Alternatively, a combination (*samuccaya*) of action and its abandonment is postulated as assisting the knowledge of the Self through a sequence, because the means of assistance differ and the impurities to be destroyed are infinite. Or else, a systematic arrangement (*vyavasthā*) is postulated based on distinctions such as Brahmin, Kṣatriya, and so forth.

Furthermore, what exactly is to be renounced here? Everything other than one's own body. But surely the sacred thread (*upavīta*) and so forth do not deserve to be abandoned? No; because there is no distinction from the *agnihotra* and other such rites. But surely, even if ritual actions are abandoned as part of the subsidiary elements (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), the sacred thread and so forth may be taken up again later? No.

In the Jābāla-śruti, after prescribing the complete renunciation of the *agnihotra* and other rites along with the sacred thread (*upavīta*) and so forth by means of the general injunction "one should go forth," and at the time of enjoining the duties of the wandering mendicant (*parivrāj*)—beginning with "Now the wandering mendicant, wearing discolored garments, shaven-headed, possessing no belongings"—the text poses the question, "How can one who does not wear the sacrificial thread (*ayajñopavītin*) be a Brāhmaṇa? It then answers, "This very Self (*ātman*) is his sacrificial thread. By the use of the restrictive particle "eva" (only/this very), it excludes the Brāhmaṇical sacrificial thread and others, because it establishes that the Self alone constitutes the sacrificial thread.

Regarding this, the proponent of total confusion (sarvasaṅkaravādī) prattles on, claiming that because the renunciation of the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*) was not previously mentioned, this statement—"How can a Brāhmaṇa be without the sacrificial thread?"—is an interpolation, since there would otherwise be no occasion for such a question. However, he merely commits an offense through his hatred for the Paramahaṃsa wandering mendicants who perceive reality and are established therein; for it is natural that he fails to recognize that the renunciation of the sacrificial thread follows as a matter of course from the total renunciation obtained by the force of the preceding injunctions.

And likewise, the Maitrāyaṇī Śruti, addressing the wandering mendicant (parivrājaka) specifically, states: "Now, the wandering mendicant, clothed in a single garment, shaven-headed, intent upon a small bowl and a water-pot, seeking alms, may enter a village until evening; he should practice the begging of alms from all castes except those who have fallen [from their status], moving clockwise and without hesitation, without the sacrificial thread, devoted to purity; at his will, he may take a single bamboo staff."

And likewise Bodhāyana also shows that the renunciation occurs only after [the stage of] saṃnyāsa, stating: "Henceforth, having discarded the sacred thread, the seat, the topknot, the staffs, the sling, the water-purifier, and the water-pot, he then takes up the staff with the mantra, 'O Friend, protect me. Therefore, renunciation is indeed as previously described, being an auxiliary limb of the knowledge of the Self. "Therefore, it has been well said"—thus concludes the commentary.

One might object: "Is it not the case that this word 'atha' (now/then) does not intend to convey a specific qualification of the qualified person by way of expressing immediate succession (*ānantarya*), but rather intends to convey the sequence [of topics] by way of expressing that [succession]? To this, he replies: "Even so, it is not as a cause (*hetutva*)."

In this regard, it must be stated: does [the author] set forth the sequence himself, or does he indicate the reasoning required by a sequence already established through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? It is not the first alternative; thus he says: "This is improper—[because it is called] a *Nyāyasūtra*. The meaning is: because there is no scripture (*āgama*); that is, because it lacks the status of being a scripture.

In the second alternative, he states that [the inquiry] is not for that purpose because there is an absence of "performance by a single injunction," which is the cause for requiring a sequence between the inquiry into Dharma and the inquiry into Brahman—namely, "Furthermore, of those [actions] having a single agent," and so forth. He introduces the Bhāṣya on this stated point with the words, "He says this."

In this regard, someone—though perceiving the mention of a distinction in the phrase "of the inquiry into Dharma and Brahman"—replies that there indeed exists a relationship of a subordinate qualification upon a primary qualification (*adhikṛtādhikāra*) between the knowledge of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice and the knowledge of the Udgītha; such a person is truly unfortunate.

Since the meditations on the *udgītha* and other such specific attributes—which have been defined by the fourfold injunctions—are treated as incidental within the context of Brahman due to their commonality as mental realizations (*pratyaya*), and because only the distinctions [between them] and so forth have been defined, there can be no subordination of the knowledge of Brahman—understood as the ultimate purport of the scripture—to ritual action, for such knowledge lacks the qualification of those already authorized for ritual. Now, it may be argued: "Let it be that the word *atha* does not intend to follow the logic required by a specific sequence implied by the necessity of performing [actions] through the impulsion of a single injunction."

However, he states the doubt regarding the subsequent commentary—beginning with "Just as in the case of the Āgneya and other [sacrifices]"—namely, that because there is a unity of the agent in the two means of accomplishment, whether by virtue of being performed through the impulsion toward a single fruit, or by virtue of being performed through the impulsion toward a single object of knowledge and inquiry, there is an implication of a sequence.

The portion of the text preceding the words "and because of the difference in the nature of sensation" is clear in its meaning. This is the intended sense here: there is no evidence for the fact that the knowledge of Dharma and the knowledge of Brahman have a single fruit, nor is it logically consistent. How so? First of all, it has already been stated in the examination of the logic regarding the verbal capacity of the *vividiṣā* passage (*jijñāsā* passage) that it does not serve as authority for their conjunction. Nor is there an injunction for conjunction in the verse: "He who knows both knowledge and ignorance together."

Because of the understanding of a difference in results from the statement, "Having crossed over death by means of ignorance, one attains immortality by means of knowledge," there is no injunction for the combination (*samuccaya*) of knowledge and action in a single person in the passage, "By that [path] goes the knower of Brahman and the doer of merit. This is because the combination is understood to apply to two distinct persons—the knower of Brahman and the doer of merit—on the path; furthermore, the use of the particle *ca* (and) in the sense of mere conjunction (*anvācaya*) allows for the connection of each [person] with the path independently. Moreover, the term "doer of merit" refers to those who rely on symbols (*pratīka*) and travel by the path of light (*arcir-ādi*) under the guidance of the non-human being, whereas those who perform sacrifices such as the *iṣṭi* are heard to follow the path of smoke (*dhūma-ādi*).

Nor is a rule for their combination understood from the passage, "Practice those [duties] constantly, O you who desire Truth," because only actions alone are heard there, and because the word "Truth" (satya) refers to the world of Satyaloka—as seen in the supplementary portion of the text, "This is your holy, well-made world of Brahman"—and because of the censure of action in the words, "For these forms of sacrifice are frail rafts; there is no uncreated [world] through the created," and because of the injunction for knowledge in the words, "To know that, one should approach a teacher alone."

The statement, "This Self is indeed to be attained through truth and austerity," is not an injunction for a combination [of means]; for the word "austerity" (tapas) denotes meditation itself, as in the passage, "The one-pointedness of the mind and the senses is the highest austerity. Therefore, there is no authoritative basis for a combination. Furthermore, it is because of a prohibition.

"There is no other path for going there"; "There is nothing uncreated by what is created"; "Neither by action, nor by progeny, nor by wealth"; "Not by other gods, nor by austerity, nor by ritual action"; and "Having abandoned ignorance, one should go to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu by means of wisdom alone. If it is argued that these passages merely prohibit mere ritual actions, we say no; for there is no qualification [to the prohibition], and since there is no authoritative evidence enjoining the combination [of knowledge and action], the prohibition of all actions is logically established. Furthermore, because the renunciation of all actions is enjoined as a subordinate element of knowledge, there can be no combination.

If it is argued that there is a combination [of knowledge and action] through the duties of the stage of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), we say no; for those duties, such as meditation (*dhyāna*) and so forth, are auxiliary to the very nature of knowledge. If it is argued that the very impossibility of enjoining obligatory rites (*nityakarman*) otherwise implies that actions bear liberation as their fruit by way of being auxiliaries to knowledge, we say no.

Because obligatory rites (*nityakarman*) are independent of results, and because if they were dependent on results, the principle of the *Viśvajit* sacrifice would apply; because it has been shown that their application [to liberation] occurs through the mediation of purification (*saṃskāra*); and because, since the injunctions regarding rituals themselves would otherwise be untenable, one must assume that the rituals alone are the means to liberation—therefore, the theory of their combination (*samuccaya*) is not established. Furthermore, since the prohibition of ritual action can be understood as being for the purpose of praising knowledge—just as the prohibition of the morning libation (*uditahoma*) serves to praise the evening libation—it would follow that knowledge and action are alternative means to liberation.

If it is argued that the knowledge of Brahman itself is postulated as the means for liberation through the ritual acts (*karma*) by way of being their *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance), we say no; because there exists another *itikartavyatā*, namely tranquility (*śama*) and so forth, and because it would contradict the injunctions since the ritual acts are established in the context of the injunction as instruments (*karaṇa*). Furthermore, the purpose is contradicted. It must be stated what the purpose to be accomplished by the ritual acts is: it cannot be the oneness of Brahman and the Self, because that is not something to be accomplished (*asādhya*); nor can it be the cessation of the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the distinctions and parts of ignorance (*avidyā*), [for that too is not produced by action].

This is because [the scriptures] understand that [ignorance] is to be removed by the vision of Brahman, as in passages such as, "The knot of the heart is severed," and "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself. Indeed, when it is said, "When He is seen," ritual actions are not understood to be auxiliary factors. Nor is the removal of the two-fold limiting adjuncts (upādhi) the fruit of ritual actions.

Likewise, because it is understood from such passages as "The knower, liberated from name and form" and "In this very way, these sixteen parts of the seer here, which have the Puruṣa as their goal, vanish away upon reaching the Puruṣa," that [liberation] is to be brought about by the vision of Brahman; and because it has been shown that karma and its adjuncts have ignorance alone as their material cause. Furthermore, for those who advocate the doctrine of the combination [of knowledge and action], there is no fruit to be accomplished even through knowledge.

Because the adjuncts of karma cannot be removed by cognition since they are real entities; because false superimposition ceases of its own accord due to its momentariness; because a stream cannot be severed independently without the cessation of the flowing elements; because it is unreal; because the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of false knowledge is not seen to be contradicted by the knowledge of reality regarding mother-of-pearl and the like, and thus is not removable; because the nature of Brahman as the Self is self-luminous and therefore not to be illumined by cognition; and because of the latent impression resulting from the practice of the knowledge of reality.

Because liberation is heard in scripture to result from the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) upon the cessation of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*), therefore knowledge bears fruit only through the cessation of that beginningless false knowledge which is the material cause of all evils; thus, there is no room for a combination [of ritual action and knowledge]. In this regard, the proponent of universal confusion (*sarvasaṅkaravādī*), being ignorant even of the qualification required for the inquiry into Brahman, prattles on about the realization of Brahman occurring after the realization of Dharma solely by the force of their combination. Furthermore, it must be investigated whether, even if such a combination were possible, the reverse might not be the case.

For instance: since only actions performed by one who possesses knowledge accomplish liberation, it would follow that the very opposite order [of stages] would be required—namely, that first the realization of Brahman must be produced, and only then is it proper for the student (brahmacārin) who possesses that realization to perform all the duties of his own stage of life, such as the inquiry into Dharma. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that the actions performed by a seeker of liberation from the very beginning until the completion of the inquiry into Dharma would be rendered useless. Furthermore, seekers of liberation are observed even in the very first stage of life.

If it is argued that the inquiry into Dharma (*dharma-vicāra*) must be performed first because it is common to all, [we reply]: O beloved of the gods! This [inquiry] has not set out to accomplish something common to all; rather, it has set out to accomplish either a desired means or that which is necessarily to be performed.
