In that regard, if both types of inquiry were considered means for attaining the desired liberation, then it was already stated that a reversal of the order would be better. Now, if the injunction for the compulsory study of the Vedas (*nityādhyayana-vidhi*) impels the inquiry into ritual action (*karma-vicāra*), then [it follows that] there is another inquiry that must necessarily be performed.

If it is argued that the inquiry into Brahman is undertaken because it is desired, this is not sound; for even after the inquiry into Brahman—which is desired—it is possible to undertake the inquiry into obligatory duty (*nityadharma*). Now, one might object: "If the inquiry into ritual action (*karmavicāra*) is not performed immediately after Vedic study, there would be sin (*pratyavāya*). This is true; however, even by performing it to a small extent as an obligatory duty, one avoids sin. Furthermore, they (the student and teacher) might simply pursue that much alone.

This is because even the duties of a student (*brahmacārin*) being performed by a learned man are obtained as means to liberation; or because in the case of "Vedic study" (*vedānuvacana*) and so forth, the instrumental case-ending is heard for each individually, indicating independence; or because it is logical that the duties of the stages of life (*āśrama*) are means to liberation as optional alternatives; and because renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is prescribed immediately after the stage of studentship.

Furthermore, the understanding of dharma, even when performed as an obligatory duty, does not exclude the inquiry into Brahman; nor is the inquiry into dharma something that must not be performed, since the duties of renunciation—distinct from the *agnihotra* and other rites—are accepted as being combined with knowledge.

Furthermore, it must be explained why the injunction for Vedic study (*adhyayanavidhi*), while impelling one toward the inquiry into ritual action (*karmavicāra*), does not likewise impel one toward the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmavicāra*). If you argue that this is because another injunction is heard in the form "He should hear [the Vedas] (*śrotavya*)," then you, O "beloved of the gods," have clearly not heard the history of Mīmāṃsā. For, since the inquiry into Brahman can be undertaken by this very injunction for Vedic study—which already possesses the established status of an impeller regarding the inquiry into Dharma—it would be redundant to postulate a separate injunction for application (*viniyoga*), qualification (*adhikāra*), and performance (*prayoga*) for the injunction "He should hear."

Because it is illogical to conceive of [the inquiry] as being merely a motivator (*pravartakatva*). If it is argued that, since the knowledge of Brahman is a means to a desired end (*kāmyamāna*), its inquiry is also a desired end and therefore not prompted by the injunction for compulsory study (*nityādhyayanavidhi*), then it would follow that even the inquiry into those Vedic passages concerning rites (*karma*) which are desired ends would likewise be prompted by that same injunction.

It might be argued: "Since the inquiry into Brahman is enjoined as having specific means such as detachment (*vairāgya*), tranquility (*śama*), self-control (*dama*), and approaching a teacher (*upasada*) as its auxiliary requirements (*aṅga*), whereas the injunction for Vedic study lacks these auxiliaries like tranquility in the case of the inquiry into ritual action (*karma*), it is impossible for that [study] to imply those auxiliaries for the inquiry into Brahman; therefore, a separate injunction including all its auxiliaries must be postulated. This is merely the talk of a loquacious person who has failed to understand the function of the injunction.

Indeed, the rule for Vedic study (*svādhyāyavidhi*), while enjoining the study of other passages even when deficient in certain auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) such as the head-vow (*śirovrata*) or eating on the ground, enjoins the study of the *Muṇḍaka* and *Kārīrī* sacrifices only after first implying those auxiliary elements like the head-vow. And when it employs critical inquiry (*vicāra*), it employs that inquiry by implying the various distinct methods of reasoning (*nyāyabheda*) which serve as auxiliaries for each individual passage, precisely because they are perceived as necessary.

Furthermore, the injunction for the New and Full Moon sacrifices (darśapūrṇamāsa) enjoins the performance of the auxiliary parts according to one's capacity when it concerns the obligatory entitlement (nityādhikāra), whereas the entitlement for optional rites (kāmyādhikāra) requires the performance of all auxiliary parts. Likewise, that same injunction implies the auxiliary of gazing at the clarified butter (ājyāvekṣaṇa) and so forth in the case of the Upāṃśuyāja rite, but the auxiliary of threshing (avaghāta) and so forth in the case of other sacrifices. In this manner, it is not contradictory that the injunction for Vedic study (adhyayanavidhi) implies the auxiliaries such as tranquility (śama) and so forth in the inquiry into Brahman (brahmavicāra), but not in other contexts. Nor is there a lack of implication [of these auxiliaries] on the grounds that they are specifications of the qualified person (adhikāriviśeṣaṇa) and thus are not things to be performed (anupādeya).

Since only those who are eligible for the injunction to study are also eligible for the inquiry prompted by that injunction, it is everywhere established that the primary injunction, depending on the specific assistance required from visible and invisible auxiliary elements, prompts the performance of whichever particular auxiliary is needed. Therefore, because both types of inquiry are prompted by the single injunction to study, when a sequence is required, the inquiry into Dharma is logically subsequent to the inquiry into Brahman; for even the inquiry into Dharma and so forth attains the status of being a means to liberation.

Therefore, it is not the case that the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*) follows immediately after the inquiry into Dharma (*dharmajijñāsā*) even because of the unity of their results. Furthermore, the distinction between the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) is established because each sentence has a distinct purport (*tātparya*). He states another reason for this: "Because of the difference in the operation of the injunction" (*codanāpravṛttibhedāt*). He explains this with the words beginning "This other," and so forth. By the term *codanā*, a word is meant which effects a verbal productive energy (*śabdabhāvanā*). And that injunction, while effecting an objective productive energy (*arthabhāvanā*) characterized by its three constituent parts, also brings about the understanding of that objective productive energy itself; for it is impossible for a person to engage in activity toward an object that has not been understood. This is the intended meaning.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the injunction (*codanā*), impelling a person toward the realization of Brahman (*brahmāvabodha*) as the goal to be accomplished, teaches a productive activity (*bhāvanā*) that is distinct from the realization itself? [Reply: No, he says—“A person is not impelled toward realization. [Objection: Is it not the case that realization is achievable through human effort? [Reply: No, he says—“For realization is according to the state of things (*yathāvastu*). The meaning is that one observes the cognition of foul odors and the like even for one who has no desire [for them] and exerts no effort.

It is said that the portion of the text preceding the phrase "discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities" is clear in meaning. Intending to state that the qualification for scriptural injunction must itself be scriptural, he says: "discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities," and so forth. In the context of the injunction, "That is to be sought," [the text] shows the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities: "Just as here the world acquired through action perishes, even so there the world acquired through merit perishes."

In the section concerning the injunction for hearing the knowledge [of Brahman], detachment from the enjoyment of objects here and hereafter is shown by the passages, "Having examined the worlds acquired through action," and "But for the sake of the self, all things become dear. Furthermore, in the section concerning the injunction for seeing [Brahman], tranquility and other qualities are shown by the passage, "Tranquil, self-controlled... In the section concerning the injunction for inquiry, "Seek to know That," the approaching of a teacher is shown by the passage, "...he approached his father Varuṇa."

Furthermore, the declarations of rewards found everywhere are intended to demonstrate the eligibility of the seeker of liberation by way of generating desire; otherwise, the mere performance of the means would render the proclamation of rewards futile. Since knowledge is not something that can be commanded, even injunctions regarding it are directed toward the injunction of its means. In this regard, the unity of the injunctions is established through the principle of the "cognition of all branches" (*sarva-śākhā-pratyaya-nyāya*).

And that single injunction, observing its own qualification (*adhikāra*) by virtue of the power of the context and in order to avoid the futility of the mere mention [of the object], accepts the previously described collection of duties as the cause for that qualification; for an injunction lacking a qualification cannot logically culminate in practical engagement. Now, how is it understood that inquiry is enjoined in these sentences? It is said: in the words "it is to be desired to be known" (*vijijñāsitavyaḥ*) and "you should desire to know" (*vijijñāsasva*), inquiry is enjoined as being implied within the desire for knowledge and the desire itself.

Because [the Self] cannot be an object of injunction; and because the inquiry itself is enjoined by the statement, "It is to be heard"; and because the statement, "For the sake of knowing That, one should approach a Guru," makes it clear that knowledge is something to be accomplished; and because the injunction to approach a Guru implies the injunction for hearing (śravaṇa) and so forth as its means. Since it is impossible to enjoin knowledge directly in the form, "One should see the Self in the Self alone," an injunction is adopted regarding its means. Thus, it is established that in all cases, hearing (śravaṇa) is enjoined as a subsidiary (aṅga) along with reflection (manana) and meditative concentration (nididhyāsana).

Now, it may be objected: "In an injunction for the means to a fruit, the mere desire for that fruit alone constitutes the full cause for qualification; what need is there for the other collection of factors? This is true; however, because the scriptural cause for qualification is explicitly mentioned, it is understood to be the cause for qualification just like [the conditions of] living, the burning of one's house, and so forth.

[Objection: Since the collection of means (sādhana-kalāpa) is something to be performed, one might postulate an injunction (*vidhi*) with respect to it and assume that it is merely an auxiliary (*aṅga*) contributing to the result, like the *prayāja* offerings and so forth. [Reply: True; even for an auxiliary, there is no contradiction in its being a qualification of the person entitled (*adhikāra-viśeṣaṇa*), as in the case of specific times such as "at dawn" (*pradoṣa*). This is indicated by such scriptural marks (*liṅga*) as "having become possessed of qualities such as tranquility (*śānti*), one should see," and because we observe that initiation (*dīkṣā*) also serves as the cause for entitlement to subsequent sacrifices. Therefore, it is rightly said: "discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities."

The subsequent commentary, beginning with "for when these exist," establishes that the entire collection of means—starting from inquiry and leading up to the experience of Brahman—possesses the status of a visible cause, as proven by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). To explain this, [the author] first states that there is no engagement [in the practice] without the desire for liberation (*mumukṣutva*), saying: "It was stated previously, under the heading of 'qualification' (*adhikāra*)," and so forth. Therefore, the meaning is that the desire for liberation is the motivating cause for engaging in the means toward the desired goal.

[Objection: But surely, when there is a desire for a fruit, since other duties are absent, one does not observe a lack of engagement in the means to that fruit. [Reply: True; however, because each preceding stage is understood as a qualifying condition (*upādhi*) for each subsequent one, it serves as the cause for eligibility (*adhikāra*) by virtue of being the condition for the desire for liberation (*mumukṣutva*). Thus he says: "Therefore, as long as this [desire for liberation] extends up to the attainment of Hiraṇyagarbha," and so forth. [Objection: But everything is indeed impermanent, because it exists, like a dream. [Reply: No; he says: "Even though this is perishing," and so forth.

Furthermore, no effect whatsoever is perceived to exist without a material cause (*upādāna*). If one effect were to have another effect as its material cause, then all preceding causes would necessarily persist within the subsequent effect; for that which does not persist cannot serve as a material cause. Therefore, rather than postulating a beginningless plurality of material causes for each stream of effects—which would entail an infinite regress—it is better to postulate a single, beginningless entity as the material cause of all effects. Moreover, this must be changeless and immutable; otherwise, it would follow that it itself is an effect.

Likewise, every effect perishes entirely at some point, because it has a single material cause (*ekopādānatva*), just like the pleasure and so forth residing in the self during deep sleep; thus, the destruction of everything extends only as far as that [single] entity. Otherwise, just as there would be no rebirth in a form similar to the previous one—since that which was destroyed at the end of a prior kalpa would lack the persistence of its own latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) due to the absence of any remainder of its material cause—so too there would follow the consequence that the present [world] could not arise, as it would likewise lack a material cause.

The construction is as follows: because one who enjoys objects perceives their imminent destruction along with those very objects. Herein the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is this: the ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) is that "as long as one does not understand impermanence, so long does one not comprehend the eternal reality. And the ellipsis is that "as long as the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal things has not arisen, so long does dispassion (*virakta*) not arise."

In the phrase “as long as there is no face-to-face destruction,” the word *yāvat* is connected with the word *virakta* by supplying the negative particle *na*, thus meaning “as long as one is not dispassionate. The ellipsis to be supplied is: “so long does one not take up the state of seeking liberation (*mumukṣutva*). And as long as one does not take up the state of seeking liberation, who would undertake the inquiry into Brahman? Thus, this negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is shown: that in the absence of the entire collection of means, there is no engagement in the investigation.

An objection is raised: "Is there not a lack of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), since activity is observed even in the absence of the entire collection of means? Anticipating this, he says: "Or somehow by the force of destiny. The meaning is that, as in the case of a *śūdra* performing a sacrifice, there would be no attainment of the final result. He states that because the rule of negative concomitance is established, positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is also established as a matter of course: "Therefore, it follows immediately after the aforementioned collection of entities. He introduces the *Bhāṣya* on this point with the words: "On this matter, the author of the *Bhāṣya* says..."

Thus, although this collection of means (*sādhana-kalāpa*) is a constituent part of knowledge (*vijñāna-aṅga*) by virtue of being something to be practiced, it nevertheless attains the status of a qualification for the seeker (*adhikāri-viśeṣaṇa*) through both scripture and reasoning. Consequently, once the inquiry into Brahman (*brahma-vicāra*) is established following the aforementioned perfection of the means, a certain "beloved of the gods" (*devānāṃ-priya*)—who is ignorant of the operation of the instruments of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), whose mind is smoldering with the defect of hatred toward the meaning of the scriptures, and who is a proponent of universal confusion (*sarva-saṃkara-vādī*)—chatters nonsense here: "For the author of the Sūtras, while establishing the necessity of inquiry, [it follows that] tranquility (*śama*) and the other [qualifications] are not... [the text continues].

It is not correct to say that [the author] cannot take an object not established by the intellect as a qualification of the qualified person (*adhikārin*) by means of the word "atha" (*now/thereupon*), whereas the inquiry into Dharma (*dharmavicāra*), being present in the intellect, is taken as a qualification of the qualified person; for the author of the Sūtras is certainly not like you, who lack the wisdom to reflect upon the preceding and following sentences.

For instance: when one undertakes to enunciate the scriptural injunction for inquiry (*vicāra-vidhi*), observing that such an injunction requires a connection with a qualified person (*adhikārin*), why would one not enunciate the specific qualification of that person—found within its own context and established by the means of knowledge consisting of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)—by means of the word *atha*? Furthermore, even if the collection of means (*sādhana-kalāpa*) were not denoted by the word *atha*, it must nonetheless be stated that they are necessary as a prerequisite for engaging with Brahman.

Because it is impossible for one impelled by passion (*rāga*) and the like to engage in that [inquiry], and because something must necessarily be required as a qualification for the qualified person (*adhikārin*), that very thing must be stated as the qualification. Furthermore, the inquiry into Dharma (*dharmajijñāsā*) does not attain the status of a qualification for the qualified person either through a perceptible means or through its scriptural nature, due to a lack of evidence. For this very reason, it is not even present in the mind, and thus it cannot be taken up by the word *atha*. Moreover, rather than taking up something already present in the mind but separated [by other thoughts], it is more appropriate to take up that which is both present in the mind and more proximate—namely, the fourfold means (*sādhanacatuṣṭaya*) contained within its own sentence. Therefore, this [objection] is trivial.

Therefore, the word *ataḥ* has the sense of a reason (*hetu*). Now, it was stated that the word *atha* itself, by way of expressing immediate succession (*ānantarya*), implies the preceding event as a reason; indeed, its status as a reason is merely implied (*ārthika*) and is not the direct denotation (*abhidheya*) of the word *atha*. This is true; for while the intention (*tātparya*) lies in the implied meaning, mere immediate succession would be purposeless. Since the principle holds that "the meaning intended by a word is the word-meaning in the employment of a sentence," the status of being a reason is established by the word *atha* alone; thus, the word *ataḥ* is not required.

If it is argued that, in the absence of the word *ataḥ*, the word *atha* would result in having one of the meanings such as "auspiciousness" (*māṅgalya*) and so forth, we say no; for this has already been refuted. If it is further argued that in the *Dharmamīmāṃsā*, even though the word *atha* was used, its status as a reason (*hetutva*) was also stated [by the word *ataḥ*], this proponent of universal confusion (*sarvasaṃkaravādī*) has nothing left but the "blind man catching the cow's tail" (*andhagolāṅgūlanyāya*) logic. For we are not required to follow the fault of redundancy (*punarukti*) simply because it exists elsewhere.

Therefore, it follows that the word *ataḥ* (therefore) is redundant—this is the prima facie view. However, it is shown that when there is a suspicion that the very causality already embraced by the word *atha* might be sublated by another reason, its refutation is performed by the word *ataḥ*, which restates the causality expressed by *atha*; this is demonstrated by the commentary beginning with "Because the Veda itself [establishes] the [efficacy] of the Agnihotra and so forth. In that regard, he shows that suspicion with the words beginning, "It might be argued: 'Because of the determination of their being produced... etc.

But when the inference based on "being produced" (kṛtakatva) and so forth is inconclusive, then since there would be no rule that even the fruit of action—which is itself produced—is impermanent, one who desires the eternal goal of man might still engage in such [action]. Therefore, the meaning is that the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal objects is not, by necessity, the cause for engagement with Brahman alone. Now, it may be argued: "Even if the fruit of action is not absolutely impermanent, there is no proof for its eternity. To this he says: "In the Veda also, it is said: 'Verily, the fruit of the Cāturmāsya sacrifice is indeed imperishable.'"

[Objection: "Even so, what follows regarding engagement with Brahman? To this he says: "Therefore, there is no necessary dispassion toward the enjoyment of sense-objects. The meaning is that, consequently, one does not engage with Brahman. Or, if one were to become dispassionate, one would engage only with objects other than those [of the Cāturmāsya sacrifice] from which one has become detached. Let there be no rule of engagement specifically with Brahman; even there, in the case of Brahman, there might be engagement by way of option (*vikalpa*). To this he says, "No, nor by relying upon an immutable and eternal reality."

[Objection: "But surely, even in the absence of identity with the entity that is the opposite [of the body], there might be attainment of Brahman characterized as conjunction (saṃyoga). [Reply: No, he says—"not its attainment. [Objection: "But the enjoyment of the bliss of Brahman exists. [Reply: No; because enjoyment consists in the perception of pleasure residing in one's own substrate, and it is not possible for the pleasure that is an attribute of Brahman to be perceived as having the individual soul (jīva) as its substrate. [Objection: "But enjoyment is merely the immediate intuition (aparokṣya) of pleasure, not the immediate intuition of pleasure residing in one's own substrate."

Because of the impossibility of qualifying [the two as identical], even if they were to exist separately, there could be no experience [of bliss] because, in the world, the happiness of one person is not perceived by another. Now, it might be argued that the Self itself is of the nature of the consciousness of bliss, and that abiding in that form is liberation; but this is not so, because it contradicts non-perception despite the conditions for perception being met. Furthermore, no one seeks liberation as abiding in a Self devoid of bliss by abandoning the bliss of gods and others.

Therefore, he concludes that one who is endowed with the fourfold means does not engage in [the pursuit of] Brahman, but rather in the fruit of ritual action, by the words beginning with "hence, from the fear of indigestion" (*ato 'jīrṇabhayāt*). To introduce the commentary which provides the statement of the reason for refuting the doubt raised therein, he asks—"How?"—referring to how the means of proof that serves as the reason for refuting the doubt is indicated by the word *ataḥ*, which expresses the causality of the fourfold means.

He says this: "Because the Veda itself [states] regarding the Agnihotra and so forth... The meaning is that it demonstrates the impermanence of all categories of human goals (puruṣārtha) other than Brahman. Now, one might object: "But surely the general scriptural statement, 'Just as here the world acquired by action,' must apply only to cases other than specific rites such as the Cāturmāsya. To this he replies: "Now, [the text says] 'of merit'... In that regard, the Cāturmāsya scripture declares the indestructibility of the *sukṛta* (the meritorious act), not of its fruit; for even when the *sukṛta* exists, the exhaustion of the fruit is logically possible through non-enjoyment.

In this regard, he states that it is contrary to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to abandon the literal meaning of the sentence and imagine that its subject matter is the non-exhaustion of the fruit: "That [sentence] does not proceed by the force of the thing itself. This means it does not proceed by the force of pervasion (*vyāpti*). It should be construed as a contradiction with scripture supported by inference. The scriptural passage, "Those who give gold attain immortality," being a statement of present fact, is contradicted by the non-perception of what is otherwise possible.

The conception that [the fruits of action] will be enjoyed is, as before, contradicted by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and it is contradicted by the scriptural texts concerning the creation and dissolution of the world of the gods, which are supported by inference. The scriptural text, "We have drunk the Soma," and the text, "He who meditates on the Self alone as his world—for him, work is not exhausted"—do not demonstrate the eternality of the fruit; for the assumption that this sentence has the fruit as its subject matter is, as before, contradicted by valid means of knowledge, since an assumption must be based on non-contradiction.

Furthermore, having begun with the statement, "If indeed one who does not know this performs even a great meritorious work, it is exhausted for him in the end," and then stating, "But he who worships the Self alone as his world—for him, work is not exhausted"—it follows that because the very act of worshipping the Self has the fruit of the cessation of ignorance through the gateway of immediate realization, the phrase "work is not exhausted" is employed here merely as a praise of the act of worship.

If it is argued that for one who does not possess such knowledge, the exhaustion of karma occurs merely through hearing [the scriptures], whereas for one who possesses such knowledge, even acts such as the *agnihotra*—when performed by him—are ordained to have liberation as their fruit and are thus rendered inexhaustible, we say no; for this would contradict scriptural prohibitions such as the indicative mark (*liṅga*) stating, "There is no other path," and "And his actions perish. Therefore, it is logically established that there must be detachment (*vairāgya*) from any human goal other than Brahman, due to its impermanence.

Now, it was argued that because the defect is equal, this [desire for liberation] cannot be the cause of activity even with respect to Brahman; to that he replies: "As for the further claim that there is an absence of the desire for liberation"—the inference that "identity with a contradictory category is impossible" contradicts such scriptural texts as "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman indeed. However, identity has been taught [in those passages] in the manner of an object and its reflection.

Nor is it correct to argue that [liberation] is not a human goal (apuruṣārtha) because of the absence of the experience of pleasure, for there is the experience of the bliss of Brahman (brahmānanda). [Objection: If there were identity [between the self and Brahman], the experience would have to be "I am happiness," and not "I am happy"; yet in the world, the experience "I am happy" is what constitutes a human goal. [Reply: This is not a fault, because the mere immediacy (aparokṣya) of happiness is itself the human goal. [Objection: Only happiness residing in one's own substrate is the human goal, not the immediacy of happiness. [Reply: No.

Since only those means of happiness that are actually perceived constitute the goal of man (*puruṣārtha*), because there is no difference in their being desired, it is understood that happiness too must be perceived in order to be a goal of man. In that regard, just as the dependence on external means and the impermanence [of happiness] are not perceived as such, the distinction between the happiness derived from objects and the Self—expressed as "I am happy"—is also not manifest as a primary goal of man; rather, it is incidental. Therefore, the bliss of Brahman (*brahmānanda*) is also a goal of man when it appears through direct intuition (*aparokṣāvabhāsa*). Now, the Naiyāyikas and others maintain that there is no eternal happiness; this is true.

There is no such thing as produced pleasure at all. [Objection: But surely its status as something produced is understood from the employment of its means. [Reply: No, because it is merely the cause for the manifestation of pleasure that is already established. Otherwise, there would be the cumbersome assumption that the capacity for the appearance of the production of a stream of pleasure depends upon means; or else, because it is not subordinate to any other goal, or because it is invariably present, or because it is the object of unconditional love, the Self in the form of pleasure appears through direct perception, without any distinction between the states of pleasure and pain.

Since the causal status of the entire collection of means (*sādhanakalāpa*) has been established by means of indicating the reason for the exclusion of the conch through the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*), there is thus a conclusion with the words "by the aforementioned means. Therein, the meaning of the sūtra’s statement was shown primarily from the perspective of desire (*icchā*). The necessity of undertaking the fourfold means was shown by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*); now, he demonstrates that very same point by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with the words beginning "since [it arises] from the persistence of duality," and so forth.

[Objection: But surely, like the collection of means [for sacrifice], the desire to know dharma (*dharmajijñāsā*) must also necessarily initiate [the inquiry]. [Reply: No; he says, "this being so, it follows by implication" (*evam sati arthāt*). The meaning is that since it is not established that the collection of dharma-necessities must necessarily be initiated solely on the basis of scripture (*āgama*) and presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), an investigation of dharma lacking those two means of knowledge cannot serve as the cause [for the commencement of the study of the Vedas].

The commentary states: "the desire to know Brahman" (*brahmaṇo jijñāsā*). Now, one might ask: why could this not be a dative compound (caturthī-samāsa), as in the expression "desire for dharma" (*dharmāya jijñāsā*)? To this, he replies: "For when there is a connection with the implied meaning of inquiry (*vicāra*... etc.). For if the desire were predominant, then because the object (*karman*) and the purpose (*prayojana*) of the desire are identical, and because of its predominance, there would be a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*) with respect to the object. However, when inquiry is predominant, there is a distinction between the object and the purpose; thus, by intending to express the purpose, there could also be a dative compound.

Now, one might ask: "What is that Brahman which exists as the object of desire by virtue of being its purpose? To this he says: "This is the occasion for the definition of the meaning of the word 'Brahman'."

In this context, by the passage beginning with "tatra yadanyaiḥ" and ending before "brahmaṇa iti karmaṇi ṣaṣṭhī," it is demonstrated that the word *brahman* does not have "genus" (*jāti*) and so forth as its meaning in this particular usage; for it is untenable to establish genus, the individual soul (*jīva*), the lotus-seated one (*kamalāsana*), or the collection of sounds (*śabdarāśi*) as either the agent or the object of the desire to know (*jijñāsā*), since they are designated by the word *brahman*.

In this context, beginning with the statement "‘Of Brahman’ is the genitive in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi ṣaṣṭhī*)", and extending up to the point where it says "furthermore, [this is] the very commencement of the treatise," the author has shown that the genitive in the sense of the object is intended; for it is better to explicitly adopt the investigation of the primary subject (*pradhāna-vicāra*) and then imply the investigations of the secondary subjects (*apradhāna-vicāra*) by implication, rather than explicitly adopting the investigations of the secondary subjects through the words and then implying the primary investigation by implication. Thus, the genitive in the sense of the object is demonstrated.

The term "remainder" (*śeṣa*) refers to the general relation (*saṃbandhasāmānya*), not to specific relations distinct from the five *kārakas*. In that regard, just as in the expression "Devadatta’s property" (*devadattasya svam*), the genitive case is capable of expressing a related meaning even when a specific relation is present, so too in cases such as "Devadatta goes" (*devadattasya gacchati*) or "Devadatta is gone to" (*devadattasya gamyate*), the expression of a related meaning is not possible within a specific *kāraka* relation; rather, it occurs within the general relation already expressed.

By implication, in some cases a specific relation between a *kāraka* and its object is understood through the sense of the matter; by this much, it is stated that "the genitive occurs in the remaining [cases]," but it is not stated that even from the sense (*artha*) there is no manifestation of a *kāraka* relation—such is the view of the opponent (*pūrvavādin*).

Furthermore, by the portion of the text beginning with "Moreover, the engagement of the treatise itself... and ending before "the desire to know is *jijñāsā*," it is shown that in the sentence which sets forth the injunction for inquiry—whose subject matter includes the qualification [of the seeker]—Brahman is indicated as the object (*karman*). And since the Sūtra has the same single purpose as that sentence, it is demonstrated that in the Sūtra as well, Brahman must be expressed as the object in this very same way through the word.

The commentary begins with "the desire to know" (*jñātum icchā*), and so forth. In this regard, since desire has as its object that which has already been cognized, the desire for knowledge of Brahman is untenable if Brahman is already cognized, and it is even more so if it is not cognized at all. To the question, "How then can there be a desire for the knowledge of Brahman?", he replies: "Because desire has the fruit as its object. What, then, is this "cognition" (*avagati*) that is desired? He says: "It is direct experience" (*sākṣād-anubhava*). An objection is raised: "Cognition arises at the very first moment"; to this he replies: "But [initial] knowledge is indirect" (*parokṣa*).

The meaning is that there arises direct knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*) regarding that which was previously understood through verbal testimony as being beyond the senses. When, however, direct knowledge arises from verbal testimony, he says: "even when [the object] is present. This means by the experience of a direct certainty (*aparokṣaniścaya*) gained through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Now, what is here called "knowledge" (*jñāna*)? The Sugatas (Buddhists), Prabhākaras (Mīmāṃsakas), Vaiśeṣikas, and Naiyāyikas maintain that it is simply consciousness (*saṃvedana*), which is the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-phala*), and that there is no such thing as knowledge—which they call the activity of the knower—apart from this consciousness and the causal complex consisting of the fourfold contact (*sannikarṣa*) and so forth. For the followers of the Vārttikakāra (Kumārila Bhaṭṭa), however, knowledge is the activity of the knower that generates consciousness. And for the Jainas (*kṣapaṇaka*) and the Materialists (*lokāyatika*), knowledge is simply the sentience of the self (*ātma-caitanya*).

For the Sāṅkhyas and Vedāntins, knowledge (*jñāna*) is the modification of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*) by way of the instrumental derivation (*karaṇa-vyutpatti*), while it is consciousness (*saṃvedana*) by way of the abstract derivation (*bhāva-vyutpatti*). In that regard, the arising of the fruit of consciousness does not occur within a permanent self (*ātman*).

[The result] is established even without the operation of an agent. Now, one might object: "From the very same cause that the operation of the agent arises, the experience itself should arise, since it is impossible for the Self to have an operation consisting of physical movement. To this, the following must be said: Is it perceived in the world that the production of a result follows from the operation of an agent, or not? If it is not, then because there would be no apprehension of the universal concomitance (*vyāpti*) and because it is imperceptible, the operation of an agent could not be understood in all cases. Yet, in the world, the operation of an agent is indeed understood.

Now, if it is argued that in the world the operation of an agent is established by perception as the cause of the effect, then it must likewise be inferred in the case of the Self, because of the necessity of universal concomitance (*vyāpti*). To this, the Vaiśeṣikas and others object: "There is no such thing as an operation called 'transformation' (*pariṇāma*), since we accept the theory of new production (*ārambha*). If so, let the effect be produced by the operation of effort, for there is a necessary concomitance between an effect and the operation of an agent. [The opponent replies: "But knowledge arises from the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*) which is the conjunction with the mind, even without an operation. [The proponent answers: No.

Because, even in the absence of a conjunction with instruments, one observes the activity of an agent when a result arises. Here, the proponent of universal confusion (sarvasaṅkaravādī) laments: "Since the dependence of the result upon the agent's activity is observed in cases such as cooking, let it be understood as such there; but here, since that is not observed, there is no activity of an agent. He, however, requires to be reminded that he is ignorant of the methodology of inference. Even for the Sugatas, the dependence of cognitions upon the activity of an agent is inferred precisely from the proof of a permanent self.

Even for the Jainas (Kṣapaṇakas), if the consciousness of the self in its own nature (*svarūpa-caitanya*), being devoid of adjuncts (*nirupādhika*), were to manifest objects, there would be the manifestation of all objects at all times. And for the Materialist (Lokāyata), since consciousness is produced (*janya-saṃvedana*), its activity must be inferred. Now, it may be argued that for the Self, which is all-pervading and partless, neither vibration (*parispanda*) nor transformation (*pariṇāma*) is possible; this is true, [but] because the Self—conjoined with the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) which is fully established through superimposition (*adhyāsa*)—undergoes transformation into the form of knowledge. However, it does not undergo transformation into the form of consciousness itself.

Because that [consciousness] is eternally established, a particular modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) serves as the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) for consciousness by delimiting its object. By the etymological derivation from the root *jñā* (to know), it is called "knowledge" (*jñāna*); however, by the etymological derivation from the abstract noun suffix (*bhāva*), it is simply "awareness" (*saṃvedana*), which is the illumination of the object, termed "cognition" (*jñapti*) or "knowledge" (*jñāna*). In this context, knowledge is immediate when it is the delimiter of immediate awareness and has an object as its adjunct. Thus, by explaining the meaning of the individual components (*avayava-artha*), it is stated that the desire for immediate comprehension constitutes the meaning of the sentence (*vākya-artha*).

The subsequent commentary (*bhāṣya*) establishes the meaning of the sentence as the necessity of performing the inquiry (*vicāra*), which is implied by way of the instruction regarding the fruit of knowledge that is desired. To demonstrate its intended purport (*tātparya*), it dispels another doubt: "How so? The meaning of this sūtra should not be described [in this manner]. For instance, if this sūtra were included within the treatise (*śāstra*), there would be the necessity of commencing the inquiry. By what, then, is the commencement of the sūtra concerning the inquiry itself effected? If it were by itself, there would be the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśrayatā*)."

If it were by means of another sūtra, there would be the consequence of infinite regress; if, on the other hand, it were not included [within the treatise], then the first sūtra would not be part of the treatise, leading to the undesirable conclusion that it should not be commenced. To this he says: "This sūtra is included within the treatise. It is precisely the rule for investigation, as initially understood, that initiates the first sūtra for the sake of the investigation required by itself. And once that rule has been investigated, it subsequently initiates the sūtras that investigate the objects of that rule; thus, even though they belong to a single treatise, there is no infinite regress.

Since the Vedānta passages, when investigated by way of their internal consistency (*samanvaya*) with respect to their own literal meaning—such as the injunction "it is to be heard" (*śrotavya*) and so forth—also have as their cause the internal consistency with Brahman, the relationship [of the treatise] consists in that very consistency. Regarding this, he states what is established by the scripture: "And by this... and so on.

The term "prayojyaḥ" (to be employed) refers to the qualified person (*adhikārī*). "Of one" [means] "of the collection of means. Its other causes are the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*), such as sacrifice and the like, and the seen (*dṛṣṭa*), such as the contemplation of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth. "Obtained by implication" means "by the force of the statement of immediate succession."

Therefore, although the word [in the sūtra] explicitly expresses causality, its actual status as a cause is stated by implication (arthāt), because its primary purport (tātparya) lies in the removal of other doubts. Thus, since there is no purpose in restating [the cause], the word "to be performed" (kartavya) is supplied, and the desire to know (jijñāsā) is declared by the scripture (śruti) as something that ought to be performed. Now, one might object: "Since knowledge is understood to be something to be accomplished (sādhya) due to its connection with desire, let that alone be what is to be performed. To this he says: "In that case, one simply knows" (tatra jānātyeva). The fact that an object of desire is to be accomplished is self-evident and does not depend on the word [of the scripture].
The meaning is: "because it is an experience of bliss. To the question "What, then, is enjoined?", he says: "But one does not know the means."

The meaning is this: it is precisely the means for attaining what is desired, when not yet understood, that is communicated by words expressing an injunction (*vidhi*). Even though [the means] is unseen (*adṛṣṭa*), the fact that hearing and so forth serve as an unseen means toward immediate experience (*aparokṣānubhava*) has been demonstrated by the injunction for hearing and the rest. Now, one might object: "Since the meaning of the sentence is understood by oneself simply from the explanation of the word-meanings, what is the use of stating the sentence-meaning? This is true.

He states that the manifestation of the relationship and so forth occurs through the explanation of the meaning of the sentence: "The relationship, subject matter, and purpose of the treatise. The meaning of the sentence is that one who desires liberation must perform inquiry for the sake of the realization of Brahman. He explains how the understanding of the relationship and so forth arises from the meaning here by saying, "This is what is meant," and so on.

Now, one might object: "Since inquiry is the means for attaining the desired liberation by way of the knowledge of Brahman, even if the connection with the fruit is established, how are the subject matter and the other [factors] established? To this, he says: "By implication, of the scripture."

Thus ends the third section, titled "The Description of the Meaning of the First Sūtra," in the *Pañcapādikā-vivaraṇa* composed by the venerable Svaprakāśānubhava, the disciple of the worshipful Ananyānubhava, a holy renunciant of the supreme order (*paramahaṃsa-parivrājaka*).

Now, regarding the fourth section, he states the purport of the commentary beginning with "That Brahman, moreover, is well-known," namely that [the commentary] implies the purpose, the subject matter, and the relationship.

He raises an objection: "How so?"—that is, since the purpose and other factors are already understood through the power of the injunction itself, how can there be an implication? He provides the answer with the words beginning "By the word 'well-known'. He asks: "Why?"—that is, since it is possible to explain by restating what has already been apprehended through a word, why would it not be the subject matter?

He offers a rebuttal, stating that this is because there would be no object not yet apprehended—namely, by the phrase "as something to be established. He further states that it cannot have a purpose either, because the purpose is already accomplished simply by the prior apprehension [of the object] through the medium of understanding the subject matter; thus he says, "and therefore, because it is not apprehended by this [treatise]. With the word "now," he raises an objection regarding the relationship and the purpose in the case where [the object] is not already established. He challenges this with the question, "How so? implying the objection: "Surely, it is only an unapprehended object that is established by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), and the purpose lies precisely therein."

He refutes this with the words: "That which is never [known by other means]. An object that has been absolutely unapprehended is what is presented by means of perception and other instruments of knowledge when they do not depend upon investigation (*vicāra*). Where an object is presented by a means of knowledge depending upon investigation, there an investigation is impossible because it cannot be directed toward something already apprehended; and since no further deliberation (*vimarśa*) is observed regarding what is already apprehended, the meaning is that there is no comprehension of the unknown through a means of knowledge that depends on investigation. Now, one might ask: "In the case of an unestablished subject (*pakṣa*), how is the relation [of the reason] implied, and not in the case of an established subject? To this he says: "But as for that which is already established... and so forth.

Based on the statement in the *Akṣapāda-sūtra*: "Tarka (reasoning) is the deliberation (*ūha*) for the sake of knowing the truth regarding a reality not yet known, by means of the application of logical grounds," tarka is that which assists the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) in order to determine the specific nature of something already known in a general way, or even something perceived in its mere appearance through a specific form. Thus, he states the purport of the *Bhāṣya*, which shows that Brahman is fit for inquiry because it is an object of an indeterminate manifestation of its specific nature, thereby resolving all three [objections]: "There exists, first of all... [asti tāvad].

[The objection is raised: "By the words 'Brahman' and so forth, it is established that Brahman alone is the subject matter and that which is to be propounded through the investigation in the *Samanvaya* (First) Chapter; whereas the specific fruit [of the inquiry] is established by the *Phala* (Fourth) Chapter. Thus, these three [subject matter, purpose, and connection] need not all be propounded here. To this, he replies: "For the sake of engaging the listener. The objection beginning with "Now, for a discerning person... and its refutation are clear.

One might object: "Is it not the case that only a specific purpose (*prayojana*) is a factor for engaging in action, and not the subject matter (*viṣaya*) or the connection (*sambandha*)? To this he replies: "Even so, [it is] only the specific purpose. One might further object: "But surely, even after knowing the result, where would one act without understanding the means (*sādhana*), which is the object of the activity and that which is capable of being accomplished? To this he says: "And [the means] has not failed to become the subject matter."

[Objection: Is it not the case that the means of achieving a result (*phala-sādhana*) is the object of activity (*pravṛtti-viṣaya*), and not the result itself? To this, he says: "It is precisely the object of the act of cutting. An entity that is inherent in the purpose becomes the object by way of being the factor of the object (*karma-kāraka*). Therefore, the meaning is that when the purpose is understood, the object is also included within it. [Objection: But the operation of the potter’s staff and so forth has the clay as its object, while the jar is the purpose; thus, there is a distinction between the object and the purpose. To this, he says: "Even of the staff and so forth..."

It is true that the subject matter (*viṣaya*), being inherent to the purpose, is included within the cognition of the subject and the purpose; however, he offers this rebuttal with the words "It is indeed so, nevertheless... and so forth: although this is the case, when the status of the subject matter is demonstrated—by virtue of its being the object of human activity characterized as an instrument (*karaṇa*) toward the purpose, and by its being unique and capable of being communicated—then there necessarily arises an engagement in the means for accomplishing that purpose, and not otherwise.

In that regard, in order to show that for the sake of regulating the engagement [in inquiry], since inquiry and the knowledge produced by it are experienced as being unique [to this context], the purpose (*prayojana*)—namely Brahman—must also be stated separately both in its own nature (*svarūpa*) and as the object (*viṣaya*), he provides an example for the opposing view: "Just as in the case of medical knowledge," and so forth. To the objection that because the object possesses an inherent relationship, the relationship is already implied within it and thus need not be stated separately, he replies with the words: "The relationship must also be stated," and so on.

In this regard, because the relationship is distinct from the exclusion of other means of proof (*sādhanāntara-nivṛtti*) due to its not being established by anything else, it must also be stated separately. To demonstrate this, he provides an example for the contrary case (*vipakṣa*) with the words, "Just as the thorough knowledge of correct words," and so forth. The meaning is this: prior to the commencement of grammar, even though the knowledge of correct words cannot be accomplished by other activities, it is nonetheless not the object of the activity of medical treatment (*cikitsā-vyāpāra*).

Because there is no connection [between them], but rather, through its connection with grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), it becomes its subject matter. Therefore, one who seeks that [grammar] does not [seek it] anywhere else. The meaning is: "the activity of medical treatment" (*cikitsā-vyāpāra*). Now, even if this were so, since the meaning of one would be established by the mention of another, there would be no need for a separate mention; to this he says: "By that, [it is shown] that they consist of human goals," and so forth. "They are distinct" means they must be stated separately. Nor is the establishment of one achieved by the other.

"Because even when one [of these] exists, the absence of the others has been demonstrated. Now, one might ask: "Even if distinct designations are required for a difference in essential nature (*svarūpa-bheda*), how is it that the triad does not collectively serve as a cause for activity? To this, he demonstrates that they are causes for activity by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) with the words: "And all three of those are factors for activity; [activity does not occur] when there is no human purpose," and so forth.

Now, it was argued that even the threefold statement [of the definition] is untenable for both the well-known and the unknown positions; to resolve this, he states the purport of the subsequent commentary up to the end of the section, beginning with: "In that regard, because of disagreement, there is no absolute certainty as to what is well-known," and so forth. In this context, the justification for instituting an inquiry based on mere general renown is established because such a reference is possible, and because the absence of absolute certainty ensures that the knowledge produced by the inquiry is unique and not shared by others.

The word *vipratipatti* (disagreement) is intended to indicate by implication the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of the word *brahman* as well. Now, one might object: "Even so, the subject matter (*viṣaya*) and the relationship (*saṃbandha*) of this treatise of inquiry have not yet been established. To this he replies: "But [is it not the case that] Brahman is the subject of the Vedāntas? One might further object: "But has not that very same subject already been indicated for the treatise itself in the phrase 'the desire to know Brahman' (*brahmajijñāsā*)?"

He says "no," [concluding] with the words: "And the scripture is for them. The sentences of the Sūtras have the *nyāyas* (logical principles) as their subject matter, and the *nyāyas* have the possibility (*sambhāvanā*) of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the objects of cognition (*prameya*), etc., as their subject matter. [Objection: In that case, then, the purpose (*prayojana*) is simply the comprehension of this possibility. [Reply: He says "no," with the words: "But the purpose... The meaning of "by way of a channel" (*praṇāḍyā*) is "even through a succession" (*paramparayā*). Since happiness alone is attained through dharma and wealth (*artha*), one is intent upon those two.

But has it not been determined in the first Tantra that the instrument (karaṇa) and the procedure (itikartavyatā) have one and the same purpose? For instance, there are three rites on the full moon day: "The cake on eight potsherds for Agni," "He performs the Upāṃśuyāja sacrifice in between," and "The cake on eleven potsherds for Agni-Soma"; likewise, there are three on the new moon day: "The cake on eight potsherds for Agni," "Curd for Indra," and "Milk for Indra"—thus there are six sacrifices, beginning with the Āgneya.

Regarding those [auxiliaries] which function as instruments, two types of limbs have been defined: those that are *arthakarma* (primary acts) and those that are *saṃskārakarma* (purificatory acts). The limbs such as the *prayāja* offerings, which assist from a distance (*ārādupakāraka*) by contributing to the result, are *arthakarma*. However, [acts] such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), which assist the very nature of the sacrifice through the medium of the substance, are *saṃskārakarma* because they provide immediate assistance (*sannipatyopakāraka*). In this regard, the purpose of both types of limbs is solely the accomplishment of heaven by means of the primary *apūrva*.

Thus, since the investigation into the power and intention (*tātparya*) of words assists the nature of verbal testimony (*śabda-pramāṇa*)—much like the preparatory rites (*saṃskāra-karman*)—and since the investigation into the nature of the object, Brahman, assists the fruit which is the realization of Brahman, it is logical that both types of inquiry have as their object the Brahman being realized. To this, the opponent objects from the standpoint of a false doctrine (*apasiddhāntin*), beginning with the words: "But [regarding] the *Āgneya* and other [sacrifices]," etc. [He asks: "But surely the Vedāntas alone are capable of bringing about the realization of Brahman; how then can there be an 'it-thus-to-be-done' (*itikartavyatā*) therein, given that the fruit is realization?"

Regarding the point that [inquiry] has Brahman as its object, he says there: "Therefore, although it is the Vedāntas alone... Now, one might ask: how can inquiry, which has those [Vedāntas] as its object by being the cause of the cognition of their possibility, have Brahman as its object by generating the comprehension of Brahman? For an operation whose object is one thing cannot have another thing as its object. To this, he replies: "For it is not the case for the cutter... etc.

For the object-agent (*karmakāraka*) is of two kinds: some possess an excellence produced by the agent's operation due to being immediate [to it], such as an axe, which—distinguished by the excellences of conjunction with and disjunction from the upper and lower regions through the operations of raising and lowering—becomes the object-agent immediately following the agent's operation; while others become the object through the mediation of the operation of the instrument (*karaṇa*), because they are the intended result, such as "the tree split in two."

In this context, although the activity of the agent is separated by the activity of the instrument, it is said to have the result of "dividing the tree" (*vṛkṣādvaidhībhāva*); for from the expression "he cuts the tree," the agent's activity is understood to have that [tree] as its object. That very tree becomes the direct object of the axe's activity, because there is no intervention. Now, one might ask: how can the instrument, the axe, be the agent? It is replied: indeed, all things are agents with respect to their own respective activities. Furthermore, the fruit of the activities of all the factors of action (*kāraka*) is to be accomplished as the object (*karman*).

In this context, the distinction between agent (*kartṛ*), instrument (*karaṇa*), and object (*karman*) arises in relation to internal subdivisions. Among these, the agent is that whose operation is independent, either by virtue of being enjoined to the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) or by way of being the primary operation (*viśeṣya-vyāpāra*) denoted by the verbal root. The instrument is that which assists toward the result through direct contact (*sannipatyopakāraka*). The object is the factor in which the result inheres (*phala-samavāyin*). Expressions such as "the pieces of wood cook" (*kāṣṭhāni pacanti*) are based on the status of being an agent with respect to their own operation, and not based on internal subdivisions.

Therefore, the tree is the object (*karman*) of the agent's activity because it is mediated by the activity of the instrument (*karaṇa*). Likewise, even for the activity of inquiry (*vicāra*), since its intended goal is the realization of Brahman through the medium of the comprehension of the possibility of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the object of knowledge (*prameya*), and since the cause of comprehension has as its domain that which is to be comprehended, its being the object of Brahman is not contradictory. Now, if it were argued that only an immediate object is an object and not one that is merely intended, to that he says: "Otherwise, the agent's activity would be directed elsewhere."

In these matters of procedure (*itikartavyatā*), there are two types of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): scripture (*āgama*) and positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). The status of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth as subsidiary parts is known from scripture; the status of clay, the potter, and the agent’s activity as subsidiary parts of the sprout, the jar, and the splitting [of wood] is known through positive and negative concomitance. However, in this case, when the meaning is understood from a word aided by the perception of the word, the knowledge of its relation, and mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), the status of inquiry (*vicāra*) as a subsidiary part is not established by either of the aforementioned means of valid cognition.

The proponent (pūrvavādī) refutes the opponent who maintains that comprehension arises from the word alone without depending on inquiry, stating: "The analogy is flawed. [The opponent objects: "But surely, although the eyes and other sense organs are causes of correct knowledge, they produce doubt and error due to the presence of defects, and furthermore, they require the removal of those defects for the production of correct knowledge; [is this not the case here as well?]"

Thus, sound produces cognition such as doubt through the defects of ignorance regarding its power (*śakti*) and intended meaning (*tātparya*), or through the opposite of that knowledge; in this regard, he raises an objection—namely, that "by means of the removal of doubt and error"—that the investigation of power and intended meaning serves as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) for the cessation of error and the like by way of eliminating those defects.

In this regard, does the word itself produce a distorted cognition due to the influence of defects, and does critical inquiry (vicāra), by removing that [distortion], attain the status of being the cause of valid knowledge (*pramiti*)? Or rather, is the word the cause of correct knowledge alone, while distorted knowledge arises from another cause, and critical inquiry merely removes the obstacle; and once the obstacle has ceased, the determination of the object occurs from the word alone? Regarding this, he states that it is not the case that critical inquiry is the cause of determining the object by means of removing error and so forth: "This is not sound."

Regarding the phrase "where there is more than one": this is the intended meaning—there is no defect inherent in the word itself, because defects reside in the person and the sense organs. Therefore, the word is not the cause of erroneous cognitions such as misconception; rather, since it is observed that in other usages of words the expressive power (*śakti*) and intention (*tātparya*) are inferred in various ways, here too, having understood them accordingly, erroneous cognitions arise through the defect of the person by means of a general observation and a cognition contrary to the actual object. From the word, however, only the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) arises.

Consequently, when many mutually contradictory cognitions have arisen from verbal testimony and from human defects, the ascertainment of the word’s power and intended meaning (tātparya) merely removes other opposing cognitions by eliminating those human defects; once the obstruction has ceased, the knowledge of reality arises from the word itself, or, if it has already arisen, it remains steadfast. Therefore, inquiry is not a constituent part of the instrument [of knowledge] regarding the subject of Brahman.

Thus, the opponent's position having been refuted, the proponent establishes his own conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words: "To this it is replied: although the knowledge of the sentence-meaning," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "based on what is observed in general" (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭanibandhanena*): the meaning is that because various capacities and intentions are observed differently in other applications, one might here too assume such a state; and because even in the world, a thing of such a kind is seen to be otherwise, one might here too assume it to be otherwise.

This is the intention: since the determination of the object occurs only when the obstacles [to knowledge] have ceased, inquiry—though its primary function is the removal of obstacles—is said to have Brahman as its object figuratively, because it is a cause for the determination of Brahman. Here, this must be considered: is the intended meaning (*tātparya*) the cause of the valid cognition of the object, or is it the cause of the removal of obstacles? Some say it is the cause of the valid cognition itself. In that regard, is the understood intended meaning the cause of valid cognition, or the ununderstood? It cannot be the ununderstood, for that is not the cause of valid cognition.

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that no deliberation would be required to comprehend the intended meaning (*tātparya*), and there would also be the consequence that cognition would not arise regarding anything other than the object of that intention. For instance, someone wishing to take another’s place might say to him while raising him up, “You have been summoned by your father. The first person, understanding the father’s summons, stands up; the other, however, remains seated. Once he has stood up, the latter realizes, “This was said with the desire to take his place.”

If it is argued that "there can be no cognition of a relation when the father’s call lacks an intended meaning," we say no; for we observe activity such as rising, and since activity cannot occur without being preceded by a cognition of a relation, it would be impossible to postulate a linguistic power or intention regarding the relation based on such activity. Now, one might object that "a word does not produce false knowledge. This is not a fault; for even when the father is indeed calling and there is a corresponding cognition, what has been demonstrated here is merely that the speaker’s intention lies elsewhere.

Therefore, intention (*tātparya*) is not a cause of valid cognition by virtue of being unknown. If it is known, then where is that intention understood? For the intention of a word must have a locus, since intention is dependent upon an object. It cannot reside in the individual word-meanings (*padārtha*), because that would be of no use for the cognition of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*). Nor can the relation (*saṃsarga*)—which is itself not yet cognized—be understood as a qualifier of the intention.

It might be argued as follows: when word-meanings have been understood from the words, their mutual relation (*saṃsarga*)—which is prompted by the fitness for mutual connection—is apprehended through *utprekṣā* (imaginative intuition), and it is this [relation] that constitutes the apprehension of the speaker’s intention (*tātparya*). However, this apprehension of the relation cannot be any one among recollection, doubt, or error. Since there is no other possibility, and because it is produced by the word, the cognition of the relation must indeed be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, the speaker’s intention does not reside in a general category, as is the case with linguistic capacity (*śakti*), because the specific intention varies with every sentence.

Furthermore, it can be inferred that the comprehension of the relation [between word-meanings], just like the comprehension of the word-meanings themselves, is based solely on the word's expressive power (*śakti*), and not on the speaker's intention (*tātparya*). Since the function of words in indicating their respective meanings is already accounted for by their utility as a means to determine the speaker's intention (*anyathāsiddhatva*), the cognition of the relation—which would otherwise depend solely on the comprehension of the intention—would consequently fail to be grounded in the words themselves.

Therefore, it is established that because words themselves possess the capacity to convey a relation—either through their primary meaning (*mukhya*) or through indication (*lakṣaṇā*)—once that relation, which is not contradicted by other means of knowledge, has been understood, the comprehension of the *tātparya* (the intended purport) serves to eliminate cognitions such as doubt or error caused by other defects. To demonstrate this justification, he concludes the point already stated in the passage beginning with "And this triad must necessarily... and ending with "...enough of this excessive detail. The phrase "There exists indeed... is clear in its meaning.

Now, an objection is raised: "Is it not the case that Brahman cannot be apprehended even in a general way in the world, because it is not within the scope of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? Nor can it be [known] through the power of scripture (*āgama*), because the meaning of the word 'Brahman' employed therein is not yet determined, and a meaning cannot be established from a mere word alone, since it is well-known to have other referents such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth. Therefore, it is not possible to enjoin an inquiry by referring to something already established. Thus he asks: "How?"

In this regard, since it is possible to understand some entity distinct from genus and so forth precisely through the power of the employment of the word "Brahman" in both the Śruti and the Sūtra, he says: "The word 'Brahman' first," and so on. Now, what is the proof for the existence of another meaning? It is the presumption based on the application [of the term]; thus he says: "Therefore, it must surely be something else. But surely, the inapplicability of the Vedic usage does not lead to the understanding of an unprecedented object.

Because the Vedic usage is dependent upon worldly usage, he says in that regard: "Therefore, [the word 'dharma' refers to] heaven, the apūrva, and the deity. By the term "apūrva," the application of the word *dharma* in the Veda—such as in the passage, "Those were the first dharmas"—is intended. Now, one might object: a word employed in a sentence does not convey a meaning not already apprehended through other means of knowledge, because the word-meaning is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) within the context of the sentence-part. To this he replies: "This is not sound."

The meaning is that [the word-meaning] is not like perception, because there is no apprehension of a [perceptual] relation, nor is it like inference and so forth. To the objection that "it has been shown to be like heaven and so on," he says "no"—"even the object such as heaven. The meaning is that the referent of words such as "heaven" is obtained through the force of the multiple sentence-meanings present [in the Vedic injunctions].

In this regard, he offers a rebuttal—stating that "in a sentence where one word..."—on the grounds that the use of a word whose meaning is not well-known alongside other words whose meanings are well-known would be impossible if one intended to convey the meaning of the sentence as a whole; rather, it conveys the meaning of the preceding word as the word's own denotation, without depending on the grasping of a relationship with the person to be instructed. The underlying sense is that the determination of the meaning of Vedic and Sūtra sentences, which are free from defects such as deception or error, must necessarily be attained.

[Objection: But surely, because there is no restrictive rule, the impossibility of simultaneous application would cause [the word] to bring to mind just any meaning whatsoever. To this, he says: "In that regard, by means of etymological derivation (nigama) and etymology (nirukta). "Etymological derivation" (nigama) refers to the occurrence of a word in another sense by following one part of it, while abandoning its well-known meaning and its constituent parts—for example, the occurrence of words such as *deha* ("body") and *ātman* ("self") in the sense of "an object that moves" (*gamanavat*) or "that which takes up" (*ādāna*), by following the single part "going" (*gamana*) or "taking" (*ādāna*), even though they primarily denote a "massed entity" (*upacita-vastu*). When a word occurs in another sense by adopting both its well-known meaning and its constituent parts...

Because it would entail the application of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) or secondary function (*guṇavṛtti*). Etymology (*nirukta*) is the application of a word to a meaning other than its conventional one by following the meaning of all its constituent parts, as in the case of the word *soma*, which applies to Maheśvara accompanied by Pārvatī. Grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) is the determination of meaning through the power of the application of suffixes, as in the case of *vādī*, where, by the power of applying the suffix *ṇini* in the sense of habitual tendency (*tācchīlya*), one understands him to be "one whose habit is speaking."

One might object: "Is it not the case that what is unestablished is accepted by the force of what is established, and that what is established is not abandoned because of what is unestablished? What, then, is the distinction here? To this he says: "For establishedness does not cease. Unestablishedness is natural antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*). The meaning is that the very impossibility of employing [the term] for the purpose of determining the sentence-meaning together with established objects is the adventitious cause for the cessation of that antecedent non-existence.

One might object: "Since the common meanings of the individual word-parts can be dispersed in every possible direction, it would be impossible to restrict them to the intended meaning; thus, there could be no fixed determination of the sentence-meaning. To this, he raises the objection: "But [it is determined] by means of etymological derivation (*nigama*) and so forth. Here, with a hidden intention, he provides the reply: "In that case, then, [there is no need for] etymological derivation and so forth. The sense is that if the restriction of the sentence-meaning occurs everywhere through the power of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) alone, then any other mode of operation (*vṛtti*) well-known in the world would be rendered useless.

The proponent states that the *nigama* and other [repetitions] possess purposefulness: "They possess purposefulness. "In a sense other than their own primary meaning" means with the intention of expressing a different meaning. "Due to application" means by taking the syntactic connection within the sentence-meaning as the occasion.

The meaning is as follows: by taking the determination of the sentence-meaning as its motive, the very impossibility of employing [a word] along with other words—while it is grasping its meaning through the force of the *nigama* and other criteria—grasps the word-meaning only as far as the purpose extends, by virtue of its fitness for connection with the meanings of the proximate words; thus, the restriction of the sentence-meaning is established. The proponent [of the Siddhānta], revealing the hidden intention, says: "In that case, it is for the sake of the restriction to a single meaning."

The meaning is this: the impossibility of a primary application (of a word) is not distinguished [in its force] from that which is established as the cause for the adoption of a specific word-meaning when it is supported by a concluding summary (nigama) and supported by the expectancy of word-meanings that connect with the sentence-meaning culminating in the result. Now, one might ask: "Even so, how does the word *brahman*—by virtue of the concluding summary—function to denote that reality which is distinct from genus and so forth, which is the unsurpassed human goal, and which is fit for the seeker of liberation’s desire to know? To this he says: "In this case, while the word *brahman* is being etymologically derived..."

[Objection: "But even so, let some entity whatsoever that is relative and possesses the nature of being a part be accepted. [Reply: No; he says this: "And because there is no conformity with the formal argument (prayoga). The reason for this is: "Because it would not be connected with the meaning of the sentence."

In this context, "smallness" (*alpatva*) refers to the limitation of an object by space, time, or other objects; its exclusion is "limitless greatness" (*niratiśaya-mahattva*). He states that when there is no restrictive factor such as a qualifying prefix (*upapada*), and when the object of inquiry can be connected to the meaning of the sentence as a human goal (*puruṣārtha*), even that [greatness] is understood through the word *brahma*—this is expressed by the passage beginning with "therefore, of that which has for its cause limitation by time... and ending before the words "and the state of being awakened" (*buddhatva*).

The meaning is that by the word "eternal" (*nitya*) in the commentary, all three kinds of greatness are shown. Now, one might object: "But qualities such as Buddhahood are not conducive to the state of Brahman; so how can they be understood from the word 'Brahman'? Thus he asks: "How? This is not a fault, because we observe that even when something is not superior in its qualities, those of small intellect regard it as such. For instance, people consider an object that is devoid of qualities and full of defects to be insignificant, as if it were non-existent; whereas they describe an object that abounds in qualities and is free from defects as "great."

Therefore, in order to demonstrate greatness by dispelling the notion of smallness regarding its qualities, [the author] states—beginning with "The reality whose nature is non-awakening"—that Buddhahood is attained because that which is devoid of the quality of awakening is small due to its inferiority in terms of qualities. Likewise, since even for a sentient being, the state of being in saṃsāra is characterized by an abundance of defects and thus an inferiority in terms of qualities, the attainment of unsurpassed greatness and so forth follows; consequently, the excellence of liberation as being free from all defects is also understood. Thus he says: "And 'liberated' means not dependent on ignorance, desire, and karma."

Even for a conscious liberated being, if there were an absence of power to govern all effects and so forth, and consequently an absence of power to govern the knowledge regarding the remaining objects of knowledge and effects, there would be a deficiency and thus a state of limitation; to exclude that possibility, he says: "It is omniscient and endowed with all powers," and so on.

Now, one might object: "Even when the word *brahman* is employed, such a meaning as this is not perceived in the case of [other words] like *jāti*, *jīva*, *kamalāsana*, or *śabdarāśi*; how then can such a meaning be understood even through common usage (*anugama*)? To this he says: "For the employment [of a word occurs] with respect to an established entity.
