When a meaning is grasped through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the understanding of that meaning arises solely from the capacity of the word's employment; whether it be small or great, the meaning of the word must be understood exactly as it is apprehended by that other means of valid cognition.

But when the meaning is understood from the power of the word's own components alone, without depending on the power of its application (*prayoga*), then—since there is an absence of other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), supplementary words (*upapada*), or context (*prakaraṇa*) which serve as causes for restriction—the primary meaning itself must be accepted according to its inherent capacity; this is the intended sense. He introduces the *Bhāṣya* regarding this stated point with the words: "He says this."

Now, an objection may be raised: "Is the meaning of a word from the Sūtra being followed, or that of a word from Śruti? It cannot be the former, because a human composition depends upon other means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and such [other means] are absent here. Nor can it be the latter, because in Śāstraic passages such as 'Truth, Knowledge' and 'From which indeed these [beings arise],' the meaning is already determined and thus requires no further following. This is not a fault.

Because the use of the word "Brahman" in the sūtra—which is rooted precisely in that [first sūtra]—has as its object a domain understood through the authority of scripture (*śruti*), it adopts its meaning by way of following the sense of the term itself, without depending on the nature of Brahman as accessible through the scriptural authority to be established in subsequent sūtras; furthermore, it would be untenable to adopt the meaning while treating as already established what is yet to be proven by the subsequent sūtras.

Alternatively, this etymological derivation (*anugama*) of the word *brahman* according to the Vedic (*śrauta*) sense is being described; for it must be stated that the word *brahman*, when employed as part of the meaning of a sentence, requires such an etymological derivation because its meaning cannot be established from any other source independently of the authority of the sentence itself. [Objection: But in that case, since the etymological derivation of a word serves merely as a cause for a conceptual possibility regarding the specific meaning already described, how can a word-meaning not yet apprehended by any other means of knowledge be connected with the sentence-meaning therein?

He raises an objection regarding its being the cause of definitive determination (*nirṇaya-hetutva*): "But even so... [and] "...by following the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti-anusaraṇena*). He replies: "True, it is so; for this very reason..."—thereby showing that since the word *jijñāsā*, standing in proximity, requires an object of inquiry that has not yet been determined, the word *brahman*—which provides the meaning required by that [word *jijñāsā*]—does not contradict its status as the cause of determining the meaning of the sentence by providing the mere object of cognition that has not yet been determined.

He states the intended meaning of the commentary (*bhāṣya*)—namely, "and because [the Self] is the Self of everything"—as follows: "This is another [point] regarding the meaning of the word *brahman*. Now, one might object: "There is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) even for the Self, because it is not an object of perception and the like; and because that which lacks a means of valid cognition is unreal, like a double moon. To this he replies: "For everyone [realizes] the existence of the Self. Furthermore, one might suspect the doctrine of emptiness (*śūnyavāda*), asking: "The Self appears as nothingness itself; how then can the existence of the Self be established? Anticipating this, he says: "If the establishment of the existence of the Self did not occur..."

[Objection: But if the category of the self (*ātman*) is already known through perception, how can there be the well-known status (*prasiddhi*) of the category of Brahman? To this he says: "And the self is Brahman. [Objection: But since the word "Brahman" is not observed to be used for the self in the beginningless linguistic usage of elders, how can the self be taken up by the word "Brahman" as the object of inquiry? Thus he raises an objection: "But how, then, is the self Brahman?"

He offers this rebuttal—beginning with the words "In the Vedāntas"—to show that even in the absence of worldly usage, the Self is presented as the object of inquiry by means of the word *brahman* in passages such as "This very Self is Brahman," on the strength of its Vedic usage. Now, one might object: "This Self, which is denoted by the word *brahman*, is not cognizable through the notion of 'I', but is rather to be understood solely through scripture"; to this he replies, "The Self alone... [and so forth].

And thus, because an inquiry is possible with respect to that which has been accepted [as the object], the fact that it is capable of being established is proven; so he says: "In this way, it is the very notion of 'I'... Now, an objection might be raised: "In the Vedāntas, the word *brahman* is not applied to the Self for the sake of mere nomenclature, but rather with the intention of expressing the identity of the Self with the meaning of the word *brahman*; therefore, since it has a distinct referent, it was stated that the Self is denoted by the word *brahman*. This is not a fault.

Because the well-known meaning [of the word] is employed by the term "Brahman" with the intention of determining the nature of Brahman as that which is beyond [all attributes], it is possible for both manifestation and non-manifestation to occur even regarding a single object, just as in the case of an original object and its reflection.

In that case, one objects: since [Brahman] is not unique by virtue of being an object of perception, its status as the object [of inquiry] is not established—this is expressed in the words, "If, then, in the world, [it is known] as Brahman and as the Self. He provides the reply: "No; because there is disagreement regarding its specific nature. He explains the meaning of the commentary with the words, "True; the notion 'I' is with respect to the Self," and so forth. Now, one might ask: when there is disagreement regarding one thing, how can another be determined? To this he says: "And these [notions], in reality..."

[Objection: But how can there be a disagreement regarding an object that is already well-known? To this he says: "Therefore, even though it is established in a general sense... [Objection: But an object whose specific qualities are not apprehended is itself unapprehended; how then can it be capable of being communicated when there is no formal enunciation (uddeśa) and injunction (vidhāna)? To this he says: "...and because it is established in a general sense, it is possible [to communicate it]. [Objection: But there is no relation of generality and particularity in Brahman. True.

The "commonality" (*sāmānya*) consists in the establishment [of the Self] through the following of the inward attributes (*pratyagdharma*), which are turned away from the external (*parāgvivṛtta*), in relation to the body, senses, mind, intellect, the void, the agent, the enjoyer, the omniscient, and Brahman-Ātman. In that regard, the establishment through the following of inward attributes is the commonality; therein, even though its pure nature is being established through the following of inward attributes, it is said to be established "in general. From that point, it is then differentiated by other specific features colored by its inwardness (*pratyaktva*).

In that regard, it is determined by its unique nature, which is opposed to the coloring [of the self] by other specific attributes. How can there be a dispute? He shows that dispute with the words beginning "the mere body" (*dehamātram*). But how can there be a dispute based on the suspicion that the *ahaṃpratyaya* (I-notion) and the word *aham* (I), which arise and are employed in respect to an object established by perception, might have multiple meanings in common? To this, he provides an example: "Just as in the case of the word 'cow' (*gośabda*)."

The meaning is as follows: the universal (*jāti*) is accepted by the medical practitioners (*vaidaka*), the individual (*vyakti*) by those concerned with number and so forth, both together by the grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*), the configuration of parts (*ākṛti*) by the Jains (*ārhata*) and others, and all three together by the logicians (*naiyāyika*); likewise, action, quality, configuration, and so forth are also [considered meanings] according to observation. Just as there is a suspicion that the universal and other factors are the word-meaning because of the rule of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka-niyama*) regarding the use of the word "cow"—since not even one of them deviates from it—so too there is a suspicion that the body and other such things are the self (*ātman*) because of the rule of positive and negative concomitance regarding them.

Because its form is clearly manifest and because its gross physicality is established through the process of elimination, he demonstrates the range of conflicting views (vipratipatti) beginning with the body, stating: "The body alone, qualified by consciousness. Regarding the doubt that the body is the self, he states perception as the means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa): "For instance, 'I am a human being. He explains the meaning of the word "body" by saying: "the body alone," etc. The body is defined as the independent substratum of the sense of touch.

In this context, although other parts [of the body] are generally cut away, the sense of touch (tvag-indriya) remains; however, with the intention that the head itself is not severed, it is described as "together with the head" (saśiraska). Now, for those who maintain that there are only four elemental principles (bhūta-tattva), one might object that a fifth principle, consciousness (caitanya), remains; to exclude that, he says: "by the word 'only' (mātra), [it means] distinct from the body," and so forth.

He states another alternative: "The senses themselves. Now, one might object: that in which consciousness arises is the conscious entity. Consciousness does not arise with the senses as its locus, because of the realization, "I, being a human, know. In that case, how can they possess consciousness? To this he replies: "Of the senses," beginning with the eye and ending with the mind.

This is the intended meaning: even though the body exists, since the cognitions of objects possess positive and negative concomitance with the sense organs, and because it is more appropriate to assume that the sense organs themselves are the substrata of cognition based on their possession of positive and negative concomitance as instruments (rather than assuming the body to be the substratum), the sense organs alone are the substrata of consciousness.

Now, if many sense organs within a single body were each conscious, there would be no recognition such as "I saw a form" or "I am hearing now," nor would the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*) regarding color, taste, and so forth occur sequentially, but rather simultaneously. To this, he says: "In succession, like a circle of suitors. The meaning is that it is precisely the fact of having a single body as their locus that is the cause of recognition and sequential enjoyment, not [the sense organs'] unity.

Now, one might object: "Even if it possesses consciousness, only that which is the objective support (*ālambana*) of the 'I'-cognition (*ahaṃpratyaya*) can be the Self; since the sense organs lack that [support], they cannot be the Self. To this, he says: "And thus, the 'I'-cognition has a coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the attributes of the senses. The underlying intention is that even for the body, the positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*) regarding its being the objective support of the 'I'-cognition can be accounted for by its serving as the locus (*āśraya*) for the senses and the self.

He states another position: "And [the self] is indeed conscious. He asks what the proof (*pramāṇa*) is that establishes this, and then says: "For it is observed in dream. This is the meaning: because in a dream, even in the absence of the eyes and other [senses], both the state of being the objective support (*ālambana*) of cognition and the state of being the object of the notion of "I" (*ahaṃpratyaya*) are seen to exist fully within the mind alone; and because if cognitions of form and so forth were based on the eyes and other [senses], then in their absence, the recollection of form and so forth would be impossible in the mind alone; and because no other substratum (*āśraya*) is established for them, [it follows that the mind is the substratum]. Of the eyes and so forth...

Furthermore, it is untenable for the positive and negative concomitances of cognition to have the instrument as their object; moreover, the "I-notion" is established as a figurative attribution of agency to the instrument, just as it is to the body; and recognition is based on unity, as in the case of the body and so forth—for if recognition were based merely on having a single locus, then it would follow that people residing in the same palace would also recognize one another. Therefore, the mind alone, which has the eyes and other instruments as its instruments and the body as its substrate, is the self.

He states another position: "Some [hold] that there is mere consciousness (vijñānamātra) which is momentary. By the term "three letters" (varṇatraya), mere consciousness—which is denoted by those three letters—is expressed. And by that, the non-existence of a self (ātman) as the substratum of consciousness is asserted. How so? Because the body and the sense organs are objects of cognition; because that which is not consciousness cannot be the self; and because, apart from the immediately preceding condition (samanantarapratyaya), no mind exists, and no other substratum is observed. What, then, is the self? To this he says: "Therefore, it is consciousness alone."

In that case, as for the Sāṃkhyas and others who hold that consciousness alone, being without beginning or end, is the Self, he says: "perishing by its own nature. But how then is unity apprehended through recognition? To this he says: "having an uninterrupted arising. The meaning is that recognition occurs due to the similarity between the continuous arisings of consciousness, just as in the case of flames. But how can a momentary entity be the locus of action, knowledge, bondage, and liberation? To this he says: "the abode of the entire course of worldly life."

The meaning is that the connection between action and its fruit arises solely from the continuum of causes and effects among the various consciousnesses. Now, one might object: "All of this is logically established in a primary sense only if there is a single, enduring self. To this, he replies: "the alternative position has been shattered by experience."

He states another alternative: "It is empty" (*śūnyam*). First, the selfhood of things distinct from consciousness has been rejected because they are objects of cognition. Nor does consciousness itself possess selfhood, because emptiness is apprehended in deep sleep. If it is argued that a stream of consciousness indeed exists even there, we say no; for there is an absence of the manifestation of objects, and a cognition devoid of an objective support (*nirālambana*) is impossible. If it is argued that only cognitions with forms (*sākāra-jñāna*) possess an objective support, while those occurring in deep sleep do not, we say no; for there is no distinction [between them], and because they are inferred to be non-distinct.

Furthermore, due to the non-recollection of consciousness upon waking, there is an absence of consciousness during deep sleep. Moreover, just as determinate cognition (savikalpaka) has for its object a non-determinate cognition (nirvikalpaka) that is contrary to its own object, it is inferred that non-determinate cognition also—because it is a valid cognition (sat-pratyaya)—has for its object a void (śūnya) that is contrary to its own object; thus, the cognition upon waking is understood to have the void as its object. This is what he says: "Because not even a trace of consciousness exists in deep sleep. [Objection: Let there be no trace of consciousness; what follows from that? To this he replies: "Precisely without cause" (akasmādeva).

The sense is that, because the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) of the arising condition would itself be empty, the cause would consequently be empty. If it is argued that "let there be no cause," he says: "of that which is causeless yet occurs only occasionally. Therefore, this is an appearance of the non-existent, having emptiness as its objective support.

He states another objection: "There exists [something] distinct from the body and so forth. But how is the self established as distinct from consciousness (*vijñāna*) and the void (*śūnya*)? To this he says: "Of the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*) which is devoid of the mental impression 'I' (*aham-ullekha*). This is the intended meaning: the enjoyer, appearing as the "I" and serving as the substratum for the cognition of objects, never experiences the state of being an enjoyer as the objective support (*ālambana*) of the notion of "mine" (*mama-pratyaya*). Furthermore, since that [self] is the object of uncontradicted recognition (*abādhitapratyabhijñā*), it cannot possibly be non-existent during deep sleep.

Therefore, the enjoyer is empty [of intrinsic nature], being distinct from momentary consciousness; for its existence is understood even during deep sleep through recognition, and because a single substratum is understood across cognition, desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, and pain.

To explain: the knowledge of the means to a desired object, which serves as the cause for activity, arises in this manner. First, when an object is seen; second, when the experience of pleasure following its enjoyment has occurred; third, when the sight of another similar object has arisen; and fourth, when there is a recollection of the commonality between the previously seen object and the current one as a means to pleasure; then, in the fifth stage, the cognition "this is a means to pleasure" arises.

Therefore, this cognition is untenable without a single self persisting through these five states; for there is no experience of pleasure by one who has seen [the object] while it was another, no recollection of what was experienced by one while it was another, and no knowledge of the cause of pleasure by one regarding what was recollected by another—since such things are never observed among distinct mental continua. Likewise, the cognition of the cause of suffering also postulates a self that persists through the five states.

For in this way, passion and aversion—preceded by the knowledge of what is beneficial and what is harmful—imagine the self to be in a sixth state. And the effort of rejection and acquisition arising from passion and aversion imagines the self to be in a seventh state. Likewise, immediately after that effort, in the eighth state...

When pleasure and pain arise, one conceives of the self as undergoing eight stages. Furthermore, such a conventional usage is not possible regarding momentary cognitions, as it is in the case of distinct continua (*saṃtāna*). Likewise, there is no mental impression of "I am cognition" (*ahaṃ jñānam*) with respect to cognitions; rather, there is the impression "my cognition" (*mama jñānam*). Nor can this be a mere metaphorical usage, as in "my self," because there is no sublation [of this experience], whereas in the other case, the notion of a relationship is sublated by the word "self. Therefore, on account of both the mental impression of "I" and recognition, the self is distinct from empty cognitions.

Likewise, for those very same reasons, the mind (*manas*) also is not the self: because even when the mind is absent during deep sleep, there is recognition of the self; because one does not perceive "I am the mind"; because there is the manifestation "my mind"; and because the mind is postulated as a mere instrument due to the non-simultaneity of cognitions. Likewise, for those very same reasons, the sense organs (*indriya*) also are not the selves.

Because there is recognition of the seer throughout the fivefold group of cognitions regarding form, taste, and so forth; because even in the absence of the functioning of the eyes and other senses during dream, there is a complete cognition of the self as "I"; and because of the understanding "my senses," which shows that the senses are distinct from the reference to "I. Likewise, the body also is not the self.

Even in the absence of the manifestation of the body's form in a dream, because there is a complete cognition of the Self as "I," and because this is distinct from the mental trace of "I" [as the body], the cognition "I" occurs with respect to the seer who is devoid of any association with the body's form; thus, there is a perceptual cognition of the Self's difference from the body. Furthermore, this is established by the cognition of distinction in the form: "The body is mine."

Now, one might object: since there is the expression of "I" with respect to the body and the senses—as in "I am one-eyed" or "I am a human"—the cognition of difference is merely figurative (upacāra). Why should the expression of "I" itself not be figurative? What, then, is the final determination? It is more reasonable that the expression of "I" alone is figurative; for it is possible that even when the Self is distinct [from the body], such usage is based upon superimposition (adhyāsa).

Nor does the cognition of difference arise from superimposition (adhyāsa) as it does in the case of a double moon; for if it did, then even in a dream—just as there is the appearance of the form of a second moon—one would have to face the contingency of perceiving the form of a human body and so forth in the manifestation "I am an animal. Likewise, the fear, joy, sorrow, and other states produced in a creature immediately upon birth, in the absence of any visible cause, lead one to postulate a recollection of causes previously experienced, just as in our own case. Consequently, since this very self possesses the perception of the causes of fear and so forth, its connection with a previous birth is established.
Because of recognition. Thus, by means of both the mental impression of "I" and recognition, the self is established as distinct from the body, the senses, the mind, the intellect, and the void.

[Objection: But even if [the self] were permanent, could it not at some time cease to exist? [Response: Its destruction cannot be caused by another; for that which is partless lacks contact with external causes. Furthermore, since that which is associated with the self is acquired as a means for attaining the fruits of its own karma, it serves as a cause for the self's persistence rather than its destruction. Nor can destruction be caused by the self itself; thus he says: "And because no cause for the termination of a stable entity is perceived. The meaning is that it is impossible for something to be a cause of its own destruction by virtue of its own existence, since such a state belongs only to the momentary.

He demonstrates how that [Self] possesses the status of agent and enjoyer with the words, "Because enjoyment is impossible for that which is changeless," and so forth. The phrase, "But how is it distinct from that? has a clear meaning.

In this regard, the Naiyāyikas maintain that bodies in the earth, the intermediate space, heaven, and the world of Brahmā are respectively composed of earth, water, fire, and air; they hold that a single body is not commenced by multiple elements. Among these, the bodies of those such as ourselves are purely earthen, based on Akṣapāda’s sūtra: "Because of the perception of other qualities of earth," which means that because a specific odor is perceived in the body. Furthermore, color, taste, and touch do not imply the presence of other constituent elements.

[The body] belongs to the earth as well, because those [qualities] are its attributes. Now, one might argue that since moistening, digestion, expansion, and space are observed in the body, it must be composed of the five elements; but this is not so, for expansion and the rest can be accounted for through contact with other elements, just as in the case of a leather bag, cloth, water, and so forth. Furthermore, scripture shows that the body is indeed earthen, stating: "The body is earthen."

The Vaiśeṣikas, however, maintain: "Because that which subsists in both perceptible and imperceptible [elements] is itself imperceptible, a body composed of five elements does not exist; since air and ether are imperceptible, a body composed of five elements would be imperceptible. Therefore, the body consists of earth alone"—thus they postulate. To them, he replies: "The body is, for its part, a composite of the elements."

Since no diminution of cloth or similar objects is observed when their moisture, heat, or destruction is removed—despite the departure of water, fire, or air—and since the body is seen to undergo diminution upon the departure of water and other elements, just as a cloth undergoes diminution through the diminution of its threads, it is understood that the body is composed of all the elements, like a cloth woven from all its constituent threads. Furthermore, scriptural and traditional declarations such as, "The food eaten is divided into three parts," and so forth, state that the body consists of the five elements.

If both the perceptible and the imperceptible were imperceptible, it would follow that all composite wholes—which reside in parts that are both perceptible and imperceptible—would themselves be imperceptible. Therefore, the body is a mere collection of elements.

Here, without depending on the operation of individual parts, he analyzes [the position] in order to show that the mere aggregate lacks the status of an enjoyer: "In that case, of the separate [parts]," and so forth. Regarding enjoyment by the separate [parts], whether simultaneously or sequentially, it cannot first be simultaneous; thus he says: "If, then, [it were] of the separate [parts]. He states the refutation there: "Because they are impelled by their own respective purposes. [Objection: Let there be no relationship of part and whole (aṅga-aṅgin); to this he replies: "And not without the relationship of part and whole."

He says that if each individual were the enjoyer, there would be enjoyment even outside of the aggregate: "Therefore, there is no enjoyment in the separate [elements]. Well then, let it be succession. But even in the case of succession, there is no occurrence of an aggregate among the enjoyers; to this he replies: "Because of contradiction, like a bridegroom's assembly. To avoid [this objection], he states the disparity with the example: "This is not so."

He analyzes the illustrative example (dārṣṭāntika): "In this case, however," etc. This is the intended meaning here: if, first of all, even one among the four—form, taste, smell, or touch—[is experienced] by the enjoyers...

Regarding the object: if the objects were common [to all], there would be no cause for their enjoyment in succession. Even if the arrangement of objects were such that the elements (*bhūta*) are the enjoyers (*bhoktṛ*) of form (*rūpa*) and so forth individually, still, when all objects are present simultaneously, a succession of enjoyment would be impossible. Just as when various marriageable girls are present at once, there can be no simultaneous union of suitors due to the distinction between primary and secondary qualities, likewise, there would be no recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) among the enjoyers.

Let it be, then, that the aggregate is the enjoyer. But how can consciousness, which does not exist in a single element, be produced in the collection? To this he says: "like the flame of sesame seeds."

In this regard, it must be stated: is the capacity for enjoyment (bhoktṛtva) a property of the combined elements, or is it a combination of enjoyers? Since a composite (saṃghāta) is not a real entity, its status as an enjoyer is untenable; even if it were a real entity, if it were distinct from the elements, it would follow that a fifth principle must be admitted; if it were non-different from them, then the composite is merely the elements themselves, and thus the elements alone would be the enjoyers. Furthermore, if the combined elements possess the capacity for enjoyment, the cause of their combination must be stated.

If it is argued that [the elements] exist for the sake of future enjoyment, then because all beings are equal with respect to that [future enjoyment], the formation of a composite through the relationship of subordinate and principal would be impossible; thus he says: "This is not so, because a collection is impossible among enjoyments. Now, one might object: since the elements possess agency prior to the connection with enjoyment, a composite is possible among those agents by virtue of their being subordinate to the enjoyment; thus he asks: "How is it impossible?"

He offers a rebuttal, stating that there is no composite aggregate of enjoyers because they lack mutual primary and subordinate status, and because they possess primacy even with respect to enjoyment: "Because the enjoyer has primacy with respect to enjoyment. He raises an objection: "But surely, even in the case of enjoyment, a collection is observed for the sake of that which is the principal object (the enjoyer)."

In this regard, the connection between the two bodies—by way of being subordinate and primary—is for the sake of the two selves who are the enjoyers and are distinct from the bodies; it is not a connection between the enjoyers themselves. Intending this, he offers a rebuttal: "This is not sound. Now, one might object that just as there is an absence of quality in sesame seeds within a flame, so too is there a composite nature in enjoyment; to this he says, "But in the case of sesame and flame, it is the reverse. For this very reason, the position that the enjoyers themselves form a composite is untenable.

Now, what indeed is this so-called "aggregate" (*saṃghāta*)? It is not merely occupying a single location, like a forest; for since the elements pervading that location exist everywhere, it would follow that consciousness and experience would occur everywhere. Nor is it the production of a composite whole (*avayavin*); for if that were different from the elements, the number of fundamental principles (*tattva*) would be exceeded, and if it were non-different, it would be nothing more than the elements themselves, and thus no aggregate would exist. Furthermore, neither difference nor non-difference is admitted [as a category]. Is it then simply the four elements in their own right?

Because the whole (*avayavin*) and so forth are dependent [on their parts], there would be no deviation from the [standard] number [of elements]. If that were the case, then the elements (*bhūta*) would not be the enjoyers, but rather the whole alone would be. In that case, since the whole as the enjoyer would itself be independent—without depending on the operations of the elements—it would result in a deviation from the [standard] number [of elements]. Furthermore, because water and the other elements are dependent on earth and the others, the number [of elements] would be deficient. Moreover, a "composite" (*saṃghāta*) is not something that attains the fitness to be the objective support for the cognition of a single substance.

Because it is impossible for things to attain oneness through their own essential nature, and because the cognition of oneness with respect to many things is an error; nor is a "conglomeration" (saṃghāta) a simultaneous conjunction [of atoms] in a single purposeful action, for if that were so, there would be the undesirable consequence of experience [of pleasure or pain] even when water is being burned by fire produced from wind supported by wood, due to the presence of a conglomeration. Nor is a conglomeration a physical cohesion like that of a mass of iron and fire, because there is no such cohesion of air within the body, and because there would be the undesirable consequence of experience even in a mass of iron pervaded by fire where water has been absorbed and air is joined. Therefore, there is no conglomeration that serves as the cause of experience.

If that is so, then [the opponent] says that experience belongs to a single element alone: "Let it then belong to one as a fixed [attribute]. [The author] refutes this, saying "Not even there," because when the objects of experience—color, taste, smell, and touch—are perceived, as well as the aggregate of elements possessing qualities such as hardness, softness, ripening, and motion, which are the locus of experience, it remains undetermined which single [element] possesses the experience; thus, experience would be indeterminate.

One might object: "Is it not the case that the intended proof—that there is no enjoyer distinct from the body—is established simply by the fact that some entity or other must be the enjoyer? To this, he replies: "What is the point of this restriction? (kimavadhāraṇena).

He refutes this with the words, "If it were so... Since all four [elements] are seen to be associated with experience and there is no basis for determining a distinction among them, a composite whole is impossible within these four elements that constitute the body if they are the experiencers; thus, it is incorrect to say that the elements themselves, which constitute the body, are the experiencers. There is a branch of the Lokāyata school which holds that the sense organs themselves, being composed of the elements, are the self; he extends the previously stated collection of objections to that view as well, saying, "The same applies even to those consisting of the causes. If each individual sense organ were produced from a single element, then defects such as the absence of recognition would follow.

If the single sense-organ were composed of the four elements, then defects such as the impossibility of its being a composite would follow; thus, other Lokāyatikas maintain that the enjoyer is the composite consisting of both cause and effect. To this, he replies: "It consists of both," because a composite [formed by] recognition is impossible.

Now, are the sense-faculties (*indriya*) merely the physical orbs? The Sugatas [Buddhists] say so; the Mīmāṃsakas say they are the potencies (*śakti*) residing therein; others say they are distinct substances (*dravya*) apart from those. They are certainly not merely the orbs, for even snakes and other creatures, though lacking such orbs, perceive sounds and objects; as it is said: "By the defects of actions born of the body, a man goes to the state of an immobile being."

Because scriptures such as "therefore trees see" indicate that even trees and the like—which lack sense-organs—understand the meaning of words through the realization of their status as locations for experiencing the fruits of karma, and because the prohibition against injuring trees and so forth indicates they possess life (*prāṇitva*), [the opponent argues: "Therefore, these are not merely capacities (*śakti*); for it is simpler to postulate capacities in those established locations than to postulate a separate substance possessing those capacities. If this is the case, then let the capacity for all cognition, acting sequentially, be postulated as belonging to the self (*ātman*) alone.

Even though the self is omnipresent, because there is a transformation of cognition in the regions of the sense-orbs—just as there is a transformation of cognition in the regions of the body—the presence and absence of the sense-orbs account for the presence and absence of cognition, despite their not being the self, just like the body. Let them, therefore, be the sense-organs.

It is not the case that substances other than the globes (golaka), which possess power, become denoted by the terms "eye" and so forth due to their connection with specific locations; for there is a lack of evidence (*pramāṇa*) for such substances. If it is argued that the very perceptions of color and so on—which are the operations of an agent—are the mark (*liṅga*) for inferring the instruments, we say no; because the argument is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) regarding instruments that do not themselves possess the operation of an agent, as they lack further instruments, and because there is likewise a lack of further instruments in the case of the agent's operation—characterized by the impelling of those [instruments]—which has the instruments as its object.

If it is argued that the sense organs are known through scripture, as in the traditional teaching that "all the vital breaths depart together," we say no; for even those devoid of the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of such scripture do not perceive the sense organs. Nor are the sense organs objects of the witness-consciousness (*sākṣivedya*) like the mind; for the existence or non-existence of the sense organs is not apprehended apart from the presence or absence of their effects. Therefore, the sense organs do not exist [as real entities].

It is said: prior to the comprehension of the scripture, the functional activity of the senses, such as sight and the rest, proceeds with respect to specific locations, just as the designation of "the sun" and so forth is applied to [reflected] circles and the like. However, once the scripture is understood, it is realized that the senses—sight and the rest—are presiding over those specific locations, just as the deities such as the Sun are the self-nature of those [reflections]. Regarding these [senses], the Sāṃkhyas claim they are distinct from the body yet composed of *ahaṅkāra*; that is incorrect, because there is a lack of valid evidence (*pramāṇa*).

Nor is there observed any understanding through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that the sense organs are produced from the internal ego (*ahaṅkāra*). Furthermore, no such ego exists as the material cause (*prakṛti*) of the elements and sense organs that pervades all effects, because there is a lack of proof (*māna*). If it is argued that the word of an authoritative person (*āpta-vacana*) is the proof, we say no; for [such an ego] is beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*). If it is objected: "But surely there are indeed statements from the Purāṇas," we reply: True. However, because this would contradict the scriptural use of the suffix *mayaṭ* in the sense of a modification of the elements—as in "The mind, my dear, consists of food (*anna-maya*)"—it is merely assumed therein that the sense organs are dependent upon the ego; thus, there is no contradiction.

The Vaiśeṣikas and others maintain that the sense organs are composed of material elements (*bhautika*); however, this too is incorrect, as there is no proof for it. If it is argued: "The sense organs are material because they possess parts due to having a medium dimension (*madhyama-parimāṇa*), like a jar and so forth," we say no, because the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*), since it is logically possible for the sense organs to have an atomic dimension (*aṇu-parimāṇa*). If that were the case, then the manifestation of objects would occur only through an atomic dimension; but this is not so, because even with an atomically small mind (*manas*), one perceives vast objects such as the self (*ātman*) and so on.

[Objection: Surely the sense organs are composed of the material elements (*bhautika*), because they invariably manifest color, taste, smell, and touch—just like a lamp, water, a mirror, the directions, or the wind that fans a substance; thus, by another inference, each individual sense organ is inferred to be produced from its corresponding individual element. [Reply: No, because this argument is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to the ear, which manifests sound but is not produced from ether (*ākāśa*), which possesses the quality of sound; for we accept that the ear is merely the ether delimited by the ear-cavity (*karṇaśaṣkulī*), and as such, it is not "produced" [from a prior cause].

Furthermore, it would follow that the mind is composed of the four elements, because it manifests them. If it is argued that the mind is not composed of the elements because the self, space, and so forth are common [to all], then the sense organs cannot be established as being composed of the elements either, since number, dimension, conjunction, disjunction, generality, particularity, inherence, and so forth are also common [to all]. If it is argued that the sense organs are composed of their specific (non-common) objects, then the mind must be composed of the self, because the self is its specific object.

If it is argued that a substance cannot be originated from a single substance, we say no; for it is only this much that is established: that which possesses parts is originated from multiple substances. But why could the partless mind not be originated from the partless self? Therefore, its material nature is established solely through scripture (āgama).

The Yogas maintained that these [the self, senses, and mind] are all-pervading, yet even that is devoid of reason. If it is argued that the self, the senses, and the mind are all-pervading because their effects are observed everywhere, like space (*ākāśa*), we say no; for the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*). If it is argued that they are all-pervading because their effects are observed wherever there is a body, this is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to the body itself. If it is argued that they are all-pervading because they move to other locations due to external adjuncts (*upādhi*), like space, we say no; for the limbs of the body also move to other locations due to external adjuncts. Furthermore, if they were all-pervading, there would be the simultaneous perception of all objects.

If it is argued that [the mind] does not [go out] because it acquires its function only within the body, then the postulation of the existence of external sense organs would be neither based on valid means of knowledge nor purposeful.

The Sugatas [Buddhists] maintain that these [senses] do not act by reaching their objects; however, this is incorrect, because it would follow that touch, taste, and smell could be perceived from a great distance. If it is argued that they require the object to be situated in a suitable location, we say no; for apart from reaching the location of the sense organ itself, no "suitable location" can be defined. Just like the tactile, gustatory, and olfactory organs, the eyes and ears are also inferred to act by reaching their objects. Furthermore, since light is observed to travel very far and very rapidly, the eye's reaching of the polar star (Dhruva) and other distant objects is not contradictory.

Furthermore, because sound is perceived at a distance, its conjunction with the auditory organ does not occur through a continuous series like a wave-train. Therefore, it is established that the sense organs are composed of material elements (*bhautika*), limited in size, and function by reaching their objects (*prāpyakārī*). What, then, is this so-called "mind" (*manas*)? The Vaiśeṣikas and others maintain that it is eternal, partless, and atomic in dimension. It is not eternal, however, because it is limited in size. If it is argued that it is eternal because it is a substance devoid of parts—just like the self (*ātman*)—we say no.

[The mind is not atomic] because, like the sense organs, it is inferred to possess parts due to its being an instrument (*karaṇatvena*), and because of the scriptural statement that it consists of food (*annamayatva*). If it is argued that it is partless because it is not struck by material objects, we say no; for the mind does not go outside [the body]. Departure (*utkrānti*) is common to the sense organs as well. Furthermore, because it possesses conjunction and disjunction, it cannot be of atomic dimension (*aṇuparimāṇatā*) like a jar or similar objects. And if it were all-pervading (*sarvagatatva*), there would follow the undesirable consequence of omniscience due to simultaneous contact with all the sense organs.

If [the mind] possesses parts due to having a medium magnitude, there is no contradiction in its assuming gross or subtle bodies, as the accumulation and diminution of parts would be possible. The Śākyas (Buddhists) maintained that the immediately preceding cognition (*samanantarapratyaya*) alone is the "mind" (*manas*) by virtue of being the cause of the subsequent cognition; but that is not so, because for one cognition to be the cause of another cognition, it must depend upon a pervasion (*vyāpti*). According to their own view, even verbal cognition is produced by pervasion. Furthermore, they hold that a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*) is produced by conjunction (*saṃyoga*), not by the cognition of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇajñāna*).

If it is argued that the subsequent cognition acquires its form from the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), we say no; for the intrinsic nature of a thing is not dependent on anything else.
Therefore, the mind (*manas*) is indeed something distinct and possesses parts.

And what is this self? Some say it is all-pervading and insentient. First of all, it has been stated that the observation of effects everywhere is not the reason for its being all-pervading. If it is argued that it is all-pervading because actions such as dancing, which have unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) as their cause, commence even in distant places—and since that action depends on the contact of the self with a locus possessing *adṛṣṭa*—we say no. For the arising of enjoyment in heaven occurs from *adṛṣṭa* inherent in [the self], due to contact with a region possessing *adṛṣṭa*, and not merely from contact with a region of the self. Therefore, its all-pervasiveness is established solely through scripture (*āgama*).

Nor is there insentience, because its self-luminosity is understood. First, this manifestation is directly perceived even in deep sleep. There is also inference: "This Self is self-luminous, because there is no absence of its manifestation when it exists, like the perception of a lamp. Or: "The Self is self-luminous, because it is the agent of the manifestation of objects, like a lamp. Likewise: "The Self is self-luminous, because it is the substratum for the manifestation of objects, like light. Furthermore, the Self possesses the quality of ungenerated manifestation, because it has the quality of manifestation, like the sun and other luminaries.
The self is self-luminous, because, while not being within the range of the sense organs, it is not non-manifest, like cognition; and scripture has been shown on this point as well.

And that [Self] is one, because it is perceived through the uniform cognition of "I" throughout all bodies everywhere, just like the nature of being a cow (*gotva*). Nor does the consequence of a lack of recollection of experiences arise merely from the difference in bodies, as in the case of past bodies and the like. Furthermore, even in a single body, a difference in bodies at every moment due to a difference in size is not logical, because it contradicts recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) and would entail a lack of recollection; for in the case of a flame, when observed closely, no difference is seen by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Therefore, it is established that the Self is one and self-luminous. The word "therefore" (*tasmāt*) serves as the conclusion.

He states another position: "The enjoyer alone [is the agent]. For agency (*kartṛtva*) consists in the penetration of action (*kriyāveśa*). And it is not possible for the all-pervading and partless Self to be connected with action characterized by motion or transformation (*pariṇāma*). Nor does the agency of the intellect belong to the Self; because there is no superimposition of identity (*tādātmyādhyāsa*), given that he is an adherent of the theory of non-apprehension (*akhyātivāda*). He states another reason: "I act, I know, and I enjoy."

If the penetration of activity were also an inherent property of the self, like consciousness, it would not deviate from the manifestation of the self; nor can any adventitious property be produced in a partless substance through the influence of a cause.

One might object: "But surely, because the appearance of the self is subject to deviation, just as its agency is, its state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*) would also not exist. To this he replies: "Is it not so that the enjoyer also... He refutes this: "It is not so. Being an enjoyer consists merely in the manifestation of the object of perception, not in a connection with pleasure and pain. Therefore, since there is no deviation from the manifestation of the object of perception even during the three states [of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep], the self is exclusively the enjoyer.

He states another alternative: "There exists one distinct from that. He explains the commentary: "Therefore, even other than that [the body and so forth], the Lord is established as distinct"—this is the connection with what follows. Here, he demonstrates the Vaiśeṣika inference regarding the Lord by means of the passage beginning with "of embodied beings, even by the mind," and so on.

The object of dispute—the world, characterized by primary matter (*bhūta*) and its derivatives (*bhautika*), which is the effect consisting of the construction of bodies and the universe—must have been preceded by an agent who possesses knowledge regarding its own nature, material cause, recipient, purpose, instruments, and so forth, because it is an effect possessing a manifold arrangement, like a palace and the like. Thus, by adopting a single agent through the principle of parsimony (*kalpanālāghava*), the establishment of omniscience and other such qualities follows. He demonstrates the inference according to Sāṃkhya and Yoga with the statement: "There is a limit for things that possess degrees of excellence."

The powers of knowledge and sovereignty that are the subject of dispute are invariably concomitant with knowledge and sovereignty over all objects, because they are qualities that pervade their respective objects as they are progressively intensified; this is like the quality of dimension which pervades the space occupied by its own object. It has been stated "or [the conclusion is] 'all-encompassing'" because the attainment of the ultimate limit is possible even if [the scope] were not yet all-encompassing; for it has been demonstrated in the inference exactly thus that God is eternally established.

He demonstrates the inference [used] by the Naiyāyikas and others: "The fruits of dharma and adharma, which have entered the scope of dispute, are bestowed by one who possesses knowledge of the action, its fruit, the recipient, and the instruments, because they are fruits of actions separated [in time], like the fruit of service and so forth. Therefore, God is established.

[The opponent] objects: "Surely, for the inner self (*pratyagātman*), which is the substratum of disagreement, the perception of the distinction between the aggregates (*skandha*) is the disagreement itself. And since God (*īśvara*) is not a distinct aggregate that qualifies the inner self, He should not be presented as a specific aggregate in the same way as the body and so forth. Thus he challenges [the author] with the words, "But surely everyone in the world [thinks], 'I... etc. The meaning of the rebuttal beginning with "It is said" (*ucyate*) is as follows: Brahman is indeed the substratum of disagreement.

Furthermore, in order to demonstrate the disagreement as to whether that [Self] is distinct from or non-distinct from the inner self (pratyagātman), the position of an Ishvara who is distinct must also be shown. Why, then, is the disagreement regarding the Self itself presented? To this he says: "Also by way of the disagreement concerning the object of the notion of 'I'."

What is meant by this? First, the inner self (pratyagātman) is indicated by other means of knowledge and then established as having the nature of non-dual knowledge and bliss, through the exclusion of specific attributes such as body, senses, mind, intellect, agency, and enjoyership; for when it is established in this way, there is the cessation of transmigratory existence and the attainment of the human goal. Therefore, in order to demonstrate the disagreement regarding whether the inner self is different or non-different from Brahman, which possesses qualities such as omniscience, a Lord distinct from it has been established, since that [disagreement] constitutes a category of conflicting views.

Regarding this, someone says: "In this context, the inner self (*pratyagātman*) is not intended as the object of inquiry by being designated with the word 'Brahman' in its specific, unique nature; rather, it is the Lord (*īśvara*) alone who is designated by the word 'Brahman' and subjected to investigation. For in the *Janmādi-sūtra*, the characteristic of being the cause of the world is stated, and this characteristic is not applicable to the inner self. Therefore, the demonstration of conflicting views regarding the self is irrelevant. To this, it is replied:

If the Lord is denoted by the word "Brahman," why then does [the author] show a disagreement regarding the cause of the world—stating, "some [say] the Pradhāna, others the atoms," and so forth? For, when the word "Brahman" is employed in reference to the Lord as the object of inquiry, it would be improper to show a disagreement regarding a different entity, namely the cause of the world.

If it is argued that because the Lord, who is the cause of the world, is non-different [from the individual self], a disagreement regarding Him constitutes a disagreement regarding the individual self, then a disagreement such as "Is the Lord primordial matter (pradhāna) or an atom (paramāṇu)? would have been shown [as a doubt concerning the self]. However, they do not doubt in that manner; rather, there is doubt regarding the internal self—the specific nature denoted by the word Brahman—with respect to the body, senses, and so forth, because those [latter] appear to them as identical with the self.

Furthermore, when the inner self (pratyagātman) is taken as the subject and its specific nature as Brahman is sought to be known, it is stated that "Brahman is that which is the cause of the origin of the world"; by this, the inner self—having shaken off distinctions such as the body—is established as being the Self of all through its status as the cause of the world.

However, when there is a disagreement regarding the cause of the world, upon the inquiry "What is that cause of the world?", it would be the case that "that which is Brahman is the cause of the world"—thus, with Brahman as the subject (uddeśya), the status of being the cause of the world is the predicate (vidheya). It does not follow the reverse, namely, that the cause of the world is the subject and Brahman is predicated of it. If it is argued that the word "Brahman" denotes the cause of the world, we say no; for that would contradict your own statement that "Īśvara" is what is denoted.

Furthermore, if it is asked: "Once God is established as the cause of the world, what does that have to do with the person's practice of meditation (*upāsana*)?", we say: no; for since such meditation is possible even through a superimposed form, the [establishment of God] would otherwise be purposeless.

Therefore, with reference to the inner self (pratyagātman), when there arises a desire to know that which is denoted by the word "Brahman" as prescribed in the Vedānta—namely, that which is the cause of the origin and so forth of the world and is characterized by existence, consciousness, bliss, and the like—it is appropriate to demonstrate the conflicting views regarding the Self in order to establish that Brahman, which possesses such characteristics, is identical with the inner self. Thus, the conflict of views concerning the cause of the world has been shown by the proponent of universal confusion (sarvasaṅkaravādin) due to his lack of familiarity with the tradition and his aversion to the meaning of the scripture.

He states another alternative: "The other [maintains] that the Self is the enjoyer. Just as Brahman is truth, consciousness, bliss, and partless, so too is the inner self (*pratyagātman*). In this regard, the individual soul (*jīva*), which is the subject of dispute, is indeed Brahman itself, though its division is delimited by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). This is because, while being a partless substance due to having the same essential nature as Brahman, it appears to have a delimited form based on the perception of those limiting adjuncts.

Whatever possesses a limited appearance dependent upon the apprehension of adjuncts (*upādhi*), while being partless substance by virtue of having the same essential nature as that [other thing], is seen to have its difference delimited by adjuncts while possessing identity with it; for example, the space within a jar (*ghaṭākāśa*). He explains the *Bhāṣya*: "This one who... [and so on]. Now, one might ask: how can there be identity between the transmigrating soul (*saṃsārī*) and the non-transmigrating [Self]? To this he says: "Of that, established by the notion of 'I' (*ahaṃpratyaya*)."

Now, it may be objected that when the "I" is thus apprehended in a general sense, and the specific distinctions such as the body and so forth are shown to be false, one must state a real, ultimate distinction, namely, "I am of such-and-such a nature. To this he says: "But in the ultimate sense... This concludes the specific [definition] as "I am indeed Brahman. As for the question, "What is the proof that [the 'I'] is not the body and so forth?", he says: "In this way, it [is called Brahman] because of its connection with the meaning of 'expanding' (bṛṃhati). Now, it might be argued that even if there is a difference from individual souls (jīvas), the meaning of "expanding" is still obtained.

"Because it pervades space and time"—this is what he says: "otherwise, of that conceptualization of its nature. He concludes: "Thus, many [hold different views] regarding something such as the body and so forth. By "Brahman," he means the "inner self" (*pratyagātman*); the meaning is that they are in disagreement. Now, one might object: "A subject is not to be investigated merely because of disagreement; rather, it must be rooted in valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), for [knowledge] arises from the cognition of reality. And since the cognition of the reality of Brahman is produced by the investigation of the *Brahma-mīmāṃsā*, the *Brahma-mīmāṃsā* is therefore necessary—this is the meaning.

Regarding the point that "misconception must be refuted," the following is the reply: the commentary beginning with "reasoning and statements" (*yuktivākya*), which he explains with the words "reasoning is [the application] of the means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇānām*) and so forth. He distinguishes between the cases by asking: "In which position do reasoning and statements belong, and where do their fallacies (*tadābhāsa*) reside?"—thus concluding that "by means of reasoning and statements, they have ascertained the final position."

[Objection: But surely, just as Brahman alone is the enjoyer because it is connected with the meaning of "becoming great" (*bṛṃhati*) through both reasoning and scriptural statement, so too Brahman alone must be [the enjoyer] within the manifold world (*prapañca*) of pleasure, pain, and their means. Consequently, since it would not be a human goal (*puruṣārtha*), Brahman would not be an object of inquiry (*jijñāsya*). For one who cannot tolerate even a connection with a few instances of pleasure, pain, and their means would certainly not accept the state of possessing all suffering and the like. [Reply: But surely, since it possesses the nature of a human goal by virtue of the characteristics of knowledge, bliss, and so forth that will be described later, why should it not indeed be an object of inquiry? [Answer: No.

If it is argued that even though [liberation] is a human goal because it is the means for the cessation of hunger, those who act with foresight show indifference toward food mixed with poison because it is a cause of harm; and that liberation is not a non-human goal because of scriptural texts such as "The one who is external is not smeared by the suffering of the world," we say no. This is because of the scriptural teaching of universal identity in passages such as "This is indeed the Self," and because [the Self] is the material cause [of the world]. If it is argued that there is no connection with harm because, due to omniscience, there is an absence of ignorance and false knowledge, we say no.

If it is argued that, because Brahman is in reality identical with the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), it does not depend on ignorance (*ajñāna*) and the like, and therefore the connection with pleasure, pain, and so forth is caused by karma; and that since such [ignorance] is absent, there is no connection with evil in Brahman—this is not so. For even apart from karma, all pleasures, pains, and their means are directly perceived as inherent in Brahman by its very nature, and karma and the rest are merely instrumental causes for that which is already present. Indeed, no transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) is observed other than the direct perception of pain and the like.

Since karma, ignorance, and the rest also expand through their connection with the same object, they are identical with Brahman; therefore, it is all the more established that saṃsāra, caused by them, is likewise [identical] in Brahman through the knowledge of reality. In Brahman, by means of the knowledge of reality...

If it is argued that there is no connection with undesirable consequences because [the world] has been sublated, we say no; for even the state of being identical with the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) would then be real. Nor can there be a distinction between the states of bondage and liberation based on a division between the causal and non-causal Brahman, or between the effected and uneffected Brahman; for such a view would entail the impossibility of the etymological application of the term *bṛhat* (the Great). Therefore, since Brahman—defined by the application of the sense of "being great" (*bṛhat*) and devoid of secondness, omniscience, the state of being a living soul (*jīvatva*), and so forth—is rendered something not to be inquired about, it is replied: [this is not so].

Even though everything is related to Brahman through direct perception, because this relation is caused by *māyā*, it is sublated by the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), just as the darkness of a reflection or the tigerhood attributed to one who is not a tiger is sublated. Since the Brahman that stands in the position of the original object (*bimba*) is eternally omniscient, there is no persistence of the self (*ātman*) in that state due to the necessity of the knowledge of reality. Furthermore, we shall explain later that the statements regarding purity are indeed more powerful. To address whose view is based on fallacious reasoning and fallacious scriptures, he says: "But the others [hold] as if they were reasonings," and so forth.

Furthermore, he explains how the body and the self possess the appearance of reasoning (yuktyābhāsatā) by stating: "the appearance of reasoning. Now, one might object that the status of being an appearance of reasoning is not established for the body and so forth merely by this much; to this he replies: "the status of being an appearance of reasoning is established for the others. Moreover, since the appearances of reasoning have already been shown, there is no need for anything else in that regard; thus he says: "and it has been shown in brief."

But are not such statements as "That person, indeed, consists of the essence of food," "This self, indeed, is Brahman," and "Consisting of earth, consisting of water, consisting of fire, consisting of air"—these and others—proofs for the doctrine that the body is the self? For the doctrine that the senses are the self, there are passages such as "They said to Speech: 'Come out for them,' and Speech went out for them. For the doctrine of the mind, there is "The mind went out for them. For the doctrine of consciousness, there is "Which is the self? It is this which consists of consciousness," and so forth. And for the doctrine of emptiness, there is "In the beginning, this was non-existent," and "This was indeed non-existent."

In the doctrine of the self as an agent, there are scriptural passages such as, "the one who permits, the one who understands, the doer, the conscious self"; and because it falls within the scope of the intellect, [it is said], "one of them eats the sweet fruit. In the doctrine of the self as an enjoyer, there is, "the other, not eating"; and in the doctrine of a distinct Lord, there are statements such as, "He who, dwelling in the self, controls the self from within. How then can the alternative positions be considered baseless? To this, he says: "But [they are] merely semblances of scriptural passages."

[Objection: "Even so, whoever develops a liking for whichever [view] may adopt that position and accomplish the human goal; what is the use of inquiry? To this he says: "In that regard, without having investigated anything whatsoever... He explains the commentary with the words beginning "In that case, such being the situation," and so forth. [Objection: "Granted that there may be no attainment of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) due to the absence of knowledge of reality in the positions lower than the final one, why would harm (*anartha*) be incurred? To this he says: "They enter blind darkness... and so forth.

Now, it might be objected that in that context, the cause of harm was said to be the destruction of the self (*ātmahanana*), not the non-comprehension of reality; to this he replies: "by means of the vision of non-self (*anātmadarśana*), which consists in reducing the self to the status of a mere fiction. He concludes the meaning of the aphorism (*sūtra*) with the words: "therefore, by way of introducing the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*)."

He explains the commentary: "By way of introducing the inquiry into Brahman" (*brahmajijñāsopanyāsavyājena*). By indicating that the word *jijñāsā* (desire to know) implies the underlying investigation (*vicāra*), it is stated that the Sūtra is intended to establish the necessity of that investigation. He states another interpretation: "Or else" (*athavā*). When it is said that "the desire to know must be undertaken," the meaning of the Sūtra results in the fact that knowledge, being the object of desire, must be accomplished as the goal to be attained. In that case, although knowledge is what is to be accomplished, the necessity of undertaking its means is understood by implication; therefore, the Sūtra is one whose purpose is established as the necessity of undertaking the investigation. The passage beginning with "For what purpose? (*kiṃprayojanā*) has a clear meaning.

If it is asked how, then, inquiry has liberation as its purpose, [the answer is] because it is accomplished by the realization of Brahman produced by inquiry—if it is further asked what that liberation is, and if it is said to be the cessation of ignorance, which is the material cause for the continuous stream of superimposition consisting of the conjunction with defects, agency, and enjoyership—[we reply: no; for even when ignorance has ceased, the perception of duality does not necessarily disappear.

For the manifold world of earth and so forth does not cease merely through the cessation of the superimposition of agency and other such attributes. It is replied: even while earth and the rest exist, once the superimposition upon the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) has ceased, there is an absence of subjecthood (*pramātṛtva*); consequently, because the consciousness of the Self lacks any natural coloring by objects, the perception of duality no longer occurs—just as one without sense organs cannot perceive form and so forth. This is one position. The other position, which maintains the cessation of all duality, will be explained under the *Samanvaya-sūtra*.

Therefore, it is fitting that the purpose of the inquiry into the Vedānta is the attainment of the highest good (niḥśreyasa), which consists in abiding in the nature of Brahman—manifesting as unsurpassed bliss—where all superimpositions such as agency have been cast off and the perception of duality has been dispelled.

Thus ends the fourth section, titled "The Determination of the Refutation of Objections Concerning the Subject Matter and Purpose," in the *Pañcapādikā-vivaraṇa* composed by the venerable Svaprakāśānubhava, disciple of the worshipful feet of the illustrious Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ananyānubhava.

Now begins the fifth section: That cause from which the birth, subsistence, and destruction of the world are established is demonstrated through two types of definitions— the essential (svarūpa) and the incidental (taṭastha).

By including the inquiry within the mention of the subject matter, he states the meaning of the commentary on the introductory verse (*vṛttasaṅkīrtanabhāṣya*) with the words: "It has been stated that Brahman is to be desired to be known," and so forth.

[Objection: But surely, since the investigation into the means (*sādhana*) and so forth is not promised in the initial proposition (*pratijñā*) regarding the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmavicāra*), it would follow that they are not to be accomplished. To this he says: "When it was said, 'This [is what is to be explained]... and so forth. [Objection: If all five types of inquiry have been promised, why is the nature (*svarūpa*) alone investigated first? Is it not because it is the primary object due to being the result (*phala*)? [Reply: No; since the accomplishment of the goal depends upon the means and so forth, let those very things be investigated first. To this he says: "Because the nature is the most venerable (*abhyarhita*) therein."

The meaning is that [the inquiry into Brahman] is primary because the specific investigations—namely, "Brahman as the means of knowledge," "Brahman as the method," "Brahman as the instrument," and "Brahman as the fruit"—are dependent upon the qualification of Brahman, whereas the determination of the essential nature of Brahman itself is independent of anything else and is what is to be established as the principal goal.

Having proclaimed the subject matter (*vṛtta*), he states the connection with what follows, preceded by a desire for knowledge: "What is its definition? He honors the Teacher for the purpose of demonstrating the nature of Brahman, which is the human goal to be sought, by addressing him as "Bhagavān. Now, one might object: "The inseparable relation between a definition and the thing defined—such that 'this is its definition' or 'this is the thing defined by this'—cannot be established without recourse to means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and logical reasoning, in order to avoid the fallacies of under-extension (*avyāpti*) and over-extension (*ativyāpti*). Therefore, how can the Sūtra be said to concern only the essential definition (*svarūpa-lakṣaṇa*)?"

Regarding this, he says: "Reasoning (*yukti*) also [is included] by implication in the determination of the definition. By the word "also" (*api*), the meaning is that the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is also included. Here, however, the determination of the means of valid knowledge and reasoning concerning Brahman—which were merely stated as aphorisms—is carried out over the course of two chapters. The portion beginning from "birth and origin" up to "the third indicative mark" is of clear meaning. Regarding the term *tadguṇasaṃvijñāna*: the meaning is that the compound is formed by treating the qualifier as being one part of the qualificand itself.

But even so, since birth, subsistence, and dissolution are all three the subjects (viśeṣya), how can there be a singular designation? To this he says: "by means of the third gender. He anticipates the objection regarding the beginning, middle, and end of birth and the rest by saying: "But [what of] the beginning?"

He refutes [the objection] with the words: "And [the fact] that birth is the beginning. He explains the *bhāṣya*: "By this sūtra... [The opponent objects: "But everything perishes immediately after being born and does not remain for any time at all, because destruction is dependent upon its own existence (*svasattā*). To this he replies: "Because momentariness has been refuted. Therefore, the phrase "having been born," etc., is clear in meaning. [The opponent objects: "But the word 'this' (*idam*) indicates only something proximate, not the entire world. To this he replies: "For thus, everywhere..."

Now, one might ask: what is the relationship intended by the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) between "birth and so forth" and the "world"? To this he says: "All indeed... One might further object: in what kind of relationship does the birth, subsistence, and dissolution of the world function as a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*)? It cannot be through a relationship with the subject (*lakṣya*) like that of a crow [perched on a house]; for these attributes have the world as their locus. Therefore, he says "from which" (*yataḥ*) to indicate the cause, meaning they function as a characteristic through a relationship with the cause.

Now, it must be stated whether the status of being the cause of the origin and so forth of the world is included within the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) or within the essential nature of the thing defined (*lakṣyasvarūpa*). If it is asked, "In what does the property of being the locus of a crow for a house inhere? Is it in the thing defined?", then the status of being the locus of a crow would constitute the meaning of the word 'house'. Consequently, upon the departure of the crow, there would arise the cognition that a part of the house has been destroyed. If, on the other hand, it is argued that [the property] is included within the definition, then the status of being a cause is likewise so.

Neither the state of being characterized by engagement in various types of activities nor the state of possessing the power to produce them can be contained within the pure Brahman that is the object of inquiry. Therefore, the causality of the world’s birth and so forth is indeed a mere secondary characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*). Now, it may be asked: are both efficient causality and material causality stated as secondary characteristics, or is it only efficient causality that characterizes Brahman? It cannot be that efficient causality alone is the characteristic of Brahman.

Because the material cause, which is non-different from the world, would exist as something distinct [from Brahman], there would follow the undesirable consequence that the word "Brahman" would lack connection with its own primary meaning. Nor is being the material cause a secondary characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*); for since the efficient cause, the omniscient one, would exist as something distinct, the designation "from whom [proceeds] all-knowingness and all-powerfulness" would not be possible; moreover, in the world, the material cause is insentient. Furthermore, the definition of essential nature (*svarūpa-lakṣaṇa*), namely "Truth, Knowledge, Infinite," would be inapplicable to both [the material and efficient causes].

Nor is being both causes [the efficient and the material] a defining characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*) of Brahman; for there is no evidence that a single entity can be both causes. Indeed, a defining characteristic established by other means of knowledge is capable of leading to the comprehension of the nature of a definiendum not yet understood. It is not possible, however, to ascertain through inference that a single entity is both the efficient and material cause of the world, because difference is observed in the illustrative examples (*dṛṣṭānta*). Since we observe various kinds of efficient and material causes among objects distinct from the five great elements (*mahābhūta*), it is impossible to enjoin Brahman by way of restating that [dual causality].

It might be argued that it is not established that a single [cause] is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the five elements; to this he replies: "The ablative case [ending] is based on its being the primal nature (*prakṛti*). This is also an indication of its being the efficient cause (*nimitta*), since the ablative is prescribed in both senses. First, a single primal nature of the five elements is inferred from the persistence of a single nature within all existing things.

For instance: the great elements (*mahābhūta*) have Being (*sat*) as their material cause (*prakṛti*), because, while being colored by the nature of Being, they possess various modifications (*vikāra*), just like jars and other objects permeated by clay. Furthermore, even non-differences such as substantiality (*dravyatva*) appear as universals (*sāmānya*) precisely because they are the very nature of their material causes; however, Being itself, because it pervades all things, is the material cause of all modifications. Moreover, the fact that derivative material objects are seen to have the gross elements as their material cause demonstrates that everything is ultimately dependent upon the primal material cause (*mūlaprakṛti*).

Therefore, by means of an inference supported by the principle that "for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), there must be only one material cause for all effects," it is established that this [one cause] is indeed the efficient cause as well. Furthermore, it is inferred that this very [cause] possesses the nature of being both the efficient and the material cause: this world ought to have a single, non-different efficient and material cause, because it is an effect produced through prior deliberation, just like the pleasure, pain, attachment, aversion, and so forth residing within the self. Nor is there any inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*) regarding jars and other such objects; for even in their case, we postulate a single, non-different efficient and material cause.

If it is argued that a difference in causes such as the unseen destiny (*adṛṣṭa*) is observed, we say no; for there is an inference of the identity of both the material cause and the presiding agent. Therefore, the fact that a single entity is the cause of both, which is already established by inference, is pointed out as a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). Furthermore, the fact that a single entity is the cause of both, as well-established in the creation-texts (*sṛṣṭivākya*), is pointed out as a defining characteristic.
