In this regard, some introduce the doctrine of transformation (*pariṇāmavāda*). They must state the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for that. If they say it is the scriptural texts concerning creation, we say no; because the word "transformation" is not heard therein. If they argue that transformation is a real change of state, and thus the texts establish that the world arises from Brahman as something real, we say no; because the word "real" (*satya*) is not heard in those passages. If they argue that, due to the self-validity of knowledge (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*), the creation is indeed of such a nature, and ask what this "being of such a nature" means—namely, reality—we say no.

Because even in a dream-creation, there is an absence of the notion of truth regarding a specific object cognized through a means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa), such as in the case of the thought, "This silver is false. If it is argued that [dreams] do not contradict the absence of their own objects within their own limiting adjunct (upādhi), we say no; for this is equally true in the case of being of the nature of illusion (māyā). Furthermore, because a creation excludes its own absence within its own limiting adjunct, all attributes conditioned by a limiting adjunct are true by virtue of being unsublated within the adjunct that is their own substratum. Thus, even creation is not sublated in its own essential form, but rather in its aspect of ultimate reality (paramārtha-satyatva).

Now, one might object that if the scriptural statement has as its object a false creation, it would lack authority; but this is not so. The beloved of the gods (the opponent) is ignorant of the operation of the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). For a *pramāṇa* does not tolerate the absence of its object (*prameya*), but it does not tolerate the absence of what is not its object. Furthermore, the scripture concerning creation does not establish ultimate reality, because there is no expression of such [reality] therein. Just as when "jar" is said, it appears as common to both existence and non-existence due to the absence of any expression of the other, so it is here.

For the scriptural passage concerning the creation of dream-objects does not establish their reality, because it lacks purpose and thus lacks a definitive purport (*tātparya*); nor does it establish the manifestation of the world from Brahman, because the transformation into suffering and its causes is a source of harm. Furthermore, the establishment of the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*) or of perception and other means of knowledge is not the purpose [of such passages], since the world’s existence is established even by its eternity, and because [the world] is already established prior to the comprehension of the scriptural account of creation.

If it is argued that even non-difference is established in the form of existence (*sattva*) and so forth, and therefore depends on words, then what is this extreme confusion of one who maintains the doctrine of universal commingling (*sarvasaṃkara*)? For Brahman—which is eternal, pure, awakened, liberated, unsurpassed bliss, self-luminous, omniscient, non-dual, and the innermost Self—is certainly not established prior to the comprehension [of it through scripture]. What, then, is the purpose of the scriptural teaching on creation?

The purpose [of this treatise] is the establishment of the nature of non-dual Brahman as not contradicted by other means of valid cognition, by first describing how the world—established through perception and other means—is absent elsewhere because it possesses origination and destruction only in Brahman, and then, even there, negating it and thereby establishing its falsity. This is because [the treatise] forms a single syntactical unit with that [Upaniṣadic teaching]; otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the primary subject matter (*śeṣin*). If it is argued that the knowledge of that [world] is invalid because it is a mere appearance of creation, like the appearance of silver, we say no.

Because there is no other primary creation like that of real silver, and because that [creation] alone is the primary creation, it possesses validity just like the knowledge thereof; for even in the case of a false effect, we hear the words "became" (*abhavat*) and "creation" (*sṛṣṭi*) in such passages as "Devadatta became a tiger" and "This is indeed an illusion created by me."

Furthermore, why this partiality toward falsity in a creation that is common to both the real and the unreal? For in such passages as "There was neither non-existence nor existence; there was only darkness," "This was then enveloped in darkness," and "Know Māyā to be Prakṛti," we hear of a primordial nature (*prakṛti*) that is indefinable (*anirvacanīya*), distinct from both being and non-being; and since the modification (*vikāra*) has that very nature as its essence, it is said: "Darkness, delusion, great delusion, gloom, and utter blindness—this fivefold ignorance (*avidyā*) has manifested from the Great Self."

This is because of the traditional teaching (smṛti), since *tamas*, *avidyā*, and *māyā* are synonyms. Thus, since the creation is understood from scripture to be illusory (*mithyā*), there would be the undesirable consequence of contradicting scripture if one were to imagine it to be real. Furthermore, in the case of the perception "the jar exists," the jar—which is apprehended under the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of the sense of existence—is seen to be sublated by direct perception itself as "it does not exist" under that very same condition; for while there is no absence of space and time within space and time themselves, leading to the negation of those two without further conditions, there is no negation of the persisting sense of existence itself.

Therefore, since the existence of space, time, and their limiting adjuncts (upādhis), as well as the jar, is sublated by direct perception itself within the reality of Brahman—which is the substratum of those perceived adjuncts—their falsity is established. Likewise, it is established that all things are indeed false, because they are sublated by the direct perception of non-existence within Brahman—the object of the cognition of all entities—which serves as the substratum of their own nature along with the adjuncts of time and so forth; for the cognition of another entity qualified by the absence of something else is indeed perceptual.

Inference as well [establishes this]: all modifications (vikāras) are superimposed upon a single entity experienced by oneself, because, while each is permeated by a single nature, they are yet distinct; like the multiplicity of moons. Because they are insentient, because they are effects, and because they are distinct; like silver [superimposed on mother-of-pearl] and like the multiplicity of moons. Because they are negated by statements such as "not gross" (*asthūla*) within the context of the locus already apprehended; like the identification of the body with the self. Because they consist in the emergence of a contrary effect without the destruction of the nature of the contrary cause; like a magical tiger.
In the state of dissolution, [the self] is non-existent along with time within its own limiting adjunct (upādhi), just like the identification of the body as the self.

Presumption (*arthāpatti*) also [establishes this]: the birth and destruction of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) are untenable unless it is false; for Brahman and the Void, which are not false, are by nature devoid of birth and destruction. Nor can there be an inference of falsity regarding the knowledge of Brahman on the grounds that it is like the knowledge of the phenomenal world, because that would contradict the scriptural statement: "That is the Truth, That is the Self. Furthermore, statements such as "not gross" (*asthūla*) do not merely express a difference from the gross and so forth; for such a negation would be illogical if there were identity between cause and effect.

Just as, when one intends to express the difference [of a cow] from what is white, a negation such as "the cow is not white" is not observed; and likewise, in that negation, one observes only the negation of the very nature of whiteness. If it is argued that there can be no inference of falsity because reasoning is unstable (*tarkāpratiṣṭhānāt*), we say no; for that would entail the non-commencement of this treatise of inquiry.

If it is argued that there is no sense of contradiction regarding Brahman because it is rooted in scripture (*śabda*), then—by the force of the two scriptural passages, "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent" and "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone"—the cause would possess both existence and non-existence; for the meaning of scripture is beyond the scope of logic, owing to the omnipotence of Brahman.

If it is argued that everything is thus consistent, we say no; for this would entail the non-commencement of inquiry into Brahman in order to resolve contradictions. For this very reason, why might Brahman not sometimes even be unreal? Therefore, since the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is understood through perception, inference, and presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), and because Brahman is inherently quiescent, the scriptural accounts of creation are purposeless and constitute nothing but an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*). Nor is there any contradiction with the persistence of the notion of "Being" (*sad-buddhi*); for that [Being] is the underlying substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*), whereas it is only the specific particulars such as jars and the like that are false. Thus it is established.

Having restated the definition (*lakṣaṇa*), he says that the subsequent commentary is intended to declare the nature of the defined object (*lakṣyasvarūpa*): "Of this world... Now, one might object: this is certainly not a defining characteristic (*viśeṣaṇa-lak�ṣaṇa*), because the causality of the origin and so forth of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is itself a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the world; for it is impossible to comprehend a property that possesses a limiting adjunct without first stating the definition of the nature of Brahman which is devoid of limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhika*). Nor is this a secondary characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*).

Because it is impossible for the indicated object (*lakṣya*) to be the meaning of the word "Brahman" due to its being delimited, he says there: "For the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) is of two kinds," and so forth. Even if it is a secondary indication (*upalakṣaṇa*), there is no contradiction with the definition of the non-dual nature; for just as in the expression "that which appeared as silver is mother-of-pearl," there is the possibility of indication even by means of something false, such as the causality of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*). For the cause of a definition is an uncommon relation (*asādhāraṇasaṃbandha*), not the reality of the definition itself; since we observe that things like crows, though unconnected, serve as indicators of a house. [The phrase] "some [regard] the effected world" refers to the following.

The meaning is as follows: the Vedāntins hold that [the world] consists of name, form, and action; the followers of the Vārttika hold that it consists of substance, quality, action, and generality; the Śaivas hold that there are five categories: effect, cause, yoga, injunction, and the end of suffering; the Vaiśeṣikas hold that there are six: substance, quality, action, generality, particularity, and inherence; the Kṣapaṇakas (Jainas) hold that there are seven: soul, non-soul, influx, restraint, shedding, bondage, and liberation; and the Prābhākaras hold that there are eight: substance, quality, action, generality, particularity, power, dependence, and application.

The Naiyāyikas maintain that there are sixteen categories: means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), objects of valid cognition (*prameya*), doubt (*saṃśaya*), purpose (*prayojana*), example (*dṛṣṭānta*), tenet (*siddhānta*), members of a syllogism (*avayava*), reasoning (*tarka*), ascertainment (*nirṇaya*), discussion (*vāda*), sophistry (*jalpa*), cavil (*vitaṇḍā*), fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*), quibble (*chala*), futile rejoinder (*jāti*), and points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). The Sāṃkhyas maintain that there are twenty-five principles: the organs of knowledge (*jñānendriya*), the organs of action (*karmendriya*), the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the gross elements (*mahābhūta*), the mind (*manas*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), the intellect (*mahat*), the unmanifest (*avyakta*), and the person (*puruṣa*). What, then, is the established tenet? To address this, he says: "In order to exclude those [views]," and so forth. Although the world is thus manifested as "form" (*rūpa*)—so called because it is "formed" (*rūpyate*)—[the following applies].

To the question, "How is it that [the world] is produced as if endowed with form through name?", he says: "For when a thing is being manifested... The meaning is this: in the world, a potter desiring to make a jar first brings to manifestation within his own mind a conceptualization of the word "jar" and a conceptualization of its form characterized by a broad base and a rounded belly; subsequently, he produces the jar exactly as it has been manifested, which is fit to be the objective referent of the word "jar" and is endowed with the form of a broad base and a rounded belly.

In the same way, the Root Cause (mūlakāraṇa) also manifests everything that has appeared within its own intellect through name and form, and subsequently makes it manifest; thus it is said to be "differentiated by name and form" (*nāmarūpābhyām itthambhūtam vyākṛtam*). The passage beginning with "connected with many agents and enjoyers" and ending before the mention of other modifications of being such as transformation (*pariṇāma*) and so forth, is clear in meaning. Now, is the essential definition (*svarūpalakṣaṇa*) of Brahman, which was indicated here, being stated?

Furthermore, there is no cognition of any object whatsoever without its essential definition (*svarūpalakṣaṇa*). Nor is there an understanding of the moon by merely saying "the moon is where the tip of the branch is," without the cognition of its nature as supreme luminosity. Indeed, there is no cognition of any object whatsoever without its essential definition; nor is there an understanding of the moon by merely saying "the moon is where the tip of the branch is," without the cognition of its nature as supreme luminosity.

The state of possessing all powers (*sarvaśaktitva*) cannot be the unique characteristic of Brahman, because it is not distinct from [the attributes of] primordial matter (*pradhāna*) and other such entities. If it is argued that "omniscience" (*sarvajñatva*) is the characteristic, we say no; for since that is a property dependent on limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), it fails to establish the nature of Brahman as being devoid of limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhika*).

And how is this omniscience to be explained? It cannot be that one knows everything through the means of valid cognition consisting of perception, inference, verbal testimony, analogy, postulation, and non-apprehension; for these do not function simultaneously, and because [if they did] the status of everything as an object of perception would be lost. Furthermore, even when these [means] exist, we ourselves lack omniscience, and because the sense organs lack the capacity to grasp objects remote in space, time, or substance—whether by way of inherence in what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*), conjunction with what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasaṃyoga*), or qualification of what is conjoined (*saṃyuktaviśeṣaṇatā*).

For if it were so, the consequence would follow that even for us [ordinary people], there would be direct perception of all objects. Furthermore, even mental cognition regarding things other than the self depends upon the sense organs and so forth; thus, nothing is accessible through mental perception alone. Nor can an object unfit for the senses be grasped by them even through the power of an excellence (*dharmātiśaya*) in the faculties; for we observe that even the vision of cats and similar creatures possesses excellence only with respect to objects such as visible forms that are already fit for their senses. Finally, a mental cognition of an omniscient being—produced by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the contemplation of everything—does not cause one to grasp all objects.

Firstly, if there is no grasping of the entire object (*kṛtsnārtha*), then mental cultivation (*paribhāvanā*) regarding it is impossible, and consequently, the cognition that grasps the entire [object] produced by that cultivation is impossible. Furthermore, if the entire object were grasped even prior to such cultivation, then this consequence would apply to us as well. Moreover, because the limits of past, future, and present objects cannot be determined, the grasping of everything is untenable; for one cannot determine that "this is all there is, and nothing beyond this remains unknown. Nor does omniscience consist in the knowledge of the [cognition's own] intrinsic nature alone, since—like the light of a lamp—it lacks the capacity to grasp past and future objects. Therefore, there is no omniscient being.

It is said: Since [the Lord] is the agent of everything, His knowledge of all objects pertaining to His present effects is established. Likewise, because He possesses the comprehension of all past objects at their respective times, memory—which consists in the non-losing of experienced objects—is postulated as being unobstructed and universal, having as its limiting adjunct (upādhi) the transformation of His own Māyā. Similarly, even prior to creation, there exists knowledge of all future objects, since such determination of the objects to be created is observed in the case of potters and others.

Since [omniscience] is attributed through the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the transformation of its own *māyā*, omniscience is logical. Furthermore, because the term "all-knowing" is applied to the cause of the universe in the scriptural passage, "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving," omniscience is established as a proven fact by both scripture and reasoning. Now, it was argued that because it is a quality conditioned by an adjunct, it cannot be the defining characteristic of the essential nature (*svarūpa*); but this is not so.

By this term "omniscient," what is intended is consciousness itself—mere representation (*vijñaptimātra*) capable of illuminating everything, like the light of the sun and so forth, which is free from the limitations of objects—as the defining characteristic of the nature of Brahman; thus there is no contradiction. As for the passage beginning with "But others also... and so forth, its meaning is clear.

One might object: "Why not take the very statement of Yāska as the basis and include the six transformations of being (bhāvavikāra) even in the Sūtra? Thus he raises the objection: "Now, [regarding] the six transformations of being. The meaning of the rebuttal beginning with "of those enumerated by Yāska" is as follows: for a Vedic (ārṣeya) statement, the source of authority is either direct perception (pratyakṣa) or scripture (āgama); inference and other means do not require a verbal statement, since we too proceed by means of them.

In that regard, if the statement of Yāska were based on perception (*pratyakṣa*), then only the modifications of material things (*bhautika-dharma*) could be apprehended through perception, and not those pertaining to the great elements (*mahābhūta*). If, in that case, Brahman were taken as the cause of these material modifications, then Brahman would be understood merely as the pentad of elements. However, since the Śruti is independent of any other root means of knowledge, it is possible to understand Brahman as the root cause of whatever possesses the property of coming into being.

Furthermore, since the sūtras have the meaning of the Śruti as their ultimate purpose, he states that the Śruti itself is the root of the "Janmādi" sūtra: "because [the sūtra] has the purpose of determining its meaning."

Is it not proper to understand that Brahman is not the root cause of the elements and elemental objects? For Māyā also is a root cause, according to the Śruti: "But Māyā, indeed, is Prakṛti. If it is argued that Māyā is merely an instrument, since *prakṛti* means "that by which something is produced," we say no; for the word *prakṛti* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in the sense of the material cause (*upādāna*), and thus its etymological derivation is inadmissible. If it is argued that it is so derived because another material cause is heard in the text, "From the Self, space [was born]," we say no.

Because the grammatical suffix is identical, because it would contradict [Māyā] being the material cause (*prakṛti*), because the ablative case is used even for the instrumental cause (*nimitta*), and because the rule that Māyā is the material cause is established by following the observed insentience [of the world]. If it is argued that in the passage "Indra by means of Māyās," the instrumental case alone is heard, that is true; however, that [instrumentality] occurs when there is the production of multiplicity in the Self. What loss is there if it is the material cause of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*)? If it is argued that two independent material causes are untenable, then they may serve as material causes in mutual distinction, like two threads of rope.

Therefore, if it were argued that since Māyā also resides in Brahman—the cause of the world—it would be characterized as Brahman itself, and that "Māyā" is synonymous with "Prajñā" (wisdom), which is none other than the consciousness of Brahman, and thus there is no contradiction—this is not so, because it contradicts the principles of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). In common usage, the word "Māyā" is observed to be employed through positive and negative concomitance regarding perceived objects such as elephants, horses, and chariots, both when their limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) are present and when they are sublated. Furthermore, this [interpretation] contradicts worldly experience.

For they do not call one who possesses superior wisdom a "magician" (māyāvin), nor do the learned apply the word "māyā" to a wise person. Since the word *māyā* has the intellect (*buddhi*) as its object, there is no possibility of applying it to the wisdom of the Brahman-consciousness. Alternatively, because the intellect manifests in various illusory forms such as dreams and the like, the proponents of the theory of the effect-in-the-cause (*kāryavādin*) maintain that the word *māyā* is used figuratively for the instrument (*karaṇa*), which is thus beyond reproach.

Moreover: "And finally, there is the cessation of the universal illusion (viśvamāyānivṛttiḥ)"; "Those who take refuge in Me alone cross over this illusion (taranti... māyām)"; "For this divine illusion (devī... māyā) of Mine, consisting of the qualities (guṇamayī), is difficult to overcome"; and "Those whose knowledge has been carried away by illusion have resorted to a demonic nature. Because of these indicators—namely, that it is something to be crossed over, that it consists of the qualities, and that it is an obscuration of knowledge—Brahman-consciousness is not *māyā*. If it is argued that *buddhi* (intellect) itself is *māyā*, we say no; for that would contradict the use of the term *prakṛti* (primordial material cause). If it is argued that *māyā* refers to spells, herbs, and so forth, we say no; [for those are not the subject under discussion].

Because the word *māyā* is applied to such things as a perceived city of the Gandharvas, but it is not so applied to spells, medicinal herbs, and the like; yet, if it is argued that the insentient power of *māyā* is ultimately real (*pāramārthika*), we say no. For the state of the world prior to its manifestation is heard in scripture to be "neither non-existent nor existent, but darkness was," thus being indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*) and distinct from both the existent and the non-existent. Furthermore, in common worldly usage, the word *māyā* is applied to the mere category of false objects, which persists even when specific instances such as elephants, horses, and chariots vary.

"The yogi crosses over the widespread ignorance and illusion (māyā) when [the Lord] is established in his heart; salutation to that immeasurable Self of Knowledge. Because of this co-referentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) between māyā and avidyā, it follows that Brahman is the cause as qualified by an indeterminable (anirvacanīya) māyā; to this, he replies: "Therefore, that which is the support upon which the entire universe evolves (vivartate)."

In this regard, three possibilities arise: either Brahman qualified by Māyā is the cause, like a rope [appearing as such] due to two joined threads; or, according to the Śruti passage, "The power inherent in the divine Self is concealed by its own qualities," the cause is that which possesses the power of Māyā; or else, Brahman is the cause by virtue of being the substratum of Māyā, which is the material cause of the world. Among these, in the case of the "qualified" (viśiṣṭa) position, the pure Brahman is established through two definitions: first, by the definition of its essential nature as knowledge, bliss, and so forth, and second, by the exclusion of Māyā from that which is characterized as Brahman in that very way.

Regarding the two subsequent positions, however, since *māyā* is dependent upon Brahman, its effect is also dependent upon Brahman; just as a cloth, though woven from threads that are themselves dependent on the yarns, is perceived as dependent on the yarns. Consequently, that which serves as the substratum and limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) for the effect being produced, and which is characterized by knowledge and bliss—that is Brahman; thus there is the attainment of the pure Brahman. This is what he expresses by the words "that which is the support" (*yadavaṣṭambha*).

However, some maintain that Brahman itself undergoes transformation (*pariṇāma*) into the form of the world, just as clay transforms into the form of a pot; they refute this by stating that "the universe is an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*). *Vivarta* is the appearance of multiple, unreal forms, contrary to its previous state, in something that does not deviate from its own essential nature (*tattva*). *Pariṇāma*, on the other hand, is the assumption of another real form by something through the abandonment of its previous form. In that case, they must provide a proof for their claim that Brahman does not undergo *vivarta* but only *pariṇāma*. [They point to] the scriptural texts concerning creation (*sṛṣṭi-śruti*).

If it is argued that [Brahman] undergoes transformation (*pariṇāma*), then it must be stated: does that scriptural passage on creation declare that Brahman—which is by nature established as prior, consisting of knowledge, bliss, truth, partless, and unlimited—undergoes a transition into an effect that is insentient, suffering, false, composed of parts, and limited, thereby abandoning its prior established nature; or does it declare that Brahman undergoes a transition into the form of an effect opposite to that [nature] without abandoning its prior established form? In the former case, through the abandonment of the prior [nature], the very essence of Brahman would be destroyed, and there would remain only the effect.

If it is argued that [Brahman] transforms again into the form of knowledge, bliss, and so forth during the state of dissolution, this would entail the consequence of no liberation (*anirmokṣa*). Furthermore, there would be a contradiction with such scriptural passages as, "The Self is unborn, great, and eternal," and "It is not born. Now, if one were to say that the scripture on creation teaches the assumption of an effect-form while not abandoning the original nature of Brahman, then it must be understood as teaching *vivarta* (illusory manifestation); for that is the defining characteristic of *vivarta*, as seen in cases such as nacre appearing as silver, or a magical illusion appearing as a tiger.

If it is argued that the scriptural account of creation concerns only the act of creation itself and does not operate regarding whether or not the prior nature is abandoned, even so, because it forms a single syntactical unit with the passages concerning the established Brahman, it demonstrates only *vivarta* (illusory manifestation), declaring that Brahman assumes the form of an effect precisely without abandoning its own nature; thus, this position is faultless. As for the one who says that even that which is partless undergoes transformation (*pariṇāma*), [that too is untenable].

For instance, when a substance of gold transforms into the form of a *rūcaka* (necklace), it must be stated whether its constituent parts (*avayava*) also transform or not. If they do transform, then those parts would likewise [transform], and thus the transformation would extend all the way down to partless atoms (*niravayava*). On the other hand, if they do not transform, then the whole (*avayavin*) would not transform either; for a change in that which is supported is impossible without a change in its substratum.

Therefore, just as conjunction, which inheres in a part of a composite whole, is preceded by a series of conjunctions of partless atoms, so too the transformation of a composite whole is preceded by the transformation of partless [atoms].

He should be asked: "What is this transformation (pariṇāma)? If it is held that transformation consists in the state of having parts congealed through the attainment of a different conjunction by its own parts from their previous conjunction, or through conjunction with other parts, then there can be no transformation in that which is partless; for the partless has no parts of its own. Furthermore, apart from the congealing of parts through a different conjunction, it is impossible to define a transformation, a change of state, or a becoming otherwise of the whole.

Furthermore, transformation (pariṇāma) is neither the conjunction of one thing with another thing, nor vibration, nor the arising of a different quality; for these do not exist in Brahman. Moreover, there is no cognition of transformation in the case of ether when it is conjoined with another thing, nor in a bee when it is vibrating, nor in a jar when redness arises, because they are substances.

Now, if it is argued that transformation (*pariṇāma*) is the production of another substance consequent upon that [original substance], then in this case, does the transformation of the gold parts occur in the form of the *rucaka* (the earring) itself, or in the form of a different substance? It cannot be in the form of a different substance, because no effect-substance distinct from the *rucaka* substance is observed there. Nor can it be in the form of the *rucaka* itself, because that [transformation] belongs to the whole (*avayavin*), and the persistence of the parts within the *rucaka* is already accounted for (*anyathāsiddha*) by the very persistence of the whole that inheres in those parts.

Furthermore, no other states of the gold particles are observed apart from the state of being a *rucaka* (necklace), by which there could be a difference in transformation (*pariṇāma*). Nor has it been stated that a mere difference in conjunction constitutes the transformation of the parts. Furthermore, it is not logical to claim that the gold particles transform into the form of a *rucaka* without a composite substance (*avayavin*), for that would entail the doctrine of new production (*ārambhavāda*). If it is argued that the transformation of the parts, though unperceived, is postulated because the transformation of the whole is otherwise impossible;

This argument—that because a modification of the substrate (āśraya) is impossible without a modification of that which is supported (āśrita)—is not sound. For if there is birth and destruction of the whole (avayavin), it would follow that its constituent parts (avayava), being dependent upon it, must also undergo birth and destruction, just as when the whole departs, the parts must also depart. If it is argued that there will instead be a transformation (pariṇāma), we say no; for while the genus "pot-ness" (ghaṭatva-jāti) inheres in the whole, the parts do not possess the inherence of that genus "pot-ness."

Now, one might object: how can there be a transformation of the whole (avayavin) without a transformation of its parts? For a substance does not undergo a change of state by becoming another substance, nor does it acquire a new quality such as blueness, or a different state. Furthermore, it has already been stated that no effect of the parts is observed apart from the effect of the whole. Indeed, even when another effect appears in the cloth, the threads do not appear as non-threads. It has also been stated that the persistence of the threads within the effect of the cloth is established otherwise, namely, through their own persistence persisting within it.

Furthermore, transformation in parts is observed only when there is the limiting condition (upādhi) of a composite whole (avayavin); thus, the transformation of a partless self (ātman) devoid of such conditions cannot be established. As for the claim that transformation occurs like the conjunction of partless entities, even in that case, the conjunction of composites that is perceived is not inherent in the atoms themselves; for if it were, it would follow that it would be imperceptible, just like the color and other qualities residing in them. Nor can conjunction in a partless entity be postulated on the grounds of its conjunction with a single part of a composite.

Just as the inherence of a universal occurs in the whole alone, so too conjunction is logically possible in the whole alone even without a conjunction among the parts. This is because the persistence of conjunction among the parts is otherwise accounted for by the persistence of the whole. If it is argued that conjunction resides only in the parts and not in the whole, we say no; for it would follow that two unjoined wholes could not initiate another effect. Therefore, conjunction resides only in the whole and not in the parts.

If it is argued that, in the case of inherence in a whole possessing parts, conjunction would necessarily involve total pervasion (kṛtsnavṛttitā), then it follows that even in the conjunction of partless entities, there would be no increase in volume due to such total pervasion. How, then, is the partlessness of Brahman established? It is said: since both the parts and the whole are self-luminous, they cannot be objects to one another; therefore, it is impossible for Brahman to experience its own state of possessing parts within itself.

If either [of the two] were not self-luminous, then because it would be known by the other—as in the case of a jar and the self—the relationship of part and whole could not be established. Furthermore, the Śruti states that [Brahman] is devoid of parts and action, saying, "Partless, actionless, and tranquil. If it is argued that actions such as being a controller are also heard of in scripture, then, given this mutual contradiction, one must postulate a distinction between reality and unreality based on Māyā; for it is heard in scripture that the activity of the conscious [Self] is dependent upon Māyā, as in: "By means of Māyās, He is perceived in many forms."

Since deep sleep is understood to be a human goal, and since Brahman lacks any purpose for spontaneous activity, and because the occurrence of a contrary effect without the abandonment of its own true nature constitutes a vivarta, this is established.

One might object: "Indeed, the status of being the cause of the origin of the world cannot be taken as an established fact to serve as the definition of Brahman, because it is not proven that the five elements are effects, since material things have the elements as their material causes. He raises this objection with the words, "Now, if one were to adopt [the definition] as indicated by the Śruti," and so forth. The meaning of the refutation beginning with "It is said" (*ucyate*) is as follows: Earth, water, fire, and air are the subjects of dispute; they possess birth and destruction, because they are objects of the cognitions of earth, water, fire, and air, just like a portion of earth, water, fire, or air.

[Objection: Is there not a counter-inference? [Thesis: Earth and the other elements are not produced; [Reason: because they are great elements (*mahābhūta*); [Example: like space. And space is not produced; [Reason: because it is a partless substance; [Example: like the Self (*ātman*). Thus, a specific demonstration (*viśeṣato darśana*) is indeed more powerful; therefore, [the position] is faultless. The author states the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of the commentary (*bhāṣya*) beginning with "not of that which possesses the aforementioned qualifications," by means of the passage starting with "reasoning also for the determination of the nature of Brahman," and so forth.

He explains the commentary beginning with "of this world" (*asya jagataḥ*) as follows: "not from anything else, such as the *pradhāna* imagined by others. This is the meaning: for all internal states (*ādhyātmika-bhāva*) have pleasure, pain, and delusion as their common material cause (*prakṛti*), because they possess a nature that is invariably associated with the commonality of pleasure, pain, and delusion. Whatever modifications (*vikāra*) possess a nature associated with something are seen to have that as their material cause, just as bowls and the like, which are associated with clay, have clay as their material cause.

Likewise, the Sāṃkhyas infer that all modifications have an undivided single material cause (*prakṛti*), because they consist of many finite modifications; for whatever consists of many finite modifications has an undivided single material cause, just as jars and other such objects have a lump of clay as their material cause—thus they infer the Pradhāna to be the root cause of the world. Similarly, the proponents of the atomic theory (*aṇuvādins*) infer: every effect-substance is produced by multiple homogeneous substances possessing a dimension smaller than its own, assisted by conjunction, because it is an effect-substance.

Whatever is an effect-substance is composed of such [parts], just as a cloth is composed of multiple substances; since inference proceeds in this manner down to partless atoms, atoms are the fundamental cause. Likewise, the proponents of emptiness (Śūnyavādins) say: "Every effect must be preceded by non-existence, because, while possessing the capacity for existence, its prior state is not perceived; just like the self imagined by others. Thus, they maintain that everything everywhere has emptiness as its objective support.

The Yogas and the Śaivas—namely the followers of Hiraṇyagarbha and Paśupati—postulate Hiraṇyagarbha and Paśupati as the cause of the world on the authority of their respective scriptures. He sets aside those positions with the words beginning "not from another," meaning "not from what is postulated by others."

Therein, first of all, he establishes the fulfillment of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with the textual portion preceding "firstly, from the insentient" (*acetanāt tāvat*). How so? First, in the Sāṃkhya inference, the connection of entities with pleasure, pain, and delusion (*sukha-duḥkha-moha*) is not accepted; for they are perceived as being either internal or external. This might be argued: "All modifications (*vikāra*) consist of pleasure, pain, and delusion, because, while being colored by the mind (*citta*), they are the cause of the appearance of those [mental] forms therein."

[The opponent argues: "Just as a reflection is the cause for the appearance of the form of a face due to its being colored by a mirror, so too is the association of pleasure, pain, and delusion inferred in entities. [Reply: This is not so, because it contradicts the perceptual evidence of the distinction between internal and external existence, and because it would entail the undesirable consequence that those perceiving a single sound would each individually perceive the triad of pleasure, pain, and delusion. Furthermore, it is impossible to restrict the causal capacity of a thing by means of the unseen (adṛṣṭa). Therefore, the reason is unestablished and inconclusive, since substances are associated with qualities and universals that are not their material causes.

As for the argument that [the world] is finite, even there, if "finiteness" refers to actual finitude, the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to the *guṇas* and the *puruṣa*. If it refers to finitude in space and time, it is inconclusive with respect to jars, hailstones, and the like, which are perceived to have origins distinct from their material cause (*prakṛti*). Furthermore, even in the Vaiśeṣika inference—that a substance is produced by something smaller than its own dimension—the reason is inconclusive because we observe that a rope made from long and wide silk cloths is itself short, despite being an effect; moreover, this inference is vitiated by a counter-inference (*pratyanumāna*).

No effect-substance whatsoever is preceded by a conjunction of partless substances, because it consists of an accumulation (pracaya). Whatever consists of an accumulation is not preceded by a conjunction of partless substances, just like a jar. Even in the case of the inference regarding the void, the prior state of the jar is perceived through direct observation; thus, the reason [in your argument]—"because its prior state, namely clay, is not perceived"—is unestablished (asiddha). Now, intending to refute the meaning [of the opponent's position], he says: "First, from the insentient, because of its very insentiency," and so forth.

Lest it be argued that while a diverse creation of effects cannot arise from a non-intelligent *pradhāna*, in the theory of atoms (*paramāṇuvāda*), however, because a presiding Lord (*īśvara*) exists, the diverse creation of the world as an effect will come about through the power of His intellect—anticipating this objection, he says: "Even from a sentient [cause]..."

The meaning is this: since God, who is inferred by the example of the potter and others, possesses a power of knowledge limited by a body and sense organs, the construction of the world would be impossible for one whose power of knowledge is thus limited according to that very same example. Consequently, there would follow the consequence of two agents for jars and other objects; therefore, such an inference must apply to the primal cause as well.

Regarding the claim that the world has emptiness (*śūnya*) as its objective support, he says: "Furthermore, because of non-existence... Nor can the world have that which is indefinable (*nirupākhya*) as its material cause, because of the persistence of existence (*sadanvaya*). Moreover, if that which is indefinable were the cause, then since the previous cycle (*kalpa*) would have perished without leaving a trace, there would be an absence of residual impressions (*saṃskāra*); consequently, there would be no regulating factor for the production of effects of the same kind again. Thus, for those who performed actions with the desire for specific animals and so forth in a particular configuration, such animals and the like would not arise in a subsequent cycle. Furthermore, this would apply to the relationship between words and their meanings, as well as to those who engage in linguistic usage.

"On the back of the firmament, for that period of time, he shines in heaven like the sun; then, at the beginning of the Kṛta Yuga, O noble ones, purified by Brahman, the omniscient and steadfast Ṛṣi is born again, remembering [his past]. Thus, regarding those things established by such scriptural passages...

Because there is destruction without any continuity (*niranvaya-vināśa*), because there would be no engagement in linguistic convention in another eon due to the lack of recollection of the conventions of the previous eon, and because in the case of a new convention, the meaning of the word "cow" (*go-padārtha*)—which is a property not accessible through other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)—cannot be established as the means to an unprecedented result; furthermore, because the composition of the sentence "One should sacrifice with a cow" (*gavā yajeta*) would be untenable if one were to apply the word "cow" after having first cognized that [meaning] as the means to an unprecedented result, he states [the consequence]: "due to the absence of the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of past eons," and so forth, [concluding that] there would be the total cessation of the linguistic usage concerning ritual action, its fruit, and its means of knowledge.

Here the proponent of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvavādin*) argues: "This [world] arises without dependence on a cause. Now, does it mean that it is itself its own cause, or rather that it arises without any cause? We say it arises without a cause. But then, would not the existence and non-existence of a jar occur simultaneously, since it would be independent of a cause that acts in succession? To this we reply: if you claim that the sequential operation of a cause is its very intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then you fall into the position of *svabhāvavāda*. If, on the other hand, it depends on another cause, then there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*)."

If it is argued that there is a sequence of effects due to a difference in time, then if that temporal sequence were inherent (*svābhāvika*), it would be the doctrine of inherent nature (*svabhāvavāda*); if it depended on another cause, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Therefore, all diverse and sequential effects arise by their very nature (*svabhāvena*) according to what is observed; to this, he replies with the words beginning "not by inherent nature" (*na svabhāvataḥ*).

The meaning is that even for entities whose capacities are established intrinsically (*svataḥsiddha*), their mutual relationship as benefactor and beneficiary (*upakāryopakārakabhāva*) is established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). The word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) serves as a conclusion. Now, one might object: "Logicians establish the Lord with the aforementioned qualifications by means of inference alone; why then is it said to be established by scripture (*āgama*) accompanied by reasoning (*yukti*? To this he says: "This very [scripture] is the inference," and so forth. For reasoning (*yukti*) merely produces a sense of probability (*saṃbhāvanā*), whereas inference (*anumāna*) brings about certainty regarding the object.

The fallacy of the non-establishment of pervasion (*vyāptyanupapatti-ābhāsa*) is the mere presentation of an example (*udāharaṇa*); the reasoning (*yukti*) is the non-deviant pervasion (*avyabhicāriṇī vyāpti*), and inference (*anumāna*) is [the conclusion derived from it]. In this regard, the fact that the omniscient Lord is the cause cannot be ascertained by means of examples such as the potter, because of the possibility of contrary examples; rather, when there is another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it can be rendered probable by means of examples such as the potter. Therefore, this is merely reasoning (*yukti*). In that context, they mistakenly consider this reasoning—which does not ascertain the object—to be inference due to ignorance.

What is that inference? It is stated as follows: "Every effect has an agent who possesses knowledge regarding its own nature, material cause, instruments, recipient, purpose, capacity, and object, because it is an effect produced through a manifold arrangement; like a jar," etc.—this is the Vaiśeṣika inference. The Sāṃkhya-Yogins [state]: "The powers of knowledge and sovereignty, increasing in degree, must terminate somewhere in one possessing the power of knowledge and sovereignty over all objects, because they are qualities that increase according to a comparative scale (taratama-bhāva)."

They infer that [the world] possesses finite dimensions (*parimāṇavat*). The Naiyāyikas, however, infer: "The entire collection of fruits of action is bestowed by one who possesses specific knowledge of the actions, their fruits, the agents who enjoy them, as well as the particularities of place, time, and so forth, because they are fruits of action, just like the fruits of actions such as service."

In that regard, concerning the Vaiśeṣika inference—namely, the inference that the world has many agents and that its agent possesses limited knowledge, power, and so forth—this is mere reasoning, because an illustrative example (udāharaṇa) is possible [only for a single agent]. Even in the Yoga inference, when one merely infers that the powers of knowledge and sovereignty reach their ultimate limit somewhere, how can omniscience and the like be established, given that this results only in the establishment of knowledge regarding the objects to be perceived? Furthermore, if one were to infer knowledge and so forth regarding all objects, there would be inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatā) due to factors such as weight, attachment, aversion, suffering, and error; thus, this too is mere reasoning.

Even in the inference of the Naiyāyikas, since it is observed that the fruit of karma has many givers possessing bodies, sense organs, and so forth, a single God is not established; therefore, [the Naiyāyikas] consider their inference to be merely a logical argument (*yuktimātra*)—serving only as a cause for a notion of probability through illustration—in order to lead to the realization of the non-dual Brahman, who is the cause of all, omniscient, the Lord of all, the giver of all fruits, and known through scripture. Thus, due to ignorance, they regard this as an inference that provides certainty as to "what that [Brahman] is."

[Objection: "But if there are already [scriptural] statements, why the effort of inference? [The author] replies: "Because it is a restatement of a matter established by inference," as stated in the words *janmādi* (the origin, etc.). [Objection: "But even in the Sūtra, these very same inferences were set forth independently as means for determining the meaning; so how can this reasoning be subordinate to scripture? [The author] raises this objection with the words *nanvihāpi tadevopanyastam* (But here too, that very same thing has been presented), and so forth.

He refutes this with the words, "Not so, because [the Upanishads] have the purpose of stringing together the Vedānta statements," and so forth. Furthermore, from mere inference, only the general existence of a cause is established, but nothing more; here, however, what is intended is the realization of Brahman as the inner self—truth, knowledge, infinite, and omniscient. Nor can a specific object be established by scripture alone or by inference whose scope is merely general; thus he says, "by those [means] introduced by the *Samanvaya* Sūtra," and so forth. It might then be argued that no reasoning (*yukti*) is set forth here, since the specific object is established by scripture alone; to this he replies, "But when [reasonings] exist," and so on.

The passage beginning with "not in the inquiry into Dharma" has a clear meaning. *Śruti* is a word that is independent of other words. *Liṅga* (indicative power) is the inseparable connection of a stated meaning with another meaning. *Vākya* (syntactical connection) is the capacity of multiple words [to convey a single sense]. *Prakaraṇa* (context) concerns matters studied as a commencement based on the lack of syntactical connection between two sentences. *Sthāna* (position) is the relationship of items occurring in a sequence with other items occurring in a sequence according to their respective order. *Samākhyā* (name/designation) is the commonality of names.

Now, it might be argued that once the nature of Brahman has been determined by the word (śabda), there is no further purpose served by direct experience (anubhava); nor can that which is an object of verbal knowledge be experienced. To this, he replies with the words beginning "because it culminates in experience" (anubhavāvasānatvāt).
The passage beginning with "nanu dharmajijñāsāyām" has a clear meaning. He raises an objection—asking "how?"—as to why dharma is independent of experience.

He shows that because *dharma* is incapable of being experienced and because experience is not required for it, there is no dependence on anything other than the word—by means of the passage beginning with "for [that which is] to be done" (*kartavyam hi*). Now, one might ask: even if an established entity (*siddhasvabhāva*) were capable of being experienced, why would experience be required? To this he replies: "But here, of that which is established... (*iha tu siddhasya*).

[Objection: "But surely, since there is no difference in being knowable through the Veda, there should be no requirement for reflection (*manana*), meditative concentration (*nididhyāsana*), and direct experience (*anubhava*) regarding Brahman, just as there is none regarding *dharma*; or else, there should be such a requirement regarding *dharma* as well, just as there is regarding Brahman. To this, he says: "For [there is no requirement] in the case of those two which terminate in what is to be accomplished and what is already established" (*na hi kartavyasiddhārthaniṣṭhayoḥ*). Let it be granted that [the realization of Brahman] is also something to be brought about by human will; to that, he says: "Therefore, [there is no application] of injunctions and prohibitions" (*tato vidhipratiṣedha*). The meaning is that, unlike [the cases of] "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) and "one should not eat" (*na bhakṣayet*), Brahman cannot be an object of injunction or prohibition. [He continues with the word] "option" (*vikalpa*).

The option based on desire (*icchāvikalpa*) is like [the injunctions] "with rice or with barley," or "it is either Brahman or a post. The conjunction (*samuccaya*) refers to the conjunction of the six sacrifices; here the meaning is "both Brahman and a post. Regarding the general rule and its exception (*utsargāpavāda*): it is like [the rules] "one should not harm any living beings," "one should sacrifice an animal to Agni and Soma," "one offers in the Āhavanīya fire," and "one offers at the footprint"—wherein there is an exception (*apavāda*) to the Brahman understood through the general rule in a specific case. Regarding sublation and addition (*bādhābhyuccaya*).

Just as the *kuśa*-grass blades prescribed for the archetype (*prakṛti*) are set aside by the *śara*-grass blades prescribed for the ectype (*vikṛti*), so too there is sometimes the setting aside of the *brahman* priest—who has been obtained through extension—by another ritual element. Furthermore, just as the five *nāriṣṭa* oblations of the archetype are performed in conjunction with the additional oblations (*upahoma*) of the ectype, so too the performance of the extended *brahman* priest in conjunction with one who is specifically prescribed constitutes "augmentation" (*abhyuccaya*).

Just as in the case of the five *prayāja* offerings prescribed for the archetype (*prakṛti*) which are extended by implication (*atideśa*) to the ectype (*vikṛti*), where the injunction "one performs eleven *prayājas*" is taught for the ectype, resulting in the performance of sixteen *prayājas* through their combination and repetition, so too is the performance of Brahman through its combination with that which is extended by implication; this is "addition" (*abhyuccaya*). As for "restricted option" (*vyavasthita-vikalpa*): it is a restriction such as "one offers when the sun has risen" or "one offers before the sun has risen" according to different recensional branches (*śākhā*), or the restriction that Brahman exists in some cases and does not exist in others.
If it is argued that there is thus an equality of nature with Brahman, he says "no"—"not in the case of a real entity. He elaborates on that very point: "And likewise, in one [entity]..."

The preceding portion, ending with "another objects," has a clear meaning. Again, those who maintain the theory of inference raise an objection: "But [if it is argued] that [the means of knowledge] has as its object an already existing thing... [The opponent continues: "Surely the sūtra does not appear to be intended to indicate inference. To this, he replies: "By the previous sūtra..."

He provides the rebuttal—starting with "Not being an object of the senses, etc."—that even though Brahman, which is the inner self consisting of knowledge and bliss, is an existing reality, its direct experience cannot be produced by the eyes and other organs, nor by inferences whose objects are merely generalities. The word "therefore" serves as the conclusion.

The phrase "nanu evaṃ sati" (if this were so) has a clear meaning. The meaning of the rebuttal beginning with "ucyate" (it is said) is as follows: although logical arguments (*yukti*) are incapable of definitively establishing Brahman—which is of the nature of knowledge, bliss, omniscience, and the inner self—they nevertheless serve as causes for a sense of probability regarding Brahman as understood through scripture, by way of general principles. How so? When Brahman is understood from the word "non-dual" (*advitīya*) as the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world, non-duality becomes probable because, through examples such as clay, the effect cannot be determined apart from its material cause.

Through the analogies of the redness reflected in a crystal, a rope-snake, and the space within a jar, it is made plausible that agency and other attributes are merely superimposed upon the Self; that there is identity between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman; that the phenomenal world (prapañca), apart from Brahman, lacks independence; and that there is the state of the pure, non-dual inner Self by way of its being unattached (asaṅga). To address the question—"What, then, is that Vedic statement?"—the Commentary says: "In every Vedāntic statement, of the word 'Brahman'... and so forth.

The meaning of the refutation beginning with "Of those Vedānta statements... is as follows: although the referent of the term *brahman*—the non-dual inner self (*pratyagātman*) characterized by reality, consciousness, and bliss—is not well-known, its mere greatness (*bṛhattva*) is well-established. Therefore, by restating that [well-known greatness], it is possible to comprehend the qualified *brahman* through the power of the connection with the proximate terms. Thus, the sentence beginning with "reality" (*satya*) is intended to propound *brahman*, and by implication, that very [sentence] constitutes its definition; consequently, there is no [defect] regarding the definition of the nature of *brahman* as reality, consciousness, and bliss.

Regarding the objection that this would result in the restatement of what is already established (*siddhānuvāda*): surely the comprehension of meaning does not follow the order of the recitation of the *svādhyāya*, but rather the reverse, according to the maxim that "the unknown is [established] by means of the known. Thus, since the cause is well-known, the function of the sentence is: "That from which space was produced—that Self is Truth, Knowledge, the Infinite Brahman"; and likewise, "He from whom this Brahman, name, form, and food are born, is the All-knowing, the All-perceiving."

It is true that, by restating the cause alone—such as "that from which the vital breaths and so forth are born, he is the divine, formless Person," or "that which is the source of beings, invisible and ungraspable," or "that from which fire, water, and food are born, that is Being, non-dual, the subtle essence, That thou art"—the specific nature of that cause is established. However, this was said with a view toward the sequence of [establishing] the qualified seeker, the knowledge, the duty, and the realization of Brahman as the Self. Thus he says: "In the same way, there is an illustration."

One might object: "Since multiplicity is also perceived in the cause of the world, how can Brahman be established by restating that [multiplicity]? Thus he asks: "How? He answers with the words beginning "by what was previously stated," and so forth.

The meaning is this: even when there is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the mere cause of the world, if there were a suspicion of its multiplicity, its oneness is also established by the designation of unity in the word "from which" (*yataḥ*). An objection may be raised: "In a restatement, a new cognition (*pramiti*) is untenable. This is not so; since there is no prior statement (*purovāda*) regarding the oneness of the cause of the world, oneness is established by the very force of the restatement itself; otherwise, the restatement would be purposeless. An objection may be raised: "If both oneness and the definition of Brahman are being cognized, there would be a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*). This is not so, because of the oneness...

The realization of Brahman is subordinate because it forms a single syntactical unit [with the primary injunction]. Alternatively—oneness itself is included within the *lakṣya* (the object to be characterized), not within the *lakṣaṇa* (the characteristic). For instance, by restating the mere cause of the world, one Brahman is enjoined. To the question, "What follows from that?", he says: "By implication, [it is] omniscient. The sentence does not aim at establishing a relationship between a name and the named; rather, it aims at conveying the meaning.

But he says that the relationship between the name and the named is based on meaning: "Desire to know That again," and so forth. The meaning is this: the cause of the world is one, all-knowing, all-powerful, and unlimited in every respect, and that is what is denoted by the word *brahman*.

[Objection: Is it not the case that without stating the nature of Brahman as free from limiting adjuncts (nirupādhika), it is not proper to understand attributes such as omniscience and so forth as belonging to something possessing limiting adjuncts (sopādhika)? [Reply: That is not so; for just as in the cases of "That which is hollow is space" (*yat suṣiraṃ tadākāśam*) and "The moon is the most excellent light" (*prakṛṣṭaprakāśaścandraḥ*), some definition of its essential nature (*svarūpalakṣaṇa*) must be stated. [Objection: Is it not the case that the very thing denoted by the word "Brahman" is the definition of its essential nature? [Reply: No, because the word merely denotes the attribute of being vast (*bṛhattva*).

If it is argued that when "a large jar" is said, the jar—being the substratum—is perceived as possessing largeness without any further qualification, and likewise here too it must be stated that the definition is that which is denoted by the word "Being," we say no; for [the word "Being"] denotes only the Great Universal (mahāsāmānya). When "it exists" is said, a particular instance of a subordinate universal, such as "jar," is required as the terminus of that Great Universal; likewise, here too, a particular instance of a subordinate universal must be stated.

If it is argued that consciousness (*vijñāna*) alone, by virtue of possessing attributes such as vastness and omniscience, is the definition of the nature of Brahman as being without limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhi*), we say no; for that [consciousness] is a great universal (*mahāsāmānya*) characterized by pleasure, pain, attachment, aversion, and so forth. Therefore, it must be stated that even this [universal] culminates in a particular instance of a subordinate universal (*avāntarasāmānya-vyaktau*). Thus he says: "And the definitive statement regarding that is 'from Bliss' (*ānandād dhyeva*). For it is bliss (*ānanda*) alone that is determined to be the nature of Brahman without limiting adjuncts, by virtue of its possessing attributes such as being Brahman-hood, omniscience, and causality.

For instance, beginning with "where one sees nothing else," and concluding with "that which is the *bhūman* (the Infinite), that is bliss," [the text] declares that bliss alone possesses the attribute of vastness (*bṛhatva*). If it is argued that consciousness (*vijñāna*) is therefore an attribute of Brahman in its unconditioned state, then is the coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of consciousness and bliss due to a relationship of quality and qualified (*guṇa-guṇibhāva*), like a blue lotus, or rather due to a relationship between higher and lower universals (*parāpara-sāmānyabhāva*), like "substance" and "pot"? It cannot be the former, i.e., a relationship of quality and qualified.

This is because of the scriptural texts, "The witness, the cognizer, alone, devoid of qualities," and "It is to be seen as one alone; there is no multiplicity here," which negate the distinction between quality and the possessor of quality, since a quality cannot be defined as either different from or non-different from its possessor.

Here, the proponent of universal commingling (*sarvasaṅkaravādī*) argues that there is no substance devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*). Let it be granted that there is no substance devoid of qualities, yet Brahman is not a substance, because there is a lack of evidence (*pramāṇābhāva*). If it is argued that it is a substance because it is an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), we say no; for the theory of origination (*ārambhavāda*) is not accepted. If it is argued that it is a substance because it is a material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*), we say no; for even qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth possess the property of being material causes with respect to their own attributes, such as the property of being perceived. If it is argued that there is no entity devoid of qualities, we reply that this is inconclusive (*anekānta*) with regard to the ultimate qualities (*antyaguṇa*).

Therefore, this is merely a hatred for the knowledge of reality, not a denial that Brahman is devoid of attributes (*nirguṇa*). Consequently, just as one says "the jar is a substance" (*dravyaṃ ghaṭaḥ*) or "the jar exists" (*san ghaṭaḥ*), there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) based on higher and lower universals (*parāparasāmānya*) in the expression "consciousness-bliss" (*vijñānamānanda*). Thus, Brahman is a particular bliss whose substratum is the universal consciousness. In that regard, because attributes such as omniscience and non-duality are indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*) due to being superimpositions upon the phenomenal world (*prapañcopādhi*), Brahman does not become possessed of attributes (*saguṇa*) or dual through them.

Even the universal of consciousness (*vijñānasāmānya*), being indefinable due to its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as suffering, passion, and the like, serves merely as the cause for the application of the word "consciousness" to Brahman. If it is argued that Brahman cannot be called "consciousness" because it lacks the quality (*guṇa*) of consciousness, we say no; for that which takes the universal of consciousness as its object falls within the scope of the conventional usage of the term "consciousness," and furthermore, it performs purposeful action (*arthakriyākāritva*) prompted by consciousness. If it is argued that since the universal is a mere appearance (*ābhāsa*), the knowledge of Brahman that takes it as its object is false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*), we say no.

Because there is no other primary generality (*mukhyasāmānya*) and because this [bliss] alone is primary, he establishes that bliss itself is the nature of Brahman—namely, that bliss is Brahman—by means of the phrase beginning with "by the indicator of what is well-known" (*prasiddhāvadyotakena*), and so forth. Therefore, he concludes: "Therefore, [the passage] has Brahman as its purport," summarizing that in all Vedāntic statements, by reversing the order of the reading and by restating the mere cause of the world, its status as Brahman is established.

Thus ends the fifth section, titled the *Janmādyadhikaraṇa*, in the *Pañcapādikā-vivaraṇa* composed by the venerable Svaprakāśānubhava, disciple of the worshipful Ananyānubhava, a holy paramahaṃsa wandering mendicant.
Now begins the sixth section.

Because they take sound as their material cause, these powers—which illuminate objects residing within the resonance—exist in Brahman alone, just as the power of fire exists in its fuel and the power of a lamp exists in relation to its object.

Indeed, the power of knowledge in the observer is not merely instrumentality; rather, like the light of a lamp, it is simply the illumination of what is conjoined [with it]. Furthermore, it is here established once more that [Brahman] possesses omniscience.

Although the Sūtra is intent upon stating two characteristics of Brahman, omniscience is primarily demonstrated through both scripture and reasoning for the purpose of establishing its distinction from causes such as Pradhāna and for the sake of explaining the creation of the world. That very same [omniscience] he now establishes by means of another reason: because of its predominance, or rather—because it is the cause of the entire universe, [it follows that] it is omniscient.

[The opponent] objects: "It is not possible [for Brahman to be omniscient], because the Vedas have no author. Anticipating this, he states the connection [of the following verse]: "This other... He first demonstrates the capacity of the Veda with respect to all objects in order to show that even Brahman possesses it by virtue of being its material cause: "by means of the various sciences and branches of knowledge concerning manifold and diverse objects. [The opponent objects: "But the Veda does not possess omniscience itself, since it functions as an instrument for the cognition of objects. [The author replies: True; for that very reason, the suffix *kalpa* is employed [in the compound].

Now, one might object: "Even if the Veda possesses the capacity for knowledge regarding all objects, how can Brahman be omniscient? To this he says: "And therefore, its cause is seen," and so forth, providing an illustration. This is the formal argument (*prayoga*): The Veda was composed by one possessing superior knowledge of its own subject matter, because it is an authoritative verbal testimony (*vākya-pramāṇa*), just like the grammatical treatises of Pāṇini and others.

Now, what is being established here by means of inference? If it is first argued that, just as a teacher utters [words] for the purpose of teaching, the utterance of all words indicated by the term "scripture" occurs even in the case of Brahman, then Brahman will not be omniscient like a teacher. Alternatively, if [it is argued that] he composes a sentence for another person after having apprehended the meaning of the entire sentence through another means of knowledge, then its human origin (*pauruṣeyatva*) follows; for that is the defining characteristic of human speech. Thus he objects: "But this being so... and so forth.

On this point, some offer the following rebuttal: a word is called "human" (pauruṣeya) when it is composed for another by one who, having apprehended an object through another means of valid cognition, desires to speak of it. In that case, the meaning of human speech is the speaker's internal state of intention (*abhiprāya*), which is passion (*rāga*)—namely, the thought, "This must be done by this person. And passion is of two kinds: eternal and non-eternal.

In that regard, since the knowledge of those who are not the Lord (*anīśvara*) regarding the means to achieve their desired ends is impermanent, the passion (*rāga*) produced by it is likewise impermanent; consequently, the human words concerning those objects are accepted as being of human origin (*pauruṣeya*) because they depend upon other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). However, since the cognitions of the Lord regarding all objects that are means to the desired are eternal, the passion rooted in them is also eternal; thus, even the Vedic words composed by the Lord are not proclaimed to be of human origin, because they concern eternal passion. This argument is not sound.

There is no evidence for the Lord possessing eternal knowledge that serves as the means for accomplishing all desired ends, since it has been shown that inferences do not have such a thing as their object. If you claim this is established by scripture (*śabda*), we say no; for that would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*): the scripture’s independent authority would depend on its being produced by eternal passion rooted in eternal knowledge of the means for accomplishing all desires, and the proof of eternal knowledge would depend on the independent authority of the scripture. Furthermore, the claims that "passion is eternal" and "it is rooted in eternal knowledge of the means for accomplishing all desires" are mutually contradictory.

And from where is this derived—that even among the words of persons, there exists a distinction between those that are dependent and those that are independent based on the difference in their intended meanings regarding what is eternal and what is non-eternal—and furthermore, it will be stated later that the intention of a person is not the meaning of a word? Therefore, this [position] is inconsistent.

Others, however, maintain that even though the words of the *Mahābhārata* and other works possess various intentions and underlying purposes attributed to Vyāsa and others, their purpose is solely that of an injunction for study, just like the speech of contemporary teachers; thus, the "composition of the Vedas" by the Lord at the time of creation consists merely in His recitation of them.

Furthermore, if the authority of the Veda and the omniscience of God are claimed on the grounds that there is no intention [on God's part] to express passion (rāga), we ask this: at the time of creation, does He manifest the Vedic sentence after perceiving the meaning through another means of knowledge, as Pāṇini and others do? Or does He utter a pre-established sentence, like a teacher? In the former case, the consequence is that the Veda would be of human origin (pauruṣeya); in the latter case, the consequence is that He would be non-omniscient, just like a teacher.

If it is argued that [the Veda] is not of human origin because there is no intention (*abhiprāya*) or purpose (*tātparya*), then how can there be an absence of passion (*rāga*) as its purpose in a composition based on perception? If it is argued that this is because the purpose is solely for injunction (*vidhi*), even so, the other [purpose] is not thereby precluded. Furthermore, it is not logical for there to be a dual purpose; for even when the purpose is an injunction, it is understood that the very act of composing based on what is perceived is the cause of dependence (*sāpekṣatva*). And since a purpose consisting of an injunction is not possible in a composition based on perception, this argument is trivial.

Others, however, think: "The Vedic sentences, being preceded by non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpajñāna*), do not incur the fault of dependence (*sāpekṣatva*); for the knowledge of the nature of Brahman is non-conceptual, whereas worldly speech, being preceded by conceptual knowledge (*savikalpajñāna*), possesses dependence. This distinction, too, is not established; for it is precisely composition based on perception that is the cause of dependence, and even the knowledge of the [Vedic] nature itself becomes conceptual when it is colored by its relation to the means for attaining what is desired. Therefore, these are no solutions at all.

[Objection: In that case, would it not follow that the Vedas are of human origin? [Reply: But the Veda is indeed not of human origin; for, while its usage has remained uninterrupted, its author is not remembered, and thus its non-human origin is inferred—just like the Self. [Reply: No, because this is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) in the case of things that occurred long ago but whose authors are now known through inference, and because the authors of the Vedas are known through both inference and scripture. For instance: "The Veda was composed by a person of exceptional and extensive knowledge, because it is an authoritative statement concerning a vast range of subjects."

As in the case of the *Bhārata*, there is the scripture stating, "He created all this," and "The Ṛg-veda, Yajur-veda, and Sāma-veda. Therefore, the Veda is of human origin. To this we ask: how can authority be established for a Veda of human origin? If you say it is because it was composed by an omniscient being—referring to Kapila, Kaṇāda, or Akṣapāda—it has already been stated that an omniscient being cannot be established through inference. If its establishment is from scripture, no; [for that would lead to an infinite regress].

Because of mutual dependence: the authority of the Veda would be established if an omniscient being were established as its author, and from that, the existence of an omniscient being would be established. It might be argued that the authority of the Veda follows from its acceptance by the great multitude (*mahājana*); but this is not so, for we hear of an infinite number of followers of the scriptures of the Sugata and others in various regions. Furthermore, we do not see authority in such things as the identity of the body and the self or the moon's size being a mere span, even though these are accepted by the great multitude. Moreover, the acceptance by the great multitude does not inherently favor what is authoritative. Therefore, no authority is attained.

Furthermore, by what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) could a person perceive dharma and adharma so as to compose Vedic statements? Certainly not by the five sense organs, because they grasp respectively color, taste, smell, touch, and sound—along with their specific qualities inherent therein—and because they are restricted to apprehending only the present, whereas dharma is something yet to be accomplished (*sādhya*).

Now, it might be argued that since dharma is inherent in the self, it is grasped as a quality of that self by the very cognition that perceives it—either by the mind alone or by the eye and other senses. Why, then, do we not perceive it? Nor can it be said that a distinguished person (the yogin) perceives it, for his senses are no different from ours. If you argue that his senses are distinguished by the power of dharma produced through yoga, even so, like the vision of a cat or similar creatures, they would merely perceive their own specific objects with greater intensity, but never an object that is outside their range, such as dharma.

If it is argued that yogins possess a divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*), based on such scriptural recollections as, "I give the divine eye," and "O Blessed One, Janārdana bestowed upon them the divine eye," we say no; for even that [divine eye] only reveals its own specific objects, such as the Universal Form (*viśvarūpa*).
