In that case, the purpose of enjoining a stream of recollections is certainly not some unseen merit (adṛṣṭa); for if it were, liberation would result in being produced by ritual action (karman), like heaven and so forth. Even if there were a visible fruit, no such fruit can be identified; thus he says: "I see no purpose for it."

[The opponent] says: "But surely pleasure is perceptible, like the pleasure of massage"—to which [the author] replies: "But [in the case of] a desired object... [The author] then says: "If that is so," meaning: since its accomplishment is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), just like massage and the like, the continuous stream of memory (*smṛti-santāna*) cannot be something to be enjoined. He then raises an objection: "In that case, let the purpose of enjoining the stream of memory be the direct realization (*sākṣātkaraṇa*) of the object being remembered. [The author] asks: Is this direct realization an unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) purpose for the stream of memory, or is it a seen (*dṛṣṭa*) one? It cannot be the unseen.

The direct perception of an object is accomplished by the totality of means of knowledge such as the eyes, and it is not produced by unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) alone. If it is argued that it is produced from the causes of knowledge belonging to another birth, aided by unseen merit, then just as in a previous birth the causes of knowledge such as verbal testimony would produce the realization of Brahman even without an injunction, so too would it be here. If it is further argued that the purpose is indeed the direct realization of Brahman through what is perceived, we say no; because it is not apprehended [in that way]. Thus he says: "This is not tenable."

He demonstrates precisely the contradiction with non-perception [of the object]: "For the object is not inferential. It is not the case that from the stream of verbal cognition and memory alone a mere direct perception (*aparokṣajñāna*) arises; rather, another cognition capable of producing that [perception] arises. He raises the objection that the stream of memory is enjoined for the sake of the fruit of that cognition—namely, "Let it not be [produced] from verbal cognition alone. Even that cognition which has direct perception as its fruit is not a fruit of an injunction by way of being unseen (*adṛṣṭa*), because comprehension depends upon a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*); nor is it so by way of being seen (*dṛṣṭa*).

He says that there is no proof for this state of affairs because a continuum of memory lacks the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), nor is there any proof that it is the fruit of a prescription (*vidhi*) regarding that [Brahman]: "There is no proof for such a state. Let it be granted that there is no prescription for a continuum of memory; rather, meditation (*dhyāna*) is prescribed with respect to Brahman as understood through verbal testimony. But what is the distinction between meditation and a continuum of memory? In this regard, a continuum of memory is a flow of homogeneous cognitions concerning the reality of an object already apprehended by a means of valid cognition, arising from that very same means of valid cognition.

Meditation (*dhyāna*) is a stream of mental volition that, even by taking as its object something superimposed, does not depend on the actual reality of the thing; that [meditation] is what must be performed. Thus he says: "Let it then be [that which is meditated upon] as understood from the word."

[Objection: Must not even that [meditation] have either an unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) or a seen (*dṛṣṭa*) purpose? It cannot be an unseen one, because, being produced by a ritual injunction (*naiyogika*), it would follow that it is non-eternal (*anityatva*), like heaven and so forth. Nor can it be a seen purpose, as he raises the objection: "For what purpose? [Reply: But surely that [meditation] is for the sake of the direct realization (*sākṣātkaraṇa*) of the object of meditation; thus, even that is not an unseen fruit, since the experience of an object is produced by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). If it is a seen fruit, [we reply]: no, because it contradicts non-perception (*anupalabdhi*). Thus he says: "There is no possibility of that," and so forth.

One might object: "Is it not seen that through the power of the accumulated practice of meditation, there is direct perception (*aparokṣya*) of things such as a deceased son? To this he replies: "It is indeed seen. He refutes this by stating: "Not so; for that which is being meditated upon is not [the reality]. For direct perception of a deceased son and the like is impossible because they do not exist at present. Rather, that which appears before one's eyes as a son or the like is of the nature of ignorance (*avidyā*) because it is sublated; therefore, it is not the direct perception of a real entity. Thus he answers: "Not so; for that which is being meditated upon is not [the reality]."

Now, it might be argued: "When Brahman is meditated upon as the Self, through the excellence of meditation, the direct perception of the object of meditation is indeed established—just as in the case of a son and so forth—and the reality of the object of meditation is established by the authority of scripture; therefore, the direct perception of the real entity will result from meditation, just as the knowledge of an elephant that arose at a crossroads in a dream becomes valid knowledge through its correspondence with the waking state. This is not sound.

The validity of immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*) would arise from its correspondence with reality by virtue of the capacity of verbal testimony (*śabdapramāṇa*) as such a form of knowledge. However, dream-cognition is not a valid means of knowledge, because it consists of ignorance (*avidyā*); as for the correspondence [of dream objects], that is due to an error of similarity. Indeed, the perception of an object is not possible without the operation of the eyes and other sense organs.

[Objection: Surely, by the very force of the injunction (*vidhi*), it is understood that the fruit of meditation (*dhyāna*) is the direct realization (*sākṣātkaraṇa*) of the object to be meditated upon; what then is the use of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)? [The author] says: "Is it not the case that [the Self] is to be seen? Even there, is the fruit something produced by the injunction (*naiyogika*) or is it a perceived result (*dṛṣṭa*)? If it were produced by the injunction, then liberation would consist of increase and decrease, like heaven and so forth. If, however, it is a perceived result, then he says: "This has already been stated."

Having accepted the existence of things to be performed (*vidheya*), [the author] states that if words were intent upon injunctions for meditation (*dhyāna-vidhi*), the identity of Brahman and the Self would not be established: "Even so, let it be from meditation. Now, one might object: "But does not the word establish the identity of Brahman and the Self? He says, "No," and explains: "The word, for its part... Now, one might argue: "Since subordinate sentences other than those containing injunctions for knowledge (*jñāna-vidhi*) are harmonized (*samanvaya*) with respect to Brahman, the reality [of Brahman] is established. To this he replies: "True; nevertheless, the reality is established."

He refutes [the objection]: "The analogy is flawed. Therefore, when there is a focus on injunction (*vidhi*), there is no establishment of a real entity (*vastu*). He extends this [critique] to all varieties of injunctions: "[This applies] even to those previously mentioned."

The application (*niyoga*) to the continuity of mindfulness (*smṛti*) and to meditation (*dhyāna*) has been refuted; now, he raises the objection regarding the application to a third kind of knowledge that has immediate perception as its fruit—namely, "as for what is said by some," and so forth. To this we reply: since the knowledge being enjoined cannot be produced by perception, inference, or verbal testimony, it must be seen together with the injunctions concerning extraordinary means (*karaṇa*) and procedures (*itikartavyatā*), just like the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices. [The opponent] says that such a thing is not observed, beginning with the words, "But what is the means for that? and so on.

He raises an objection: "With this [text], 'by the recitation of the Vedas... The meaning is that one who desires liberation, by means of hearing (*śravaṇa*), reflection (*manana*), and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*)—which are assisted by the recitation of the Vedas, sacrifice, charity, austerity, fasting, tranquility (*śama*), self-control (*dama*), and so forth—should produce the knowledge that has immediate realization as its fruit regarding Brahman. He refutes this: "In that case, it would be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for another means of valid cognition. The meaning of this is: the direct realization of Brahman, together with its procedural requirements (*itikartavyatā*) and its qualification (*adhikāra*), is itself another means of valid cognition.

If it were cognized by words as something to be performed (*kartavyatā*), then words would not be a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding Brahman, but rather a means of valid knowledge regarding the means of knowing Brahman. Therefore, by the principle of parsimony (*kalpanālāghava*), it is more appropriate that their authority resides in Brahman itself. Now, one might object: "It is not appropriate for words to have authority regarding Brahman alone, without reference to an injunction (*vidhi*. To this he says: "Cognizable through the effect" (*kāryagamyam*). The authority of the Vedāntas is cognizable through the effect consisting of the certain cognition (*niścita-pramiti*) of Brahman arising from the Vedāntic sentences for one who has grasped the relationship [between word and meaning].

In that case, since validity is understood through the fact that a cognition is produced regarding an object that is to be enjoined, why should the sentence concerning the *agnihotra* not be intent upon enjoining the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices? If it is argued that this is because no valid cognition arises there due to a lack of verbal capacity [to enjoin], then here too, since the capacity for injunction and the resulting valid cognition are understood from the statements "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, Infinite" and "That thou art," it is logical that validity resides in Brahman alone.

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that worldly validity is understood solely through its effect (*kārya*), whereas scriptural validity is understood through injunction (*vidhi*)? To this he says, "It has been stated," and so forth. Here, when it is impossible for worldly words to convey Vedic meaning by means of expressing their primary sense (*mukhyārtha*), there arises a doubt: do we grasp a separate relationship in the Veda, or do we convey the meaning from the very same worldly relationship even by means of another mode of operation (*vṛttyantara*)? In this dilemma, it is proper to accept only the worldly [relationship].

He states that this is because it would involve an extraordinary postulation: "Or there might be a designation based on a quality. Thus, it is logical that authority is strictly worldly; the meaning is that it would otherwise require an extraordinary postulation. Therefore, the Vedānta passages do not terminate in an injunction by virtue of having a visible fruit.

Now, what indeed is this so-called *niyoga*? Is it not well-known from such expressions as "the command (*niyoga*) of the teacher"? True; in that context, *niyoga* is a specific intention (*abhiprāyabheda*) consisting of the impelling of a superior person toward an inferior person, and this is not possible in the case of the impersonal Veda or in the perceptual activity of a child. Now, it might be argued that the object cognized through the notion of "what is to be done" (*kārya*) is designated as *niyoga* because of the commonality of being an instigator (*pravartakatva*). But what is this "what is to be done"? If it is merely the fitness for action (*kṛtiyogyatāmātra*), no activity follows from that.

Because everything that possesses antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is capable of being produced by effort (*kṛti*). Now, if it is argued that the "thing to be done" (*kārya*) is that which is conjoined with effort, no; for it is accepted that the cognition of the "thing to be done" has the very conjunction with effort as its cause. If it is then argued that the "thing to be done" is some extraordinary entity (*alaukika*) that is merely capable of being produced by effort, then [this would apply] to one who is unlearned.

Regarding the empirical usage expressed as "the fetching of water must be done with a jar" and so forth, it must be stated: is something non-worldly (alaukika) other than the action (kriyā) and its factors (kāraka) apprehended therein, or not? If it is apprehended, then there is nothing non-worldly [in this case]. Furthermore, this [non-worldly element] must be demonstrated by means of another term as being "thus. [Objection: One acts after having apprehended [something] as a "task to be accomplished" (kārya). Therefore, the fact that the task possesses an impelling form constitutes its distinction from the action, its factors, and their results. [Reply: No.

Because it is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) itself that prompts action by being the means to achieve what is desired, and because it is precisely that which falls within the scope of the cognition of "what is to be done" (*kārya*). Now, one might object: "The 'to-be-done' (*kārya*) is one thing, and the means to achieve what is desired is another. True; however, it is the means to achieve what is desired alone that is called "the to-be-done," insofar as it is fit for purposeful action (*kṛti-yogya*) and thus prompts activity. Nor does the means (*sādhana*) differ in its objective basis for these two cognitions merely due to a difference in its relation to the excellence (*śreyaḥ*) and the purposeful action. Furthermore, we do not perceive any "to-be-done" distinct from the means to achieve the desired that could serve as the cause for engagement.

[Objection: But surely even the result (*phala*) is seen to be capable of motivating activity because it is something to be accomplished (*kārya*). [Reply: No, because the state of being a result lacks the quality of being a cause for a specific kind of activity. It is only that which is to be accomplished (*kārya*)—namely, the means to what is desired—that serves as the cause for activity, which is the mark for grasping the relationship [between word and meaning]. As for the result, however, it is the cause of mere desire. Furthermore, nothing called "that which is to be accomplished" is observed in the world as something transcendent (*alaukika*). It cannot be apprehended through perception, because its nature is unestablished (*asiddha*); nor can it be known through inference, because the relationship [of concomitance] has not been grasped.

Because it is not [previously] understood, it cannot be known through scripture (*āgama*). Since there is no impossibility (*anupapatti*) without a non-worldly effect (*alaukika-kārya*), the effect cannot be apprehended through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). If it is argued that the state of being an instigator (*pravartakatva*) is untenable, we say no; for activity proceeds even from that which is a desired means (*abhilaṣita-sādhana*) merely because it is fit for effort (*kṛti-yogya*). Nor is the status of being a means (*sādhanatva*) devoid of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-śūnya*) like the effect itself; for it is understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with the arising of its result, and even when [the specific result] has not been experienced, the status of being a means is established by the observation of a general rule (*sāmānyato-darśana*).

Nor does it follow that there would be an inclination toward the means for achieving [objects] such as the past; for there is the qualification "a means to a desired end that is fit for action. Therefore, it is established that whatever functions as an instigator in the linguistic usage of one who is unlearned by means of another instrument of knowledge, that very same thing is inferred to be the instigator for the listener as well, by virtue of being the object of verbal cognition. In that regard, the connection with an injunction in the knowledge of the identity of Brahman and the Self consists in its capacity as a means to a result.

In this regard, since there is no fruit of liberation apart from the cessation of ignorance, and since that [cessation] is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the fact that the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) is the means to liberation is apprehended through positive and negative concomitance and is not a matter to be known solely through verbal testimony (*śabda-prameya*). Thus, it is established that verbal testimony is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) only with respect to Brahman.

Now, for the sake of refuting those who think that—having accepted a difference between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman, and having admitted both that Brahman exists in another location and that it is all-pervading—liberation will result as a fruit from the meditation enjoined in the form of a superimposition, "I am Brahman," just as heaven results from a sacrifice, he states the subsequent commentary beginning with: "But then, that light which is beyond this heaven... and so forth.

[Objection: But even so, if the word is intent upon an injunction for meditation (*upāsanā-vidhi*), would it not follow that the true nature of Brahman remains unestablished? To this he says: "By the same logic as [the proof of] the deity’s possession of a body. Nor is there any contradiction with other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); for [in that case], Brahman would be subject to modification (*vikāra*) and would consequently be accompanied by a second entity (*sadvitīya*). [Objection: But if liberation were a fruit resulting from an injunction (*naiyogika-phala*), it would be non-eternal like heaven and so forth. [Reply: No; he says: "And even though it is something to be accomplished (*sādhya*)," etc.

[Objection: But how can the Śruti, being contradicted by the inference of non-eternality, establish non-return? To this he says: "For this [is not... [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22]. [Objection: But since the inference and the scripture are contradictory and non-erroneous, they cause doubt; to this he says: "Of that which is to be known through the Word. The meaning is that scripture is stronger than inference. He introduces the Bhāṣya as a refutation of this [objection] with the words: "Not between the fruits of ritual action and the knowledge of Brahman," and so forth.

He states the intended meaning of the commentary with the words: "The meaning of this is, in brief," and so forth. Now, an objection is raised: there is no difference in the results [of knowledge and action], because liberation, too, being achievable through meditation (*upāsanā*), is produced by karma; consequently, one might also possess a body, sense organs, and so on, subject to increase and decrease. To this, he replies: "From scripture and from reasoning."

From such scriptural passages as, "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself," "Through knowledge one attains immortality," "Established in Brahman, he attains immortality," and "Now this bodiless, immortal life is indeed Brahman," liberation—characterized by being bodiless and immortal—is shown to consist in identity with Brahman. Furthermore, the eternality of liberation is understood through reasoning, because if there were a return [to worldly existence], there would be a recurrence of bondage, which would result in the term "liberation" (mokṣa) being used in a figurative sense; moreover, a distinction is recognized between worldly prosperity (abhyudaya) and the supreme good (niḥśreyasa).

The scripture also establishes its beginninglessness through two logical arguments. For the scripture states: "The liberated one is liberated," and "Being Brahman, he merges into Brahman. Furthermore, there is the logical principle that if it had a beginning, it would necessarily have an end. Consequently, liberation is not something to be accomplished by action. He explains that if it were accomplished by action, then like the fruit of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*), liberation would be subject to the destruction of its connection with the body, senses, and so forth, and would likewise possess the qualities of increase and decrease—stating this with the words beginning, "If [it were] like the twilight worship (*sandhyopāsana*)," and so on.

Now, one might object: "Just as the fruit of action consists of the body, the senses, and so forth—which are subject to increase, decrease, and decay—and is thus something to be experienced, so too should the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), characterized by the bodiless, immortal Brahman, which is the opposite of that, also be the fruit of action; for we observe that actions are the cause of various fruits such as those of animal births. To this, he says: "And bodilessness itself is not the effect of dharma."

What is this "bodilessness by nature" (svābhāvikamaśarīratvam), and what is "bodiness due to a cause" (naimittika)? Bodilessness by nature is the absolute absence of any kind of connection whatsoever between the body and the self, other than the connection consisting in false knowledge; whereas bodiness due to a cause arises from the connection with false knowledge.

In this regard, since disembodiedness—which is characterized by the cessation of the connection with false knowledge and is to be accomplished through right knowledge—cannot be achieved by ritual action (*karman*), and since disembodiedness characterized by the cessation of other [karmic] connections is innate (*svābhāvika*), liberation is not something to be accomplished by *dharma*. Now, one might object: "This fruit, characterized as the immortal Brahman devoid of a body, is transformed into something else by means of rituals. To this he says, "nevertheless, in some way," and so forth, denying that objection.

Now, let it be granted that liberation—characterized by being natural, bodiless, immortal, and eternal—is of a single, constant form; nevertheless, it will arise from the continuous practice of meditation (*upāsanā*) as it is so prescribed, since meditation has the nature of knowledge. To this, he replies with the passage beginning, "In that case, like gold forgotten in one's hand," and so forth.

Now, one might object: "If liberation were to be accomplished through meditation like the fruit of a sacrifice, would it not be subject to increase and decrease, be perishable, and involve a connection with a body? To this it is replied: It must be stated whether there is a limitation—whether by nature, by time, or by number—of the meditation enjoined for the sake of the fruit of liberation, or whether there is not. If such a limitation exists, then, just as there is a limitation for the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices along with their ancillaries, the limitation of this meditation must be demonstrated as being "this much"; yet no such thing is observed. Nor is there a limitation by way of number.

There is no restrictive rule that a hundred thousand or a million mental impressions (*pratyaya*) constitute the means to liberation, for no such regulator is observed. Nor is there a limitation by time; there is no evidence for a fixed rule that liberation belongs to one who meditates for one hundred, a thousand, or any specific number of years. If it is argued that death itself is the limit, even then, as in the case of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, a fixed measure of the means consisting of a single uniform form cannot be established.

For, due to the death of someone at one time, another time, ten times, a hundred times, or a thousand times, there would follow an increase or decrease in the cultivation of meditation (*upāsanā*) among different individuals. If it is argued that the limit is the direct realization (*aparokṣya*) of the object of meditation, even so, because for some person direct realization occurs at some particular time, the increase or decrease of the means remains in that same state. Therefore, a uniformity of the means to liberation characterized by meditation cannot be established. Furthermore, a superimposed direct experience is not the means to liberation, because it is not prescribed [by scripture] and because it is a false cognition (*mithyājñāna*).

Now, suppose it is argued that there need not be uniformity [in liberation], because—due to differences in place, time, number, and magnitude—there will be a nature of increase or decrease in the means among different persons, as in the case of repeated performance of the *agnihotra* sacrifice. In that case, liberation would not be of one form for all; for, just as a flame increases with an increase in fuel, or as heaven increases with an increase in the *agnihotra*, it would follow that liberation undergoes increase or decrease through an increase in meditation (*upāsana*). If, on the other hand, it is claimed that the fruit remains uniform despite the disparity in the means, then the performance of the means would be rendered futile.

Now, it might be argued that even if meditation (*upāsanā*) is enjoined, because there is no restrictive rule, it may consist of increase or decrease, and its fruit, according to scripture, is uniform. This is not sound. For, as ignorance, its latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), desire, and karma are being destroyed through meditation, the arising of immediate, perfect knowledge (*aparokṣa-samyag-jñāna*) is possible due to one-pointedness of mind; and because of the dissimilarity among the decaying karmas and other factors, the attainment of immediate knowledge is indeed possible.

Therefore, liberation would be of the nature of an accumulation, like the fruits such as heaven; because it would be achievable through the meditation being enjoined, it would—like pleasure and pain—be dependent on the visible causal complex consisting of the body, senses, and so forth, and it would be subject to decay due to the exhaustion of its means. Thus he concludes: "Therefore, [liberation] is not [an end] by way of being a remainder of what is to be done."

Now, it may be argued that while scripture and inference rely upon generalities—such as "Just as here, those who perform ritual acts... and "Whatever is created is impermanent"—the scriptural statement regarding non-return, which concerns liberation, is more powerful; thus, the text reiterates the stated point: "But he does not return again. To this we reply: first of all, if the Vedāntas were intent upon injunctions, then the scriptural mentions of results would be mere *arthavādas* (explanatory praises), like the case of [the sacrificial ladle] being made of *parṇa*-wood; and non-return cannot be established as a fact by means of *arthavādas*.

It is like the scriptural mention of the fruits of substances, qualities, purificatory acts, and ritual actions. Now, it might be argued that scriptural mentions of fruits do not lose their authority because they are *arthavādas* (eulogies); rather, they lack authority here because, being stated as present facts, they contradict the non-perception of such a possibility. If that is so, then in this case as well—"and he does not return"—the prohibition of something not yet established means that the *arthavādas* do not possess authority. For instance, in the passage, "He attains the world of Brahman and does not return," the return at the time of attainment is prohibited even though it has not [otherwise] occurred.

If it is argued that the meaning of the sentence is to be construed as a prohibition against future recurrence—namely, "surely he will not return"—we say no; for to abandon the directly stated meaning (*śruta-artha*) in favor of imagining an unstated meaning (*aśruta-artha*) contradicts both scripture and inference, such as the scriptural statement, "Whatever is made is impermanent," and the inferential principle, "As here [in this world], those built of action [perish]. This same reasoning should be applied to other passages concerning non-return. Therefore, this is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*).

Through both general scriptural statements and inference, the impermanence of liberation as a goal has been shown; now, by the force of the specific qualification "non-return," he declares its finitude: "Furthermore, for them here... The qualification "here in this world" indicates that return is naturally expected in another cycle of existence.

Now, it might be argued that since this sentence teaches non-return within this kalpa, if it were to teach return again in another kalpa, there would be a syntactical split (vākyabheda) due to redundancy; however, this "beloved of the gods" who advocates for universal confusion is ignorant, because this objection applies equally to all sentences containing qualifying attributes.

If it is argued that a sentence with a qualifier directly expresses a qualified object, while the exclusion of other qualified objects is understood by implication—and thus there is no split in the sentence—then here too, non-return qualified by this specific eon is directly expressed, while the prevention of his return in another eon is established by implication; therefore, there is no split in the sentence.

[Objection: Is it not the case that even in another *kalpa*, the prohibition—"there is no returning here again"—is the same due to the commonality of the scriptural statement? [Response: True. For us, first of all, the return of those who have attained [liberation] in this *kalpa* to another *kalpa* is established by the force of the qualification at present. If there were also the cognition of non-return for those attaining [liberation] in another *kalpa* regarding that [other *kalpa*], then such a systematic rule (*vyavasthā*) would be postulated: "For those who have attained in this *kalpa*, there is return in another *kalpa*; for those who have attained in another *kalpa*, there is no return therein. Otherwise, there would be a deficiency in the qualification.

Furthermore, the meaning of the section of the text beginning with "abhyupetya" and ending before "tathā taddhaitat" is as follows: when Brahman has been understood through verbal testimony and rendered immediate through repeated practice because it is an experience of bliss, that which constitutes its direct realization in the absence of any injunction is called the knowledge of Brahman.

When that [knowledge] has arisen, it is logical that the fruit occurs simultaneously with the realization of Brahman, because the defects such as ignorance are removed immediately thereafter. However, when meditation—which has a superimposed self as its object—is prescribed and called "the realization of Brahman," then, since the fruit resulting from a ritual injunction (naiyogika) occurs at a later time, the designation of simultaneity is not tenable.

Therefore, since Brahman known even from the word proceeds by itself toward immediate knowledge and produces its fruit, there is no entry into the sphere of ritual action prior to that. The passage beginning with "Thus, seeing this, the seer Vāmadeva... and ending before the words "Furthermore" (kiñca) has a clear meaning.

Moreover, the scripture shows that the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman is the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā*). And that ignorance does not cease without the immediate knowledge of reality (*tattva*), characterized by the removal of immediate superimposition (*adhyāsa*). If, however, meditation (*upāsanā*)—which consists of a superimposed form—were itself the knowledge of reality, then ignorance would not be removed by it. Therefore, only the knowledge of reality produced by a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the remover of ignorance; thus, because the cessation of ignorance is heard as the fruit [of knowledge], the Vedāntas are a valid means of cognition regarding the Self that is Brahman. He states this with the words: "Furthermore, to him whose impurities have been wiped away," and so forth.

Now, it might be objected that the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā*) is not explicitly heard here [in the text]. This is not a fault; for, having introduced the knowledge of the Self as the means for crossing over sorrow in the passage, "He who knows the Self crosses over sorrow," and concluding with, "He shows the further shore of darkness," if the text did not indeed speak of the cessation of darkness (*tamas*), then the initial reference to the cessation of the superimposition of sorrow and so forth would be inconsistent. Therefore, it is understood that by the statement, "He shows the further shore of darkness," the very cessation of the beginningless ignorance which is the material cause of sorrow and the like is intended.

Likewise, by stating that one "causes [the seeker] to cross to the further shore of ignorance," the text—speaking of the attainment of Brahman through the transcendence of ignorance—indicates cessation itself, since such transcendence would otherwise be impossible; thus, in accordance with the Śruti, it has been stated that the Vedāntic authority culminates in the knowledge of reality for the sake of achieving the fruit, which is the cessation of ignorance.

Now, he demonstrates that even according to the treatises on logic (*tarkaśāstra*), the fruit of the cessation of false knowledge is the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*)—with the words "For this reason also, it is thus. This is the meaning: "Upon the successive disappearance of suffering, birth, activity, defects, and false knowledge, there follows the non-existence of each preceding one; from this, liberation (*apavarga*)."

Regarding these twelve categories—self, body, sense organs, objects, intellect, mind, activity, defects, rebirth, fruit, suffering, and liberation—there exists this beginningless false knowledge. When that [false knowledge] is removed through the purification resulting from the vision of the true nature of the twelve categories, such as the self and the supreme self, then attachment, aversion, and delusion do not arise toward them. Consequently, due to the absence of a motivator, the activities of engagement and withdrawal, which result in pleasure and pain, no longer occur.

Consequently, due to the emptiness of mixed karma—both auspicious and inauspicious—accumulated through the doors of engagement and withdrawal, one is not born among the various types of wombs from Brahmā down to the level of stationary beings; the meaning is that one does not enter into connection with a body. Therefore, since pleasure and pain do not arise in the absence of a body, [the text] demonstrates that liberation consists precisely in the removal of false knowledge.

Likewise, for the Vaiśeṣikas as well, false knowledge—which has proceeded without beginning due to a lack of discernment regarding the true nature of substances, qualities, actions, universals, particulars, and inherence by way of their similarities and differences—is removed through the contemplation of reality; and thus it is said that liberation occurs because of the absence of further [existence]. Similarly, it has been shown by the Sāṃkhya-Yogins: ignorance, characterized by the non-discrimination between the seer and the seen, which has proceeded without beginning, is removed by the knowledge of reality.

Consequently, the afflictions—ignorance, egoism, attachment, aversion, and the will to live—are abandoned. Then, for one whose afflictions have been destroyed, liberation occurs because the cycle of worldly activity no longer arises. This has also been stated by the Sugatas: "Cognitions are defiled by the conceptualization of continuity, by defects such as attachment and aversion, and by delusions regarding objects that culminate in the arising of activity and its fruits. When these delusions cease through the cultivation of reality (*tattva-paribhāvanā*), the emergence of the final moment of pure cognition is liberation."

Thus, since liberation occurs upon the cessation of ignorance, how can the act of meditative worship (*upāsti*) be postulated as the means to liberation, setting aside the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) produced by valid cognition?

But has it not been demonstrated that the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) which removes false cognition (*mithyājñāna*) is something quite different? For instance, it has been stated by the Naiyāyikas that ignorance (*avidyā*) is removed by right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) produced from the contemplation of the principles (*tattva*) among the twelve categories; and previously accumulated karmas are removed by the affliction (*saṃkleśa*) produced from the contemplation of the principles, by the exhaustion (*kṣaya*) produced by its intensification, and by the experience (*upabhoga*) of present [karmas]. Thereafter, liberation (*kaivalya*) ensues. Thus it was said.

It has been shown that even for the Vaiśeṣikas, false knowledge is sublated by the knowledge of reality produced from the contemplation of the six categories and supported by meditation on the Lord; thereupon, attachment and the other afflictions gradually diminish; consequently, there is the absolute destruction of previously accumulated demerits, which result from the exertion of contemplating the categories, and the cessation of merits through the bliss of the purity of the vision of reality; and from that, liberation (kaivalya) is attained.

The yogis, however, have maintained that one is liberated when ignorance, egoism, attachment, aversion, and the will to live are being destroyed by the knowledge of the distinction between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*—a knowledge produced by *asaṃprajñāta-samādhi* which culminates in the mere nature of the *puruṣa*—and when previously accumulated *karman*s are being destroyed according to the principle of "belonging to a single birth."

The Sugatas [Buddhists] maintain that liberation is the cessation of the continuum when the delusions regarding the objects of activity—namely, permanence and agency—are eliminated through the arising of the final moment characterized by pure knowledge, which is produced by the cultivation of the truths of momentariness, selflessness, suffering, and the path. Thus, they hold that liberation is accomplished by means of distinct cognitions. To this, he replies: "And the removal of false knowledge occurs through the realization of the identity of Brahman and the Self."

One might object: "Even among those who have demonstrated the vision of reality, why is it that the knowledge of Brahman alone is accepted as the remover of false cognition (*mithyājñāna*), when there are other counter-arguments? Thus he raises the objection: "How is this understood? He answers: "Because the perception of difference is a manifestation of false cognition, its cessation occurs only through the vision of the non-dual Self as Brahman, which is its direct opposite, and not through the aforementioned perceptions of difference. This he establishes with the passage beginning, "Indra by means of his powers of illusion" (*indro māyābhiḥ*).

Is it not the case that the scripture does not have as its primary purport the identity of the self with the non-dual Brahman? For there is no such intentionality therein; rather, [its purport lies] in [the self] as distinct from the individual soul (jīva).

He presents the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that, regarding Brahman as understood through scripture and not contradicted by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the identity statements have as their object meditative identifications (*saṃpad*) and the like—starting from the words "But it might be so" up to the point before "To this [we reply]". The text, however, is clear in its meaning. In this regard, the following must be said: Is the syntactical connection of the words intended for the purpose of meditative identification and so forth due to contradiction with other means of valid cognition, or because of a lack of purport (*tātparya*) regarding that [actual] object? It cannot be due to contradiction with other means of valid cognition, because those two [Brahman and the Self] are not within the scope of such means.

He states—beginning with "For in the form of identification (saṃpad), etc."—that even when there is an appearance of difference, the logic of the original object and its reflection (bimba-pratibimba-nyāya) applies; and that the absence of a primary intention (tātparya) does not entail an absence of referentiality toward the meaning.

For instance: regarding the statement "That thou art," which is repeated nine times, explanatory passages (arthavādas) such as "Having entered with this living self" are cited for the sake of establishing oneness; likewise, the perception of difference is censured in the passage, "Now, those who know otherwise than this become subjects of other kings and dwellers in perishable worlds. Similarly, for the statement "I am Brahman," there is the explanatory passage beginning with "He has entered here."

Furthermore, the negation of difference found in passages such as, "Now, he who worships another deity [thinking], 'He is one and I am another,'" is employed as an indicator of the [text's] intended meaning (*tātparya*). Likewise, the intended meaning of the passage "This is your Self," which is repeated many times, is understood through the sublation of difference in statements such as, "There is no other seer but He. Similarly, the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), "That which is here in the person and that which is yonder in the sun, those are one," serves to explain the statement, "Having created that, He entered into it."

Likewise, the passage, "But he who perceives a difference therein, fear comes upon him," is a negation of the perception of duality. Similarly, the statement, "He saw this very Person as the most pervasive Brahman," has as its explanatory purpose (arthavāda) the passage, "Having split open this very boundary, he enters through this door. Thus, it should be understood that throughout all the Vedāntas, in various places, the oneness of Brahman and the Self is being established by means of the exclusion of the three states [of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep].

For it is not reasonable to say that the identity of Brahman and the Self—which is established here and there through the sublation of the perception of difference, through the explanatory passages concerning the entry of Brahman itself as the individual soul (jīvātman), and through the removal of contradictions regarding the connection with the three states—is devoid of purport. Furthermore, the cessation of ignorance and the realization of the nature of Brahman-as-Self are heard in scripture as the fruit of knowledge; and this is not possible if the texts were intended merely for meditative identification (saṃpad) and the like, because it is a contradiction for one thing to be the self of another, and because such [identification] lacks authoritative validity.

Therefore, he states that the syntactical connection of the words has as its purport the identity of Brahman and the Self, even by the force of the statement regarding the fruit: "and because it is the cause of the realization of That. He concludes: "Therefore, it is not like a meditative identification (saṃpad) and so forth."

On this point, someone says: "This individual soul (*jīva*) is both different and non-different from Brahman. Consequently, the distinction between the eternal liberation of Brahman and the eternal bondage of the soul is maintained; for if there were absolute non-difference, how could Brahman itself produce the world for its own worldly existence? Furthermore, it is contradictory for that which is pure to be perceived as impure. To this, it is replied: Of what nature is this difference-and-non-difference? It is certainly not based on the relationship of genus and individual, quality and possessor of quality, cause and effect, qualified and qualification, or part and whole.

Because of the absence of both the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman among those [categories], and because difference and non-difference are perceived through another mode [of existence]. If it be argued that they stand in the relation of part and whole based on the Smṛti text, "The world of living beings is indeed a portion of Me," we say no; for this contradicts the Śruti text, "Without parts, without activity. Furthermore, the statement, "All beings are a foot of Him," is spoken merely with the intention of indicating their smallness, since the purport of the passage is to establish the infinity of Brahman; moreover, if Brahman possessed parts, it would follow—like a cloth—that it must be composed of constituent parts.

If it is argued that partlessness is inherent while having parts is caused by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the intellect (*buddhi*), we say no: the individual soul (*jīva*) cannot be split apart from itself by means of an adjunct. For even when space—which is partless—is struck by the edge of a sword, no division is observed. Furthermore, if Brahman were to experience transmigratory existence by splitting its own self through adjuncts, it would merely manifest delusion within itself. Moreover, the creation of adjuncts is not for the sake of some other purpose [such as splitting the Self].

Because of the absence of otherness—since there is no difference among individual souls (jīvas) who were previously non-distinct—and because it is only by means of a substance that a substance can be divided, as well as because karma, ignorance, and latent impressions, though existing, do not constitute limiting adjuncts (upādhis).

If it is argued that difference, though unestablished, is manifested as being adventitious (*aupādhika*), then difference must indeed be beginningless (*anādi*). Furthermore, that [beginningless difference] could not be based on the relationship between genus (*jāti*) and individual (*vyakti*) in the case of Brahman and the individual soul (*jīva*). If it is argued that difference is intrinsic (*svābhāvika*)—like blue and yellow—and non-difference is based on the genus of substantiality (*dravyatva*) and so forth, then, just like that [intrinsic difference], there would be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) such as "This Self is Brahman," and the scriptural texts concerning its entry [into the world] would be contradicted. Moreover, the inference for unity has already been demonstrated.

If it is argued that [the difference] is not established, nor is it beginningless, but rather that difference appears there based on limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), then that would indeed be a delusion (*vibhrama*), consisting in the superimposition of something onto what it is not. Furthermore, it has already been stated that the difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman is not apprehended by perception or other means of knowledge. Moreover, scripture negates difference in the passage, "There is no other seer but He. If it is argued that those passages merely express non-difference, do not say so.

Since non-difference has been established by such passages as "This is your Self," and difference is subsequently negated in that very same context, how can there be a systematic distinction (vyavasthā) regarding ignorance, desire, and action even while non-difference exists? For when space is delimited by a jar and smoke or the like enters within it, the connection of space with the smoke cannot be avoided. [Objection: But surely, because of difference, there is also a systematic distinction; [Response: In that case, both the association and the non-association of ignorance and so forth would have to exist in Brahman.

Is it not the case that a contradiction is being urged here? What indeed is this so-called "contradiction" for one who maintains both difference and non-difference? If you argue that non-difference does not mean non-existence, but rather that within a single substrate there is the acceptance of both existence and non-existence of the same thing—namely, that unity itself is a distinct attribute (*dharmāntara*)—even so: since we observe sublation through the cognition of difference and unity in cases such as "I am a man" and "there are two moons," why should those who accept difference and non-difference in one place not likewise accept existence and non-existence in Brahman?
Furthermore, when each individual part of the cloth of the body is in contact with impurity, one thinks, "I am a dirty cloth," or "I am dirty."

Furthermore, because there is a certainty of the contact with impurity in the whole (the body), and because statements regarding results—which describe present states—are merely *arthavādas* (explanatory or figurative passages) since they contradict direct perception, it would follow that even if there were a distinction, Brahman as a whole, being associated with the impurities inherent in the individual soul (*jīva*), would be determined to be predominantly impure. Moreover, how can one whose inner organ overflows with supreme devotion—being unable to tolerate even the contact of ignorance and other impurities in Brahman—tolerate non-difference from those very same impurities! If you argue that non-difference is untenable due to its contradiction with the faultless scriptures (*śruti*), we say no.

Because of the scriptural teaching that [Brahman] is the self of all. For this very reason, it was said that this position is the most wretched. Now, one might object: "Is it not established by the distinction of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*)? No; for since there is no real distinction in meaning, and since the connection with transmigratory existence—which is ultimately real—is non-different, any systematic arrangement (*vyavasthā*) is untenable. However, a systematic arrangement of illusory transmigratory existence is logical through illusory distinction, as is seen in the case of an original object and its reflection. Furthermore, does Brahman perceive all individual souls as its own self, or not? If it does not, its omniscience would be lost.

If it perceives, it would perceive saṃsāra within its own self. But surely it also perceives difference; in that case, one might say that Brahman perceives saṃsāra in itself and yet does not perceive it. Furthermore, even while perceiving difference, one perceives the attributes of the body in the self due to the false conceit of identity; what then need be said regarding [perceiving them] through the conceit of real non-difference? For when there is the immediate perception of non-difference, difference is never seen to appear as an immediate manifestation.

Furthermore, for Brahman—the support of all and the omniscient one—who perceives everything as real and directly within Himself, there would necessarily be a connection with the entire cycle of transmigratory existence. Moreover, even if a single individual soul were dissolved into a single limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) through the means of knowledge, meditation, and absorption, no purpose whatsoever would be served; for the connection with all remaining limiting adjuncts and their attributes would still continue to manifest. And it is impossible for anyone to effect liberation from all limiting adjuncts.

For me, however, even though the nature of Brahman as the Self—manifest as the original image—is directly perceived through the relinquishment of a single limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), there is no connection with the transmigrations of the individual soul (*jīva*), just as there is no connection with the darkness of a reflection. This is because such transmigrations are false and are sublated by the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). Furthermore, just as in the case of dreams and the like, liberation from all limiting adjuncts through the knowledge of reality is logically consistent.

If it is argued that, upon the liberation of Vāmadeva and others, there would now be no perception of saṃsāra, [we reply: even though each individual is liberated, since infinite souls have been liberated over infinite ages, the non-perception of saṃsāra at this time is equal for both of us. Furthermore, the observation of saṃsāra at present is equally common to you as well. And the logical inconsistency is the same for both of us. Therefore, while You, the unconditioned Consciousness, are Brahman manifest before our eyes, your perception of liberation within conditioned consciousnesses amidst the appearance of bondage is an illusion.

Since the scriptures and other authorities concerning that [Brahman] are not contradicted by perception, they are merely *arthavādas* (explanatory or commendatory statements). Furthermore, since the distinctions of conditioned consciousness (*sopādhika-caitanya*) are imagined within You, who are the manifestation of unconditioned consciousness (*nirupādhika-caitanya*), the doubt does not arise for you as to which single entity undergoes bondage and liberation; this is because there is a delusion of liberation among those with conditioned consciousness, and because their words are merely *arthavādas*. Thus, each individual self has no such doubt. Therefore, this confusion belongs to the proponent of universal commingling (*sarvasaṅkaravādin*); in our position, there is systematic order (*vyavasthā*).

Thus, since the realization of Brahman culminates in immediate perception (*aparokṣa*) as its fruit even without an injunction, and because there is no other goal to be accomplished, there can be no connection with an injunction; this he states: "This being so" (*tatraivaṃ sati*). What then is the fruit of the means of knowledge? To that he says: "Therefore, [the world] is indeed false" (*ato mithyaiva*).

Now, is it because of the absence of a purpose that Brahman is not the object of an injunction, or rather because of the absence of its being an objective factor (*kāraka*)? As for the purpose, liberation, which is the goal to be accomplished, will be explained; [Brahman is not the object of an injunction] not because of the absence of its being an objective factor, but because it is the objective factor of the act of knowing (*vidikriyā*). Thus he says: "Is it not the object of the act of knowing? The commentary itself provides the answer: "And it is not so. Now, one might object: if Brahman is not the object of the act of knowing, then since the knowledge produced by the scripture would lack a defining characteristic (*vyāvartakatva*), Brahman would not be something accessible through the scripture. To this he raises the objection: "This is like the case of a rite for pacification (*śāntikarman*)."

It establishes that Brahman is the object of knowledge (prameya) of the scripture by demonstrating that, although Brahman is self-luminous and thus independent of the production of a manifestation of its own object, it nevertheless takes on the form of the knowledge generated by the scripture; thereby, it possesses the fruit of removing defects such as ignorance (avidyā) and serves to differentiate [Brahman] from other things.

To this, the following reply is given: "It is not imagined by ignorance," and so forth. Now, one might object: "Without the illumination of an object not previously apprehended, the operation of a means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa) would lack its fruit. To this he says: "For the scripture [says] 'This is that,' and so forth. Again, one might ask: "In that case as well, how can there be an operation of a means of valid knowledge directed merely toward what is to be removed, without the apprehension of an object? To this he says: "For it is thus..."

This has already been stated: since the identity of Devadatta is established by recognition itself, the validity of the two sentences of recognition arises through the removal of the difference imagined by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) by means of the knowledge produced by those sentences. Now, one might object that since there is no misconception regarding the Self that is Brahman, their validity cannot arise even through the removal of such [misconception]. To this, he says: "In the same way, so too is the referent of the term *tvam*."

By what form of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then, is error dispelled? To this he says: "attaining oneness with the referent of that word" (*tatpadārthaikatām upagacchan*). The meaning is that the identity of Brahman and the Self, indicated by the two words *tat* and *tvam*, is the form of the cognition. What, then, is dispelled by that cognition of such a form? To this he says: "produced by the adjuncts of the 'I'-aspect and the 'this'-aspect of the Self. He states that the operation of a means of knowledge consists precisely in the arising of the form of the object; and because of the very nature of the thing being cognized, there is the dispelling of error—hence he says: "by implication" (*arthāt*).

[Objection: Is it not the case that consciousness (*saṃvit*), which resides in the knower and takes the form of the object known, is the fruit of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and by this [definition] error is excluded? For luminosity itself is opposed to non-luminosity, and since the luminosity of consciousness is eternal, there can be no fruit of a means of knowledge for it. To this, he says: "The fruit of the means of knowledge is the manifestation of that which is not 'this' (*anidamparāmarśa*) as being delimited. Consciousness pertaining to an object made its own by a means of knowledge is called the fruit of the means of knowledge; it is not something produced by the means of knowledge, because even in common worldly usage it is unproduced (*ajanya*).

Therefore, consciousness (caitanya), which was previously delimited by the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge, removes the knower and the rest; for there is no contradiction between the delimitation and its removal, as they exist in the relation of preceding and succeeding moments. Now, an objection is raised: if the fruit (phala) is the remover, then because it arises immediately after that which is to be removed, the fruit would persist for only as long as that duration. To this he says "no"—"that [fruit] also consists in the destruction of the delimiting factors. But if Brahman is not manifested by the knowledge produced by the scripture, then it would not be accessible through the scripture. To this he says: "by that [knowledge], of the fourfold set beginning with the means of knowledge."

Now, one might object: "Why is it said that only the cessation of ignorance is the fruit of valid cognition? Let the illumination of the object also be called the fruit of valid cognition. To this, he replies: "And thus, of such a kind..."

"It is unknown to those who know," as in the passage beginning with "from which words turn back. Now, an objection may be raised: since it is heard that "it is to be seen by the mind alone" and "that person is the one to be known from the Upanishads," it appears to be an object of the activity of cognition; this is not a fault. For the following systematic distinction is established: being the object of the scripture's teaching means being the differentiator through the provision of a form by the immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*) produced by the Vedānta; whereas being non-objective means being devoid of any excellence of illumination produced by cognition. Thus, the arrangement is logically consistent.

For there is no arising of another quality of illumination within a quality of illumination itself. Now, one might object that since even the cessation of ignorance is accomplished by knowledge, liberation must be non-eternal; to this he says, "And thus, [the Self] is eternally liberated."

Now, who is this so-called *jīva*, whose essential nature—as indicated by the term "thou" (*tvam-pada*)—becomes Brahman itself as the meaning of the sentence? We say that it is Brahman itself reflected through ignorance (*avidyā*). Consequently, when the term "thou" excludes all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), the very nature of the Self thus indicated becomes none other than Brahman—the object indicated by the term "that" (*tat-pada*)—by virtue of the power of the two words together. Nor can the knowledge of the pure Brahman-Self be attained through the exclusion of these two sets of adjuncts by means of a single word alone.

Because there is no arising of contradiction. Now, one might ask: why could the meaning of the sentence not be "identity-in-difference" (*bhedābheda*)? It cannot; for if that were the case, since the referent of the term *tvam* (the individual self) is qualified by its body and senses, the meaning of the sentence would be established as being merely the identity-in-difference of that [self] with Brahman. Consequently, there would be no sublation of superimposition through the knowledge of Brahman-as-Self via secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*). Furthermore, because statements describing a present state and those stating results are contradicted by the non-perception of what is otherwise possible, even when the knowledge of reality exists, there would be no realization of the cessation of the bondage of the scriptures.

Furthermore, if the meaning of a sentence were both different and non-different [from its constituent parts], the cessation of the aspect of difference would not result from the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*); for that knowledge does not destroy its own object. To assume that such cessation occurs through ritual action, meditation, or direct experience is contradicted by the scripture whose subject matter is both difference and non-difference at all times. As for the proposed systematic arrangement—that the usage of terms like "knowledge" and "liberation" pertains to the aspect of non-difference, while the usage of terms like "ritual action" and "science" pertains to the aspect of difference—that is merely a deceptive lure for those of dull intellect.

For instance, if the soul (*jīva*) as a whole were [composed] of both difference and non-difference, and the non-different part were Brahman itself, then the meaning would result in this: that Brahman possesses parts and that the soul is a part of Brahman—a conclusion that would indeed befall one who considers himself a scholar. If the different part were not Brahman, there would be absolute difference between them. Nor can the soul be a composite of both parts, for that would entail the consequence of its being a non-entity. Nor can the non-different part alone be the soul, for that would entail the consequence of the soul being nothing other than Brahman itself. Nor can it be both parts, for that would entail the consequence of there being two souls.

Nor is the individual soul (*jīva*) merely the aspect of difference, for that would entail the consequence of absolute difference, whereby the conventional practices of the knowledge of reality, liberation, and so forth, would be impossible. If it is argued that the soul is the non-differentiation of the aspects of difference and non-difference, then, if these two are indeed non-different, the soul is simply Brahman; in that case, how could there be a systematic distinction between the conventions of bondage and liberation? If, on the other hand, it is held that the aspects of difference and non-difference are themselves both different and non-different from one another, this is not so, as it would lead to an infinite regress of difference and the like.

Furthermore, whether one considers the whole (*aṃśin*), the collection of its two parts, or the two parts themselves as non-different from each other, if these constitute the individual soul (*jīva*), it is impossible to avoid the conclusion that Brahman is a part of the soul. Moreover, for whom is this scriptural instruction intended? It cannot be for the non-dual part, because that, being the very nature of Brahman, does not require instruction; nor can it be for the dual part, because the realization "I am Brahman" would be impossible for it. Furthermore, a return to non-duality for that which possesses the aspect of duality is not possible.

Because of contradiction, and because it would follow that transmigratory existence (saṃsāra) would belong to Brahman itself. To whom does this defect of ignorance belong? It cannot belong to the aspect of non-difference, for that would result in its belonging to Brahman itself. Nor can it belong to the aspect of difference, because difference does not exist prior to the production of limiting adjuncts (upādhi). If it is argued that the defect of bondage belongs to the individual soul (jīva)—which is the substratum possessing the aspect of difference by its own nature—then upon the destruction of that [aspect], the soul itself would be destroyed; for in liberation, the aspect of difference is destroyed, while the aspect of non-difference is eternally liberated. To whom, then, is this liberation taught?

Even in that case, if it were both different and non-different, there would be a contradiction with the word "only" in the passage, "One who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself," and there would also be no distinction from the state of transmigratory existence.

Furthermore, how could this person—who perceives all things as intermingled and proceeds to establish heaven, hell, bondage, liberation, and so forth in a state of confusion—not feel shame before those of refined intellect? If everything is established through distinction alone, then what is the use of this barren, imagined distinction which serves no purpose of its own application, since there is no basis for the attribute of "distinction" apart from the substratum and the counter-correlate?

The determination of difference and non-difference based on a distinction of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) precludes actual difference and non-difference in a single entity, because the locus (*dharmin*) and its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) are distinct. Furthermore, the scripture—through such passages as "There is no other seer but He" (*nānyo 'to 'sti draṣṭā*)—establishes non-difference precisely by subverting difference; and likewise, "This is your Self" (*eṣa ta ātmā*). Nor can the non-difference of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman be established through universals such as existence (*sattva*), for that would be proven by inference alone and thus would not depend upon scripture. [Objection: But for you, who maintains absolute non-difference, everything would become confused; it would not for me.

This is not so, because difference is admitted [only conventionally]. Since the manifold of effects has an unascertained nature, the distinction between difference and so forth is accepted only according to how it appears, while non-difference is accepted as belonging to the Self alone. Therefore, this position of difference-and-non-difference is adopted by those of dull intellect, whose minds are oppressed by the heavy burden of many bamboo-like arguments, for the mere purpose of self-satisfaction.

Consequently, it is most excellent that this very Brahman is established by the sentence as having its distinctions sublated—like Devadatta—through the reflection of distinctions caused by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
He states the purport of the subsequent portion of the commentary, beginning with "But for whom liberation is something to be produced," as follows: "Now, even in the case of Brahman..."

He asks, "How is it that action is not possible? because the status of being an agent (*kārakatva*) is possible [in knowledge]. To this, he says: "How so? In this regard, the following must be stated: Is knowledge enjoined to bestow a fruit such as the *apūrva* (unseen potency) inherent in the agent, like the sacrifice (*yāga*) and other rites? Or is it for the sake of a fruit consisting of an excellence produced in the object or the instrument? It cannot be the first alternative, because it has already been refuted starting from the passage: "Because there is a difference between the fruits of ritual action and the knowledge of Brahman. Nor can it be the second alternative; thus he says: "If, first of all, it were something to be produced," and so forth.

On this point, some say: even if liberation (*mokṣa*) were something to be produced, there would be no fault of impermanence; for only that which is accomplished by action (*kriyā*) is impermanent, whereas liberation is accomplished by knowledge alone (*jñāna-mātra*), and nothing accomplished by knowledge alone is seen to be impermanent. Furthermore, it is not merely the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā-nivṛtti*) that is accomplished by knowledge, since the state of being Brahman (*brahma-bhāva*) is also to be accomplished. [Objection: But the state of being Brahman is natural (*svābhāvika*) to the individual soul (*jīva*) and thus not something to be accomplished. [Reply: No, because it is identity (*tādātmya*) itself that is natural.

Identity (*tādātmya*) consists in the contradiction of being merely that which is differentiated. However, the state of being that [identity], namely the state of Brahmanhood of the individual soul (*jīva*), is accomplished through knowledge, according to the force of both types of scriptural statements: "The knower of the Self crosses over sorrow" and "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself. To this, it is replied: Is liberation accomplished by means of the correct knowledge produced by the scriptures, which has identity as its object, or by that which has the state of being that [identity] as its object? It cannot be by the latter, because that would entail the consequence that it is eternally established.

If it is argued that even in that case, once identity (*tādātmya*) has ceased with respect to its object, the existence of that [object] is either established or not, then it must be stated: if it has ceased, it would follow that knowledge is shown to be the destroyer of its own object. Furthermore, if it were removable by knowledge, ignorance itself would have to become identical [to knowledge]. On the other hand, as long as identity has not ceased, the existence of that [object] is not tenable; for it is impossible for mere identity and its contradiction to coexist simultaneously.

Furthermore, it must be stated whether "that state" (*tadbhāva*) is simply the cessation of identity (*tādātmya*), or something else. If it is the cessation itself, then it would be said that liberation is merely the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā*). If it is something else, then another form must be described apart from both identity and that state. For no other form can be defined for the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman than absolute difference, which is distinct from identity and that state. And what indeed is this so-called "that state"? It cannot be Brahman alone, because it is not something to be accomplished (*asādhya*).

For this very reason, the individual soul (jīva) is not [identical with Brahman]; nor can a third entity, whether conscious or unconscious, be established as being that [Brahman]. Furthermore, if the soul were characterized by an identity-distinguishing difference (tādātmya-lakṣaṇātireka), it would undergo destruction upon the destruction of that [Brahman]. If the soul were [Brahman] with its identity abstracted, it would be nothing but Brahman alone, since absolute difference is not admitted. Therefore, the state of being that [Brahman] through identity with it is devoid of both scripture and reasoning. Nor is identity perceived between the individual soul and Brahman, which are indicated (lakṣyamāṇa) by the two words "that" (tat) and "thou" (tvam).

Because a single reality is perceived through the apprehension of different limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), the appearance of difference is not removed when that reality is indicated by a single word alone. Furthermore, the scriptural declarations of results can be appropriately applied to the cessation of ignorance. Nor is there the attainment of eternity for that which is accomplished by knowledge; for we observe that a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) produced thereby is non-eternal. Moreover, such a mental impression is not produced by an action, because—like other impressions—it cannot serve as a cause for recollection, and because this would contradict the principles of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

If it is argued that because the knowledge of Brahman is something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), it must be produced by action (*kriyājanyatā*), we say no; for [the reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to action. Therefore, only "coming into being after not having been" (*abhūtvā bhavanam*) is the cause of impermanence. To this, one might raise the objection: "In that case, let the third kind of fruit be accepted as that which is accomplished by action"—this is expressed in the phrase "for the sake of avoiding impermanence."

In this regard, the following must be stated: Is Brahman identical with the inner self (*pratyagātman*), or is it distinct? If it is distinct, is Brahman all-pervading or does it reside in a specific location? Regarding the case of identity, he states the refutation: "That also is not so. If it is distinct and all-pervading, since there is no attainment other than conjunction (*saṃyoga*), conjunction would be eternally established; thus he says: "Even if it is distinct... He raises the possibility of its residing in a specific location: "Now, [if it resides] in the modification (*vikāra*)."

In this regard, it must be stated: is the existence [of Brahman] in a specific location asserted in order to avoid contact with modification, or is it due to the force of the scripture? Furthermore, the scripture shows that Brahman is indeed all-pervading, and even though it is all-pervading, there is no contact with modification; thus he says: "Nor even in the place of modification. Now, one might suspect that because all-pervasiveness is merely figurative, Brahman exists only in a particular location; to this he says: "Now, [if it is argued that] it does not abide in the place of modification... No; it is not so.

Because an object of intermediate size, like the earth and so forth, possesses parts. To demonstrate the divisions of the refutation, he analyzes [the position] and states the refutation regarding the first alternative—that it is indeed the attainment of that [Brahman]—as follows: "In that case, there would be the destruction of its own nature. For in that regard, neither the state of Brahman for the individual soul (*jīva*), nor the individual soul being Brahman itself, is possible; because [such a state] is not something to be produced (*asādhyatvāt*). Nor is it a distinct substance (*dravyāntara*) being commenced from the individual soul and Brahman.

Because it would follow that [Brahman] is subject to destruction, and because it is impossible for the all-pervading Brahman to possess parts. Nor is there any relation called "identity" (tādātmya) between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman; for there is no relation between two distinct substances other than conjunction (saṃyoga). Nor can there be an attainment of the nature of Brahman while the soul remains of atomic dimension (aṇuparimāṇa), due to contradiction; and if the dimension were not fixed, the very nature of the substance would be destroyed. Regarding the second alternative as well, he states the refutation: "of conjunction," etc.

[Objection: But surely, since non-return is established by the authority of the scriptures (*śāstra*), how can a return be proved by means of reasoning (*tarka*)? To this, he says: "Nor is there a scriptural statement regarding non-return. This is because, if taken according to the literal sense, it would result in a prohibition of what has not been attained; because the conceptualization that "he will not return" contradicts the inference based on the fact of being produced (*kṛtakatva*); and because if he were to remain in his own essential nature, it would entail the consequence of multiple lords, contrary to the scriptural text, "He becomes self-ruling" (*sa svarāḍ bhavati*). Therefore, there is no attainment of Brahman residing in another location.

But is it not heard in scripture: "Going upwards by that, one attains immortality"? If so, then even those who rely on symbols (pratīka) would attain immortality upon departing through the cranial artery to reach the person of the Manava, since there is no distinction made in the scriptural statement. But is it not the case that for those traveling by the path of light and so forth, the attainment of Brahman is heard in the text: "He leads them to Brahman"? No; [that refers to a different context].

Because its object is the effected Brahman (*kāryabrahman*). Now, one might argue that since the primary meaning of the word "Brahman" is [the Supreme], the Supreme Brahman alone is understood; but this is not so. If the primacy [of the meaning] is asserted on the basis of usage among the elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*), then this word is indeed already conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in the sense of the effected Brahman as well. If, on the other hand, the primacy of the meaning is asserted by following the etymological derivation (*avayavārtha*), it is not so; for it is impossible for a single word to simultaneously employ both conventional (*rūḍhi*) and etymological (*yoga*) functions. When usage determines primacy, the effected Brahman alone is understood.

Furthermore, from the phrase "He leads them to the worlds of Brahman" (*brahmalokān*), indicated by the word *brahmaloka* and the plural number; from the hearing of the locus and those who occupy it in "They dwell in them as far as the distant regions" (*parāvataḥ*); from the hearing of a limitation of time in "They dwell there for eternal years" (*śāśvatīḥ samāḥ*); from the hearing of the number and the word "heaven" in "On both sides of the third heaven" (*tṛtīyasyābhito divi*); and likewise from the mention of the lake Airammadīya, the Aśvattha tree, the Soma-savana, the city Aparājitā, and the golden palace (*hiraṇmayaṃ veśma*).

Because of the mention of various objects of enjoyment, such as the ocean and couches, and because of the statement, "I enter the assembly hall and the palace of Prajāpati," it is understood that the assembly hall and palace of Prajāpati are the effected Brahman (kāryabrahman) reached by the path beginning with light. Furthermore, the compound is not *brahmaiva lokaḥ* ("Brahman itself is the world"); for the term *brahmaloka* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) as referring to Satyaloka, and even if it were etymological (*yaugika*), the word "world" (*loka*) would be in contradiction when applied to Brahman, since it more immediately evokes that [Satyaloka] in the mind.
