Nor is it appropriate to assume for the single word "Brahman" a primary meaning of the object itself—beyond its primary status as a designation—by way of setting aside these marks of the effected Brahman (kāryabrahma); for the word "Prajāpati" is conventionally established in the sense of the effected Brahman, and the word "world" (loka) denotes a specific place of enjoyment.

Furthermore, on this view, even those who know the five fires would attain the supreme Brahman. Nor is it reasonable to claim that the word "he" in the passage "He leads them to Brahman" refers to those other than the knowers of the five fires; for it is the knowers of the five fires alone who are the primary subject under discussion, and [otherwise] there would be the undesirable consequence of leaving them without a stated fruit.

Furthermore, it must be stated whether the fruit of the Gāyatrī, Śāṇḍilya-ṣoḍaśakala, Upakosala, Vaiśvānara, Bhūman, and Dahara-Paryaṅka meditations is of a single uniform nature as the attainment of Brahman, or whether it consists of degrees of increase and decrease. If the fruit were of a single uniform nature, then the increase and decrease of the meditation resulting from the addition or omission of qualities would be purposeless; for an increase in the fruit does not arise from an increase in the performance of the Agnihotra and other rites. If, however, an increase and decrease in the fruit are admitted, then there can be no attainment of Brahman, which is untouched by modification.

Because that [result] is absent there. Furthermore, it must be stated whether the attainment of the three worlds is intended as the fruit of the meditation on Vaiśvānara or not. If it is intended, how could the attainment of the fruit of being the self of the three worlds occur in Brahman, which is unassociated with modifications (*vikāra*)? If it is not intended, there would be a contradiction with the scripture stating, "In whatever way they meditate upon Him... Moreover, it must be stated whether enjoyment occurs in Brahman, which is unassociated with modifications, through the volitions regarding fathers and so forth, or not. If it does not, there would be a contradiction with the scripture concerning the volitions regarding fathers and so forth.

If it were so, Brahman would exist within the realm of modification and would be joined with fathers and the like. Furthermore, even for one who has attained Brahman existing within modification, the statement "Beholding these desires with the mind, he rejoices; endowed with that world of the fathers, he is magnified," would indicate that Brahman itself possesses the enjoyment of means [to pleasure]. Consequently, there would be a contradiction regarding the state of having all desires fulfilled, and creation would be motivated by self-interest.

Furthermore, it must be stated whether the subtle body (liṅgaśarīra) exists or does not exist for one who has attained Brahman, which abides in modification. If it exists, the scriptural teaching regarding the dissolution of the constituent parts (kalā-pravilaya) would be contradicted. If there is no subtle body, the scriptural passage stating, "By the mind [he attains] these desires," would be contradicted. Moreover, the cause for the dissolution of the subtle body in that state must be stated. If it were knowledge alone, it would have to occur at the time of departure [from the body], since the karma that initiates it has been exhausted. If it were the touch of the hand of the non-human being, it would have to occur at the station of lightning.

Furthermore, no cause for the dissolution of time is heard of in the subsequent [passage]. Moreover, in the view that the individual soul (jīva) is conditioned by limiting adjuncts (upādhi), it is not possible for the soul to go to Brahman, which does not abide within modifications; for it is impossible to extract and carry away a portion of space delimited by a jar, as space is partless. If such an extraction were to occur, this region would become devoid of Brahman, and furthermore, Brahman would undergo increase. Therefore, the illusion of movement in the Self arises from the movement of the limiting adjunct. But surely, even the movement of the adjunct is not possible?

Because Brahman, which is its material cause (*upādāna*), is devoid of motion—just as there is no movement of a jar while the clay remains stationary—it follows that the appearance of going and so forth is a manifestation of *māyā*, like the movement [perceived] in a dream. [Objection: It is not claimed that enjoyment (*bhoga*) occurs in Brahman through the volitions (*saṃkalpa*) of the father and others; rather, whatever enjoyment exists therein is included within the attainment of eternal bliss (*nityānanda*), and thus it is described as a variety of sovereignty (*aiśvaryabheda*). [Reply: No.

Because it would be improper to resort to a figurative interpretation of the many scriptural declarations of rewards for fear of abandoning the etymological meaning of the single word "Brahman," and because it would result in the futility of the final section of the Śāstra; therefore, the proposal that there is an injunction of ritual action for the sake of attaining the Brahman residing in another location is untenable.

He states the refutation regarding the position that [the self] is an object of refinement (*saṃskārya*)—namely, "even the state of being refined" (*saṃskāryatvamapi*). He raises the objection: "Is it not the case that refinement is the manifestation of the existing Brahman-nature through the removal of defects?"—this is expressed as "Now, of that which is already existing" (*atha vidyamānasya*). To this, it must be said: Is the removal of defects by an action residing in the Self, or by one residing in something else? First, there can be no vibration or transformation for the Self, which is partless; thus he says: "Because the Self is devoid of action" (*nātmanaḥ kriyārahitatvāt*). Nor [can it be] by an action residing in something else.

He says that because there is no conjunction with a substance possessing action (*kriyāvad-dravya*), no excellence (*atiśaya*) can be produced therein—namely, "because of its nature as something ever-new" (*pratyagrūpatvāt*). He raises an objection: "But surely, just as poison is dispelled by meditating upon a mantra-deity, so too might faults be removed by meditating upon the Lord (*īśvara*)," which he introduces with "But surely, by meditating upon the Lord. The refutation beginning with "It is said" (*ucyate*) has a clear meaning. An objection is raised: "But is it not heard in scripture that a refinement (*saṃskāra*) characterized by the addition of qualities to the self occurs through scriptural rites? To this he replies, "No," and says "nor... (*na ca*).

"By means of actions such as bathing," etc. This is the meaning: that which impels the instruments—the body, the senses, and the mind—is the agent, the enjoyer, and the one to be refined (*saṃskārya*). And that is the *ahaṅkāra* (ego) permeated by consciousness, according to the Vedic scripture: "Consciousness performs the sacrifice. And since it persists uninterruptedly until the end of *saṃsāra*, experience is possible. Furthermore, an excellence of merit and demerit arises therein, not in the changeless Self (*ātman*). Therefore, its status as the object to be refined is not tenable.

Therefore, the passage beginning with "it is not something to be refined" and ending before "nanu" has a clear meaning. The objection and its resolution, beginning with "But even for knowledge... and ending before "this other [point]," have already been mentioned previously; however, as they are relevant to the present context, they are brought forward here again with their meanings clarified.

The distinction between action and knowledge has been stated on the basis of their having produced and unproduced fruits respectively; now, he states the distinction based on their causes—namely, that action is to be accomplished through human desire and effort, whereas self-knowledge is independent of those. This is another distinction: [knowledge] is not produced by an injunction (*codanā*) in the way that it is produced by human desire and effort, because we observe that knowledge of foul odors and the like occurs even for one who does not desire it.

One might object: "Since knowledge produced by words lacks being produced by its object, it is not dependent on the thing itself; therefore, it must be produced solely by the injunction (codanā). To this, he replies: "Even there... [meaning] even in that case, [the cognition] is produced by the indicative suffixes (*liṅgādi*) and so forth, independent of the human desire and effort generated by the injunction. Thus he refutes: "Even there..."

But surely, what is this so-called "action" (*kriyā*) other than a collection of conjunctions and disjunctions? Is it not the case that this movement is indeed directly perceived through the cognition "it moves"? True; yet even that movement has as its objective basis only conjunctions and disjunctions. But then, would there not be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that a post (*sthāṇu*) also "moves" when it possesses conjunctions and disjunctions with a hawk? No; because the cognition [of movement] has as its objective basis conjunctions and disjunctions with one's own location, and the post does not have the hawk’s location as its own. If it is argued that everything has space (*ākāśa*) as its location, we say no.

For even when darkness is enveloped in dense gloom such that it is not perceived, one observes the cognition of motion in a firefly. Nor can conjunctions and disjunctions be perceived without perceiving space. Therefore, the cognition "it moves" has as its objective basis an action distinct from conjunction and disjunction. As for the one who infers action from the conjunctions and disjunctions with its own location—how so? Because conjunctions and disjunctions produced by a substance, occurring occasionally in their own substratum, must be preceded by some extraordinary property (atiśaya).

[The opponent argues: "Because [the action] occurs only occasionally (kādācitkatva) in a substance that is already established, like an effect produced by conjunction and disjunction. [The proponent replies: This reason is inconclusive (anaikāntika), because even though the conjunction with and disjunction from the water in its own location exist in the stable and immovable parts of the substrates—the currents of water such as crocodiles and the like—there is an absence of action and cognition in those [parts].

Furthermore, the excellence (*atiśaya*) that is the cause of conjunction and disjunction—which is what we designate as "action" (*kriyā*)—must arise either from a stable substance itself or from a substance already possessing another excellence. In the first case, since action would arise from a substance that is not yet established [as having motion], the production of conjunction and disjunction would likewise proceed from that very same [stable] substance; thus, the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). If one postulates a further excellence [to account for the initial motion], there results the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

For, just as an action residing in the foot initiates a conjunction with the foot that is inherent in it but not connected to its own substratum, so too the conjunction of the self—possessed of effort—with the foot initiates a conjunction between the earth and the foot; thus, there is no room for an excellence in the action residing in the foot. Therefore, the cognition of action is perceptual.

[Objection: But how can an action that is momentary persist for two moments, characterized as the conjunction with the sense organ and the resulting cognition? [Response: There is no contradiction, just as in the case of sound, lightning, and so forth. Therefore, there exists [an action] distinct from the cognition of the action itself. The phrase "moreover" (*kiṃca*) has a clear meaning. Furthermore, it is stated that the means to liberation is the knowledge of reality, which has as its object a determined meaning, as in the passage: "Those whose objects are well-ascertained through the wisdom of Vedānta. And that [knowledge] is possible only if it is produced by a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Thus he says: "In this way, because it is established as being correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*)."
He states the illustrative example: "This being so..."

[Objection: But surely injunctions regarding the knowledge of Brahman are heard in scripture; how then can they be set aside by reasoning? To this he says: "Therefore, even though they are heard... [Objection: But if there is no injunction due to the absence of anything to be performed, the word would be useless; to this he says: "No, because it serves as a mere explanatory praise (arthavāda). [Objection: But if, like other explanatory praises, it functions as a glorification, the injunctive word would be devoid of meaning; to this he says: "Because it directs the mind toward that [Brahman]."

With the words beginning "Hearing thatness," etc., [the author] analyzes and demonstrates those means such as hearing by which the Self is praised. Now, one might ask: "What benefit is produced by hearing and the rest, such that the Self would be praised by being made the object of these exalted practices? To this he says: "Therefore, because of stability regarding the meaning of the sentence. One might further object: "An explanatory passage (arthavāda) is connected only with that which is to be enjoined, because praise has the fruit of inducing activity, not with an already established entity. Thus he raises the objection: "But what then..."

Since even the praise of the fruit is useful for engaging in practice, it is logical that the praise of the Self—which is the fruit itself—is also useful for engaging in hearing [the teachings] and so forth; with this intention, he says: "This is what is relevant here," and so on. The text, however, is clear in its meaning.

Now, it might be argued that since right vision (*samyagdarśana*) is of the nature of a fruit and is dependent upon the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it is not something to be enjoined, and thus its status as an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) is logical; whereas hearing (*śravaṇa*) and the rest, being of the nature of action, are indeed to be enjoined because they provide both visible and invisible assistance to right vision. To this he says: "And all this [is established] by the very first sūtra. The meaning is that the first sūtra was composed by accepting the injunction of hearing—augmented by reflection (*manana*) and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*)—for the sake of right vision.

It has been stated that even injunctions (*vidhi*) possess a commendatory character; now, he states another meaning of the word—namely, "Furthermore, this is not at all... [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.7]. Now, one might object: "Granted that there are no injunctions for knowledge (*jñāna-vidhi*), yet an injunction for meditation (*upāsanā-vidhi*) is indeed heard in scripture. To this he replies, "No," with the words "Therefore, one should meditate [on the Self] as 'This indeed is the Self'" (*tenātmetyevopāsīta*) and so forth. Because the restrictive particle *eva* is heard everywhere [in such passages], a specific object is being established by way of restating the recurrence of the notion already obtained through its own nature as "I" (*aham*); thus, he concludes that [the knowledge of Brahman] is devoid of rejection and acquisition (*hānopādāna-śūnya*).

He explains the commentary with the words: "This is its meaning. It has been stated in the second section—and in the first section as well—that for the purpose of defining Brahman, which is the object of knowledge enjoined for the fruit of liberation, the Vedāntas are authoritative regarding Brahman independently of any injunction; thus, the authority of the Vedāntas regarding Brahman without dependence on other means of knowledge was asserted. Now, having raised an objection to the meaning of both those sections, he resolves it with the words beginning: "As for what some say," and so forth.

How is it that the self (*ātman*) is taught by the Vedāntas? Is it only that which is determined by the notion of "I," or is it something distinct from that? If the former, then because such a self would be a subordinate factor (*aṅga*) in ritual action, the Vedāntas would share syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) with injunctive sentences. If, on the other hand, something distinct from that is taught, then since there would be no object to be designated (*uddeśyatā*), there could be no teaching at all—following the principle that "something must be taught with reference to something else. Furthermore, if that [distinct self] were conscious, it would likewise not be a subordinate factor in ritual action. Therefore, the Vedāntas are authoritative only with respect to ritual action.

And thus Āpastamba demonstrates that the authority of the entire Veda lies solely in ritual action (karman): "The conviction of those learned in the three Vedas is that the Vedas are authoritative. In this regard, whatever is heard concerning rice, barley, cattle, clarified butter, milk, potsherds, and the wife—such as 'the rite should be performed loudly' or 'in a low voice'—any conduct contrary to these is considered non-authoritative. Likewise: "The Vedas have the Agnihotra as their fruit; sacred learning has character and conduct as its fruit."

To this, he states the answer with the words beginning "tannopaniṣadasya" (that is not [the case] for the follower of the Upaniṣads). The meaning is that the Self, which is distinct from the qualified self apprehended by the notion of "I" and is devoid of the connection between action and its factors (kāraka), does not lead to the Vedāntas being subordinate to injunctions as a subsidiary part of ritual action.

[Objection: But surely, if this [Self] is also conscious, it must be a constituent of ritual action (*karmāṅga*) by virtue of being accessible through the notion of "I" (*ahaṃpratyaya*). [Reply: No, he says—"Not by anyone. [Objection: But why should that which is accessible through scripture (*śāstra*) not also be a constituent of ritual action? [Reply: To this he says—"For that which is not established by another means of knowledge... This is because, having referred to the qualified person (*adhikārī*) and the agent (*kartṛ*) as already established by other means of knowledge, the text merely teaches the injunction (*vidhi*); otherwise, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).

[Objection: But surely, because the conscious self (cetana) is not accessible through other means of knowledge, it is not known even by the scripture (śāstra). [Reply: No; he says, "And it is not the case that it is not cognized. [Objection: But it has been stated by the authors of the Smṛtis that the entire Veda is applied to dharma. To this he replies: "Precisely for this reason, [it is said] 'being based on the Upaniṣads' (aupaniṣadatva). The secondary derivative suffix (taddhita-pratyaya) in the word "aupaniṣada" applies the Vedāntas to Brahman.

Likewise, from the Śruti and Smṛti passages, "That goal which all the Vedas proclaim" and "By all the Vedas I alone am to be known; I am the author of the Vedānta," it is understood that the Vedāntas have Brahman as their ultimate purport. Now, one might object: even if Brahman is perceived through the syntactical connection of words (*padasamanvaya*), it must be a false cognition because it is sublated by perception and other means of knowledge. To this he replies: "This [Brahman], though being perceived... He further says: "And for this reason also, it cannot be [sublated]... [meaning it cannot be sublated because there is no other object to be apprehended]. As for the objection that because there is no subject to be enunciated (*uddeśa*), the predicate (*upādeya*) cannot be established as an object of valid cognition, he says: "For this reason also, it cannot be [established]... [meaning it is not impossible to establish it].

Now, one might object: "Even if one points to the self as the object of the notion of 'I' (*ahaṃpratyaya*) and then teaches that it is Brahman—the non-dual, unsurpassed knowledge and bliss—then because the self would be a non-entity, [the teaching] would be without a basis (*nirālambana*). To this he replies, "No," with the words beginning, "And because the self is not to be rejected" (*ātmānaścānirākāryatvāt*).

He concludes the meaning of the section with the words, "Therefore, [the Self] is devoid of the three limitations," and so forth. An objection is raised: "But surely, by the force of the author of the Sūtras’ statement, the entire Veda is enjoined solely for the purpose of action. To this he replies with the words, "But [regarding] the scripture... Now, one might ask: how can there be a determination of the meaning of the beginningless collection of Vedic words based on a human statement? It is said in reply: from the beginningless practice of usage, cognition, and application, which occurs solely for the sake of action, this is understood. Thus he says: "Therefore, [the Veda teaches] engagement and withdrawal..."

[Objection: But surely, immediately after hearing a word, a cognition arises even regarding an object that has already existed. [Reply: No, he says—"From that, there is no comprehension of the real thing. [Objection: But how could the comprehension of Brahman, which was previously unknown, be an error? [Reply: To this he says—"Therefore, that is false. The meaning is: because of the absence of the word's own power [to denote it] and because of the absence of corroboration. [Objection: If a valid cognition (*pramiti*) does indeed arise regarding an object that has already existed, then one should not postulate the word's power in that case. Thus he raises an objection: "But how then..."

He refutes this with the words: "of the word, there [in that case]. Now, one might object: just as smoke, whose relation has been grasped in a general sense, makes known a particular [object], so too a word whose relation has been grasped for the sake of an action (kriyārtha) could convey a past (bhūta) object. To this he says, "No," with the words: "and not when its capacity has not been grasped. Then, one might suggest: let the relation be grasped even with respect to a past object. To this he says, "No," with the words: "and the grasping of capacity..."

[Objection: "But surely, since activity occurs even toward an object that has already come into being, one may grasp the capacity [of words] through the inference of knowledge. [Reply: No, he says: "In its absence, from where [could it arise]? Activity occurs toward what is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), not toward an object that has already come into being. It is replied: the refutation begins with the words "Not so, by the author of the Sūtras," and so forth. How is this established by the Vārttikakāra, who follows worldly reasoning? He states: "It is *abhihitānvaya* (the connection of what is expressed). *Abhihitānvaya* is the cognition of the mutually related meanings of word-meanings once they have been understood from the words.

In that regard, having inferred through the listener’s activity that the cognition of a specific relation is the effect of the word, one understands that the collection of words possesses the capacity for the collection of meanings. Therein, through the methods of insertion (*āvāpa*) and deletion (*uddhāra*) in various usages such as “Bring the cow” and “Tie up the cow,” although there is deviation regarding the act of bringing and its relations, because the word *go* (cow) is invariably connected with the mere cow even when [the verb] *badhāna* (tie up) is used, one understands that the relationship of the word *go* pertains to the mere cow, and not to the act of bringing or its relations, because of their deviation.

Thus, when one observes that the capacity of all words is understood only with respect to the individual natures of word-meanings, the question arises: what is the basis for the cognition of their mutual relation (*saṃsarga*)? In response to this inquiry, it is postulated—on the basis of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that cannot be explained otherwise—that the cognition of relation is based on the word-meanings as apprehended by the words themselves. Therefore, the view of those who maintain the theory of the "relation of the expressed" (*abhihitānvayavāda*) is that meanings arise from words, and the relation arises from those meanings.

In this regard, if it is claimed that words expressing non-action lack an objective referent (*ālambana*), or alternatively that they lack a purpose (*prayojana*), then: if it is the absence of an objective referent that is meant, he says: "You see Devadatta, drive the cow hither. Now, if it is not the absence of an objective referent, but rather the absence of a purpose, he says: "If it is understood... If it is argued that words whose meaning is not action lack a purpose because action itself lacks the status of being a purpose, he says: "And the purpose is immediate."

Now, if it is argued that the purpose [of words] consists solely in action (*kriyā*), he says "True, for some"—meaning this applies to certain [words]. Therefore, [he says] "of those which express objects not conducive to such purposive action. But if it is asked, "Is it not the case that everything has action as its door to purpose? he says "No," [adding] "in the realization of Brahman as the Self. Thus, even when the expressed word-meanings convey their own meanings as connected with a purposeful object, it is possible for them to convey an already existing reality (*bhūtavastu*).

Here the Prābhākara objects: the capacity of a word resides in its own meaning as conjoined with an action (*kārya*), not in the mere meaning of the word itself; thus he says, "This might be so, even though... [and so forth]. Now, if the capacity is perceived in the case of an existent fact (*bhūtārtha*), then let the connection with that existent fact also be cognized; to this he replies, "No," saying, "even so, it is not [cognized] without [the action] being understood. The meaning is that only the action qualified by the existent fact is what is cognized.

[Objection: "But if the word's capacity [to convey meaning] resides in its sense as conjoined [with something else], then let the conjunction be cognized in the case of an already existing thing (bhūta). [Reply: No, he says—"[only] by virtue of being for the sake of action" (kriyārthatayā). This means "only by virtue of being conjoined with an injunction" (niyoga). [Objection: "Even if the word's capacity resides in its own sense as conjoined with what is to be done (kārya), since the sense as conjoined [with another] is included therein, then by that very motivator, the conjunction should be cognized even in the case of an existing thing. [Reply: No, he says—"for [the sense] of that [cow] is not [conveyed] from the word 'cow'..."

This is the intended meaning: after hearing the words "Bring the white cow with a stick," one observes the listener's activity toward bringing the cow; thus, one understands that the necessity of bringing the cow was apprehended by him from this verbal expression. Consequently, one ascertains the capacity of the collection of words to denote a purposeful action (kārya) associated with an existing entity (bhūtārtha).

Furthermore, in other usages such as "Bind the cow! Bring the horse!", because the word *go* (cow) is associated with the form of the cow as connected with an action (*kārya*), and because when that [action] is excluded, the form of the cow as connected with the action is likewise excluded, the word's capacity (*pada-sāmarthya*) is determined to reside in the cow as connected with an action; for even though there is deviation regarding the specific action of bringing or its connection therewith, there is no deviation regarding the connection with an action in general.

And thus, since there is no sublation of the fact that words are the cause of the cognition of the relation first apprehended, and because one avoids the conceptual complexity (*kalpanā-gaurava*) of postulating an intervention by word-meanings and their powers among them, it is more appropriate to postulate the capacity of the words themselves to convey the relation; this is also due to parsimony (*lāghava*). Therefore, the power of words resides in their own meanings as related to an action (*kārya*). This [position] he refutes with the words: "The presentation is unequal."

For in various applications [of words], it is not only the connection with the action (*kārya*) that is invariably perceived from the form of the word "cow" (*gavākṛti*), but rather the connection with qualities (*guṇa*), individuals (*vyakti*), actions (*kriyā*), and factors of action (*kāraka*). Thus, when it is said, "Bring the white cow," the relations between the quality, the factor of action, and the action are perceived; and the connection with the action occurs by way of the action itself. In that case, in order to establish the apprehension of an immediate relation, the capacity of a word to convey a meaning as connected with another is grasped.

And gradually, the connection between qualities, actions, and so forth, appearing as appropriate until the completion of the utterance of the final word, subsequently results in the cognition of the meaning of the great sentence (mahāvākyārtha), which is delimited by a single purpose through the synthesis of all those words; thus, there is no contradiction regarding their mutual connection. Furthermore, like that which is graspable by other means of knowledge, the "thing to be done" (kārya) invariably follows [the word] as the cause for the sign of activity (pravṛtti), but not as the object of the capacity of every word.

Therefore, for the sake of parsimony, the capacity [of words] resides in their own meanings as connected [with one another]; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of mere restatement (*anuvāda*). If the capacity of a word were understood through another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding its own meaning as connected with an action (*kārya*), then even when that much alone is understood from the word itself, it would be a restatement. Furthermore, there is no direct relationship between all word-meanings and the action, by virtue of which the capacity [of words] could reside in them as thus conjoined. As for the claim that there is a relationship characterized by the status of the subordinate (*śeṣa*) and the principal (*śeṣin*), what indeed is this so-called "status of the subordinate and the principal"? It cannot be ownership (*svāmitā*).

Because that [intention] has volition as its object, there is no relationship of principal and subordinate (aṅga-aṅgin) between them, as in the case of Devadatta; for the others lack the status of being its constituent parts. If it is argued that being the "thing to be accomplished" (sādhya) constitutes the state of being the principal, then the action itself—being accomplished by the auxiliary factors (guṇa-kāraka)—would be the principal. If, on the other hand, the ultimate goal to be accomplished is heaven alone, then why this superfluous "thing to be done" (kārya) acting as the principal?

Therefore, qualities are connected with substances, substances—conjoined with the meanings of case-endings—are connected with the action, and that action is connected with the result; thus, due to this mediation, it is logical that the capacity [of words] resides in their own meaning as conjoined with another. Furthermore, since a result cannot be conjoined with another result, its conjunction with something else must be stated. If it is argued that the result is conjoined with the result consisting of the meaning of the verbal root, we say no; for the status of being a result belonging to the meaning of the verbal root is caused by its conjunction with the *niyoga* (the mandate).

However, the *niyoga* (the mandate) is connected only with the meaning of the verbal root, not with the "task" (*kārya*); for the status of being its task occurs at a subsequent time. For this reason as well, the capacity of a word resides in that which is connected with something else.

Furthermore, the fact that an object is apprehensible by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would also be within the scope of the word's capacity, because there is no deviation [between the word and that fact]. If it is argued that the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is established otherwise by virtue of being the cause for the application [of the word], then the necessity of positive concomitance for "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) also exists simply by its being the reason for the mark of activity (*pravṛtti*), and not solely by virtue of being the scope of the capacity of all words. Moreover, in the world, verbal cognition is experienced even regarding the connection of past events—for example, in such cases as "Devadatta went out after eating."

In this regard, should one supply a word denoting an action (*kāryapada*) in every response; or should another means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*) distinct from verbal testimony be postulated; or should one accept that [the cognition] is erroneous; or rather, should one establish its validity by understanding the capacity of words to denote what is connected with something else? This must be investigated, for it is simpler not to postulate a linguistic usage regarding an uncontradicted real object, since the comprehension of meaning occurs through the apprehension of the relationship itself even for those who have not grasped the purpose or those who are mistaken about the purpose. Furthermore, [this is clear] from the teachings of the *Nighaṇṭu* and grammar.

If it is argued that the capacity of a word is understood through its non-deviation from objects when they are conjoined with other things—even without first apprehending the object as something to be accomplished (kārya)—and that because such conjunction with an effect is observed in some cases, it is inferred elsewhere as well; this is not so. For, by observing mere conjunction with another thing in one instance, it is logical to assume that even in the case of conjunction with an effect, the cause is merely the conjunction with another thing, rather than assuming an unobserved cause. Since it is more reasonable to adopt a cause that has been observed, it is established that the capacity of a word lies in its own meaning as conjoined with another thing.

[Objection: But surely, since the word *go* (cow) also conveys many meanings such as its connection with the act of bringing, and the word *ānayana* (bringing) also denotes numerous functions such as its connection with the cow, there would be no restriction on the specific relation conveyed by the two words together. [Response: This is not a fault; for a restriction is established by the fact that when each individual word is uttered, only so much meaning as is perceived is understood as being in relation [to the other] when they are uttered together. Indeed, all possible relations are not perceived from the utterance of each individual word.

Because the cognition of a relation arises from other words acting as cooperative causes. [Objection: But in that case, there would be synonymy; for instance, the meaning of the word *go* (cow) would be "cowness" as conjoined with "bringing," and the meaning of the word *ānaya* (bring) would also be "bringing" as conjoined with the cow. [Response: This is not sound; for if the same amount of meaning that is cognized from one word were also cognized from another word, then indeed there would be synonymy.

But when two objects that are mutually related are perceived together by means of two words, how can there be synonymy? [Objection: When the word "cow" (go) is uttered, why is only the form of the cow (*gavākṛti*) perceived, and not everything that falls within its semantic range? [Response: Because of the deviation from concomitance (*anvayavyabhicāra*); [the form] is perceived because of the greater strength of the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) regarding the cow's form, whereas for other things there is such deviation. Thus, the position is faultless.

Now, if it is argued that the word *go* (cow) conveys the universal *gotva* as connected with another word-meaning already denoted, then the word *ānaya* (bring) would likewise convey its own meaning as connected with the word *go* already denoted; thus, there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatā*)—namely, that once *gotva* is denoted, the bringing connected with it is denoted, and once that is denoted, the *gotva* connected with it is denoted. This is not a fault; for when words are uttered in succession, their respective meanings, which are invariably concomitant, are perceived in that very same sequence.

Furthermore, immediately after the utterance of the final word, the words—being apprehended by a single unified recollection—convey the denoted word-meanings as already expressed in a state of mutual connection; thus, the syntactic relation (*anvaya*) is established precisely through what has been denoted (*abhihita*). The same objection and its resolution apply equally regarding the word-meanings themselves as they convey that connection. "Denotation of the related" (*anvitābhidhāna*) is the name for the fact that the words themselves convey their own meanings as already connected. Thus, it is established that the capacity of words exists even with respect to an accomplished (*bhūta*) object, without depending upon a task to be performed (*kārya*).
Intending all of this, he says: "By means of the connection with the denotable object of the word 'cow'," and so forth.

He states that even in the Veda, the cognition of a connection [between words] is admitted without depending on an action, by means of the passage beginning with "And likewise for the one who utters the *vaṣaṭ*. Now, it might be argued: "In that case too, the word 'is to be done' (*kartavya*) is supplied as an ellipsis, and by accepting it as forming a single syntactical unit with that [word], the meaning of the sentence is cognized. To this he replies: "But as for [the claim] that 'it is to be done'..."

But surely the author of the Sūtras himself, following the usage of the elders, has demonstrated that the capacity of words resides in their own meaning as connected to an action, in the statement: "Of those [words] which have attained [their own meanings], [there is connection] with a word denoting action. To this he replies: "As for the statement 'of those which have attained... etc. The meaning is that the Commentator himself has shown the syntactic connection (*samanvaya*) of qualities, possessors of qualities, and so forth, through the relationship of qualifier and qualified. But how can there be a relationship of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between quality and possessor of quality, given the expression "with a word denoting action"? To this he says: "With a word denoting action... etc.

And likewise, the portion of the Commentary beginning with "The Commentator also... up to "...for this very reason" has a clear meaning. Furthermore, why is it that the Vedāntas are held to be concerned with *kārya* (what is to be done) based on the statements of Jaimini’s Sūtras, while they are held to be concerned with *brahman* (the Absolute) based on Bādarāyaṇa’s Sūtras? To this he says: "For this very reason, by means of the previous system (*tantra*). [An objection: But if there is no difference in the subject matter (*artha*), how can there be a separate commencement? To that, he states the distinction in the passage beginning with "In that regard, of the Veda... and ending with "...the primary [purpose] has been demonstrated."

[Objection: "But surely, even when the meanings of the nominal stems (*prātipadika*) are construed as having the single-flavored Brahman as their ultimate referent, the meaning of the nominative case-suffix (*prathamāvibhakti*) must still be construed as a *kāraka* (grammatical factor), because that [nominative] is never absent [from such constructions]. [Reply: He says "no"—"And thus the venerable Pāṇini [says] 'it is not distinct'. The meaning is this: although gender, number, and so forth are perceived from the sense [of the words], they will be *anirvacanīya* (indescribable/unreal), because they would contradict such scriptural statements as "Brahman is a mass of pure consciousness, without a second."

[Objection: Even in the absence of another action, when there is a syntactic connection with the meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the connection is established as being centered on the sense of "existence" (the verb *asti*), because of the traditional rule of Kātyāyana: "The verb *as* (to be), in the present tense, should be employed in the first person when it is not explicitly understood. [Reply: No, he says: "Only when there is an agent of the action of existence. [Objection: But even setting aside the action of existence, no such syntactic connection is observed. [Reply: To that he says: "And it is seen, as in 'the trees have borne fruit' (*phalitāḥ*)."

[Objection: "But surely, even there, the connection with the action of 'being' (asti-kriyā) should be postulated. [Reply: No; he says this: "Nor here, [in the case of] 'those who have borne fruit'. [Question: "Then where does the sentence find its final completion? [Reply: He says that: "Thus, of that which is established in a general sense..."

It has already been stated that, because the relationship between words is grasped merely through their connection with other meanings, it is logical for there to be a connection with the meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*)—which is non-distinct and of a single flavor—while setting aside the action (*kriyā*); now, he says—"Furthermore, 'A Brāhmaṇa must not be killed'"—to show that even for those who maintain that [words] denote a connection with action, the syntactic coherence of prohibitive sentences regarding a past object must be explained. Now, one might object: "Is not the absence of the killing of a Brāhmaṇa itself an action, or at least something intended for an action? To this he replies: "It is neither an action nor something intended for an action."

The meaning is: because it has the characteristic of being the cessation of an action that has been undertaken. Now, one might object: in passages such as "One should not look at the rising sun," an act of volition (saṃkalpa) opposed to looking—namely, "I shall not look"—is enjoined; likewise, in "I shall not kill," let it be that an act of volition opposed to killing is what is enjoined. To this he says: "Because of the connection with the word *vrata*. This is the meaning: the negative particle (*nañ*) primarily denotes the very absence of that which is being conjoined [with it].

In cases such as [the injunction] "one should fast on the Ekādaśī," because it begins with the word *vrata* (vow), which denotes something to be performed, the term refers by secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to another action that is contradictory to what is being conjoined; however, here there is no such sublater (*apavādaka*) whereby the negative particle (*nañ*) would have to function through secondary indication to denote an act of volition (*saṃkalpa-kriyā*) that is contradictory to what is being conjoined. [Objection: But surely the negative particle can have its primary meaning even when conjoined with something other than that [which it negates], or even with something contradictory to it? [Reply: No, he says—"Not merely from the connection of the negative particle."

Here the Prābhākara objects: "In this context, three things are perceived—the Brāhmaṇa, the act of killing, and the meaning of the suffix. Among these, the negation cannot be construed with the Brāhmaṇa, because that would contradict direct perception. Nor does it convey the non-existence of the killing, because that [act] has already commenced. Nor can it convey the non-existence of the meaning of the suffix, because the desire for the fruit or the cognition of an obligation (kāryabuddhi), which are the causes of activity, are directly perceived."

Therefore, by means of an attachment to the sense of "killing" as it is naturally acquired, the very act of volition that is opposed to it is conveyed by the negative particle (*nañ*). And that [act] is enjoined by the suffix. Now, there is no such thing as "non-existence" apart from another positive entity, such that the sentence would terminate in that [negation]. Consequently, the sentence is intended to enjoin another positive entity; this is what he states with the words beginning, "by its very nature, due to the cause of passion and so forth."

He refutes this, saying: "And this is not tenable. Nor can non-existence (*abhāva*), which is the object of that cognition, be negated. Furthermore, non-existence is not simply another positive entity (*bhāvāntara*), because the latter is necessarily dependent upon a counter-correlate (*sapratiyogika*). Moreover, non-existence alone is the primary meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*); for when it is possible for the word to function through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) toward things that are either different from or opposed to the primary object and related to non-existence, it is improper to assume a conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*). Now, one might object: "But when joined with the meaning of a noun or a verbal root, the negative particle is certainly not a negator [of existence]."

"It expresses non-Brahminhood and non-dharma, which are opposed to something else. Thus, the word *nañ* has been shown to function even in a different sense; this is true. Even there, by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) through connection with the primary meaning, a restriction of the cognition to another sense is demonstrated; thus, there is no contradiction.

The Prābhākara says: "The injunction (niyoga) pertains to the absence of killing; therefore, the sentence culminates in the injunction. To this he replies: "But [you claim] the injunction has the meaning of the negative particle (nañ). He refutes this: "This is mere talk. Either a positive entity such as curd or some quality is the cause for the cessation [of an action] by being the object of an injunction, not the prior non-existence of killing; for, being established from time immemorial, it cannot be something to be performed (*anuṣṭheya*) by means of an injunction. He states another refutation: "In this way, [there would be] the [absurdity] of a prohibition..."

The meaning is that the worldly linguistic practice of distinguishing between injunctions and prohibitions would not exist. Therefore, he concludes that [the inquiry] does not terminate with the "task" (kārya): "Therefore, while being combined... and so forth.

It has been stated that, by accepting the connection of the negative particle (*nañ*) with the meaning of the verbal root itself—namely, "killing"—neither a state of being (*bhāva*) nor a different object is to be enjoined. Now, however, he says that it is the meaning of the suffix alone that is connected with the negative particle, because the meaning of the verbal root is subordinate to another, and [grammatical] elements connect with the principal element: "And that, when combined... and so forth.

Since injunctions and the like are impossible in the context of empirical transactions such as perception because they lack dependence on another person, the term "one's own duty" (*svadharma*) means that which is to be performed as a property of the person being instructed. The phrase "the fruit of the action being prohibited" means the fruit of the action being turned away from. Consequently, if the fact that killing is a means to a desired end is the motivator, that very thing is restated by the suffix and then prohibited: "Killing a Brahmin is not a means to a desired end."

[Objection: Is it not the case that the fact that killing is a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) is directly perceived, and that this is not opposed to the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*), because the word "desired" refers to a visible purpose? [Response: This is not opposed to the unseen; for "prārthanā" means that which is sought after, i.e., the means to a result. Therefore, if the fact that killing is a means to a desired end is the motivator, then that very thing is restated by the suffix and then prohibited: "Killing a Brāhmaṇa is not a means to a desired end. [Objection: But surely the fact that killing is a means to a desired end is directly perceived and is not opposed to the unseen.

Since that which has a visible purpose is denoted by the word "desired" (*iṣṭa*), this [prohibition] is opposed to the invisible (*adṛṣṭa*); "prārthanā" means that which is sought after, i.e., the means to a result. Therefore, if it is the fact that killing is a means to a desired end that prompts one to act, that very thing is restated by the suffix and then prohibited: "Killing a Brāhmaṇa is not a means to a desired end. But surely, the visible status of killing as a means to a desired end is not opposed to the invisible?

Because that which has a visible purpose is designated by the term "desired" (*iṣṭa*), the meaning is that this [killing] is not a means for achieving a visible end that is contrary to the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*). Furthermore, in all cases, because of the connection with benefit (*artha*) and harm (*anartha*), a benefit that exceeds [the mere avoidance of] harm is called a human goal (*puruṣārtha*), and a harm that exceeds [the mere absence of] benefit is called a non-human goal (*apuruṣārtha*). Thus, when it is said that killing is not a means for achieving a human goal, it is effectively said that there is no benefit exceeding [the mere avoidance of] harm. Consequently, because the harm exceeds the benefit, it is said that "harm results from the benefit."

Thus, it is established that the negation of the meaning of the suffix (pratyaya) is not something to be performed; so he says: "And that is prior non-existence" (*saca prāgabhāvaḥ*). If one asks, "What then is to be performed?", [the answer is: since the arousal of passion and the like might occur due to the delusion regarding the means to achieve human goals, the destruction of its cause is what must be performed; thus he says: "The arousal of its latent impression" (*tatsaṃskārodbodhaḥ*). If it is argued, "Then let that very thing be enjoined by the sentence," he says, "No," adding: "And although that is something to be accomplished" (*sa ca yadyapi sādhyaḥ*).

Since killing is understood to be neither desired nor undesired, the cessation of the causes that arouse the impulse to kill must be practiced through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) alone; therefore, there is no dependence on verbal testimony (*śabda*) in that regard. Furthermore, he says "tatpratipādaka" (that which establishes it) because the sentence lacks direct authority regarding the duty to cease the causes. Now, one might object: if the cessation of the cause occurs through the power of words concerning what is an undesirable means, then that cessation is also a meaning of the word. To this he replies: "yaścārthādarthaḥ" (and that which [is obtained] from the sense of the meaning).

He concedes the point with the words, "Now, however... He then refutes it with, "Granted; nevertheless... The meaning is that even so, since the portion to be performed is established through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), the word does not terminate in an injunction (niyoga) that is to be performed. An objection is raised: "But the apūrva is conveyed by the suffix (pratyaya); how then could it be non-performable? To this he replies: "Where has its relationship [with the word] been grasped? Not, first of all, in common worldly usage."

Because that [intermediate entity] is not perceived. Now, one might argue: "The necessity of performing a sacrifice for one desiring heaven is untenable without a means to achieve heaven; and since that status as a means is untenable for an action that perishes in a moment without an intervening entity, the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) is inferred through presumptive testimony (*śrutārthāpatti*), and the expressive power of the word is grasped therein. This, however, is like the "catching of a crane" (a futile pursuit).

If the necessity of performing the action (*kriyā-kartavyatā*) is expressed by the word according to its worldly capacity (*laukika-sāmarthya*), why then is a connection [of the word] with the *apūrva*—which is obtained through that very capacity—grasped? Or, if the necessity of performing the action is not expressed, then the *apūrva* itself is not obtained; so how could there be a grasping of a connection? [Objection: But surely the necessity of performing the sacrifice (*yāga-kartavyatā*) is expressed as being untenable without the expression of the *apūrva*. [Reply: In that case, that too is untenable; for heaven (*svarga*) cannot be established without a connection between the body, the senses, and their objects.

If it is argued that the suffix (pratyaya) may denote the body and so forth because they are understood through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) and thus do not depend on verbal expression, this is equally true for the *apūrva*. Therefore, the meaning of the suffix is simply the means to achieve a desired end (*iṣṭasādhana*), characterized by the necessity of performing the root-meaning (*dhātvartha*). Thus, the portion beginning with "following the usage of elders" and ending before "the answer to this" is clear in its meaning. To begin with, the initial verbal cognition (*śābdajñāna*) is not enjoined, nor is its continuous flow (*santāna*) to be enjoined for one who desires the experience of pleasure.

And from those two very [means], when they have proceeded spontaneously, direct knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*) arises. With reference to one for whom such direct knowledge has thus arisen, he says the subsequent [passage]: "Not for one who has realized the identity of Brahman and the Self. Now, an objection: the connection with the body is caused by karma and the like, and from that comes transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*); so what is the use of direct knowledge? To this he replies with the passage beginning "The connection with the body is not, first of all, caused by karma" and ending with "the experience of pleasure and pain."

It has been stated through both positive and negative concomitance that when ignorance is removed by the knowledge of reality, transmigratory existence ceases. Now, in this regard, he states the authority of scripture (*āgama*): "And likewise, the declarations of the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*. For they, although directly experiencing the oneness of Brahman and the Self, nevertheless exhibit the appearance of dualistic perception.

[Objection: But once false knowledge has ceased due to immediate (aparokṣa) realization, how can there be any perception of duality? To this he says: "But that which pertains to objects... [The opponent objects: But since even the karmas have ceased, how can there be a perception of duality caused by them? This is not a fault; for because of the statement, "For him, there is delay only so long," which establishes a limit distinct from knowledge, it is assumed that the body, senses, and so forth persist for some time, and thus it is assumed that the karma which causes them also persists.

We reply: "Surely, since there is a scriptural statement regarding the destruction of all karma, how can the presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) derived from that scripture be sublated in only one part? For if the presumptive testimony does not arise, it would follow that the scripture itself is sublated. Therefore, the systematic arrangement is established by the scripture itself through the relationship of the general and the particular. [Objection: But if all ignorance is removed by immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*), from where could there be any persistence of karmas? It is said in response:

Knowledge of reality itself, arising from its own causes, being obstructed by the persistence of prārabdha-karma as understood from the scriptures, is produced devoid of the capacity to remove the appearance of duality required for that [prārabdha], yet it does bring about the cessation of other karmas, ignorance, attachment, and so forth. Now, one might ask: "How can the experience of Brahman as the Self and the perception of duality coexist? We do not say they coexist.

At one time there is the vision of the oneness of the Self through non-discerning [samādhi], and at another time there is the vision of duality caused by defects presented by the karma already set in motion (*ārabdhakarman*). Now, it might be argued that for one who still possesses a body, there can be no direct perception (*aparokṣadarśana*); but this is not so, because we accept that such a vision exists as the cause for the destruction of all prior and subsequent karma, with the exception of the karma already set in motion. Furthermore, the destruction of all karma is not possible without direct perception; and for one possessing *ārabdhakarman*, the vision of reality (*tattvadarśana*) is possible only while still embodied. Moreover, it is heard in scripture that Vyāsa and others possessed direct perception even while they were still embodied.

If it is objected that even for one who perceives reality, there would still be the perception of duality—and consequently, the performance of ritual injunctions—this is not so; for the performance of such acts depends upon the realization of specific place, time, qualification, and agency.

For one who has realized the Truth (tattvadarśin), however, because there is no restriction of place or time regarding the arising of defects caused by karma already set in motion (prārabdha-karman), it is impossible for them to remain until the completion of that commenced performance. Furthermore, since the karmas already performed are sublated by the repeated realization of the Truth, there is no purpose in their further performance. Moreover, transgression (pratyavāya) is ceased by the realization of the Truth itself. [Objection: But if there is no restriction from the scriptures for one who has realized the Truth, would they not engage in acting as they please? [Reply: No.

Since conduct is motivated by the desire for the attainment of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful, how could there be the possibility of acting as one pleases for one who directly experiences unsurpassed bliss and the cessation of all misfortunes within his own self, and who thus lacks any desire for further human goals to be accomplished? If it is asked, "How then does he maintain a body? the answer is that it is due to the force of *prārabdha* (commenced) karma; furthermore, the accumulation of new karma cannot occur because of ignorance, attachment, and other such causes [which have been eliminated].

Because [duality] has ceased, and because the karmas already set in motion have as their sole cause the production of their own respective fruits; therefore, even for one who perceives reality, the appearance of the perception of duality is logically possible.

Now, it might be argued that because reflection (*manana*) and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*) are enjoined in addition to the knowledge arising from hearing (*śravaṇa*), there must be some further goal to be accomplished; to this he replies "no," stating: "And of reflection and meditative absorption..."

And it has been stated that reflection (*manana*) and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*) are causes for the vision of reality (*tattva-darśana*). Now, he restates the meaning set forth in the two expositions (*varṇaka*), beginning with the passage "Thus, of the established entity... and ending with "...therefore, independent of injunctions, Brahman itself is the object of the authority of scripture through the systematic concordance (*samanvaya*) of the Vedānta texts. Furthermore, he states that when there is the exposition of an existing entity independent of injunctions, the distinction in the commencement of the scripture is established: "And this being so, of the words..."

[Objection: But surely the very distinction between the motivating factors (*pravartaka*) is the reason for the commencement of a separate treatise. [Reply: No, he says—"Otherwise, here... [Objection: But there is indeed another differentiator: in the *Karmakāṇḍa*, the various injunctions (*vidhi*) to be accomplished by means of the body and the senses were described, whereas here, an injunction to be accomplished solely through the mind is being described. [Reply: To that he says—"Even so, [there are] external means (*abahiḥsādhana*)."

Thus [the opponent] objects: "Even so, there is the inquiry into the remaining duties (dharma) starting with the words 'Therefore, next'. He concludes the meaning of the section: "In this way, prior to the realization of Brahman as the Self... After the direct perception (*aparokṣa-darśana*) of Brahman as the Self, because the cognizer—who is a synthesis of the internal organ and the self—is sublated, and because the connection with objects of cognition is no longer established, the worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) characterized by the knower, the means of knowledge, the object of knowledge, the agent, the action, the effect, the enjoyer, and the enjoyment, indeed ceases.

[Objection: But surely, because it consists of both difference and non-difference, the vision of non-duality does not sublate the vision of duality. [Reply: In that case, there would be no such thing as the identification of the body with the self; even pleasure, pain, and so forth would be sublated, since they too consist of both difference and non-difference. Furthermore, "difference and non-difference" is a contradiction in terms; there would also be an absence of the distinction between prima facie arguments (*pūrvapakṣa*) and established conclusions (*siddhānta*), due to the total confusion of everything. [Objection: But for you as well, in the state of non-duality, the same total confusion applies. [Reply: No; for the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is established in its difference exactly as it is perceived, whereas Brahman alone is non-dual.

But is it not observed that an object is both different and non-different through perception? What is that perception? It is not the case that the perception "this is a broken cow" has as its object something both different and non-different; for there is no such appearance. If it is argued that non-difference appears precisely as mutual identity, then difference would likewise have to appear as mutual non-identity. If it is argued that difference appears through a difference in form (*rūpa*), then non-difference must be said to arise from the identity of form.

Now, if it is argued that there is non-difference because of mutual identity, and difference because of the difference in form—where has such "mutual identity as non-difference" been observed? It is certainly not seen in the case of "this is one jar. Therefore, in the case of "this is a broken cow," there is no appearance of both difference and non-difference.

It might be argued that the two cognitions, "This is a cow" and "He is a hornless one," manifest both difference and non-difference; but this is not so, because two cognitions lack the capacity to produce a single valid cognition (*pramā*) by acting together, and without recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), the connection of a single object with both [attributes] cannot be established. If it is then argued that difference and non-difference are established through three cognitions by implication, that is already refuted by the case of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Because the three—the syllable *khaṇḍa*, the cow, and the individual entity that is the substratum of both—appear in perception, and because grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇya*) has as its object the individual entity that is the substratum of both, there is no inference (*arthāpatti*) either; for even by means of the three cognitions—"the short vowel *a*," "the long vowel *ā*," and "this is that same vowel *a*"—neither difference nor non-difference is established, since they are admitted to be mere errors. Therefore, an object is neither different nor non-different. Nor can difference be proven with respect to the self (*ātman*).

If it is argued: "The individual bodies of stationary and moving beings under dispute possess a self by means of the very nature of the opponent's own body-individual, because they are body-individuals, like the opponent's body-individual"—this being an inference based on their being a single self; and if it is further argued that "a difference between the substrates (the selves) is inferred because they are the locus of contradictory properties such as simultaneous birth and death, like fire and water"—we say no, because [the reason] is unestablished due to its being in a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇāsiddha*), since [birth and death] have the body as their substrate.

If it is argued that the distinction between perceivers is postulated based on the non-connection with, or connection to, the experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth in each respective body, we say no; for even when there is a difference of bodies, one and the same self is observed not to connect with experiences from other births. Furthermore, even though unity exists, no mixing of colors is observed among different reflections. Nor is the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman established by perception; for while one might infer a distinction based on their being substrates of contradictory attributes, such an inference is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to the case of the original object and its reflection.

If it is argued that there is a difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman because the distinctions between the controller and the controlled, the ruler and the ruled, the seer and the seen, and so forth, serve as indicative marks (*liṅga*) of such difference—this is not so. For, since the Śruti itself, in passages such as "There is no other seer but He," prohibits difference, it is impossible to infer a difference on the basis of indicative marks; furthermore, because their means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) are not equal, it is improper to postulate both difference and non-difference. If it is argued that the number two is heard in the text "Two birds..."—this is not so.

Because of the scriptural hearing of the number one in the statement, "That which is in this person and that which is in yonder sun are one," oneness is established through the restatement of duality—which is itself established by error—since there is no means of valid knowledge for plurality. For if difference were apprehended by perception, it would depend upon the determination of the relation between a locus and its counter-correlate, and since such a determination depends in turn upon difference, there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*). Therefore, neither difference nor non-difference exists; thus, the vision of duality is sublated by the vision of non-duality (*advaita*).

Furthermore, since perceptual error is seen to be sublated by authoritative testimony, and since statements regarding results—being descriptions of the present—are contradicted by the non-perception of what is otherwise perceptible, liberation is simply the cessation of bondage through the means already observed.

Furthermore, he states the purport of the three verses beginning with "Moreover, they say" (*apicāhuḥ*) by means of the passage starting with "of the secondary and false self" (*gauṇamithyātmanaḥ*). He explains the verse by saying, "stating this, he says," in order to confirm it. He states the purport of the second verse by means of the passage beginning with, "How, then, is its authority established? (*katham idānīm asya prāmāṇyam*).

He explains the third verse: "Prior to the direct realization (*aparokṣānubhava*) of the Self as Brahman—which is non-dual, unsurpassed bliss, pure consciousness, focused on unity, omniscient, the Lord of all, omnipotent, partless, transparent, unattached, and inward—the entire empirical transaction proceeds according to its appearance, just like the notion that the body is the self. And when that [Brahman] is manifest in direct realization, because the notions of being a knower (*pramātṛtva*) and so forth are sublated, the entire empirical transaction ceases; such is the meaning of the verse."

Thus ends the ninth section, titled the Section on Concordance (*samanvayādhikaraṇa*), in the *Pañcapādikā-vivaraṇa* composed by the venerable Svaprakāśānubhava, the disciple of the worshipful Ananyānubhava, a holy wandering ascetic (*paramahaṃsa-parivrājaka*).
